News.title: Student, 19, ‘strangled to death by her stepdad in uni halls after he developed sexual obsession with her’
News.content:
UNI HORROR Student, 19, ‘strangled to death by her stepdad in uni halls after he developed sexual obsession with her’







Next

A STUDENT was strangled to death by her stepdad in her university accommodation after he developed a sexual obsession with her, a court heard.

Carla Georgescu, 19, was discovered dead on what would have been her 20th birthday on the University of Lancashire campus in Preston.



Her stepdad Nathan Owens, 34, is accused of driving through the night to murder Carla after becoming “sexually fixated” with her, jurors heard.

Preston Crown Court heard he was possibly driven by “sexual jealousy” after discovering his stepdaughter was due to meet up with a new lover.



Owens allegedly left the home he shared with Carla’s mum Janina in Hartlepool in the early hours of February 4 and strangled her to death.

The second year clinical psychology student was found the next day slumped against a wardrobe door with injuries to her face.

Nicholas Lumley KC, prosecuting, said: “Her death was the culmination, the end point, of weeks, months and perhaps years of a one-sided sexual obsession.

“And it was the beginning of a complex murder investigation, which led to his door in Hartlepool.

“For it was he who was sexually fixated on Carla and it was he, Nathan Owens, who had killed Carla.”

Jurors heard Owens made up a story about visiting Carla’s flat to collect her mother’s purse after she left it during a previous visit.



But he did not tell his wife about the journey and spent around 90 minutes in the flat, it was said.

Owens also parked his car “some distance” from the accommodation and covered himself with a blanket, the court was told.

When he left, he was allegedly “shielding” himself with an umbrella and wearing a face-mask and Carla’s trainers, while carrying several bags.

Carla’s mum raised the alarm when she failed to contact her daughter and the police were called.

Officers initially believed the student had taken her own life but a forensic examination suggested there was “more” to her death, jurors heard.



A post mortem also revealed Carla had been subjected to two heavy blows to her head, slash marks on her cheek and cuts and bruises to her mouth and nose.

Carla’s hands were covered in blood after she attempted to defend herself and she had sexual injuries, the court heard.

The jury was told sex toys and Owens’ DNA were found at the scene.

Mr Lumley said “some form of grievous sexual activity” had taken place which was “hardly surprising” given Owens’ sexual obsession with her.

He alleged in the months leading up to Carla’s murder, Owens had been collecting photos of her taken without her knowledge.



Owens had also allegedly filmed himself having sex with her dolls and toys – including one that was a life-sized “effigy” dressed in Carla’s nightie.

He was also said to have manipulated innocent selfies of Carla into sexual images which he viewed in the week before she died.

“The only possible reason for looking at those images is that Nathan Owens had a wholly improper and dangerously entrenched sexual obsession with his stepdaughter,” Mr Lumley told the court.

Jurors were told Carla – a second year psychology student at the University of Lancashire – was fit and well in the weeks before she died.

The prosecution also alleges Mr Owens removed Carla’s phone and laptop and dumped them on the drive between Preston and Hartlepool.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Owens denies charges of murder, intentional strangulation and grievous bodily harm with intent.

The trial continues.

News.title: Ex-World Conker Championships winner, 84, QUITS as mascot two years after being cleared in cheating scandal
News.content:
CONKED OUT Ex-World Conker Championships winner, 84, QUITS as mascot two years after being cleared in cheating scandal







Next

A FORMER World Conker champion has quit as mascot two years after he was caught up in a major cheating scandal – from which he was later cleared.

David Jakins, 84, had held the honorific position for two decades but is now walking away due to old age.



The stalwart of the brown seed smashing contest had rocked the sport in 2024 over allegations he cheated his way to his first ever win.

Jakins, then aged 82, was caught with a steel conker in his pocket.



He was accused of swapping the all-natural conker for the metal replacement to take his first title after 40 years of trying.

The veteran was cleared of any wrongdoing after a probe reviewed video footage.



But the controversy cast a shadow over last year’s event and led to “airport-style” security checks being brought in.

Mr Jakins says he is stepping down “with great sadness” due to reduced mobility.



The crown will be passed to his daughter Fee Aylmore and World Colmer Championships chairman Jim Packer, who become the new King and Queen Conker.

Mr Jakins said: “It is with great sadness that I step down from my role as King Conker after 20 wonderful years.

“However, I am extremely pleased to pass this role onto my daughter, Fee, who will be a wonderful Queen Conker, supported admirably by Jim, who will be supporting her as a new King Conker.”

Organiser StJohn Burkett said: “It will be sad to see David go as he has served his role admirably.

“He is struggling with his mobility due to arthritis in his knees so feels now is the right time.



“I don’t think the cheating scandal weighed that heavily on his decision – he feels he has cleared his name regarding that matter.

“However, we have since kept his steel conker in a Perspex box which we display at the event to make sure there is no repeat of the events of 2024.”

Fee said: “It is a great honour to take over from my dad, who loved his conkers and served with honour all these years. His will be a hard act to follow.”

Jim said: “He never let on about the steel conker, even to me. I hope I’m up to the job.”

This year’s event takes place in Southwick, Northamptonshire, on Sunday.

News.title: Pressure will be on Kemi Badenoch to capitalise on her recent momentum at Tory conference today
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Pressure will be on Kemi Badenoch to capitalise on her recent momentum at Tory conference today







Next

KEMI Badenoch is adamant that young people simply can’t be left on the jobs scrapheap.

The Tory leader vows to slash Labour’s so-called “Jobs Tax” to help young people take their first step on the jobs ladder.



She is attempting to assert her position and challenge Chancellor John Healey to follow suit at the Budget later this month.

Badenoch recognises the national scandal of nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.



She highlights that not being in work at a young age will negatively affect lifetime earnings.

For a young person, lifetime earnings drop by £52,000 but this figure rises to £293,000 for those aged 18 to 24 who are out of work or education.



So she will lower taxes for employers hiring people aged 21 to 24 to encourage them to take on more youths.

Labour is awaiting the outcome of a report by Labour grandee Alan Milburn on youth inactivity before making its next move on young people.

The Treasury know better than anyone that money is tight and pledging a £2.3 billion tax cut will likely prove out of reach for Mr Healey.

Kemi Badenoch has so far had a strong few days with the party faithful in Birmingham.



Her biggest challenge is to elevate the Tory brand and try and put some distance between the Conservative party that was booted out of office two years ago.

But as she addresses the conference in Birmingham today the pressure will be on her to capitalise on her recent momentum.

News.title: Kemi will slam Burnham for being a dangerous left-winger who uses slick TikTok videos in Tory Party conference speech
News.content:
Next

KEMI Badenoch will today accuse Andy Burnham of being a dangerous left-winger who uses slick TikTok videos.

She will use her Tory Party conference speech to hammer the Labour PM, and warn it is not kind to spray money on more benefits.



She will say: “They claim what they are doing is compassionate.

“But these ideas will make every single person in this country poorer.



“Your taxes will be higher.

“Your bills will go up.

“You will find it harder and harder to make ends meet.

“Just because these ideas are delivered on TikTok, it doesn’t make them any less dangerous.”

Ms Badenoch will say she is up for “a fight we have not seen for more than half a century.

“A battle for the soul of this nation”.



She will add in Birmingham that she would cut but not axe inheritance tax.

Her reason will be: “We are running out of money and running out of time to put it right.”

News.title: Half of French sixth form schools close as student clashes with cops worsen & Macron convenes emergency meeting
News.content:
Next

MORE than half of France’s sixth forms have shut down as President Emmanuel Macron called an emergency meeting to address violent clashes across the country.

A baby in a pram has been hit with a firework, a teen’s hand has been blown off and college set alight as pupils raged at school conditions.



But a students’ union warned that clashes will worsen until pupils demands are met.

Spokesperson Alice Cohen-Morzadec told BBC News that the movement will “amplify even more until we get our demands”.





Around 3,700 Lycées – the French equivalent of sixth-form colleges – have shut as arrest numbers climb and riot police crack down on teens chucking fireworks at cops and burning buildings.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called today’s protests the most violent student demonstrations in decades.

He said at least 215 teens and 85 staff had been injured in the clashes, as well as more than 700 police officers.

Feared French riot police were deployed to control the chaos, firing tear gas and water cannons at crowds to break up violent fringes on the edge of protests.



France‘s interior ministry said more than 250,000 people took part in dozens of cities, but organisers put the figure much higher, claiming 450,000 had marched.

Teens first took to the streets to protest water leaks in schools are fixed, rat infestations tackled and other maintenance issues.

But as unrest grew across the country so did the list of demands.



Students are calling for more teachers, shorter school hours, and an end to racial discrimination.

Riot police used teargas, flashball guns and baton charges to try and restore order.

Since the protests kicked off around three weeks ago, 6100 people have been arrested, according to the interior ministry.

Some of the worst trouble in Paris on Tuesday was at the Place de la Nation – one of the city’s major squares, where march came to an end in the early evening.

An officer at the scene said: “Gangs of youths are trying to attack us constantly, while others are lighting fires.”



The widespread chant echoing around him was: “Everyone hates the police.”

A police officer allegedly fired a tear gas grenade into the face of a 14-year-old protester at point-blank range was charged with causing bodily harm “leading to mutilation or permanent disability“, prosecutors said.

The attack in said to have taken place place on September 28 during a demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Ouen.

And on Monday a 15-year-old schoolboy lost his left hand when a police grenade exploded in the northern town of Lens.

Meanwhile, buildings have been burned to the ground, and fire engines vandalised so as to stop them dealing with blazes.



Carole, 17, protesting in Paris, said: “Classrooms are full of rats, and teachers are not always present – the conditions are terrible.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Students from ethnic minorities are also terribly – especially by the police. This is why we are out on the street.”

French Lycées teach 15 – 18-year-olds their equivalent of A levels.

News.title: Scammers helping migrants to escape deportation shows ministers must grow a backbone and rip up the ECHR
News.content:
Human blights







Next

BRITAIN’S soft-touch asylum system has become a goldmine for dodgy lawyers, sham charities and greedy racketeers.

An unscrupulous minority make a small fortune by helping illegal migrants exploit human rights laws to win refugee status.



There’s no stunt they won’t pull to con officials into believing they are fleeing war or persecution.

Now a shadow industry is charging thousands of pounds to help migrants pretend to be gay to escape deportation.



Cynical fraudsters use an LGBT group to manufacture fake lives for Bangladeshi men so they can avoid being sent home, where same-sex activity is illegal.

Our revelation has led to 100 asylum applications being reviewed — but it’s probably the tip of the iceberg.



Bangladesh accounts for the second largest number of asylum claims based on sexual orientation, behind Pakistan.

Feigning victimhood is a despicable act that undermines faith in a discredited system — and the European Convention on Human Rights, which has now become a big part of the problem.

It harms real refugees by clogging up the system while taxpayers are left to foot the £4.9billion asylum bill.

The Home Office talks tough about rooting out the perpetrators.



But illegal migrants and those who make fortunes by facilitating them know the odds are stacked in their favour.

Until ministers grow a backbone and rip up the ECHR, Britain will remain an easy target for scammers.

Neet idea, Kemi

LABOUR’S tax hikes have triggered a youth employment crisis which is costing £125billion a year.

More than a million young people are not in work, education or training — more than any other European country apart from Romania.

Bosses hit by the crippling rise in business rates and the inflated minimum wage simply can’t afford to hire any kids.



Kemi Badenoch’s plan to halve Employer National Insurance on under-25s will give small firms, pubs and restaurants a better chance.

It’s a lifeline that could save many youngsters from a life on benefits.

Handout chaos

WORKING families seeing their pay packets gobbled up by tax and inflation will be appalled by the spiralling benefits bill.

It’s a measure of Labour’s priorities that welfare costs are rising more than twice as fast as wages.

Labour-held seats account for 29 of the top 30 benefits bills in the country.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

This is not what we expected when Andy Burnham promised “growth in every postcode”.

The PM must get a grip of this madness and fast.

News.title: How October 7 massacre was the day Britain became mired in antisemitic hate and turned so many in this country insane
News.content:
Next

EVEN on October 7, 2023, as Hamas terrorists rampaged through Southern Israel, murdering, raping and taking hostage every man, woman and child they could lay their hands on, it was clear this was an event which would change Britain too.

That night, while most people in this country were shaken with revulsion about the unfolding massacre, there were people across our country who were celebrating.



They were lighting fireworks and they were dancing.

Jewish TV presenter Rachel Riley was among the first to document this astonishing behaviour.



Tweeting a video of apparently rapturous people near her home in West London, she wrote on X: “People have been brutally murdered, kidnapped, and there are people in London dancing. Make no mistake, this is a dangerous and terrifying time for all Jews around the world.”

The spike in antisemitism — on social media, in the street — started that day too.

Novelist Howard Jacobson has described it as a “bloodlust” — the idea that seeing Jews being hurt encourages other people to want to hurt more Jews.

The pattern has continued in the three years since, from the terrorist attack on Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester a year ago, to the stabbings and firebombs in Golders Green, North West London earlier this year.

Every time a Jew is hurt, for most people the response is sympathy.

But for some people, it elicits excitement. They want to hurt more Jews.



It tells us something about antisemitism but also the society that houses it, that allows it to flourish.

Just in the past few days, as we hear about a pilot trying to crash a plane-load of Israelis, British police arrest Iranians allegedly plotting a terrorist attack and the Green Party passes a Jew-hating motion.

The temperature for British Jews like me feels as though it keeps getting hotter.

As I write this, I am waiting for a call from the Metropolitan Police after I was assaulted while being called “Zionist scum” and a “Zionist fascist”, threatened and hemmed in by a giant banner held by a mob at a supposed anti-racism demonstration on Sunday.

The irony was that this was an event celebrating the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street when the working class helped defend their Jewish neighbours from Oswald Mosley’s fascists.



But the mob turned on me when they heard I was a Zionist — someone who believes in a Jewish state on our ancestral homeland.

For me, there is little difference between the people in keffiyehs who dress up as Islamist terrorists and the fascist Blackshirts who also used to want to hurt Jews and march through where we live.

And we have allowed them to run rampant for three years now.



It was just after midday on October 7, 2023, that the Palestine Solidarity Campaign applied for its first demonstration for Gaza.

Hamas — a proscribed terrorist group — was still killing Israelis, yet these people wanted to march in favour of the other side.

From October 7, 2023, to the end of that year, there were 900 protests in favour of Gaza.

From the start, they were steeped in antisemitism, waving placards with the Jewish Star of David entwined with a swastika or thrown in a bin.

And protesters dressed as terrorists with images of the paragliders who had invaded Israel.



Cries of “baby killer” and “genocide” started on October 7 as Israel was fighting for its life.

Those demonstrations have continued.

Successive governments have struggled to know how to deal with them, even as they have led to entire parts of our cities being closed every weekend for months.

While right-wing protests against immigrants are quickly shut down, the pro-Gaza crowd have been given practically free rein.

How have we got to the point where all the Metropolitan Police can do about a planned pro-Gaza demonstration by London university students today — on the anniversary of Hamas’s attack on Israel — is to ask them to change the date?



How are we so toothless against what is essentially the celebration of terrorism?

Against a terrorism that isn’t just about Jews but about the West and the freedoms we all take for granted.

That free rein on our streets has given the green light to hatred in this country, which I could never have envisaged.



From classrooms where children are bullied for saying they are Jewish to university students who have been shunned by housemates, to the NHS where a doctor was suspended for a rant about “Jewish supremacy”.

While one Jewish man — in the middle of an operation — had to suffer a doctor telling him about how much Jews liked to hurt children.

There’s the overt hatred, the violence and the terrorist attacks.

And then there are the quieter, silent attacks — the Jewish comics or musicians banned from appearing on stage, the Israeli restaurants that have had to rebrand as “Mediterranean”.

The mob that comes after them also comes after everyone who dares to show sympathy with Jews.



Boy George could no longer perform in a musical because he had written a song with the lyrics “I stand with the Jews”.

Ed Sheeran, for daring even to say that he didn’t want to be political, faced death threats and mass cancellation.

In the meantime, a terrorist group called Palestine Action smashes up British military equipment and violently assaults police officers and guards, yet thousands stand up for them.

This is pro-terror radicalisation happening with Israel as an excuse.

October 7 was a catalyst, showing something has broken in our country.



How else to explain that we have four MPs voted into Parliament “for Gaza”, a war more than 2,000 miles away over which we have no influence?

Or that a political party, the Greens, should be so overrun by obsessive Jew haters that anyone who believes in the right of Jews to have their own state in their ancestral homeland — that is most of us — are now deemed officially racist by them.

Or that Labour, so determined to win the same antisemitic voters who have abandoned them for the Greens, have blown up our relationship with Israel, an ally that has prevented multiple terrorist attacks in this country.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It is important today to remember the terrorism of October 7, those who died on that awful day and in the war that inevitably followed it.

And to wonder how it ended up turning so many in this country insane.

News.title: Insane cost of executing death row inmates vs life in prison – & that’s before Christa Pike’s life-saving medical bills
News.content:
Next

THE staggering price of putting a killer to death is often millions more than keeping them locked up for life.

Now the cost of capital punishment is under renewed scrutiny after murderer Christa Pike was left critically ill when Tennessee’s attempt to execute her failed.



Pike, 50, survived two doses of lethal drugs after spending three decades on death row for the brutal 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, with her case estimated to have already cost taxpayers more than $3 million.

Her legal team said on Tuesday that Pike is now “conscious, speaking” but remains under critical medical care.



Her lawyers claim botched IV lines caused the drugs to leak into tissue, leaving both arms “swollen, burned and blistered.”

And the taxpayer bill is still mounting, with the state now facing the cost of Pike’s hospital treatment, an investigation into the failed execution and potentially further legal proceedings.



Six days of intensive care and ventilation alone could carry charges of around $26,000 based on published Nashville hospital rates, before other treatment is factored in.

Stacy Rector, executive director of Tennesseans for Alternatives to the Death Penalty, told The U.S. Sun, “I would guess her case has exceeded $3 million, before this botched execution attempt.

“I can’t even begin to guess what her hospital bill will be once this is all over – a hundred thousand plus?

“All is being paid by TN taxpayers.”



Pike had been held at Nashville’s Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, formerly the Tennessee Prison for Women, since March 1996 before being transferred to Riverbend Maximum Security Institution for her attempted execution.

She was then taken from Riverbend to an off-site medical facility after the lethal injection failed.

Rector based her estimate for Pike on a detailed Maryland study of 1,136 death-eligible murder cases from 1978 to 1999, covering the period in which Pike was convicted.



Cases where prosecutors did not seek death cost around $1.1 million over their lifetime.

That rose to around $1.8 million when prosecutors sought death but no death sentence was imposed.

Cases resulting in a death sentence cost around $3 million — almost $2 million more than those where death was not sought.

The $3 million included the trial, penalty phase, state and federal appeals and prison costs.

Prosecutors decide before trial whether to seek death.



If they do not, there is no separate capital sentencing hearing after a conviction, explaining the $0 penalty phase cost.

When death was sought, that additional phase cost an average $71,000 when no death sentence was imposed and $263,000 when it was.

Newer studies have also found a major gap between the cost of death penalty and non-capital cases.

A 2021 review by the Ohio Legislative Service Commission looked at studies from several states and found death penalty cases cost between 2.5 and five times as much as non-capital cases, with some studies putting the additional bill at between $1 million and $3 million per case.



A 2025 Indiana analysis found an even bigger difference at the trial stage, with an average death penalty trial costing $290,022 compared with $36,173 for one seeking life without parole.

That works out at around eight times as much at the trial stage alone.

Tennessee’s own research found death penalty trials cost taxpayers an average of 48 percent more than cases where prosecutors seek life imprisonment, while state estimates have put the added cost of capital trials and appeals at more than $750,000 per case.

Rector said, “I think the cost is a colossal waste of tax dollars spent pursuing death for a handful of people who are already incarcerated.”



She questioned the spending when Tennessee “solves only about half its homicides” and said the state’s victims’ compensation fund was difficult for those impacted by violence to access.

She added, “Too many Tennesseans lack access to mental health care, and our Department of Children’s Services continues to struggle to serve children like Christa Pike, who have experienced terrible trauma and violence.”

Rector said many Tennesseans remain unaware of how much is being spent in her state.

She said, “Our organization, TADP, continues to educate people about these costs, but too many Tennesseans don’t know how expensive it is.

“Our state has no centralized mechanism to track these costs so taxpayers are in the dark.”



Rector feels the money spent pursuing executions could instead be used on victims, unsolved murders and crime prevention.

She said, “We are paying for a system that does not achieve anything for us. It does not make us safer.

“It traps surviving families of murder victims in decades of trauma without the resources and space they need to begin their healing process.

“It is not applied fairly. It diverts an inordinate amount from investments in real crime prevention and solving unsolved crimes.”

She added, “And it sometimes gets it wrong: over 200 people sentenced to death in the US since 1973 have later been exonerated and released from death row.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We don’t know the number of innocent people we have executed.”

She added, “The bottom line is that the death penalty system is a costly government program that is totally unnecessary and distracts us from investing in real solutions.”

News.title: Waitress injured as dine and dash customer 'attacks her' at UK restaurant
News.content:
Waitress injured as dine and dash customer 'attacks her' at UK restaurant

The waitress was taken to hospital after chasing after the dine and dasher, and police have now released an image of a man they want to speak to in relation to the incident

View 4 Images The staff member chased after the dine and dashers

A 'young' waitress has allegedly been assaulted at a UK restaurant by a dine and dash customer who tried to flee without paying.

‌



‌



Noodle Alley, an Asian restaurant in Manchester's Chinatown, shared CCTV footage on social media, claiming a young staff member was attacked after a customer left without paying for their food. The incident is thought to have occurred Sunday, September 27 just after 6pm and led to the waitress being sent to hospital for her injuries.

‌



In the footage, a staff member is seen running up the stairs after three customers, reports the Manchester Evening News. Noodle Alley owners said: “What has the world come to? A violent man sent our staff to A&E over an unpaid meal.

‌



View 4 Images The restaurant says a member of staff was 'assaulted' during the incident

Nicole Scherzinger shows off painful scars from horrific injury before Pussycat Dolls tour performance READ MORE :

“We’re a small family business, and lately it feels like small businesses are being targeted again and again. But this time, it went far beyond anything we have experienced before. One of our young staff members — a girl simply doing her job — was assaulted after going beyond her duty to try to recover what had been taken from our restaurant. She ended up in A&E.

“What hurts us most is seeing how emotionally affected she has been by what happened. She told us she had treated them kindly and never expected that kindness to come back to her like this.

‌



“We work hard to look after our staff and our customers, and nobody should have to go through this simply for doing their job. We have reported the incident to the police.”

View 4 Images Police would like to speak to this man

Greater Manchester Police has released an image of a man they would like to speak to. Officers say they believe he can help with their investigations.

‌



Anyone with information is asked to contact us on 101, on LiveChat or via the reporting mechanisms on our website quoting CRI/06A2/0030137/26. Alternatively call Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

In a previous statement, a spokesperson for Greater Manchester Police said: “Officers received reports of an assault and a pair making off without paying a bill from a restaurant on Faulkner Street. No arrests have been made at this stage and enquiries are on-going.”

View 4 Images Noodle Alley, owned by Ken and Wendy Chen, in Manchester's Chinatown

‌



Noodle Alley, which specialises in Szechuan-style street food dishes, first opened its doors three years ago in the former China City spot. Run by owners Wendy and Ken Chen, the pair said they wanted to ‘share the food’ they grew up on, and add to the variety on offer in Chinatown.

Following their reports of the incident, customers took to social media to share their support for the venue. One person said: “Omg this makes me so sad to see. I love your restaurant so much, you don’t deserve this!” Another posted: “Unbelievable. We really hope your staff member is OK.” One other commented: “we’re so sorry, you guys are always SO EXCELLENT.”

It’s the latest incident for the Noodle Alley restaurant in as much as six weeks, with owners Wendy and Ken Chen previously speaking to the Manchester Evening News back in August after a customer left without paying.

Article continues below

Earlier this year, Noodle Alley was nominated for Affordable Eats Venue of the Year at the Manchester Food and Drink Festival Awards, with the honour later going to popular pizza spot Double Zero.

News.title: Shocking moment passenger ferry crashes into mansion after losing control
News.content:
Shocking moment passenger ferry crashes into mansion after losing control

No injuries were reported from the crash as videos of the aftermath show a trail of destruction left by the ferry, which also collided with a boat moored up infront of the property in Istanbul, Turkey

View 3 Images The boat smashes into the mansion and another vessel, CCTV appears to show

Shocking CCTV footage shows the moment a passenger ferry appears to collide with a mansion and a boat moored in front of the glitzy home.

‌



‌



Videos from Turkey show a large boat careering straight into an outside terrace of a waterfront property, smashing into a smaller vessel in front of it. Turkish news outlets say the incident took place in Üsküdar, an Istanbul suburb on the Asian side of the Bosphorus.

‌



Reports suggest the incident took place at 10:30pm on Tuesday, October 6. It’s thought the mansion and boat were owned by a businessman. Both have been damaged, according to DHA news. It added no injuries were sustained in the incident.

‌



View 3 Images Moments before impact

CCTV footage shows the larger ferry approaching the smaller boat, initially sending birds flying away in fear. The bow of the ferry then collides with the side of the boat, pinning it against the outside terrace.

‌



The boat is then thrown backwards as the ferry continues to head careen into the terrace, quickly destroying a metal fence and retaining wall.

It then goes a few metres into the terrace, before slowly sliding back into the water, leaving devastation in its wake. As it retreats, people onboard the ferry can be seen rushing to its bow to express their disbelief at the incident, with hands placed on heads.

View 3 Images A trail of destruction is left behind by the vessel

Article continues below

Videos on social media taken from inside the mansion show the chaos left behind, with fences destroyed, furniture broken, and plants ripped apart. The mansion occupants and ferry personnel can be heard shouting at one another.

News.title: 'Rejecting a Reform coalition isn't a reason to vote for Kemi Badenoch's Tory party'
News.content:
'Rejecting a Reform coalition isn't a reason to vote for Kemi Badenoch's Tory party'

"Reform UK has dragged politics so far to the right that even the Conservatives now want to keep their distance - and Kemi Badenoch would rather fight another election than "

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The Tories were once branded Britain’s “nasty party”.

‌



‌



Reform has dragged politics so far to the right that even the Conservatives now want to keep their distance. Kemi Badenoch says she would rather fight another general election than enter a coalition with Nigel Farage.

‌



On that, she is right. But rejecting Reform is no substitute for giving voters a reason to return to the Conservatives.

‌



A week ago, at the Labour conference, Andy Burnham offered difficult choices, big ideas and a clear argument about how Britain should change. Given her moment, Ms Badenoch offered a party that was still largely talking to itself.

Voters are not crying out for lectures about Conservative identity. They want to know how their bills will come down, when they will get a GP appointment, whether their children can afford a home, why wages feel squeezed and how crumbling public services will be fixed.

Mr Burnham at least tried to answer those questions. Ms Badenoch talked about saving the Tory Party.

‌



Voters need someone focused on saving the country.

Speed, certainty and care

For cancer patients, every week of waiting can mean the difference between hope and heartbreak. That is why the warning from Cancer Research UK is so alarming.

On current performance, England will miss a key cancer treatment target by more than three years, with the 62-day standard not expected to be met until April 2032.

‌



Ministers have promised that by March 2029, 85% of patients will begin treatment within 62 days of an urgent referral. That commitment must be more than another date on a Government spreadsheet.

Patients facing one of the most frightening moments of their lives deserve speed, certainty and care.

Ministers must act now, put whatever resources are needed into cutting these waits and make certain that no cancer patient is left paying the price for delay.

Article continues below

Brilliant and brazen

Jeffrey Archer was a bundle of contradictions: a bestselling storyteller who became a convicted liar, a political insider who ended up behind bars, a man of immense ambition repeatedly undone by his own behaviour.

Yet he kept returning. Brilliant, brazen, disgraced and resilient, Archer’s life was as compelling as any of his plots.

News.title: Andy Burnham issues powerful anti-Semitism statement on October 7 anniversary
News.content:
Andy Burnham issues powerful anti-Semitism statement on October 7 anniversary

The Prime Minister has told Britain's Jewish community 'we stand with you' as he marked the third anniversary of the horrific October 7 attack in Israel and voiced his anger at antisemitic attacks in Britain

View 2 Images Andy Burnham pictured at the scene of the terror attack at the Heaton Park Synagogue last year (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham has told Britain's Jewish community "we stand with you" as he marks the third anniversary of the October 7 attack.

‌



‌



The Prime Minister said the country will today remember the hundreds of people senselessly murdered by Hamas terrorists in Israel. He said the impact of the horrifying killings are still being felt across the world - and said he was horrified by anti-Semitic attacks that have happened in the UK since.

‌



Mr Burnham said in a statement: "Three years on from the October 7 attacks on Israel, we remember those who were senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists. The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day."

‌



He said that the UK has seen a number of antisemitic attacks in the past three years, including the killing of two British Jews, Melvin Kravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 55, at Heaton Park Synagogue on October 2 last year. The PM stated an attack on Jewish people in Britain is an attack on all.

View 2 Images Hundreds of people were killed in the October 7 attacks three years ago (Image: Andy Commins / Daily Mirror)

Mr Burnham said: "In the years since, we have seen a disturbing rise in anti-Semitic behaviour in the UK.

‌



"A year ago we witnessed a horrifying terrorist attack on the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation in Manchester, with further attacks against Jewish people and institutions since.

"I want Britain's Jewish community to hear this from me directly. We stand with you. Abuse and violence against you, in any form, will not be tolerated. Not on our streets, not online, not in our schools or universities.

"That's why we are funding protection for synagogues, schools and community buildings, and why we will come down hard on anti-Semitism wherever it is found - in classrooms, on campuses and in neighbourhoods.

‌



"At home, we are committed to protecting our citizens from vile hatred. Abroad, we continue to work towards a two-state solution, with Israelis and Palestinians living side by side in peace and security."

And he concluded: "An attack on Jewish people in Britain is an attack on all of us. Anti-Semitism has no place in this country, and we will do everything we can to stamp it out."

Around 1,200 people were killed in a series of co-ordianted attacks on Israel, including 378 in a massacre at the Nova music festival during the Simchat Torah Jewish holiday.

Article continues below

Dozens of children were among the dead, while 251 civilians and soldiers were taken as hostages into Gaza. The horrific attack triggered a huge Israeli assault on Gaza, estimated to have claimed over 74,000 lives.

News.title: Christa Pike's horrific injuries revealed as she 'wakes up and speaks' after lethal injection
News.content:
Christa Pike's horrific injuries revealed as she 'wakes up and speaks' after lethal injection

Christa Pike's injuries have been revealed after the murderer survived two doses of pentobarbital last week, but is now awake, conscious, and talking, her lawyers say

View 3 Images Christa Pike has survived two lethal injections (Image: Tennessee Department of Correction/AFP via Getty Images)

Christa Pike’s horrific injuries have been revealed after the prisoner woke up and started talking after surviving two lethal injections.

Pike’s lawyers announced late on Tuesday she remains in intensive care, but is now conscious and talking. She was injected with two doses of pentobarbital last Wednesday, a drug widely used in the US for executions.

But when the second dose did not end Pike’s life, and she was heard snoring, she was rushed to hospital with horrific injuries.

“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.

Her attorneys added they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her.”

A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalised Tuesday.

It’s now been revealed the lethal injection has caused horrific burns and blistering on Pike’s arms. Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery.”

View 3 Images Christa Pike murdered Colleen Slemmer (Image: WVLT 8)

But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her.

“She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well.”

Pike’s attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection. The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.

View 3 Images In this image from video provided by WBIR-TV, Christa Pike cries after being sentenced to death on March 30, 1996

Pike’s attorneys said in their Tuesday statement that they continue to ask Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

“Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” her attorneys said.

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder and torture of classmate Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.

News.title: Lufthansa passenger ‘tries to open plane door at 30,000ft’ as crew wrestle him
News.content:
Lufthansa passenger ‘tries to open plane door at 30,000ft’ as crew wrestle him

Passengers and crew grappled with a man as he allegedly tried to open a plane door at cruising altitude in the middle of a Lufthansa flight from Bogotá to Frankfurt

View 2 Images The chaos erupted on a Lufthansa flight from Bogotá to Frankfurt (file) (Image: Getty Images)

Passengers and crew were forced to wrestle with a man who allegedly tried to open an exterior aircraft door at 30,000ft in the middle of a commercial flight.

‌



‌



The Lufthansa flight from Bogotá to Frankfurt descended into chaos, with the passenger accused of standing up from his seat and shaking the plane door.

‌



The crew asked the man to stop shaking the door but he ignored their instructions, German newspaper Bild reports.

‌



The situation on board the Boeing 787 escalated to the point that the cabin crew had to physically pull the man away. Two passengers joined in efforts to subdue the man and they eventually managed to get him away from the door.

View 2 Images A Lufthansa Boeing 787 at Frankfurt Airport, where the plane was met by police (file) (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Tanzania safari plane carrying 30 faces emergency after striking and killing zebra READ MORE :

The flight was able to continue as scheduled, according to Lufthansa. At cruising altitude, the cabin door cannot be opened due to the high pressure.

‌



Police met the plane when it landed in Frankfurt and a 33-year-old man was taken into custody. A police spokesperson said: "Due to his condition, the man was taken to a nearby psychiatric hospital."

Criminal proceedings have been started against the man, on suspicion of endangering air traffic.

This comes as a safari plane carrying 30 people was forced to make an emergency landing after striking and killing a zebra during take-off in Tanzania.

Article continues below

The Sindbard Air aircraft was carrying 26 passengers and four crew from Seronera to Zanzibar when it hit the animal on the runway in the Serengeti National Park at around 11.30am local time on Sunday, according to Aviation Herald.

The aircraft was a 1990-built Embraer EMB-120ER Brasilia, registered 5H-HLL, Aviation Safety Network records show. The crew diverted towards Kilimanjaro International Airport after the collision but were unable to lower the aircraft’s main landing gear.

The Embraer EMB-120 was eventually forced to land with its main gear up on runway 09 at Kilimanjaro. Dramatic footage showed smoke coming from the aircraft as its underside scraped along the runway during the landing.

News.title: 'Trump said 'Iran bombing LA is small price to pay' - and it matters even if he didn't mean it'
News.content:
'Trump said 'Iran bombing LA is small price to pay' - and it matters even if he didn't mean it'

No other politician in the world gets taken "seriously but not literally". It's unreasonable to expect Americans to all possess a Donald Trump decoder ring

View Image (Image: Getty Images)

By now you've probably seen the footage of Donald Trump apparently suggesting that sacrificing the cities of Los Angeles or San Diego, which between them have a population of about 4 million and a million and a half respectively, would be a small price to pay for ending the war in Iran.

‌



‌



This is objectively a mad thing to say. So it got me wondering if he really said it. Here's the full transcript, with a bit of context before and after.

‌



"It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego. And it's going to be over with very soon. Essentially it's almost over with."

‌



So ...yeah, those are the words that he said.

And understandably they have gone down very poorly indeed - particularly in California, which - it appears - Trump would be happy to see largely reduced to rubble if it meant winning his poorly defined war of choice. LA Mayor Karen Bass said the comment was "an attempt to encourage attacks on American lives."

And governor Gavin Newsom said the remarks were "dangerous - if not treasonous".

‌



Trump suggests letting Iran 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego

The White House, as you can imagine, interpreted it differently. Comms chief Steven Chung - who is one of the most combative people alive who isn't also an ultimate fighter - said we'd got it all wrong. Branding it a "media freakout", he said Trump was "clearly stating US Cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped."

‌



Which...isn't what he said. If we were to give Trump the benefit of the doubt - and after creating the most dangerously divisive decade of politics in modern history, lying, cheating and upturning societal and geopolitical norms to a hugely damaging effect for entire world, largely for his own gain, there's no reason he deserves the benefit of the doubt....

...but if we were to give it to him, you could argue that it's what he meant to say. But it's not what he said.

And while it's obviously important to drill into what a politician actually means, the words that they say aren't irrelevant. You can't just say 'oh ignore the things he says' just because he's doddery and imprecise.

‌



For more of our coverage of Trump's America: Subscribe to The Trump Update on YouTube

Subscribe to the US Dispatch - our weekly newsletter exclusively for Mirror+ readers - following all the gossip and intrigue from Trump's DC swamp

- following all the gossip and intrigue from Trump's DC swamp Follow Mikey Smith on Twitter, TikTok, Bluesky or Facebook.

Back in his first term, when he said there were "very fine people on both sides" of the racist Charlottesville 'Unite the Right' March, Trump - and a lot of his water carriers - argued that he was not, in fact, saying the Neo nazis responsible for the march were 'very fine people'.

But it was implicit in the words that he actually, in reality, used.

Article continues below

And you know who didn't spend too long trying to work out if he was really praising the Neo nazis? The Neo nazis. They took it as a barely coded high five from the president of the United States.

Nobody else gets this kind of treatment. No other politician in the world gets taken "seriously but not literally". It's unreasonable to expect Americans to all possess a Donald Trump decoder ring, with which to decipher his lunatic ramblings and get to the root of what he really means.

More to the point, I'm pretty sure the decoder rings aren't sold in Iran either.

News.title: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum
News.content:
Two people were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds in cash. A third person was arrested on suspicion of being in the country illegally.

Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said the fake claims were connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London.

He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months.

"We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between Â£1,000 and Â£4,500," Foster said.

"It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants."

More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted.

Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs.

The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim.

The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year.

A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May.

In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence.

She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim.

Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay."

The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims.

Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay.

Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection".

"To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said.

"And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country."

A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

News.title: Watch: Police raid on gang behind fake gay asylum claims
News.content:
Three people have been arrested after a raid on a suspected criminal network believed to be behind dozens of fake asylum claims from people pretending to be gay.

News.title: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.

The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".

Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.

As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.

Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.

She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles, external.

Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.

She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win.

"The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority.

"My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."

A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election.

Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."

Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".

She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".

Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches.

Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received, including a Â£5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.

Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down.

"That's what we're about."

Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.

Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.

Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.

Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party".

News.title: Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court
News.content:
The Green Party member behind a motion which declared Zionism to be racism was named in court documents as a "close friend" of a man who was jailed after being accused of plotting a suicide bomb attack at Heathrow Airport.

Lubna Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

Court documents from 2015 show she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.

The BBC has contacted Speitan for comment. The Green Party said she holds no official positions and the party "takes all allegations of this nature seriously".

The motion proposed by Speitan, which was passed on Sunday to become party policy, called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

In response, Israel banned Green leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Lib Dem MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.

Speitan argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

On Tuesday, it emerged she wrote a letter in 2016 to the New York judge in the Pham case describing him as "one of the kindest, honest, most sincere" people she had known.

The existence of the letter was first reported by the Jewish Chronicle, external and it has been seen by BBC News.

Pham, a Vietnamese-born British national who had lived in London, was arrested at Heathrow Airport in July 2011 after spending seven months in Yemen. He was found in possession of a live round of ammunition.

In 2015 he was extradited to the US and in 2016 sentenced to 40 years in prison after he admitted three counts based on his support for the group al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), an offshoot of al-Qaeda.

News.title: From 'woke' ridicule to real car - new electric Jaguar unveiled
News.content:
Two years ago, JLR relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy. Its bizarre teaser ad was described as "woke" and its "Barbie pink" concept car was ridiculed.

Now, the first of its new models has appeared in public for the first time. The all-electric Type 01, unveiled in New York, represents a radical new direction for the classic brand.

The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.

But it marks a gamble for JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar, despite the risk of collateral damage from the culture wars.

The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.

The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".

However, it comes at a hefty price tag, with a minimum cost of Â£130,000.

Under normal circumstances, the launch of a car like this might generate few headlines. But in this case the attention has been much greater, and for good reason.

News.title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor
News.content:
Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035.

The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters.

Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade.

Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in".

He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas.

"It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it."

Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas.

Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said.

Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.

Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".

News.title: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notification to app users
News.content:
Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers.

Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app.

The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt.

Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed.

In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident.

The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach.

Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times.

The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets.

Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday.

Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history.

Shares in the company fell by around a tenth on Tuesday.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note".

But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts.

News.title: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
A 22-year-old British national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford, counter-terror police said.

He was arrested in Westminster, London, on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire on 27 September.

It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident but no one has been charged.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

Senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said it "remains a live investigation" and police are continuing to "pursue multiple lines of enquiry".

Five men were arrested on 27 September near the base in connection with the incident and were subsequently released on police bail.

The men, aged between 23 and 25, were detained in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster and was also later released on bail.

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

On Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

While speaking to a group of reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.

He replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.

"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy.

"But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."

Earlier, US Vice-President JD Vance said the bombers were moved "out of an abundance of caution".

The comments came after US media reports suggested the decision was made after intelligence suggested Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not verified those reports.

On Tuesday, a spokesperson for US European Command, which coordinated American military activity in Europe, said it would be "inappropriate to discuss matters of intelligence" but that the US would "continue to assess the threat environment" at bases.

The spokesperson added the US remains at the "highest state of readiness" and would take "appropriate actions to protect our people, our platforms, and the bases where our forces operate".

Prior to Trump's intervention on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to his previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

News.title: Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC
News.content:
Broadhurst acknowledges that term is "politically loaded" and the modern care system is very different from the coercive practices that took place mainly between 1949 and 1976 - and for which the government recently apologised for cases in England.

But she says it "is actually what's happening because parents do not agree".

"They want to continue to be in contact with a child," she says. "Even parents who feel they couldn't look after a child at that point find it particularly brutal that they're going to have no contact, or very little contact, with that child until they're 18."

One birth mother, Jean, tells us she never wanted to give up her daughter, Tye, for adoption - and describes it as "forced". Her local council says it followed a lawful process.

Jean was separated from her daughter for 16 years, after Tye was taken into care at 11 weeks' old and then adopted at the age of two.

Now, with Tye an adult, they are reunited. When she turned 18, having struggled with adoption and questions about her identity, Tye looked for her mother on social media.

"I knew I had a mum somewhere and it wasn't the people I was growing up with," she says - describing her adoption as something that had left her "completely alone" without a "whole chunk of heritage".

When Jean became pregnant, she was looking forward to being a mother. But she had concerns too: "The only thing I knew for certain was that I was disabled, I couldn't look after myself properly, so I wasn't sure how I was going to be able to look after a baby, so I needed help."

Her local authority at the time, Newham Council in east London, told her such help was not available, she says. Tye was put into foster care, but Jean was able to see her often.

There had been multiple assessments and residential placements as Jean tried to keep Tye. But professionals, including doctors and social workers, ultimately advised the court that Tye needed a stable, permanent family and that Jean could not provide it.

Jean says she fought and "gave it my all" through years of court proceedings. She even asked if she could have visiting rights, in a similar way to a parent in a divorce. "I was told that was an unrealistic expectation," she says.

News.title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
News.content:
A Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home.

Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care.

Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife.

The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after.

Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children.

The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16.

At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care.

News.title: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vaping
News.content:
More than a million people who say they have never smoked are now vapers, latest data for 2025 reveals, external - up from around 940,000 in 2024.

People aged 25-34 are vaping more than any others, overtaking 16 to 24-year-olds, with 16.4% using e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.

For the second year in a row, more over-16s in Great Britain are using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Meanwhile, the number of smokers in the UK continues to fall to nearly one in 10 adults, or 4.9 million people, down from 5.3 million in 2024, with more over-16s now vaping than smoking at 5.4 million.

News.title: Man charged with GP's murder
News.content:
A man has been charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home.

The man was arrested after the body of 45-year-old Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday.

Norfolk Police said 45-year old Mark Cain, of Fern Hill, Dersingham, has been charged with her murder.

He has been remanded in custody until a court appearance on Wednesday.

A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where Dr Terry is listed as a member of the practice team, said it was "temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team".

Tributes have been left outside the centre, including a teddy bear and flowers on a bench. A card from two patients reads: "Dear Dr Hannah Terry. We are so shocked and saddened to hear such tragic news."

News.title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates
News.content:
Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced.

On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said.

The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically.

Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials.

If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer.

Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said.

News.title: First minister to face no-confidence vote over Drumcree row
News.content:
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill is to face a no-confidence vote at Stormont over her handling of the Drumcree parading dispute.

The motions against her and three other Sinn FÃ©in ministers are set to be debated after receiving the backing of unionist parties.

But the attempt to oust them will fail as it requires cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly.

It comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and other senior Sinn FÃ©in politicians have been heavily criticised by unionists for joining protests which have blocked the parade from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.

Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry.

O'Neill has defended her actions, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents and adding that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it".

In the assembly on Monday, the Sinn FÃ©in vice-president described the planned Orange march as "unwanted, sectarian and triumphalist".

The exclusion motions have been submitted against O'Neill and fellow Sinn FÃ©in ministers John O'Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins.

They are expected to be debated as early as next Monday.

News.title: Insurance exec fatally shoots wife, daughter before taking his own life inside their NJ mansion, police say
News.content:
