Ronaldo left the national team squad in Copenhagen on the eve of a Nations League fixture against Denmark after he was an unused substitute for a 2-1 win away to Norway on September 27.

The Portugal captain chose not to applaud the travelling fans with his team-mates, for which he apologises in his statement, and reports subsequently emerged of a rift between Ronaldo and Jesus.

Ronaldo claims in his statement that Jesus had told him he would play 30 minutes against Norway on the day of the game only to go back on his word.

"Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said. "The coach had broken his word to me."

On failing to show his appreciation to the fans, Ronaldo added: "At the end of the match I only wanted everything to finish with the victory and to be alone. A failing that is solely my responsibility and that should not have happened.

"I apologise to the Portuguese who supported us intensely there, I apologise to the fans, and I apologise to those who, without being Portuguese, may have travelled there to see me and whom I may have disappointed."

The eight points Jesus 'agreed' to say to the media

Ronaldo and Jesus, who used to work together at Al Nassr, subsequently held a meeting, which was also attended by the sporting director of the Saudi Pro League club, Simao Coutinho.

According to Ronaldo's statement, Jesus agreed to clarify the situation and say that his captain never demanded minutes and that it was a mistake to let him warm up without bringing him on.

Ronaldo says an eight-point document was drawn up to summarise what had been discussed in a subsequent meeting between Jesus, Al Nassr sporting director Coutinho and Tiago Craveiro, the player's strategic adviser.

The eight points Ronaldo says Jesus agreed to say in his press conference 1. I myself, and no one else, proposed to Cristiano a plan for him this sporting season with the National Team. It was a long and very good conversation.

2. I know how much he lives and loves the national team and the weight he has in the world, and even more the weight and the positive influence he has had on the national team for 24 consecutive years.

3. The plan I proposed to Cristiano was accepted.

4. He never questioned my options. He was exemplary, loyal and professional.

5. The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.

6. I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it.

7. To close the subject: I want Cristiano in the National Team. In fact I do not want him a little, I want him a lot. Fortunately he also believes in me. He believed at Al Nassr and he does here as well.

8. About not greeting the fans. We have already spoken about that. Someone who has played more than 230 matches for the national team does not receive lessons from me on love for Portugal. It was a moment of frustration that erases nothing. He is the player who gives the most autographs, takes the most selfies, and shows the most affection to the fans. Let us not invent problems where they do not exist. When we are not happy we react.

However, Ronaldo felt the Portugal head coach's press conference bore no reflection to the conversation they had shared, which he claims ended in Jesus asking him for a hug.

"I heard expressions and an aggressiveness that I do not believe I deserved, an attitude of 'I want, I can and I command' that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before," said Ronaldo.

He added: "It was the second time he had broken his word to me. I decided to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises."

Jesus denied that any such agreement had been made with the player in a later press conference.

Ronaldo's apologies and Portugal farewell 'promise'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cristiano Ronaldo returned to Al Nassr training after he left the Portugal squad. Pictures courtesy of @AlNassrFC.

Ronaldo admitted he never should have left the Portugal camp "despite the absolute breach of trust" from Jesus.

"Never, at any moment, have I interfered in any technical or tactical decision of any coach or national team manager in almost 25 years of career," said Ronaldo. "I accept, for better or worse, what they propose that I do. I respect the decision, and when they break their word to me, I feel that my place is not there."

He added: "I felt that, from that point on, my remaining would only harm the working group, and I did what I have always said I would do if I did not feel useful: I packed my bags and left."

Ronaldo apologised to his team-mates and the Portuguese people over his departure from the squad and said he will accept whatever punishment is handed down to him by the Portuguese Football Federation.

The forward said he hopes his international career will not be limited to a farewell but promised he would end his Portugal career in the right way.

Ronaldo added: "I can promise all my fans, naturally and especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches; there will be time for that. But when I think of the national team, what I really think of is competing.

"That is what I thought on the day I was given the news of my father's death. I was at a camp with our national team and I decided to stay there until the end of the match the following day. I did for the country what I would never do for any club."

How Ronaldo nearly retired from international football

Ronaldo publicly admitted earlier in this international break that he considered retiring from international football following the World Cup.

His statement on Instagram reveals that he had written his retirement statement only to be talked out of it by the president of the Portuguese Football Federation Pedro Proença on the plane back from North America.

Ronaldo says Proença then asked him for his opinion on his former head coach at Al Nassr Jesus becoming Portugal's next manager.

"I told [him] that, in my opinion, it would be the right choice," Ronaldo said. "That is why, on the day the current head coach was presented, I was genuinely happy with the choice. It was the right option, as the results are confirming."

Sports.title: O'Neill confirms decision to stay on as Celtic boss
Sports.content:
Martin O'Neill has confirmed his decision to stay on as Celtic manager after reflecting on his future over the international break.

The Celtic manager admitted before the international break that he would consider his future after three consecutive defeats and talk to the board.

The 74-year-old has now declared himself up for the challenge after two defeats by Rangers sandwiched a Europa League setback against Ferencvaros.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Scottish Premiership match between Celtic and Rangers

When asked how ready and determined he was to lead the team forward, O'Neill told the club's Celtic Player: "I am. I'm extremely prepared for it.

"We had a difficult week. It can happen, you can lose to your arch-rivals, you can lose a European game.

"It's certainly not the end of the world, as it seemed to be described. But (I'm) ready to go.

"I did think I would take a little bit of time and it didn't take me that much time to think about it.

"I want to lead the club, I want to try and win the league, which is what we set out to do, and just as determined now as ever before.

"It was a time of reflection for a moment or two and, yes, some things that you think about.

"But overall, I'm back, I'm raring to go and the team's ready."

O'Neill, whose side face Motherwell at Fir Park on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, added: "What you try and do is analyse the things that you've done or perhaps the things that you haven't done.

"Throughout my managerial time, I've been exactly that. I think I look to myself, first of all. Maybe a wee bit different as a player, because I think I used to blame every other player for my own bad performance. But as a manager, you've got to look at yourself.

"And if you feel as if something has dropped away, of course you have to analyse it.

"Now, there wasn't a great deal in some of the games. If we get the equaliser just after half-time in the Rangers game, totally different ball game, totally different. But it wasn't to be. So you have to reflect on a few things like that.

"But overall, did the reflection, did all of that and a bit of self-analysing and just prepared for the battle."

O'Neill also revealed that Jota had played 45 minutes of a training-ground friendly against Falkirk on Friday, as the Portuguese winger steps up his comeback attempts following 18 months out with a knee injury.

The Celtic manager has also been encouraged by Alistair Johnston and Callum Osmand getting back on the training pitch following hamstring injuries.

O'Neill added he would assess the fitness of Hyun-Jun Yang on Friday after the South Korea winger experienced hamstring trouble on international duty.

Analysis: Celtic were always calm over O'Neill future

Sky Sports News' Anthony Joseph:

Martin O'Neill was never going to be sacked by Celtic after three humiliating defeats in one week before the international break - but there was a real potential of him walking away from the job.

After losing 1-0 at home to Rangers on September 20, O'Neill said he would take some time to think about whether he would continue as manager of the club.

Those comments sparked widespread reports and supporter speculation that the 74-year-old was on the verge of resigning.

Sky Sports News understands Celtic have always remained calm about the situation, despite the recent results. There was no appetite to pull the trigger themselves, especially when the teams are sitting at the top of the league.

That was proven when Celtic CEO Michael Nicholson backed O'Neill in a statement announcing the club's latest financial results. He said: "We will now come together and support Martin and the players, as we focus our efforts on achieving success domestically and in the Europa League."

The ball has been completely in O'Neill's court and - as he has said today - he very quickly indicated his intention and desire to stay.

Celtic face a tricky next five games back - Motherwell away (live on Sky Sports), Benfica away, Hearts at home (live on Sky Sports), Celta Vigo at home and Hibernian away (live on Sky Sports).

It's going to be an interesting month ahead for O'Neill and Celtic.

Sports.title: FIA directives questioned after formation lap 'farce' at Bahrain GP
Sports.content:
David Croft has questioned the FIA after the chaotic formation lap scenes at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, describing a software glitch that saw several drivers slowing to a crawl or stopping completely as a "farce".

F1 and the FIA have new technical regulations this year which saw the introduction of a new power unit which is almost 50 per cent electric.

Sepang saw the first wet conditions of the season, and the FIA later confirmed that a combination of low engine speeds, low grip, wet-weather energy-management settings and the configuration of the circuit had caused an unintended loss of power.

Speaking on the F1 Show podcast, Sky Sports F1 commentator Croft questioned why such a scenario had not been simulated before the season began.

"We had a shakedown in Barcelona and six days of testing in Bahrain before the season started. Why on earth were situations like this not tried out before we went racing?" he said.

"Nikolas Tombazis [FIA single-seater director] says there are bugs all the time with software. Behind the scenes, people are working on those bugs, and what they try and do is do updates during the night time when people aren't actually using their computers.

"Not during the course of a Grand Prix, when someone has now suddenly realised we've got a situation on our hands.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit.

"Before the start of the race, it looked like it was the day where we were going to break the duck and have some wet weather running.

"We've had dry weather all the time, so we've had plenty of time to simulate this, to stop it happening in front of hundreds of millions of people during the course of a race.

"This falls on the FIA. I'm sorry, but you are the governing body. You are supposed to have the upper hand when it comes to these rules and regulations, the directives, the power units and everything.

"You weren't on top of things when it came to that race, and it was a farce."

When the drivers left the pit lane following a rain-delayed start, several almost ground to a halt, including race leader Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with numerous other drivers in the midfield also experiencing issues.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chaotic formation lap halts race start at Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

The unusual scenes left spectators and viewers unsure what was happening, with the aborted start followed by a lengthy wait while the problem was resolved.

The FIA said its emergency software fix took around 20 minutes to issue and install, although the overall disruption was considerably longer.

"We had no idea why those cars were going so slowly," Croft said. "We had no idea why we were waiting around for 40 minutes to get a race on.

"There's a lot going on, and we need to understand and appreciate that the FIA are trying to keep across a million and one different things.

"But sometimes taking a step back, identifying issues that could come during a season, during a scenario, and taking preventative measures is the best way forward, rather than just trying to react on the spur of the moment.

"I want to see a bit more strategic thinking when it comes to these sorts of issues.

"Let's go through other simulations, FIA, and other things that could go wrong with these power units. Let's get the bugs fixed and get the simulations in place now."

Tombazis acknowledged after the race that the software had not been tested sufficiently in the specific conditions encountered at Sepang.

The FIA added that the issue had not been detected during testing or the laps to the grid and has promised a full review with the teams and power-unit manufacturers.

The controversy ultimately overshadowed what became an eventful and competitive Grand Prix as Verstappen emerged victorious, with Kimi Antonelli second and Hamilton completing the podium after a dramatic recovery.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player SkyPad ANALYSIS of Lewis Hamilton's P15 to podium recovery drive!

"I'm just really frustrated that I've come away from Sepang - a brilliant weekend commentating, talking about a great track, brilliant drivers, some sensational racing - and what's dominating the headlines is F1 farce because we see cars slowing down and stopping," Croft added.

"I don't want that for the sport that I love. I actually want people to be talking about great racing.

"That's what we should be talking about, but these issues need addressing."

Sports.title: Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past Czechia
Sports.content:
It was a night that belonged to Harry Kane. Yet another one. It began with him being shown a replay of his first England goal during a pre-match interview with ITV – the header against Lithuania in 2015, just 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for his debut. It ended with him reflecting on two more in what was a supremely comfortable Nations League victory over Czechia. Some things never change.

It remains a numbers game for Kane. They are getting bigger and ever more impressive. On the occasion of his 125th cap, the one that took him level with Peter Shilton at the top of the all-time England list, he moved to an astonishing 91 goals. Nobody will be surprised if he reaches the century. The only question appears to be when.

England know how to beat the game’s smaller fry. Under Thomas Tuchel, they have played 16 matches against teams ranked outside the world’s top 20. They have won 15 and drawn one – against Ghana at the World Cup. They have conceded only once – against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also at the World Cup. Czechia, who are ranked No 50, were never in the contest.

Kane is similarly inevitable. The captain even claimed the assist for the breakthrough goal with a cross into the corridor of uncertainty that spooked Vladimir Coufal so severely he shot into his own net. Kane’s passing was very good. When he was withdrawn in the 82nd minute, he left to a great ovation.

The victory meant that England virtually guaranteed their progress into the Nations League quarter-finals and, perhaps more importantly, saw them close out this elongated window with plenty of optimism. One of the main goals was to put as much distance as possible between themselves and the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina. It was mission accomplished.

Kane will break the caps record when England host Croatia in November and that will be the night when he is truly feted. As an aside, he would want to do it at Wembley rather than in Madrid against Spain where England’s next-but-one game will be staged. Was that why he was so keen to play in all four of the matches during this window? It might have been a part of it.

Then again, Kane always wants to play. He was one of only three England players to start each of the matches in this series. The others were Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Elliot Anderson. Was the City manager, Enzo Maresca, happy about that? Probably not. Does he have bigger problems at the moment? Yes.

Kane’s act of drawing level with Shilton was the box-office detail. His name was on everybody’s lips; his face on the big screen before kick-off. He was pictured alongside Shilton when his name was read out with the teams. The Wembley crowd roared.

Kane was at the heart of the opening goal, providing the teasing cross from the right and it was some finish from the player just inside the six-yard box. One that Kane would have been happy to call his own. The problem from a Czechia point of view was that it came from their right-back. Coufal could feel Eberechi Eze at his back as he faced towards his own goal, albeit the England winger was not that close. Coufal stretched and everybody had the time to have the same thought: you do not have to do this. Coufal did it. He could not check his momentum and steered firmly past his goalkeeper.

View image in fullscreen Czechia’s Vladimir Coufal scores an own goal to put England ahead. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Trent Alexander-Arnold, who Tuchel recalled at right-back, was involved in the buildup and he caught the eye, especially when surging up and inside. He repeatedly got into advanced areas and there was one moment in the first half when he stormed into the No 9 position on to an Anderson pass. He just could not bring it under his spell. Alexander-Arnold had extended Lukas Hornicek with a whipped free-kick at the outset.

Jude Bellingham was excellent. Of course he was. There were fizzed passes from him that took the breath, getting England into dangerous positions, including one for Morgan Rogers in the 25th minute that the Chelsea attacker wasted. There were those strutting runs and it was Bellingham, as much as anybody, who advertised the fact that England were going to break through.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Anderson should have made it 2-0 after a Bellingham lay-off; Kane sparked the move and Alexander-Arnold’s cross drove it. The second goal arrived before half-time and it had to be Kane. It would have been all about the buildup were it not for the identity of the scorer. Anderson’s lofted ball up the inside right was a beauty and Rogers’ first-time cross on the half-volley was even better, cut unerringly towards you-know-who in the middle. Kane was unmarked. Hornicek was helpless.

Kane wanted more. As usual. He got it. As usual. There was the moment shortly after the restart when he unloaded from the edge of the area and watched the shot kiss the top of the crossbar. Hornicek was beaten. Then he was for real.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s header puts England 3-0 up at Wembley. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

It was Lewis Hall – impressive at left-back – who swung over the corner, which came after Hornicek kept out an audacious Bellingham flick. Only Jiri Slama knows why he gave Kane so much room in front of goal. It was always going to end badly for the Czechia defender. Kane rose and the header had too much power for Hornicek.

There was the minor irritation for Tuchel when Myles Lewis-Skelly got himself booked in the 53rd minute for pulling back Pavel Sulc. The midfielder will be suspended for England’s next game and it was certainly not a great idea for him to get in the face of Michal Sadilek shortly afterwards. Sadilek had fouled Rogers and was booked. It was a needless risk from Lewis-Skelly.

England toyed with Czechia in the second half with Eze running through some of his party tricks. It was Kane who provided the substance.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi farewell match live – updates and analysis from Argentina v Benin
Sports.content:
1m ago 20.47 EDT 50 Min: Argentina with a pair of subs, the first of many I’m sure. Otamendi and defender Nicolás Tagliafico make way for Lisandro Martinez and Facundo Medina, respectively. Share

4m ago 20.45 EDT Goal! Argentina 1 – 0 Benin (Otamendi, 48) Lionel Messi with a well-placed corner kick and it’s Otamendi, the man we all came to see score tonight, who volleys it home at close range. Messi, at least, won’t be leaving empty-handed tonight. That’s his 68th assist with the national team. Share

10m ago 20.39 EDT Second half begins Both teams out for the start of the second half – Argentina’s XI remains unchanged. Let’s see if they can deliver some badly-needed joy in the second 45. Share Updated at 20.41 EDT

29m ago 20.19 EDT Halftime at Estadio Monumental It has to be said: this has been a pretty dreadful match to watch, far from the celebration we were promised. We’ll see what Argentina have in store for us in the second 45. What did you guys think? Use the link above to reach me and we’ll unpack it all here. Share Updated at 20.40 EDT

31m ago 20.17 EDT Guardian reader Peter reaches out via email: If Messi doesn’t score, they’ll have to organize another farewell match. I would not put this past the AFA! Share

32m ago 20.16 EDT 44 Min: Benin with another effort, again easily handled by Martinez. Share

34m ago 20.14 EDT 43 Min: Olaitan is again the danger man for Benin, as the midfielder puts a decent effort on goal from 15 yards, but it does little to challenge Martinez. Share

37m ago 20.12 EDT 40 Min: Benin doing their best to generate a little danger but they’ve had few chances, all of them generated on the counterattack. Still, it feels almost unbelievable that Argentina haven’t found any joy against such an outmatched opponent. The longer this stays 0-0, the longer the unthinkable remains a possibility! Share

43m ago 20.05 EDT View image in fullscreen Messi grimaces after a missed chance. Photograph: Marcos Brindicci/Getty Images 32 Min: Messi with another chance as Argentina striker Lautaro Martínez plays a driven cross to Messi, who sends his volleyed effort wide of the far post. Certainly not a sitter by any measure, but I’d have put money on Messi to finish at least one of his three big chances thus far. Guys, what if he doesn’t score? Share Updated at 20.32 EDT

50m ago 19.58 EDT 26 Min: Messi lines up for a free kick 30 yards from goal and puts it on target at the near post, but it’s dealt with easily by Benin goalkeeper Marcel Dandjinou. Similar distance to one of his all-time greatest efforts – his free kick goal against the United States at the 2016 Copa America. Different result, though. Share

53m ago 19.56 EDT 24 Min: Messi laughs after he misses a golden chance. Messi’s Inter Miami teammate Rodrigo De Paul found him at the edge of the six with a driven cross. Messi, fully outstretched, redirected the cross just wide of the near post. Feels like it’s only a matter of time before the inevitable. Share

1h ago 19.52 EDT 19 Min: Benin midfielder Junior Olaitan gives The Cheetahs their first real chance of the game, streaking towards the byline and driving his shot from eight yards wide of goal – Argentina keeper Emi Martínez (who has a tribute to Messi shaved into his hair tonight, by the way) seemed to have it covered regardless. Still, impressive fight from a vastly outclassed opponent. Share Updated at 20.31 EDT

1h ago 19.47 EDT 14 Min: Messi receives the ball 25 yards from goal above the semicircle and deftly plays Nicolás Otamendi through with a one-touch service. Otamendi, though, is offside. Predictably enough, Argentina with the bulk of the action in this one thus far. Share

1h ago 19.44 EDT View image in fullscreen Messi is embraced by Benin players during the 10th minute pause. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters 10 Min: The match is stopped at the 10th minute for a one-minute ovation. More fireworks, more tears as Messi salutes the crowd, which are serenading him – “Olé, Olé Olé Olé, Messi, Messi.” Not sure what Ifab or Fifa have to say about any of this but honestly who cares at this point. Share Updated at 20.30 EDT

1h ago 19.42 EDT Guardian reader Simon shares a personal memory of Messi. Can you imagine? Simon, are you sure this wasn’t a fever dream? I was lucky enough to meet Leo Messi a few times at the hotel I work at. An incredibly unassuming guy, we stood and watched our kids playing 3 v 3 for an hour or so. At the end he told my son “eres muy rápido” and I’ll be taking that to my grave. Share

1h ago 19.39 EDT 7 min: Messi sees his first true action of the match, rounding his defender and letting a left-footed effort go from 25 or so yards, handled with relative ease by Benin’s keeper. Share Updated at 19.44 EDT

1h ago 19.32 EDT We are underway! 31 minutes late, but the ball is finally rolling at the Estadio Monumental! Share Updated at 20.40 EDT

1h ago 19.31 EDT Another reader email, this one from Dion in Australia, who legitimately invited me to his wedding (thanks so much, but I don’t have that budgeted) and then offered his thoughts – it’s been incredible, honestly, to watch the compare/contrast between Messi and Ronaldo’s experiences this window: Devastating to see Messi go. Although I once saw them as equals, Ronaldo has disgraced himself this month with his Keane-’esque’ blow up at the nations league. To be a champion you must age gracefully, which Messi has done. To have such a great career in this era is an even greater achievement than in the past. The standard of defending faced by Maradona or Pele was hopeless by comparison. Share

1h ago 19.25 EDT Messi is not the only one crying now, as Argentina Boss Lionel Scaloni tears up during the Argentine anthem. Guardian reader Julia is also feeling it – she reaches out with this tribute: I’m 29 years old and have watched the World Cup as long as I can remember, but 2006 is the first one that’s really clear for me. My family are Argentina fans (to put it mildly), and my dad was a Messi believer from the beginning. I hate to be that person, but I’ve literally been a Leo fan for more than two-thirds of my life, and he’s seen me through growing up, losing a parent, graduating law school, and everything else. Today feels monumental, and I’m both pretty devastated and parasocially thrilled that he’s getting all the love he deserves. Share

2h ago 19.17 EDT Kickoff was delayed from 7 to 7.15 and we still don’t have teams on the pitch. We’ll see how long this drags out – the pitch, as of now, is covered by a massive Messi jersey, and the stadium is in full voice singing “Muchachos,” Argentina’s iconic battle call as of late. Share Updated at 20.29 EDT

2h ago 19.14 EDT By the way, if any of you have comments, questions, compliments, criticisms, or memories of Messi in an Argentina shirt, feel free to use the link at the head of this page to email me and we’ll navigate them together. It’s lonely here in the basement. Share

2h ago 19.12 EDT A lot of chatter on the Vix broadcast about ticket prices, which has been a central point of discussion in Argentina ahead of this match, with some accusing the Argentine Football Association of price gauging. “Sorry to those of you who couldn’t be here,” says the pitchside commentator, in Spanish, “maybe because of decisions made by people far away from the pitch. The prices for this match certainly were not for ‘the people.’” Reminds me a bit of the World Cup, obviously, and just like those matches, this one is fully sold out. Share

2h ago 18.59 EDT Guardian reader Paul reached out via email and is apparently deep in the comments section of a 20-year-old Messi article we published here at the Guardian. I can only hope Guardian reader “snafuclarke” has fully recovered from such a scorchingly terrible take: don’t kid yourselves. messi is currently hugely overrated. the amount of hype this lad gets has never matched his performances on the pitch the last game aside. the fact is that all too often he’s peripheral to the game and rarely has any effect on the result. one game where he bags a hat trick does not make him the superstar some are desperate to acclaim him. if he continues to put in that sort of performance over the course of a few years, fine he’ll be up there, but anyone saying, “oh he’s great player, even now” is either devoid of anything to compare him against or just not very clued up about football. potential is one thing, performance is what counts and this far one game in what 40 odd first team games perhaps, is not a very good record. Share Updated at 19.00 EDT

2h ago 18.49 EDT We’ve seen a lot of tears out of Messi over the years – tears when he briefly retired from the national team in 2016, tears when he won in 2022, tears of joy and sadness alike at the 2026 World Cup. Today we add “tears on the bus ride to the stadium” and “tears during warmups” to the archives. A moment of appreciation, please, for athletes who emote so openly. It’s lovely to see. Allow content provided by a third party? This article includes content hosted on embed.bsky.app . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue Share Updated at 18.54 EDT

2h ago 18.39 EDT Absolutely electric atmosphere at the Estadio Monumental, the home ground of Argentine side River Plate and the largest stadium in the country – it is filled to capacity well ahead of the opening kick. Argentina are near-unbeatable at the venue and Messi himself has never lost a match at the stadium, having won 22 of the 28 matches he’s played there with Argentina and drawn the other six, scoring 19 goals along the way. Something tells Benin will not be breaking that streak tonight. Share

2h ago 18.27 EDT View image in fullscreen Argentina players line up with their families. Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty Images Argentina’s starting XI is out and Messi, unsurprisingly, is in it, as are many of the players who helped guide Argentina to the 2026 World Cup final. Goalkeeper: Emiliano Martínez

Defenders: Agustín Giay, Cristian Romero, Nicolás Otamendi, Nicolás Tagliafico

Midfielders: Enzo Fernández, Alexis Mac Allister, Rodrigo De Paul

Forwards: Julián Álvarez, Lautaro Martínez, Lionel Mess Share Updated at 20.29 EDT

2h ago 18.27 EDT View image in fullscreen An overhead view of El Monumental Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/AP Messi, like any other megastar, has his haters and believers. I can’t say I fall into either side, but I find myself a bit sad watching the early scenes at Estadio Monumental. I’ve covered him in person dozens of times at this point, both with Argentina at this summer’s World Cup and over the entirety of his club career at Inter Miami. I can’t say it ever gets old – his magic is so predictable at times but never ceases to amaze. As I told a friend the other day – watching Messi is like watching a comedian tell the same joke over and over again, and you still laugh every time. Let’s see what he has in store for us tonight. Share Updated at 20.28 EDT

3h ago 18.00 EDT I could populate the entirety of this pre-match coverage with milestones and statistics from Messi’s illustrious career – his international career alone is a statistician’s dream, especially in the past two World Cup cycles, which saw him solidify his status as an immortal. Our own Ryan Benson unpacks the statistical absurdity of it all, arguing that Messi has at this point “completed football.” It’s hard to disagree: For now, though, it’s time for Argentina to celebrate what they have achieved with Messi because there is no guarantee it will ever be as good as this again. Argentina had already won the lottery once before with Maradona; it’ll surely be a while before they strike gold a third time. Luckily, Messi provided them with memories to last a lifetime. More at the link below. Lionel Messi has completed football and can bid Argentina farewell with pride Read more Share

3h ago 18.00 EDT If you’re watching tonight’s game in the United States you’re likely tuned into Vix, a Miami-based streaming service that operates in the US, South America and Spain. It’s probably unfair to call it an odd fit – the service regularly broadcasts matches from a host of competitions across North and South America but still – you’d think the final international appearance of the world’s best-ever footballer would find a wider audience elsewhere. Share

3h ago 18.00 EDT Pablo Iglesias Maurer Hi folks, Pablo Iglesias Maurer here, settled in and ready for Lionel Messi’s swan song as Argentina welcome 93rd-ranked Benin to El Monumental for an international friendly.



First things first – if you’re wondering why Argentina is playing a team like Benin, you likely haven’t been paying much attention to the types of friendlies the Albiceleste typically schedule. It’s far from their first encounter with a bottom-rung opponent; the average FIFA global ranking of their friendly opponents over the past several years is 85, at the moment, having faced other minnows like Burkina Faso and Mauritania.



This dynamic offers little in the way of competition but offers the Argentine Football Association a huge amount of control in terms of logistics and financial terms. Tonight, it may lead to all of us seeing Messi score a dozen goals or more. Who knows. Share

3h ago 18.00 EDT Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game. Then Messi retired, distraught after a missing a penalty in the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision. Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more. Read more from Jonathan Wilson: Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Jonathan Wilson Read more Share

Sports.title: USMNT v Canada live – updates, analysis and more from international friendly
Sports.content:
now 20.48 EDT 39 min: Ellis brilliantly sets up Albert, and it seems for a moment that the US youngster might create a promising angle to shoot, but he loses possession, and Canada end up with another free kick deep in their own half. Share

47s ago 20.47 EDT 37 min: I’m trying to think who Shaffelburg, with his mustache and semi-mulleted curls, resembles. Maybe a member of .38 Special? Some other 70s or early 80s band? He’s a persistent thorn in the USA’s side in any case. Share

3m ago 20.45 EDT 36 min: Shaffelburg again draws a free kick to the side of the box, this time on a foul from Freeman. Share

4m ago 20.44 EDT 35 min: Bad US pass picked off, but Eustáquio squanders the opportunity with a shot that Schwake easily smothers. Share

5m ago 20.43 EDT 34 min: Foul on the USA – second time in a few minutes that they’ve ended their possession with an unnecessary infraction. Share

6m ago 20.42 EDT 33 min: Trusty does well to leap high and get a head to a menacing Canadian cross. Share

6m ago 20.41 EDT 32 min: The USA test the other side of the field for the first time in a while, but they end up retreating. Share

7m ago 20.40 EDT 30 min: Yellow card to Oluwaseyi at his old home ground. Clearly late, and he caught a US player’s foot. Can’t argue with that one. Share

9m ago 20.38 EDT GOAL!! USA 1-0 Canada (Ellis 29) Freeman and Tillman combine wonderfully down the right, and Freeman rips one toward the far post. Ellis, last seen with a woeful limp, bangs the ball into the net from about two feet away. Replay shows he was … maybe offside? Share Updated at 20.39 EDT

11m ago 20.37 EDT 28 min: Resume passing around on the US back line. And it’s … a goal? Share

12m ago 20.36 EDT 26 min: The USA have looked a bit dangerous down the right when they’re not griping about no-calls. US fans may disagree, but I think Madrigal, the referee from Costa Rica, has done well thus far. Share

13m ago 20.34 EDT 25 min: The referee can’t ignore this one, as Tillman is late to a challenge. Shaffelburg sends the free kick somewhere toward the border. Share

15m ago 20.33 EDT 24 min: Another good ball from Canada, and it’s Campbell making the vital intervention. Potential fouls each way, but the referee is probably getting tired of blowing the whistle. Share

15m ago 20.32 EDT 23 min: Dangerous diagonal ball from Millar, but the US center holds firm. Ellis comes back onto the field looking like me after I banged up my knee hauling musical gear this weekend. But he’s barely one-third my age, so maybe his recovery will be faster. Share

17m ago 20.30 EDT 22 min: Reyna puts the free kick into heavy traffic, and Canada clear. Share

17m ago 20.30 EDT 20 min: Free kick USA, as Ellis is down 25 yards from goal. He’s rolling around in evident pain. Eustáquio was the guilty party, as Ellis got a leg ahead of him as he attempted to play the ball. There’s a mildly ill-tempered confrontation. Ellis limps off. In a World Cup game, maybe he plays through it, but it seems imprudent to leave him on here. Share

20m ago 20.28 EDT 19 min: Freeman with a clever midrange pass ahead to Musah as he races to the sideline, but Musah loses control and dings it out of play. Share

21m ago 20.27 EDT 18 min: More Canadian pressure, and Schwake has to boot it away. Freeman almost ends up with it but can’t control it. I’ve made it 18 minutes without mentioning I’ll be seeing Canada’s most legendary band this month. Share

22m ago 20.26 EDT 16 min: Some lunging but fair tackles each way, and Shaffelburg unleashs a shot from 25 yards that has some power but is straight at Schwake. Then it’s Shaffelburg again from an acute angle – probably more of a cross than a shot – but Schwake handles well. The US keeper, making his first start, has been up to the task thus far, though he hasn’t been asked to do anything spectacular. Share

24m ago 20.24 EDT 15 min: David with a nonviolent but completely unnecessary foul in his own half. That’s eight fouls, and I wouldn’t say they’ve been bad calls. Share

25m ago 20.23 EDT 14 min: Belated call to give the USA a free kick. Canada had started to go off to the races. That’s Canada’s seventh foul. On pace for 45! Share

26m ago 20.22 EDT 13 min: Eustáquio surprises everyone with a short pass to Liam Millar, who scuffs his shot well wide. Share

27m ago 20.21 EDT 12 min: Corner to Canada. Not a great delivery from Eustáquio, but Shaffelburg fights for possession and draws a foul. Free kick a few yards away from the upper corner of the box. Share

28m ago 20.20 EDT 11 min: This is the second time St. Clair has been forced to play the ball with his feet and wound up scrambling to keep the ball from rolling out for a corner. Awkward. Share

29m ago 20.18 EDT 10 min: A bit more direct from the USA here, seeking Albert on the left wing, but the young US player fouls Sigur. Canada play quickly upfield and end up with a wayward shot. Share

30m ago 20.17 EDT 9 min: Reyna draws a foul, perhaps a little embellished, but there was contact with his ankle. The USA are choosing to do nothing aggressive with free kicks at midfield, like they’re resuming a possession drill. Share

31m ago 20.16 EDT 8 min: Play is confined to a 30-yard stretch along the far sideline. Share

32m ago 20.15 EDT 6 min: The font for the names on Canada’s shirts looks like a rejected design scheme at Epcot Center. Canada foul at midfield, but they reclaim the ball soon after the free kick. Share

34m ago 20.14 EDT 5 min: Canada’s press gains possession, but an erratic pass from Oluwaseyi gives it back. Reyna is fouled deep in his own half, and the USA attack. Share

35m ago 20.13 EDT 4 min: Schwake gets his first touch, handling the ball with confidence. Resume passing around at the back while Canadian forwards lurk like icebergs. Share

37m ago 20.11 EDT 2 min: Canada isn’t messing around with this press. But the USA break through and force the Canadian defense to be alert. Share

38m ago 20.10 EDT Kickoff USA in the red and white hoops. Canada in stealthy dark kits. Share

39m ago 20.09 EDT US fans unveiled a giant banner that said “MAKE NOISE.” I thought at first it said “DRAKE NOISE.” That would be surprising. Share

45m ago 20.03 EDT Jeff Rueter A few players I’ll be watching closest in this one: Goalkeeper feels like a re-opened competition after shaky halves from World Cup incumbents Matt Freese and Chris Brady, while Diego Kochen shone bright in his first start against Mexico. Brian Schwake will try to make his case from the opening whistle, looking to carry his fine form with Nashville into his second appearance.



I was hoping to see Auston Trusty partner with Chris Richards, as he seems like the best partner in a post-Tim Ream US side, but he looks set to deploy at left-back. That said, Alex Freeman will likely advance further up the right, and Trusty could deputize as a wide center-back in build-up phases.



Mathis Albert may not yet be a regular with Dortmund’s B-team, much less the senior side, but his dynamism throughout this camp earned him a surprise start over the more polished and proven Zavier Gozo. A fascinating chance to get a long look at another star of the program’s future. Share

46m ago 20.01 EDT More game facts Weather: Beautiful. Currently 69 degrees and clear. Referee: Steven Madrigal (Costa Rica). Follow him on Instagram. Share

1h ago 19.50 EDT First email of the day is from JL Kalanga … double quotation mark As a foreign neutral in this affair, I will be following the match through the cheers that flow in my apartment window across the street from Allianz Field while watching Benin vs Messi on my laptop. I wanted to mention that the beloved Tani Oluwaseyi is currently playing for Villarreal in Spain, not Minnesota United FC. But it will be his first time back at Allianz Field since being sold last summer, so it will be emotional for him and other Loons fans. Messi’s playing in that game? This is his farewell? Incidentally, I’m still seeing kids at the local elementary school arguing about Messi vs. Ronaldo. Share Updated at 19.54 EDT

1h ago 19.34 EDT Earlier today … In case you missed it, the Faroe Islands drew Kazakhstan, which had to come back from 0-2 down. Also, England won by a lot. Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past Czechia Read more In the Americas, Uruguay beat India 6-1, Venezuela drew Jordan 0-0, Colombia and Peru will kick off soon, Mexico and Chile are up later, and Argentina have started their match against Benin. Share

1h ago 19.26 EDT Canada lineup Dayne St. Clair (29, Inter Miami); Niko Sigur (23, Toulouse), Luc De Fougerolles (20, Fulham, on loan to Real Salt Lake), Richie Laryea (31, Toronto FC); Ralph Priso (24, Vancouver Whitecaps), Stephen Eustáquio (29, Swansea City), Nathan Saliba (22, Villarreal), Liam Millar (27, Birmingham City), Jacob Shaffelburg (26, LAFC); Jonathan David (26, Atletico Madrid), Tani Oluwaseyi (26, Villarreal) Alphonso Davies won’t be here because he’s on his honeymoon. Clubs have been corrected. Share Updated at 19.45 EDT

1h ago 19.18 EDT US lineup Giving clubs and ages here … Brian Schwake (25, Nashville SC); George Campbell (25, CF Montreal), Auston Trusty (28, Celtic), Alex Freeman (22, Villarreal), Chris Richards (26, Crystal Palace); Gio Reyna (23, Borussia Dortmund), Brooklyn Raines (21, Houston Dynamo), Yunus Musah (23, AC Milan), Malik Tillman (24, PSV Eindhoven), Mathis Albert (17, Borussia Dortmund); Justin Ellis (19, San Jose Earthquakes) Matt Freese is not dressed. Alex Freeman, Gio Reyna, Chris Richards, Malik Tillman and Auston Trusty started against Mexico. This is Schwake’s second appearance after coming on as a sub against Chile. You may safely deduce this is his first start. Share

2h ago 19.10 EDT Preamble Ah, the friendly. It’s a can’t-lose game. Win, and it’s proof that the team is on the upswing. Lose, and it was all just an experiment. That said, when a bunch of youngsters are romping over Mexico, it’s hard to suppress the optimism entirely. And this one has all the added subplots of two countries sharing the world’s longest border – 5,525 miles or 8,891 kilometers – who aren’t really on speaking terms right now. Did we mention that the Canadian coach, Jesse Marsch, is from the USA and has a tendency to take a few jabs at his native land? Jesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’ Read more So this one might be worth more popcorn than the typical friendly. Enjoy. Share

2h ago 18.45 EDT Jeff Rueter on the kids, after Cavan Sullivan’s long-range chip helped the US to a 3-0 win over Mexico: The more incredible thing about Sullivan’s moment, aside from its historic nature and its semi-dreamy origins, is how normal it is for this window for the US. All but one of the 13 potential debutants called in by Mauricio Pochettino have seen time on the field, most of them impressing. Julian Hall, 18, has scored in all three of his appearances. Mathis Albert broke Christian Pulisic’s decade-old benchmark to become the program’s youngest goal scorer and held the record for a whole four days before Sullivan’s chip. Given the opponents so far, it’s fair to say these players aren’t inching into the shallow end of the pool. They’ve been thrown in at the deep end, and they are swimming. The USMNT’s kids are thriving, and ‘they have a bit of swag to them’ Read more Share

Sports.title: Sturm warning rocks Pocognoli as abject Scotland turned over by Slovenia
Sports.content:
The nature of this Scotland defeat felt far more significant than the fact it arrived at all. Sébastien Pocognoli is already in tricky territory, just four games into his tenure as Scotland head coach. Slovenia comprehensively outplayed the fragile hosts at Hampden Park, which leaves Pocognoli staring at a third-placed finish in a soft Nations League section. Brave new dawn or beginning of an error?

Scotland were defensively disorganised. Their attacking play was timid. Long before full time, the 39-year-old Belgian had the look of a coach throwing darts blindly at a board. And missing. Wastefulness from Slovenia prevented Scottish embarrassment.

A scathing assessment arrived from the Scotland captain, Andy Robertson, who admitted his team were “outfought”. Robertson added: “They looked a lot fresher, a lot more hungry.”

Pocognoli was more circumspect. “We didn’t play the game we wanted to,” he said. “We were not at the level we expect to be. I will not say everything is perfect or everything is bad but we need to improve many things. We have enough quality.”

A pre-match presentation to Robertson, who reached the 100-cap mark during Scotland’s win in North Macedonia on Saturday, carried wider meaning. Gordon Strachan and Alex McLeish, Robertson’s first two Scotland managers, were joined on the Hampden pitch by Steve Clarke. This marked a swift and welcome return to the national stadium for Clarke, who departed the Scotland job in unsatisfactory circumstances following failings at the World Cup. Clarke, bashful by nature, took as significant a bow as was ever likely before supporters.

Scotland find themselves in a post-Clarke state of flux. He was the manager who made this country relevant on the wider stage once again. There was, however, widespread criticism that Clarke’s team lacked ambition. Pocognoli has been charged with not only maintaining at least decent results but also delivering an alternative brand of football. It is a fanciful quest, perhaps.

The first quarter mirrored the opening half when these teams met in Ljubljana. Scotland looked uncertain. Slovenia were perfectly comfortable, not only in a defensive sense but when springing into attack. Adam Gnezda Cerin should have afforded the visitors a 13th-minute lead but failed to connect with appropriate force, allowing Jack Hendry to boot clear when just three yards from his own goal. This venue, which should be an asset to Scotland, was eerily quiet.

Ryan Christie raised the mood. That the goal was horribly ugly mattered not a jot to the Scottish contingent. A short free-kick was played wide to Ben Gannon-Doak, whose deflected cross was headed on to a post by Hendry. Modern football’s madness means Oli McBurnie will be credited with an assist for the header with which he was undoubtedly trying to score. The ball instead landed at the feet of Christie, who tapped home from close range.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Christie gives Scotland the lead from close range. Photograph: Robert Perry/EPA

Robertson demonstrated his ongoing value before the break. Zan Vipotnik seemed certain to equalise before the Tottenham full-back’s rescue act, courtesy of a sliding block. Ominously for Scotland, Danijel Sturm had totally bamboozled their three-man defence when supplying Vipotnik.

It was impossible to argue Slovenia were not worthy of their equaliser, which arrived 11 minutes after half-time. It came from a Scotland throw-in, where possession was cheaply conceded. Sturm played through the centre and towards Aljosa Matko, who brushed Luis Binks aside as if the Brøndby defender was not even there. The Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn, as is something of a theme, was weak in trying to deal with Matko’s shot. Sturm should have sent Slovenia in front two minutes later but saved the blushes of a hilariously open Scotland defence by shooting over. This had to be alarming for Pocognoli.

Slovenia were swaggering around their hosts. Pocognoli switched to a back four for the first time in this elongated international window shortly before Matko was denied his second goal of the night by an offside flag. The decision was not at all debatable.

View image in fullscreen Scotland’s Sébastian Pocognoli looks away in horror on the touchline. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

Neither was the goal which took Slovenia ahead. This time Matko turned supplier, having rampaged down the right flank and crossed for the onrushing Sturm. Gunn was left with no chance as Sturm slammed the ball past him. Pocognoli was now subjected to Tartan Army boos.

Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake had penalty claims rejected for Scotland. Desperation had indeed become the order of the day. McPake was at least lively, having stepped from the bench. Too many of his teammates either underperformed or are not cut out for this level. It is up to Pocognoli to source answers, and sharply. This is no patient football domain.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promises
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway drove him out of the camp but insisting he remained available after any punishment.

In a lengthy statement, the 41-year-old gave his ⁠account of the dispute ⁠that prompted his ​departure from Copenhagen before Portugal’s Nations League match against Denmark last week.

Ronaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would ⁠miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 ⁠minutes.

“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called ​on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his ‌word to me.”

Portugal’s captain and ‌all-time leading scorer said a subsequent meeting with Jesus, attended by his club side Al-Nassr’s sporting ‌director Simão Coutinho, produced an agreement for the coach to clarify events at his next press conference.

According to Ronaldo, an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus’s decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Ronaldo said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him ‌but said the coach’s public remarks bore no resemblance to their private discussion.

“It was the second time he had broken his word to me,” Ronaldo said. “I decided ​to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises.”

The statement provided Ronaldo’s account but on Sunday, after Portugal’s win over Norway, Jesus denied he had made any agreement with the player but left the door open for his return.

The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) did not immediately respond to a request for ⁠comment about Ronaldo’s statement.

Ronaldo apologised for failing to greet supporters after the Norway ​match and for leaving his ​teammates, accepting that his captaincy made ​his conduct more serious. “The consequences of my actions must be assessed and punished ​by the Portuguese Football ‌Federation,” he said.

Despite ​the rupture, Ronaldo said ​he was not limiting his international ambitions to a farewell appearance. “If I’m physically fit, playing for my club – scoring goals, I hope – after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I’ll be available, as I’ve always been until now, to compete and win for our national team,” he added.

Sports.title: Fifa reportedly allowed DR Congo into World Cup despite ineligible player in qualifying
Sports.content:
Fifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’s World Cup despite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying.

The player in question, the goalkeeper Lionel Mpasi, starred for his nation at the tournament, including against England in the last 32. Mpasi, who was born in France and played for Les Bleus at youth level, had never completed the process of switching nationalities, Fifa reportedly found. No punishment was levied against the Congolese federation, Fecofa.

The news will again raise questions over the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with a series of governance scandals having brought heightened scrutiny on his position. Fifa’s investigative teams are independent and the president has no input into their proceedings. Fifa is understood to have denied that Infantino played a part in the decision-making process over Mpasi, but his name is likely to remain in focus owing to a former university associate, Véron Mosengo-Omba, being elected unopposed as president of Fecofa this May.

The Nigerian Football Federation submitted a complaint over the DRC apparently fielding ineligible players during a World Cup playoff tie between the nations, which the DRC won on penalties, in November.

According to reporting by the New York Times and Le Monde, Fifa investigators were aware of Mpasi’s situation before the DRC defeated Jamaica in a final intercontinental playoff round in March. Faced with a series of possible responses, including banning the DRC from the playoffs, Fifa chose to reject the Nigeria complaint on the grounds it had not been submitted within the necessary timeframe.

Nigeria appealed against the decision and government representatives have suggested they could seek financial compensation for their loss, with a member of the national sports commission , which regulates Nigerian sport, telling ESPN: “Nothing has been decided yet, but we will seriously consider seeking compensation from Fifa for all of the economic losses this has cost Nigeria.”

Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, which includes Jamaica among its members, said it “takes player eligibility matters very seriously and expects the applicable regulations and procedures to be applied consistently and fairly in all competitions”. In a statement it asked that any “concerns regarding player eligibility” be “thoroughly reviewed and addressed through Fifa’s appropriate governance and disciplinary bodies”.

Fifa, Concacaf, Caf, the Nigeria Football Federation and Fecofa, were all approached for comment.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

On Tuesday the Norwegian football federation confirmed it had submitted a three-pronged complaint to Fifa over its governance, including the decision to overturn a red card awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun after a telephone intervention by Donald Trump. The other instances cited by the NFF are the Fifa peace prize and the abandoned plan to sell a share in the World Cup to investors, known as the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme.

“Each of these cases must be assessed based on the facts of each individual case,” said the president of the NFF, Lise Klaveness. “At the same time, the cases point to a more fundamental question: has Fifa’s position, authority or influence been used in a way that was not appropriate, and if so, did the mechanisms that were supposed to prevent this function work as they should?”
