Christa Pike is awake and communicating after surviving a botched execution attempt in Tennessee last week, according to her attorneys.

Pike remains hospitalised in Nashville, where she is receiving critical care after suffering severe injuries to her arms during the failed execution, her legal team told TMZ.

Her attorneys said Pike’s condition has shown some improvement, although her prognosis remains uncertain and she is expected to face a lengthy recovery.

The legal team is expected to visit Pike and speak with her at the hospital.

Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during the execution attempt before the procedure was halted. She was subsequently taken from the prison by ambulance for medical treatment.

Her attorneys also said she remains restrained to her hospital bed with handcuffs and shackles while receiving treatment.

World.title: Libya’s parliament speaker ousted after 12 years
World.content:
Libya’s parliament speaker, a supporter of eastern strongman Khalifa Haftar, was ousted on Tuesday after 12 years in the post, in what experts said may be a sign of a shifting political balance.

MPs voted to replace Agila Saleh with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, the parliament’s spokesman announced on X.

Libya has been beset by violence and instability since the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

It remains divided between the UN-recognised government in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Haftar.

Haftar’s camp relies in particular on the parliament, which sits in the eastern city of Benghazi under their control.

Saleh, 82, has long been considered a staunch ally of the Haftar clan, but he appeared to be weakened as Haftar’s sons, in particular Saddam Haftar, consolidated their positions.

Emadeddin Badi, an analyst at the London-based Chatham House, said: “Agila Saleh appears to be the latest casualty of Saddam Haftar’s drive to centralize decision-making in eastern Libya and bulldoze his way into a political role.”

His removal comes as a US initiative aimed at reviving the political process and unifying Libya’s institutions is under discussion.

World.title: Ondo Crash: ADC questions NAF aircraft maintenance funding
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress, ADC, has questioned the implementation of defence budgets for the maintenance of Nigerian Air Force aircraft following Monday’s crash of an ATR-42 aircraft at Igbokoda, Ondo State.

The opposition party said the tragedy should not only prompt investigations into the immediate cause of the crash but also renewed scrutiny of how much money meant to keep military aircraft operational is actually released and spent.

In a statement released in Abuja on Tuesday by its National Publicity Secretary, Mallam Bolaji Abdullahi, the ADC described the crash as tragic and unfortunate and expressed condolences to the families of the victims.

The party said official figures showed that as of December 2025, only N4.5 billion, representing about 13.98 per cent of the N34.71 billion budgeted for the maintenance of Nigerian Air Force aircraft, had been released.

By contrast, it said N20.74 billion was allocated for the maintenance of the Presidential Air Fleet, with N20.27 billion, representing 97.76 per cent, released within the same period.

“Put simply, while the fleet that serves a handful of people in power got almost every kobo it asked for, the fleet that serves and protects 200 million Nigerians was left with crumbs,” the ADC said.

The party stressed that it did not want to prejudice the ongoing investigation into the crash but said the incident provided another opportunity to examine the funding and maintenance of military equipment.

“While we do not intend to prejudice ongoing investigations into the cause of this tragic crash, we believe that this sad moment also provides an opportunity to raise, yet again, questions about the non-implementation of the defence budget and the perennial neglect of military equipment,” it said.

The ADC said the safety of military personnel should receive the same level of attention as the safety of political leaders.

“The safety of the President matters. But what also matters is the safety of the pilots and airmen who put their lives on the line in defence of the country. Patriotism does not replace spare parts, and condolence messages do not take the place of accountability,” the party maintained.

The party therefore called for the crash investigation to go beyond determining the immediate cause of the accident to examining the maintenance of defence equipment, particularly the Nigerian Air Force fleet.

It also demanded an audit of maintenance expenditure and budgetary releases to determine whether funds appropriated for the upkeep of military aircraft were released and properly utilised.

World.title: Go out, collect your PVC irrespective of who you want to vote — Makinde
World.content:
Gov Seyi Makinde

By Efe Onodjae

Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, Seyi Makinde, has urged Nigerians to collect their Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs, ahead of the 2027 general elections, irrespective of their preferred candidates.

Makinde made the call in a short video shared on his official Instagram page, where he was seen displaying his PVC.

He said the voter card remained an important tool through which Nigerians could exercise their constitutional right to choose their leaders.

According to him, Nigerians should not allow their political preferences to discourage them from participating in the electoral process.

Makinde said: “Fellow Nigerians, INEC has said October 9, 2026, as the date for people to start collecting their PVC.

“This is your power, irrespective of who you want to vote for. Please go out, collect your PVC, and you will use it wisely in the 2027 election cycle.

“Thank you and God bless.”

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo opens door for Portugal return, apologises for walk-out
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has confirmed his continued availability for Portugal after explaining his decision to leave the national team camp and accusing head coach Jorge Jesus of breaking an agreement over his playing time.

The 41-year-old Al Nassr forward had raised questions about his international future following his departure from the squad, but said he remained committed to representing Portugal.

“If I am physically well, playing for my club, with goals I hope, after serving the suspension that may be applied to me, I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team,” Ronaldo said in a statement shared with Reuters.

Ronaldo also apologised to his teammates and the Portuguese public for leaving the camp, adding that he would accept any disciplinary action imposed by the Portuguese Football Federation.

The forward left the squad after remaining an unused substitute during Portugal’s 2-1 away victory over Norway in the Nations League on September 27.

According to Ronaldo, he and Jesus had previously agreed that he would miss the Norway and Denmark matches as part of a plan to manage his fitness.

However, Ronaldo said the coach changed the arrangement on the day of the Norway match and told him he would play for 30 minutes.

“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from halftime onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called on,” he said.

“The manager had broken his word to me.”

Ronaldo said it was the second time he believed Jesus had failed to honour an understanding between them and that the coach’s public comments did not correspond with their private discussion.

“It was the second time he had broken his word to me. I decided to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises,” he said.

Jesus, however, denied after Portugal’s victory over Norway that he had reached such an agreement with Ronaldo, while leaving the door open for the veteran forward to return to the national team.

Ronaldo also rejected suggestions that he had interfered with tactical or technical decisions during his international career.

“Never, at any moment, have I interfered in any technical or tactical decision of any coach or national team manager in almost 25 years of career,” he said.

“I accept, for better or worse, what they propose that I do. I respect the decision, and when they break their word to me, I feel that my place is not there.”

Addressing speculation about a possible farewell to international football, Ronaldo said he expected to have one or more farewell matches in the future but remained focused on competing for Portugal.

“I can promise all my fans, naturally and especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches; there will be time for that. But when I think of the national team, what I really think of is competing,” he said.

Ronaldo, Portugal’s record goalscorer and most-capped player, has scored 146 goals in 234 international appearances.

He also recalled remaining with the Portugal squad following the death of his father during an international camp, saying his commitment to the national team had remained strong throughout his career.

The dispute between Ronaldo and Jesus has cast uncertainty over the forward’s immediate international involvement, but his latest statement makes clear that he intends to remain available for Portugal, subject to his fitness and any disciplinary sanction.

World.title: WHY DO MILITARY AIRCRAFT CRASH SO OFTEN?
World.content:
Military aircraft should be properly maintained, writes ETIM ETIM

The frequency of air crashes involving Nigeria’s military aircraft and helicopters in the last few decades should compel our military authorities to look critically into the causes of these accidents and put an end to them or reduce drastically. It is so embarrassing for the military and the nation as a whole to lose so many well-trained officers and resources to these crashes. What could be the problem? Is it poor maintenance, age of the aircraft or human factor? While the NCAA and other regulatory agencies in civilian aviation have worked hard to achieve zero accident involving commercial jetliner in the country in the last 14 years, the military continues to suffer catastrophic accidents almost on a yearly basis. It’s so bad that a Chief of Army Staff was killed in one of those crashes in 2021. We cannot continue to lose senior military personnel to these senseless air accidents.

This has to stop.

The latest in the series of these military crashes occurred on Monday, October 5, 2026, and it involved a Nigerian military surveillance and maritime operations aircraft (tail number NGR 931) carrying 25 passengers and crew en route from Benin to Lagos. It crashed in Igbokoda, Ilaje, Ondo State, triggering a search and rescue operation by the Nigerian Air force. There are no survivors. My thoughts and prayers are with victims’ families.

But one question continues to bother me. Why has Nigeria experienced so many tragic military plane and helicopter crashes in the last few decades resulting in loss of key military leadership, service personnel, and aircraft? And why has no solution been found for this problem?

On May 21, 2021, a Nigerian Air Force Beechcraft King Air 350i crashed near the Kaduna International Airport during bad weather. The crash claimed the lives of the late Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Ibrahim Attahiru, along with 10 other military officers and crew members. That same month, a Nigerian Air Force Beechcraft King Air 350i surveillance aircraft crashed near Abuja airport due to reported engine failure, killing all seven military personnel on board.

On September 17, 2006 a Nigerian Air Force Dornier 228-212 military transport aircraft carrying 18 people—including senior military officers traveling for a retreat in Obudu—crashed in Vandeikya, Benue State. The tragedy resulted in 15 fatalities, including high-ranking generals, with only three survivors.

On September 12, 1997, a Nigerian Air Force Dornier 228-212 crashed with 10 people on board. Between 2015 and 2023, data shows that the Nigerian Air Force suffered approximately 14 separate military air incidents and crashes, destroying around 15 aircraft and causing over 35 fatalities. Aviation safety experts have frequently attributed these frequent incidents to aging fleets, inadequate maintenance infrastructure, and challenges with spare parts supply chains.

Of all these military air accidents, the 1992 Nigerian Air Force C-130H Hercules crash on September 26, 1992, was the deadliest in history, resulting in 159 to 165 fatalities with no survivors. The plane took off Murtala Muhammed International Airport, and was heading to Kaduna. But three minutes after take-off, it crashed into Ejigbo/Oke-Afa canal, burying those on board in the swamp. The victims were predominantly middle-ranking military officers and students from Armed Forces Command and Staff College, Jaji, who were returning from Lagos after a study tour. Students from other African countries like Ghana, Tanzania, Uganda and Zimbabwe were on board. Reports said the cause of the crash was excessive take-off weight, combined with multiple engine failures. Coming just two years after Col. Gideon Orkar’s coup and a year to the end of IBB’s eight-year tumultuous régime, the accident triggered all sorts of rumours across the country.

The civilian aviation has been relatively safe. The last civilian commercial air accident recorded in Nigeria was Dana Air Flight 0992 which crashed near Lagos , killing all 153 people on board, and about 10 people on ground. The flight originated from Abuja and was headed to Lagos. According to the final investigation report by the Accident Investigation Bureau (AIB), the aircraft suffered a progressive loss of power in both engines during its final approach to the Lagos airport. Investigators also attributed the cause of the accident to improper maintenance of the aircraft and the lack of situational awareness by the flight crew. The crew ‘’omitted critical checklists, failed to recognize the severity of power loss and delayed declaring emergency’’, according to the AIB report. Every air accident is a moment to learn lessons and improve on safety standards. The Dana crash prompted stricter enforcement of safety regulations and major reviews of commercial airline procedures. Authorities have since revoked Dana’s license and barred it from flying in Nigeria after series of other poor maintenance reports.

Other African countries with large militaries seem to have relatively better safety records. The last time South Africa military recorded an air crash was on December 2012. All the 11 people on board were killed. Egyptian military recorded an air crash in May 2025 when an air force training aircraft crashed, killing all crew members on board. The year before – in November 2024 – Egyptian military helicopter suffered a technical failure, resulting in the deaths of two air force officers. Kenyan military also recorded a crash last year, but it involved a trainer aircraft, killing the two pilots on board.

It is important to note that Nigeria’s military aircraft are not under the supervision of NCAA and other civilian regulatory agencies. It is therefore difficult to understand how well our military aircraft are maintained. But I urge our military authorities to spare no efforts in making their aircraft more airworthy. We cannot continue to lose our fine officers in such tragic circumstances.

Etim is a Journalist

World.title: A TIME FOR NIGERIAN WOMEN
World.content:
With each day that brightens and darkens, the crucial 2027 general elections draw near, bringing Nigeria closer to a critical conference with fate.

For Nigerians, what is perhaps the most unfortunate fixture of their national life is the fact that politics defines everything else, serving as a principal determinant of the direction of life in the country.

These days, everything depends on politics. The economy, security, name it. This would have been no problem were the country’s politics above board or played by people of value. Nigerians would have had no issues with politics conducting every other aspect of their national life like an orchestra were Nigerian politicians not among the worst the world over.

So, as the 2027 general elections gradually take shape on the horizon, shaping everything else around it, many Nigerians are waiting with bated breaths. For Nigerian women, very little, if anything, is predicted to change regarding their place in Nigerian politics and public life.

While there is some unanimity that Nigerian women have been scandalously shortchanged in politics, there has never been any real commitment to improving political participation and representation for women in Nigerian politics.

Every election cycle, suffusive lip service is paid to including women in politics and public life. Suddenly, the critical roles women play in sustaining Nigeria’s democracy are hailed to no end, and promises of allowances and accommodations being made for them flow anew. Pathetically, all these last only for as long as campaigns and elections are on the horizon, which is often not very long.

Many countries around the world have shown up the horrid hypocrisy of the argument that women cannot power governments and countries. In countries like Sweden and Rwanda, women have shown that they can heal systems and countries largely ripped apart by men. In fact, if anything, it is time in Nigeria for women to be given a chance to show what they can do, for as things stand, they are the last demographic that has not been tested by the treacherous waters of Nigeria’s politics.

Now, this is no guess. Since Nigeria’s political class has largely proven itself to be an ageing clan of kleptomaniacs with a few young people who have shown disturbingly sticky fingers, women may hold the secret to solving Nigeria’s leadership conundrum. They may have something up their sleeves that can finally send Nigeria on the long road of recovery as a country.

They should be given the chance. Their nature and priorities can shine a bright light on those Nigeria has long left for dead.

Where men and young people have failed, women may just hold the unique formula for succeeding there.

There is no level playing ground for women and as such this must be intentional. The odds are heavily stacked against them. To make this work, some of the biases that have kept them in the dark all these years must be carefully stripped away.

Ike Willie-Nwobu is a social thinker and policy practitioner

World.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND TELECOMS INVESTMENTS
World.content:
SONNY ARAGBA-AKPORE argues for more investment in infrastructure

To achieve a robust telecommunications connectivity and take service to unserved and underserved areas of Nigeria, between 70,000 and 80,000 telecoms towers are required. Only about 40,000 telecoms towers currently exist leaving a short fall of between 30,000 and 40,000 thus creating an opportunity for investors. The existing towers host 145,141 base equipment units across the country.

Indeed, infrastructure deficit remains a primary hurdle to meeting national broadband targets thus creating new avenues for investors. There are only three infrastructure service providers in the country currently. They are IHS Towers, ATC Nigeria Wireless Infrastructure limited and Globacom Limited. This leaves a yawning gap to be filled by existing and potential investors.

In 2025 alone, data consumption rose from 1.13 terabyte to 1.66 terabyte, accounting for about 47% thus putting enormous pressure on existing infrastructure, a situation that has made the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) to beckon on investors to intervene and reduce the pressure on the networks by boosting services.

When it hosted the Digital infrastructure Investment forum in Abuja recently Executive Vice Chairman (EVC), Dr. Aminu Maida said the forum was designed to provide a strategic platform for fostering dialogue between regulators, investors, infrastructure providers, and development partners to examine the investment requirements needed to expand connectivity, identify barriers to infrastructure deployment, and explore partnerships capable of accelerating digital transformation and economic development with the overarching objective of mobilising investments that will improve connectivity. Cumulative Value of Investments in the sector so far are over $76 billion across infrastructure and operations since liberalization in 2001.

In 2025, capital expenditure stood at N2.13 trillion (approx. $1 billion+) but 2026 projections by operators is N1.8 trillion to N1.86 trillion for network expansion alone. But Capital importation and foreign investments dropped significantly by about 91% ($7.24 million) in Q1 2026 compared to prior periods), showing a heavy reliance on domestic reinvestment by major players like MTN and Airtel.

Maida told his audience, ”The investment challenge before us is not merely one of expanding coverage. It is also about ensuring that those already connected enjoy better service quality, improved user experiences, and infrastructure capable of supporting future technologies”. Among the measures already implemented, he cited the telecommunications tariff adjustment approved in 2025 to support operators’ capacity for network investment and service improvement, ongoing engagements with state governments on Right of Way issues, and the designation of telecommunications infrastructure as Critical National Information Infrastructure by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. These initiatives, he said, are aimed at reducing barriers to network deployment and enhancing investor confidence in the sector.

He said that “the investment we advance today must ultimately translate into better opportunities for Nigerians, improved access to services, and a stronger digital economy that supports sustainable national development,”. Maida commended Swed fund and Ookla for their strategic partnership and contributions toward the successful hosting of the forum, noting that both organizations have played critical roles in supporting the Commission’s efforts to deepen data-driven decision-making and improve understanding of connectivity realities across Nigeria.

According to him, the collaboration with Swed fund and Ookla provides independent insights into the actual connectivity experience of consumers and supports the Commission’s efforts to identify service gaps, monitor network performance and assess areas requiring additional investment. The Forum brought together organizations that could help answer questions on the way forward. These included government and regulators, investors, development finance institutions, operators, infrastructure providers, technology companies and development partners.

Although Nigeria has made significant progress in expanding digital infrastructure, but infrastructure need does not automatically translate into an investable project. Investors and infrastructure providers need a clearer picture of where infrastructure is most needed; where demand is growing; what infrastructure already exists; and where coverage, capacity and performance gaps remain. What is constraining deployment and what would make projects commercially viable or financeable are part of the questions asked for informed investments, especially to determine where public and private resources can work together.

As digital adoption grows, so does the demand for reliable infrastructure. Nigeria’s internet usage illustrates the scale of this growth. Monthly data consumption increased from about 518,000 terabytes in January 2023 to more than 1.66 million terabytes in July 2026, more than three times the January 2023 level. July 2026 usage was also about 47% higher than July 2025, according to NCC’s published industry statistics.

At the same time, network performance and infrastructure capacity vary across locations, while some communities remain difficult or costly to serve. This creates a continuing need for investment in fiber, mobile networks, towers, data centers, satellite connectivity, energy and other supporting infrastructure. The wider economic context makes this increasingly important. The Federal Government has set an ambition of building a US$1 trillion economy by 2030, with the 2026–2030 National Development Plan supporting that ambition. Digital infrastructure is not the only requirement for achieving this goal, but it is an important enabler of productivity, enterprise, innovation, investment and inclusion.

In terms of investment opportunities, the forum covered a wider digital infrastructure ecosystem, including Fibre, backhaul and broadband infrastructure to support growing data demand. Reliable and sustainable power for digital infrastructure and potentially surrounding communities formed one of listed especially in reality of poor electricity supply in Nigeria. Technologies that can improve the cost, speed, reach or resilience of deployment were also on the list of investment opportunities.

Conscious of underserved communities in the country the forum listed opportunities for Commercial financing and partnership models for harder-to-serve locations. The NCC boss said that “the investment we advance today must ultimately translate into better opportunities for Nigerians, improved access to services, and a stronger digital economy that supports sustainable national development.” Industry, Trade and Investment Minister, Mrs Jumoke Oduwole said the forum was timely as quality of a country’s digital infrastructure increasingly determines the quality of investment climate, the competitiveness, and ability to participate meaningfully in international trade. This is because the future of trade is now digital and the nature of trade has changed as today “private networks, data centres, digital platforms, and secure data systems for transactions.”

Aragba-Akpore is a member of THISDAY Editorial Board

World.title: WHAT IF ATIKU TURNS THE TABLE IN JANUARY 2027?
World.content:
TUNDE OLUSUNLE argues against the optimistic projection by The Economist in the 2027 elections

With just over three months to go until Nigerians vote in the 2027 general elections, the script that the All Progressives Congress, (APC), has circulated — that Nigerians may grumble about President Bola Tinubu but will re-elect him anyway — is beginning to fray. The Economist of Thursday, October 1, 2026, made that proposition in “Nigerians Dislike Their President, But May Re-elect Him Anyway.” It rests on three tired assumptions: incumbency is invincibility, a divided opposition is a defeated opposition, and cynicism will keep turnout so low that money and machinery can finish the job. Borno tells a different story. And Lagos, on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, told another. Tinubu returned that afternoon from Paris after a month-long sojourn billed as a working holiday. What awaited him on the streets of Lagos was not the choreographed welcome of old, but booing — raw, irreverent chants from young Nigerians. Lagos does not boo its son lightly. When it does, it is saying something has snapped.

To understand why that rupture may become a national tide, you must travel North. Borno, APC-governed, remains in the grip of an insurgency that has become an economy of its own — extortion, abductions for ransom, looted grain stores, farmers taxed until farms are abandoned. A 27-year-old grain trader in Maiduguri told me he now takes grain to Chad to sell because kinsmen cannot afford to buy. Young men pack and leave for Chad, Cameroon or Ghana, “because if you sit down here, there is no food.” This is the context in which Tinubu’s pitch — subsidy gone, naira floated, revenue up, inflation easing to about 15% in August, growth projected at 4.1%, collapses. Food inflation still hovers near 20%. One litre of petrol averages N1,500; diesel, which powers generators, is over N2,000 per litre; kerosene, when available sells for N1,950. In a country where minimum wage is N70,000. The World Food Programme, (WFP), says malnutrition is at its worst in ten years.

Dr Nura Tukur, who runs a Save the Children clinic, reports a sharp spike in severely malnourished babies and anaemic mothers in three years, July being the worst since 2016. Aisha Umara arrived months ago with two of her triplets — one died on the road — each weighing 2.5kg at six months. She can now breastfeed, but to what home? A village policed by gunmen, a hut without food. What does a mother say to a child who survived starvation only to return to nothing? The weight of that was captured not by opposition but by one of Tinubu’s oldest allies. Senator Babafemi Ojudu — comrade from the anti-military struggle, wrote in an open Independence Day letter that hardship had become “the defining experience of too many Nigerians,” and progress must mean “food on the table, a child in school, treatment for the sick,” not projections. When a friend must publicly beg a President to “widen the circle” and commission independent polls because official briefings no longer capture reality, the fortress has cracked. His line, “No farmer should have to choose between tending a field and staying alive,” nationalises what the Maiduguri trader said.

All this has cratered Tinubu’s standing in the North, where his party, not necessarily he himself, once had goodwill from the Buhari years. In 2023, he reportedly polled 54% in Borno. Recent SBM Intelligence polling now places him behind Atiku and Obi in that state. That is not a blip; it is a mood swing — articulate, historic bile against APC. The party that came in 2015 promising change is seen by many northerners as having institutionalised pain: markets of lies, politics as palliative rice, governance as press release. “Renewed Hope” has not provided succour even in its fourth year. In Maiduguri today, people don’t say they have given up on voting; they say they will “fight back” with the ballot. This is where Atiku’s final shot acquires potency. If Tinubu has no organic base in the North-East, Atiku is its native son — former Vice President, businessman with pan-Nigerian rolodex, who knows every emirate by name. He is not parachuting in. He is returning at a time northern Nigeria feels orphaned.

Atiku’s challenge rests on four pillars. First, memory and economic nostalgia. Northern traders, farmers, civil servants remember Obasanjo-Atiku years between 1999-2007 not as utopia but as relative predictability — debt relief, telecoms revolution, security, budgetary discipline, a sense government tried to make life cheaper, not dearer. That nostalgia is powerful when a mother must say thank you for paracetamol. Second, political arithmetic. Obi is popular with the urban youth and in the South-East, but the constitutional path to Aso Rock still runs through the North-West and North-East — Kano, Kaduna, Sokoto, Maiduguri, Yola, Bauchi. Atiku does not need a formal coalition with Obi to consolidate anti-APC vote, resentment itself is coalition. As Joachim MacEbong of Control Risks put it, anti-APC vote may not be coalesced on paper, but on the ground is driven by hunger and humiliation needing no MoU. Third is the symbolism of presence versus absence. Tinubu’s long absence and manner of return have become campaign issues.

From his first interview upon landing on Tuesday, to his Independence Day engagements on October 1, to the premiere of the documentary on Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola, acclaimed winner of June 12, 1993, public commentary focused on energy, demeanour and delivery. At that premiere, widely circulated images showed him flanked closely by his wife, Senator Remi Tinubu, and aides. Whether fair or not, perception of a presidency being “managed” between foreign trips has become a political fact. Ojudu, with tenderness, opened his letter with “I hope your time away has brought you some rest.” Politeness from a friend confirming the month-long sojourn is now a political fact. Fourth, Atiku’s finality. This is his last shot, and Nigerians know it. There is moral clarity in a final battle. He is not building dynasty, he is closing circle, offering what Tinubu can probably no longer credibly offer to many: a bridge to the North that does not insult the North, market-friendly economics that does not punish the poor first, and a calm temperament that feels less combustible in a fraying nation.

But disaffection is no longer northern monopoly. That makes 2027 different. In the South-East, the terrain remains firmly Obi country. Every vote that goes to Obi in Anambra, Enugu, Imo, Abia, Ebonyi is a vote that will not return to the APC column. In the South-South, revolt has taken visceral, infrastructural form. Decrepit federal roads — where commuters spend nights on highways triggered open protests in Edo and Delta. A government that cannot move goods can not promise growth. And South-West itself, long presumed a given for Tinubu, is no longer given. In 2023, he lost Lagos to Obi, was flattened in Osun, and the Osun electorate voted against APC again in the most recent governorship, a local referendum of sorts. Oyo is tougher because incumbent Seyi Makinde, formidable operator, is himself pitching for presidency on the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement, (APM), and controls structures that will not be warehoused for Abuja. All these fractures whittle Tinubu’s numbers ward by ward.

Atiku, by contrast, is not without friendships across the Niger. Having spent substantial parts of working life in the South, customs postings, business, politics — he has built formidable relationships where his name does not sound foreign. Renowned banker and businessman, Akin Kekere-Ekun from Lagos State, was Chairman of the Board of Trustees of the American University of Nigeria, (AUN), Yola, owned by Atiku. Ben Ndidi Obi, CON, a revered statesman from Anambra State, is the Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of Council of the same institution. Atiku is, therefore, not a sectional candidate learning South; he is man with former colleagues, partners, friends, and godsons across it. The old argument says northern cynicism will keep turnout below 20% in Borno, 27% nationally in 2023, thus helping the incumbent because people who expect nothing won’t vote. That was true when suffering was resigned. It is less true when suffering is angry. Hunger, unlike disappointment, mobilises. APC strategists bank on religion, believing the Muslim-Muslim ticket with Kashim Shettima still insures North. Governor Uba Sani of Kaduna has moved smartly to redress the secular injustice of Nasir el-Rufai, his predecessor, by picking Christian running mate Jerry Adams for 2027.

But northern voters are not voting catechism. They are voting survival. At some point, as Cheta Nwanze of SBM argues, people stop trusting God and government and start trusting their own rage. That rage needs vessel. What if that vessel is Atiku? If the Lagos boos of September 29 were the sound of a fortress cracking, and Independence Day optics of October 1 were picture of presidency that looked laboured and tired to many viewers, then January 2027 may not be the expected coronation. It may be reckoning. Ojudu ended his letter with prayer that Tinubu should “finish well” and a reminder that credible election must be protected, security neutral, INEC truly independent, and President ready to accept verdict. That too reminds us democracy, the very freedom Ojudu and Tinubu fought for under Abacha, is larger than any incumbent. It may be the moment Nigeria decides it does not have to re-elect a man it “dislikes” because it is told there is no alternative.

There is an alternative. He is from Adamawa. He has waited thirty years. He will be 80 on November 25, 2026, a milestone he intends to mark with the Founder’s Day and groundbreaking of specific projects in AUN, Yola. And this time, the wind may finally be at his back. In that final accounting, two outcomes become plausible where once only one was imagined: an outright Atiku triumph on the wave of cross-regional discontent, or, for first time in presidential annals in Nigeria, a runoff, the type engendered by the Brazilian presidential election which has compelled the scheduling of a rerun for Sunday October 25, 2026. There, the myth of invincibility may finally meet the arithmetic of rejection.

Olusunle, PhD, Fellow of the Association of Nigerian Authors, (FANA), is also a Fellow of the Nigerian Guild of Editors, (FNGE)

World.title: A NEW DAWN IN HEALTHCARE
World.content:
Redeemer’s Health Village medical feat is commendable

In a remarkable medical feat, a cancerous kidney tumor was recently removed from a patient’s body in Abuja while the doctor worked remotely 500 kilometres away at Mowe, in Ogun State. Spearheaded by Redeemer’s Health Village (of the Pastor EA Adeboye-led RCCG ‘Redemption City’) the doctor, Professor Obi Davies-Ekwenna, controlled a surgical robot to carry out the operation in Abuja. Known as tele-robotic surgery, it came through Redeemer’s Hospital collaborative effort with RoboMed Global and Nisa Premier Hospital, the first of its kind in West Africa.

The Chief Executive Officer of Redeemer’s Health Village, Dr Adedamola Dada, stated that the operation included safeguards, with a medical team physically present with the patient in Abuja and prepared to intervene in case of complication. “We were able to operate on a patient with a cancer tumour,” said the robotic surgeon Dr. Ekwenna. “Telesurgery can be done from any part of the world with precision, with excellent results.” Alexander Idachama, the first patient to undergo robotic-assisted surgery at RHV for a radical prostatectomy, expressed delight at the outcome of the operation, with significantly less pain.

We congratulate Redeemer’s Health Village Hospital on this significant milestone. In a country often overwhelmed by healthcare challenges, Redeemer’s sophisticated landmark is an inspiration. It is yet another proof that we have what it takes to stand and compete with the best in any part of the world when provided with the right incentives.

Indeed, over the years, the country has recorded many historical medical achievements. As far back as 1974, for instance, the University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN) through its clinical arm, the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital (UNTH) performed Africa’s first open-heart surgery. Since then, it has carried out hundreds of other routine heart surgeries through local leadership and collaborative missions. Besides, many other institutions, including privately-run outfits, have also performed other complex medical feats ranging from neurosurgery to separation of conjoined twins.

Unfortunately, these could not be sustained due to inadequate attention. Many of our hospitals suffer from infrastructure decay, erratic power supply, and poor working conditions. Many of the government teaching hospitals operate with shoe-string budgets. Successive budgets for health in the country have consistently fallen short of the 15 per cent Abuja Declaration target agreed upon by African nations. Only recently, the Health Ministry disclosed that the total money released to it for capital projects in 2025 was a mere N36 million, money perhaps insufficient for a department’s logistics.

The breakdown of vital tools, in addition to low wages, has led to mass migration of health workers abroad in a phenomenon called the ‘Japa’ syndrome. At the last count, more than 50,000 Nigerian-trained doctors, many of them specialists, practice abroad. Expectedly, the medical brain drain, exacerbated by poor equipment, has triggered medical tourism involving Nigerians seeking treatment abroad for cancer, kidney failure, heart diseases and related ailments. According to the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, the country spends about $2 billion on medical tourism annually, a heavy financial drain on the economy. Ironically, many of specialists they meet abroad are Nigerians who left because of the poor working conditions at home.

This is why we are heartened by the increasing investment in the domestic health ecosystems. Dr Adedamola Dada said the health facility in Ogun has acquired multiple robotic systems and is launching a Robotic Academy to train Nigerian medical professionals. The purpose is to slash the cost of medical tourism by offering quality services locally. “We just don’t want it to happen only once,” he said. “We want it to become a routine.” In the last few years, private initiatives and state-level projects across the country are also striving to provide the best health facilities locally, many of which are already attracting patients from the diaspora because of affordability.

World.title: World Teachers’ Day: 60 Years After ILO/UNESCO Recommendation, Nigerian Teachers Still Seek Improved Welfare
World.content:
This year’s World Teachers’ Day marks the 60th anniversary of the 1966 International Labour OrganiSation/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. As Nigeria joined the rest of the world to observe the day on October 5, Uchechukwu Nnaike reports that improved welfare still tops the demands of teachers in the country

World Teachers’ Day is observed annually on October 5, to celebrate the teaching profession while renewing a collective commitment to the rights, status, professional autonomy, working conditions, and wellbeing of teachers worldwide.

The day commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers, which sets benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions.

With the theme: ‘Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures’, UNESCO said that the 2026 edition will centre on reviewing the current challenges related to teacher status and the strategies to address them, calling on society and policy-makers to protect, promote and elevate that status.

In a joint message, UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany; International Labour Organisation Director-General Gilbert Houngbo; UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell; and Education International General Secretary David Edwards stressed that “the value we place on teachers reflects the value we place on future generations”.

According to them, 60 years on, the Recommendation’s core purpose remains as relevant as ever.

“Standing with teachers begins by ensuring that they have the conditions necessary to carry out their work effectively. This includes high-quality initial teacher education, opportunities for continuous professional learning and safe, supportive working environments,” they stated. “It also means trusting teachers’ professional judgement and ensuring that their experience helps inform education policy through meaningful social dialogue.”

They said the priorities have become increasingly urgent, as the world is projected to need 50 million additional teachers by 2030, including 44 million to achieve universal primary and secondary education and 6 million for pre-primary education.

“Recruiting new teachers is as necessary as retaining experienced ones and ensuring that teaching offers motivating, rewarding and sustainable career pathways, including opportunities for female teachers to take up leadership positions. Advancing gender equality in and through teaching is essential to addressing persistent gender norms, barriers, and inequalities,” they explained.

They added that protecting and promoting the status of teachers demand concrete action to enhance the esteem accorded to teachers and the support provided for their work, noting that this is reflected in the resources invested in schools and teachers, the quality of their working conditions, and the confidence placed in teachers’ professional judgement and that “governments bear a central responsibility in this regard, working alongside employers, teacher organisations, teacher education institutions, communities and international partners”.

The message noted that today teachers educate learners in a world shaped by rapid technological change, including artificial intelligence, as well as climate change, conflict, displacement, persistent inequalities and increasingly diverse learning environments.

“In this context, teachers are expected not only to impart knowledge and skills, but also to foster critical thinking, inclusion, resilience, lifelong learning and responsible citizenship. As expectations continue to grow, the teaching profession must evolve alongside the transformation of education, with teachers empowered not only to adapt to change, but also to help shape the futures of education.”

“As we work with member states to revise the 1966 Recommendation and ensure that it reflects the realities of teaching in the twenty-first century, its fundamental purpose remains unchanged. It continues to provide a strong foundation for strengthening the teaching profession and expanding access to quality education for every learner,” the officials pointed out.

UNESCO, ILO, UNICEF and Education International therefore called on governments and partners to stand with teachers by advancing the status of the profession and ensuring that every teacher, everywhere, is empowered to help build more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable societies.

Sixty years after the ILO/UNESCO Recommendation, the welfare of Nigerian teachers remains in a critical state, marked by poor remuneration, minimum wage delays, teacher shortages, decaying school infrastructure, insecurity, and more.

While congratulating Nigerian teachers, Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate Peter Obi described them as critical to shaping the country’s human capital and future. In a post on his X account, he commended teachers for their resilience and sacrifices, particularly amid difficult socio-economic conditions, while calling for improved welfare and working conditions.

He also called for the restoration of the profession’s dignity, saying more investment in education is necessary to tackle some of the country’s major challenges, such as out-of-school children, unemployment, poverty, and underdevelopment.

Speaking at the commemoration of the day in Abuja, National President of the Nigeria Union of Teachers (NUT), Titus Amba, appealed to the federal government to implement the special salary scale approved for teachers without further delay, saying the four-year wait has adversely affected their morale and welfare.

Amba, represented by Deputy National President Kizito Kalu, said the special salary structure for teachers in basic and secondary schools, approved in 2022 by the administration of President Muhammadu Buhari alongside other welfare packages, has yet to be implemented four years after its approval.

He decried the poor working conditions in schools, overcrowded classrooms, inadequate furniture, insufficient instructional materials and dilapidated infrastructure. He called for increased investment in school infrastructure and the provision of a safe and conducive environment for teaching and learning.

He also attributed the shortage of teachers in schools across the country to some state governments’ failure to recruit teachers for several years, urging governments to recruit enough professionally qualified teachers, particularly for rural and underserved communities, and to provide incentives to retain them in the profession.

Amba also called for regular training and retraining to equip teachers with the skills needed to respond to changes in curriculum, technology, and societal expectations. He also appealed to the government to ensure that the increasing use of digital technology and artificial intelligence in education supports teachers, rather than displacing them.

He also called for greater participation of teachers and their representative organisations in the formulation, implementation and evaluation of education policies. The president also called for stronger security measures to protect teachers and pupils, stressing that safety should form a permanent part of education planning.

Some teachers, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that appreciating educators through cash incentives, awards, public commendation, among others, will encourage them to carry out their duties and respond to new demands in the classrooms. According to them, Teachers’ Day reassures educators that their sacrifices are recognised, contrary to the saying that “teachers’ reward is in heaven”.

World.title: UNN Responds to Manpower Needs, Secures NUC Approval for 12 New Academic Programmes
World.content:
Emmanuel Ugwu-Nwogo in Enugu

The University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN) has continued to expand and fine-tune its academic programmes to align with workforce demands of the high-tech-driven global economy.

The institution has secured the approval of the National Universities Commission (NUC) to commence 12 new full-time undergraduate academic programmes with effect from the 2026/2027 academic session.

According to a press release from the Public Relations Unit, the NUC conveyed approval for the programmes in a letter dated September 11, 2026, signed by the Director of Academic Planning, Abubakar M. Girei, on behalf of the executive secretary.

The NUC letter of approval was addressed to the Vice-Chancellor of UNN, Prof. Simon Ortuanya, and authorises the university to establish the programmes at its campuses.

The approval followed a resource verification visit by a panel of experts from the regulatory agency to assess the human and material resources available for the proposed programmes. The newly approved programmes cut across engineering, nuclear science, health, education and information technology, thereby “expanding the university’s academic offerings in emerging and specialised fields.”

The new programmes include B.Eng. Automotive Engineering; B.Eng. Nuclear Engineering; B.Sc. Nuclear Science; B.Sc. Pharmacology; B.Sc. Health Care Administration and Hospital Management; Optometry; and B.Ed. Educational Management. This programme offers options in Politics, Philosophy and Economics; English and Literary Studies; Political Science; Geography; Social Studies; and Business Education. Other approved programmes are B.Sc. Cyber Security; B.Sc. Artificial Intelligence; B.Sc. Data Science; B.Sc. Software Engineering; and B.Sc. Information Technology.

The NUC approval covers the full-time mode of delivery only, with the NUC emphasising that the University should notify it “for further processing” before commencing part-time delivery or the postgraduate components of the approved programmes.

The commission also directed UNN to retain the approved titles and nomenclature of the programmes, adding that any changes would require its approval. It further enjoined the University to provide adequate human and material resources to support the development and growth of the new programmes.

Reacting to the development, Ortuanya said the approval was an important step in the University’s ongoing efforts to expand opportunities for students and strengthen its capacity to respond to the needs of a rapidly changing world. He added that the university would ensure the approved programmes were supported with the requisite human and material resources, in line with NUC standards.

The introduction of the 12 new academic programmes marks a significant expansion of the university’s academic portfolio ahead of the 2026/2027 academic session.

World.title: YABATECH Accountancy 1986 Alumni Invest N100m in Legacy Project
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

The Accountancy Alumni Association (1986) of Yaba College of Technology (YABATECH) has invested about N100 million in rehabilitating and upgrading facilities at the institution, 40 years after graduating from the college.

The legacy project, which focused on the former School of Management and Business Studies, now known as the School of Financial Studies, was recently inaugurated as part of activities marking the association’s 40th anniversary.

The rehabilitation covered accountancy classrooms and a resource centre, as well as windows and doors, plumbing, toilet facilities, drainage, gutters and water infrastructure. The alumni also provided computers, a printer and internet access to support teaching, learning and research.

Speaking at the unveiling, the Chairman of the Governing Council of YABATECH, Prof. Funso Afolabi, said that the project represented “history, friendship, gratitude, reunion and enduring institutional loyalty”. He commended the Class of 1986 for returning four decades after graduation to contribute to the institution’s development and leave a legacy for succeeding generations.

“Forty years is a remarkable milestone. It represents four decades of memories, accomplishments, personal growth and professional contributions by the members of the Class of 1986,” he stated.

He noted that the project demonstrated the alumni’s appreciation for the institution that provided them with the knowledge, skills, discipline, and foundation on which many members built their careers.

The chairman noted that the decision to mark the anniversary with a legacy project went beyond celebration, describing it as a conscious commitment to giving back to the institution. According to him, institutions were strengthened not only through government and management efforts but also through alumni contributions and continued commitment to their development.

“This legacy project will therefore serve as a lasting reminder to present and future students that they are part of a long and proud tradition. It will also inspire them to remember, when their own time comes, that one of the most meaningful ways to honour an institution is to contribute to its progress,” Afolabi said.

He reaffirmed the governing council’s commitment to strengthening the relationship between YABATECH and its alumni, urging the class to sustain its engagement through mentorship and continued support.

In his remarks, the Rector of the college, Dr Ibraheem Abdul, described the project as an investment in the institution’s future and generations yet unborn. He said the alumni had returned not merely as former students but as builders who had turned their gratitude into a practical contribution to their alma mater’s development.

“Forty years after walking through these gates as young men and women determined to master the discipline of accountancy, the class of 1986 has returned as builders. Through this project, you have chosen to invest in the future of your alma mater and in generations yet unborn,” he said.

Abdul said the alumni had transformed their memories and affection for YABATECH into a lasting physical legacy, adding that the project was more than bricks and mortar. He explained that the former School of Management and Business Studies had been restructured as the School of Financial Studies to provide a clearer academic identity and specialised training in finance and related disciplines, while the School of Management and Business Studies would focus on management education, marketing and business leadership.

He called on other alumni sets, corporate organisations and friends of the institution to emulate the Class of 1986 by supporting the development of YABATECH. He also urged staff and students to protect the renovated facilities and ensure that the investment translated into improved academic outcomes.

Earlier, the President of the Accountancy Alumni Association ’86, Mrs Itunu Omotayo, said the legacy project was conceived to ensure that the 40th anniversary celebration went beyond reunion, ceremonies and photographs.

She said members of the set asked themselves what they would leave behind after the anniversary and subsequently committed their resources, expertise, time and networks to rehabilitating the college facility. She said the project represented the culmination of a 40-year journey that began when members entered YABATECH as students in 1981 and graduated in 1986.

“Four decades later, after building careers, raising families and achieving professional milestones in Nigeria and beyond, we returned to the institution with a simple message that encapsulated the essence of our anniversary: We came, we learnt, we left, we grew, and we returned to give back,” she said.

The Chairperson of the 40th Anniversary Committee and Chairman of the Legacy Project, Alhaja Simiatu Shittu, said the project was funded through contributions from members of the set, donors, friends, corporate supporters and professional networks.

She noted that the alumni wanted their 40th anniversary to produce a tangible, lasting benefit for present and future students, urging beneficiaries to make good use of the facilities and the College community to develop a strong maintenance culture.

World.title: Tebello Motsoane’s father reflects on painful coincidence [video]
World.content:
Sylvester Motsoane, father of the late Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane, has reflected on how the anniversary of his wife’s passing painfully coincides with the murder trial of his son, which began on 5 October 2026.

Tebello’s mother, Rayhab Niniwe Motsoane, passed away in October 2023, just months after losing her son. The celebrity chef was fatally shot alongside rapper AKA in February 2023 in Durban.

Their untimely passing shook the nation, their families and the entertainment industry, as both men were regarded as trailblazers in their respective fields.



The trial is taking place at the Durban High Court, where seven accused are facing multiple charges, including two counts of murder, attempted murder, conspiracy to commit murder, and firearms and ammunition-related offenses.

TEBELLO MOTSOANE’S FATHER SPEAKS OUT

In an interview with eNCA, Sylvester Motsoane fondly reflected on the close bond Tebello shared with his wife.

“My son was close to my wife. They were like a team. I was like an outsider. Today is the worst day to remember my son because today, the 5th of October, is when my wife passed on, and it coincides with this court case, so that’s why I decided, no, maybe my son is watching over me somewhere, and my wife is watching from somewhere to see if I follow her son’s death (trial).



When asked, “What will justice look like to you?” he responded, “Justice is something that is very difficult to say because it’s in the hands of the judges,” he said.

“If they give good justice, I’ll be happy; if they don’t give good justice, I have no word. It’s out of my control, but I’d like to see them have penalty for whatever they’ve done,” he added.

Sylvester Motsoane, father of Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane, says October 5 marks three years since his wife’s passing – an anniversary that now coincides with the start of the long-awaited trial into the murders of Motsoane and rapper Kiernan “AKA” Forbes. Seven accused are facing a string of serious charges, including conspiracy to commit murder, two counts of murder, attempted murder, and firearms and ammunition offences. Tune in to #eNCA on #DStv403.  October 5, 2026

RAYHAB: ‘THE BEGINNING OF MY MISERY’

During an interview on Carte Blanche shortly after Tebello’s passing, his parents reflected on losing their son, with his mother saying:

“I felt numb. I couldn’t cry. [A] feeling of disbelief: ‘No, it can’t happen to Tebello.’ That was the beginning of my misery,” she said.

World.title: WATCH: Severe hailstorm batters Zimbabwe, damaging homes and vehicles
World.content:
Hailstorms cause extensive damage to homes, vehicles and other property. Image: AI illustration

A severe hailstorm tore through Masvingo in neighbouring Zimbabwe, damaging homes, vehicles and infrastructure and leaving some families in need of temporary shelter.

The storm struck on Monday evening, 5 October, bringing heavy rain, strong winds and large hailstones to parts of the city.

I am deeply saddened to hear that our people in Masvingo, in the south-eastern part of Zimbabwe, have been hit by a severe hailstorm.



I pray that there have been no fatalities and that the government will move quickly to assist those affected. If you have family or friends in… pic.twitter.com/cyFVR0OwtJ  October 5, 2026

Homes and vehicles damaged by severe hailstorm

Masvingo City Council said the storm caused extensive damage to homes, private property and critical city infrastructure.

Strong winds ripped roofs from some homes, while hail damaged windows, sliding gates, vehicle windscreens and solar panels.

Some families were left with their homes exposed to the weather following the storm.



The storm also uprooted trees and brought down power infrastructure in parts of Masvingo. Businesses in the city centre were also affected, with broken windows reported at shops and other buildings.

Flash flooding was also reported in several parts of the city after the heavy rain.

No injuries reported in early assessments

Speaking to NewZimbabwe.com, Civil Protection Unit chief director Nathan Nkomo said authorities initially received reports of damage to 60 households.



“We received calls that 60 households have been affected. The wind uprooted trees and a car was damaged in the process. No injuries have been recorded so far,” Nkomo said.

Authorities continued assessing the damage following the storm.

Temporary shelters opened

Masvingo City Council opened Mucheke Hall and Rujeko Hall to provide temporary shelter for families whose homes suffered severe damage.



The halls are also available for residents to store furniture and other household belongings while assessments continue.

Masvingo Mayor Aleck Tabe described the extent of the damage as “significant and deeply distressing”, adding that several families had been left with their homes exposed to the elements.

Tabe urged residents to remain cautious and help vulnerable members of the community, including children, older people, people with disabilities and families whose homes suffered severe damage.



Masvingo City Council and the Masvingo District Civil Protection Unit continued assessing the affected areas to determine the extent of the damage and the immediate needs of residents.

World.title: Clifton beach chaos: Booze, brawls and matric mob [videos]
World.content:
Clifton beach was the destination for thousands of underage youth last weekend. Images via TikTok

Police clamped down on unruly behaviour as thousands of minor beach-goers, many of whom were matric learners, descended on Camps Bay, Clifton and surrounding Cape Town beaches over the weekend.

According to city officials, five underage individuals were arrested for assault and driving under the influence, while dozens of fines were issued for drinking in public. Over 1000 units of alcohol was confiscated.

CLIFTON CHAOS: BOOZE AND BRAWLS TAKE OVER THE BEACH

According to reports, close to 4 000 underage youth descended on Clifton’s first through fourth beaches, as well as neighbouring Camps Bay and Maiden Cove, to celebrate the last weekend of the third term school holidays.



Much of the crowd were Matric learners who returned to their fourth and final school term this week.

Western Cape SAPS spokesperson Sergeant Wesley Twigg said that a 16-year-old had been arrested for driving under the influence. Four other minors were arrested for assaulting law enforcement personnel.

Twigg added that 64 fines were issued for alcohol-related offences whilst police confiscated around 1 000 units of alcohol.

Cape Town City Law Enforcement spokesperson Wayne Dyason stated that between 3 000 and 4 000 youth descended on the Clifton and surrounding beaches over the weekend.

The City was alerted to the planned youth gathering and had implemented a contingency plan that included City Law Enforcement, Metro Police, Traffic Services, and Camps Bay SAPS, who covered several popular beach areas along the Atlantic Seaboard.

Take a look at various videos taken over the weekend…



MATRIC SAFETY

Mayoral Committee Member for Safety and Security for the City of Cape Town J Smith, issues a stern warning to minors and matric learners following the Clifton Beach incidents over the weekend.

Smith urged the youth to be responsible during the outdoor social activity.

He shared on Facebook: “A little bit of ‘innocent fun’ can sometimes have lasting consequences. Don’t lose sight of the mission. Many matriculants are gathering at our beaches to celebrate reaching this final milestone with their friends. Make those memories ones you can look back on with pride, not regret.

“Alcohol is not permitted in our bathing areas.

“More importantly, alcohol impairs judgement, slows reaction times and can dramatically increase the risks associated with swimming, driving and other activities.

“Every year, too many lives are lost on our roads because of alcohol. So, if you encounter our enforcement officers on the beach and they confiscate alcohol, understand that it is about more than simply enforcing a by-law. It is about protecting you.

“You are the leaders, professionals, entrepreneurs, parents and citizens who will shape our city and our country tomorrow. We want you to get there”.

TEEN PRESUMED DROWNED AT CAMPS BAY

Meanwhile, the search continues for a teen boy who was swept out to sea at Camps Bay.

The 18-year-old from Mfuleni is presumed to have drowned after he disappeared in the surf in a strong rip current at Glen Beach over the weekend.

On Monday, 5 October, city officials confirmed that an 8-year-old had drowned in the Camps Bay tidal pools.

World.title: CheckPoint Podcast | Are We Raising Boys For Violence? Prof Malose Langa On How Masculinity Is Made
World.content:
Violence Prevention Starts Long Before The Police Station

South Africa often talks about violence at the moment it becomes visible: after an assault, a murder, an arrest or another national outcry. By then, however, the story may already be years in the making.

That is one of the more uncomfortable implications of psychologist Professor Malose Langa's work with boys growing up in Alexandra. His research did not begin by asking which boys would become violent. It asked what it meant to be a boy, and then listened closely enough to discover that the answer changed depending on who was in the room.

Individually, boys could express relatively progressive ideas. In groups, Langa found that some shifted towards familiar masculine expectations: toughness, multiple girlfriends, fighting and other performances of what a boy was supposedly meant to be. He describes this tension as a difference between a public and private script. Beneath the bravado, he encountered shame, uncertainty, vulnerability and the emotional cost of trying to perform an approved version of masculinity.

That finding matters because it moves the violence conversation upstream.

If masculinity is partly learned, reinforced and policed socially, prevention cannot begin only when someone reaches the criminal justice system. Langa points instead towards the institutions surrounding children much earlier: homes, schools, churches, streets and early childhood development spaces. His argument is not that these institutions mechanically produce violent men. It is that everyday messages about strength, fearlessness, gender and acceptable behaviour accumulate long before society encounters their possible consequences.

South Africa's own policy architecture increasingly recognises that prevention must be broader than policing. The National Strategic Plan on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide includes prevention and rebuilding social cohesion as one of its central pillars, while a Cabinet-approved Programme of Action has called for greater engagement with men and boys to challenge harmful norms.

The problem, then, is not simply recognising prevention as important. It is turning that recognition into sustained practice.

There is evidence that this can work. Langa refers to Stepping Stones, an intervention evaluated by the South African Medical Research Council, as an example of programmes that created spaces for young people to discuss relationships, gender, sexuality and violence. SAMRC reporting on the intervention found changes in young men's sexual practices and violence perpetration, while cautioning that further research remained necessary.

Langa's own research offers another lesson: boys cannot be reduced to the worst stereotype available to describe them. His earlier academic work with 32 adolescent boys in Alexandra found multiple and sometimes contradictory masculinities, including boys simultaneously complying with and resisting dominant masculine norms. Wits University later summarised his decade-long work as a challenge to the homogenised portrayal of young black men as inherently violent or destructive.

This does not minimise violence or excuse perpetrators. It changes the prevention question.

Instead of asking only how to punish violence after it occurs, institutions also need to ask what they reward, tolerate and teach before it occurs. What does a five-year-old learn about being a boy? What behaviour wins approval at school? Which emotions are permitted among friends? Which versions of manhood are celebrated in communities and popular culture? And where can boys practise something different without being humiliated for it?

Late in his CheckPoint conversation with Nkepile Mabuse, Langa's frustration shifts from individual behaviour to institutional implementation. Researchers, he argues, repeatedly produce findings and examples of interventions, yet the country can behave during every new crisis as though no answers exist.

That may be the larger accountability question. South Africa has invested heavily in understanding violence. The next test is whether institutions can become as serious about preventing its social production as they are about responding once the damage has already been done.

References

· Malose Langa, Becoming a man: exploring multiple voices of masculinity amongst a group of young adolescent boys in Alexandra Township, South Africa, University of the Witwatersrand.

· South African Medical Research Council, Stepping Stones evaluation.

· South African Government, National Strategic Plan on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide and Programme of Action on GBVF.

· CheckPoint: The Podcast, interview with Prof Malose Langa, 6 October 2026.

World.title: Number Of The Day | R6.4 million | 06 October 2026
World.content:
What Does A R6.4 Million Cow Actually Buy You?

A cow selling for R6.4 million sounds almost impossible to reconcile with ordinary agricultural economics. But Queen Arusha is not an ordinary cow, and understanding why someone would pay millions for her requires looking beyond the animal standing in the auction ring.

The Ankole heifer comes from Ntaba Nyoni, the cattle operation owned by President Cyril Ramaphosa. Her multimillion-rand sale provides a window into a specialist part of agriculture in which the value of an animal can lie as much in what it may reproduce as in the animal itself.

When The Product Is Genetics

For commercial cattle farmers, value can be closely connected to familiar outputs: meat, milk, fertility, weight gain and the efficiency with which animals turn feed into something that can be sold. Elite breeding introduces another commodity: genetics.

Queen Arusha's family illustrates the economics. Her brother, the Ankole bull Optimus Prime, also featured in the conversation between Gareth Edwards and Francis Herd on Number of the Day. Sexed semen from the bull reportedly sold for R250,000 a straw.

That changes the way a valuable breeding animal should be understood. A buyer is not necessarily spending millions for the economic output of one cow. The investment can include the offspring she may produce, embryos carrying sought-after genetics and the possibility of extending a prized bloodline across future generations.

Edwards compared the market with thoroughbred horse breeding, where the value attached to lineage can vastly exceed the immediate productive value of an individual animal. As he put it, buyers are purchasing “the lineage”, “the genetics” and “future generations”.

Modern reproductive technology can multiply that potential. Herd pointed to the cattle equivalent of assisted reproduction: embryos can allow valuable genetics to be reproduced beyond what would be possible through a cow's natural calving cycle alone.

The R6.4 million price therefore represents something more complicated than the purchase of livestock. It is a wager on future genetic value.

Scarcity Can Become An Asset

That also introduces risk.

An extraordinary auction price does not guarantee an extraordinary return. Breeding outcomes are uncertain, reproductive programmes cost money and the future value of offspring depends on buyers continuing to prize a particular lineage and breed.

Scarcity matters too. When desirable genetics are difficult to obtain, buyers may be prepared to pay a premium to enter that bloodline. As those genetics spread through breeding programmes, however, the economics can change.

This makes elite cattle breeding an unusual combination of agriculture, biological inheritance and asset valuation. The physical animal matters, but so does the market's belief about what that animal could produce tomorrow.

When The Farmer Is Also The President

Queen Arusha carries another dimension that most multimillion-rand cattle do not: the operation that sold her belongs to South Africa's sitting president.

That inevitably returns attention to Phala Phala, where the theft of foreign currency linked to a buffalo transaction triggered years of political and legal controversy. In the podcast discussion, Edwards raised the question that follows naturally from Queen Arusha's sale: how much involvement may a sitting president have in private business interests?

The distinction matters. Ownership of an economic interest is not automatically the same thing as personally performing paid work for that business. Herd described the position advanced by Ramaphosa's lawyers as being that his farming interests constitute business interests rather than prohibited paid work.

That question should not be collapsed into an assumption that Ramaphosa personally received R6.4 million from Queen Arusha's sale. An auction price is business revenue, not automatically the owner's personal income or profit. Nor does ownership by itself establish that the President manages the operation day to day.

Yet the scale of the transaction explains why the distinction attracts public attention. Queen Arusha is not merely evidence that unusual cattle can command unusual prices. Her sale demonstrates that the President retains an interest in an agricultural operation dealing in potentially very valuable assets.

That leaves two very different questions standing side by side. Agricultural economics asks how a cow can become worth R6.4 million. Democratic governance asks how a country should manage significant private economic interests when their ultimate owner occupies its most powerful public office.

One remarkable animal manages to illuminate both.

World.title: To hike taxi fare or not to hike? Industry in talks amid fuel price pressure
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - This week taxi operators are mulling over one big question; this is to hike taxi fare or not to hike taxi fare?

It comes amid the latest announcement of fuel price increases, which are set to kick in at midnight.

SANTACO national spokesperson Rebecca Phala said they find themselves in a difficult position.

While they have to navigate the fuel price hike that continues to add pressure on taxi operators, they also need to consider commuters, whose household budgets she said are already stretched.

Taking this into account, Phala said they have to be "incredibly careful to strike some sort of balance despite the difficult circumstances".

READ | Govt warns against panic buying as record fuel prices take effect

According to Phala, the taxi association has not yet made a decision on whether or not to hike fare prices, but those conversations are already underway.

“There are a number of things that we want to exhaust from our end. We'll be engaging with the leadership of all provinces tomorrow. “So far, though, the national office bearers, which is the highest decision-making body, have already decided to say, we are going to engage with those in the fuel sector, because the industry does have buying power, considering the number of vehicles that we have and the consumption that we do to fuel. But we're also going to engage with the government.”

With engagements with relevant sectors taking place, Phala said they will have a decision by Thursday at the very least.

READ | Fuel price increase could push up cost of goods, freight industry warns

“The reason why we're not immediately announcing whether we'll be increasing fares or not is that we know that our commuters complained already. I mean, since March, when these increases started to be announced, we've only ever increased once, and they were already complaining about that.

World.title: 'We are struggling with population expansion' - Joburg Water
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Johannesburg Water has partly blamed Ebony Park residents for years of erratic water supply.

The Johannesburg community has had intermittent water flow for three years.

This has made them suspicious that the problem is manufactured for financial gain.

But Johannesburg Water spokesperson Nombuso Shabalala said water challenges are not only bound to Ebony Park.

She said similar issues are also witnessed in Kaalfontein and the greater Ivory Park.

READ | Joburg inner-city power outages leave thousands without water

According to Shabalala, this is because the system that supplies these areas, which is President Park Reservoir and Tower, is highly constrained, leaving the water utility to resort to throttling daily in order to build capacity.

“We throttle the system every day at two o'clock, and we open it again at four o'clock the following morning. This is so that the reservoir is not completely depleted.

World.title: Rand holds steady
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Rand may be getting its mojo back.

The currency has strengthened more than half a per cent against the US dollar.

After showing resilience during most of the war in the Middle East, expectations of higher interest rates had placed the currency under pressure.

READ | Rand falls to weakest level in two months

The Rand was trading close to R16.70 to the dollar at the start of October, its lowest level since late July.

But in recent days, it has regained ground and today strengthened to below R16.50 to the dollar.

A weekly auction of government debt spurred on the currency, attracting the strongest demand in four months.
