World.title: Kenya: Young People Must Shape Their Own SRHR Future, Says Kenyan Activist
World.content:
Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in Eastern and Southern Africa continue to face a disproportionate burden of HIV, early and unintended pregnancy, and poor sexual and reproductive health outcomesâparticularly during key life transitions such as leaving school, early pregnancy, migration, or exposure to violence.

Across Africa, young people are being told that their sexual and reproductive health and rights matter. But for many, accessing those rights remains a daily struggle.

Progress on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) has been made by governments and health systems, but this progress is not equal. Many adolescents, particularly girls and young women, still face obstacles to accessing the information, services, and legal protection they need to make informed choices regarding their bodies and futures. Fear of being stigmatized and concerns about confidentiality and who to go to for help can also be reasons why young people are not able to access sexual and reproductive health information and services when they need them.

Millions are still being affected by preventable risks, such as new HIV infections, early pregnancies, child marriage, gender-based violence, and period poverty. The gap between the rights that are promised on paper and the rights that are experienced in everyday life is further exacerbated by the fact that access to contraception, HIV prevention, comprehensive sexuality education, and youth-friendly health services remains a challenge for many.

Young people are increasingly demanding that this gap be taken seriously. They are calling for better access to sexual and reproductive health services and for comprehensive sexual and reproductive education in schools and health centres, free of stigma and shame.



Kenyan HIV and SRHR activist Jerop Limo said that closing that gap means moving beyond simply talking about young people and giving them a meaningful role in designing, implementing and holding health systems accountable.

"The reality is that we have made progress, but that progress is not being experienced equally by young people," Limo said. "We have more knowledge, more HIV prevention options, more conversations around SRHR, and stronger recognition of young people's leadership. But for many adolescent girls and young women, especially those living in poverty or in underserved communities, the ability to actually benefit from these advances remains a dream."

She said the biggest gap lies between what exists on paper and what young people experience in their everyday lives. She said policies, guidelines and new technologies mean little if a young woman cannot get accurate information, afford transport to a facility, or find a service in stock, or if she encounters stigma from a provider or fears being judged.

Limo warned against treating young people as a single group.

Their realities, she said, are shaped by where they live, their economic circumstances, disability, gender, HIV status, relationships, and many other factors. She added that the response has to be much more community-centered and responsive to those different realities.

Limo's own experience with HIV shaped her path into adolescent health advocacy. She began working in the HIV response eight years ago as a facility peer educator. As a young person living with HIV, she quickly discovered that access to treatment was only one part of what young people needed. Young people were also grappling with adherence, disclosure, fear, grief, relationships and self-worth, and with the question of what life could look like beyond an HIV diagnosis.

Her work has since taken her beyond Kenya and onto the global stage.

In 2025, Limo was recognised by the Gates Foundation's Goalkeepers community for her leadership in HIV and youth reproductive health. But she said the recognition is not hers alone. It belongs to the young people who have shared their experiences with her and the peer educators working in health centres every day.

The platform, she said, allows her to carry their everyday priorities directly to global decision-makers.

One of the biggest lessons she has learnt is that young people do not need adults to constantly tell them what their problems are or what solutions they need. They need people and systems that are willing to listen, trust them and create space for them to shape those solutions.

Today, Limo is Executive Director of the Ambassador for Youth and Adolescent Reproductive Health Program (AYARHEP), a youth-led organisation working on adolescent HIV and SRHR in Kenya.

A central part of Limo's advocacy is changing how institutions understand youth participation.

"Youth leadership, for me, is not simply putting a young person on a panel or giving young people a speaking slot," she said. "It is about young people having actual influence over decisions, programmes and resources."

At AYARHEP, she said, young people are not only beneficiaries but also peer educators, advocates, community mobilisers, programme designers and accountability actors. Limo said that peer connection is one of the strongest tools youth-led groups have.

"There is something very powerful about a young person sitting with another young person and saying, 'I understand what you are going through,'" she said. That peer connection, she said, can open conversations that may not happen in a formal institution.

Youth-led organisations also tend to sit closer to the realities of communities, she added. They hear first when a service is failing, when a product is unavailable, when a young person is too afraid to visit a facility, or when a national policy is failing to translate into meaningful change at community level. However, Limo said that youth-led organisations cannot be expected to carry the responsibility alone. Governments, donors and larger institutions need to recognise young people's expertise and provide the resources needed for youth-led organisations to lead at scale.

Misinformation is a growing concern too.

The challenge is particularly acute in an environment where misinformation and opposition to SRHR continue to shape what young people hear and believe. Young people need information that is accurate, understandable, relevant to their realities and delivered through channels they actually use and trust.

AYARHEP uses peer engagement, community dialogues, social media and youth-friendly spaces to allow young people to ask questions without fear of judgement. The organisation also engages caregivers, teachers, health workers, community leaders and other gatekeepers because young people's SRHR needs cannot be separated from the communities around them. Creating an enabling environment is essential, said Limo.

Limo said misinformation must be countered without shaming those who believe it. "If we want young people to trust us, we have to create spaces where they can say, 'I heard this, is it true?' and receive a respectful answer," she said.

Digital platforms have become increasingly important in the HIV and SRHR response, but Limo believes that young people should not only consume information online. They should also have the skills to identify misinformation and make informed decisions.

Limo said that stigma remains one of the biggest barriers preventing young people from accessing care. It surrounds HIV, sexuality, contraception, pregnancy and abortion, and extends to young people simply wanting to make decisions about their own bodies.

She said practical challenges, including services that are not youth-friendly, inconvenient operating hours, stock-outs, transport costs, lack of confidentiality and judgmental providers, can further discourage young people from seeking care.

Limo also said another major challenge is the information gap.

Young people today can reach enormous amounts of information, she said, but not all of it is accurate."Access to information has to mean access to trusted, evidence-based and understandable information," she said.

For Limo, one of the most urgent issues is ensuring that the incredible progress we are seeing in HIV prevention science actually reaches the people who need it. She cited lenacapavir, an injection that protects against HIV for six months and is given twice a year. Kenya became the first country in East Africa to roll it out in February. Limo said clinical studies show it can be up to 96% effective.

For many young women, she said, taking a pill every single day is hard to keep up, so an option they need only twice a year gives them real choice and more control over their own protection.

The rollout has begun in 15 high-burden counties, with plans to expand to all 47.

"Making the injection free at public health facilities isn't enough," Limo said. The next hurdle is ensuring that adolescent girls and young women know about the injection, can obtain it locally, and feel safe asking for it without judgment.

Young people as decision-makers

Limo said meaningful participation means far more than consultation. Young people, she argued, should be involved at every stage: identifying the problem, designing the response, implementing it, monitoring it, and holding institutions accountable.

"Young people are experts in their own lived realities," she said.

Even a team of highly experienced technical experts can produce an excellent programme on paper, she said, but if young people are not part of designing it, they can still miss important realities about how it will work in someone's life.

At AYARHEP, she said, the value of this approach has been clear through community scorecards, peer-led programming, youth support groups and community dialogues. Young people can tell you not only whether a programme is reaching them, but whether it is actually working for them.

Limo believes the question should therefore change. "We need to move from asking, 'How can we involve young people?' to asking, 'What decisions should young people have power over?'" she said.

What frustrates Limo most is when young people's participation stops at the conversation.

She said conferences and policy dialogues matter, and that she values every opportunity to be in those rooms. They are where community realities reach decision-makers directly, and many of the partnership discussions most important to her work begin there.

"My frustration is when young people speak, our quotes go into a report, and we are not included in the discussions and decisions on the next steps," she said.

Young people are often described as the leaders of tomorrow, Limo said, but they are already leading today. They are implementing programmes, mobilising communities, collecting evidence, shaping policies and creating solutions.

Sustained youth leadership, she added, needs sustained investment. Partners and funders can work with advocates who keep showing up and delivering results when they invest in young leaders.

"The opportunity now is to move from youth visibility to youth investment by bringing young people in early and keeping them in the process, from design through to accountability," she said.

Funding under strain

The push for meaningful youth leadership comes at a difficult time for HIV and SRHR programmes, as funding pressures affect community-based organisations across Africa.

Funding pressure is being felt most directly at the community level, she said. When funding shrinks, it is not just an organisational budget that changes.

"We have seen fewer community activities, fewer peer educators, reduced outreach, fewer spaces for young people to access psychosocial support and less capacity for youth-led organisations to hold systems accountable," she said.

Limo said there is a contradiction in asking communities to take greater ownership of the HIV and SRHR response while the organisations rooted in those communities struggle to survive.

"We need to stop seeing youth-led and community-based organisations as temporary project implementers," she said. "They are part of the infrastructure of the response. Communities built the response."

Close 

Sustaining that infrastructure, she said, will require longer-term and more flexible funding, investment in organisational capacity, and genuine recognition that communities hold expertise that cannot simply be replaced.

"We also need to protect the gains we have made. We cannot keep rebuilding community systems every time a funding cycle changes," said Limo.

A call to policymakers and funders

For policymakers and funders, Limo said, is to listen differently.

She said that young people need more than programmes designed for them. They need the opportunities, resources and decision-making power to help design and lead those programmes themselves.

She urged decision-makers to recognise that young people's priorities do not always fit neatly into programme categories. HIV, mental health, education, economic empowerment, relationships, violence, SRHR and digital safety are interconnected in a young person's life, she explained, and responses need to reflect that.

She also urged decision-makers to invest in choice.

She pointed to the exciting scientific developments in HIV prevention, but said innovation only becomes meaningful when communities can access it, understand their options, and make informed choices about what works for them.

Limo asked funders not to stop at paying for activities.

"Invest in the people and organisations that make the activity possible, the young leaders, peer educators, community organisations and networks that remain in communities long after a particular project has ended," she said.

What gives Limo hope, she said, is young people themselves.

She has watched young people who were once afraid to speak in meetings grow into peer educators, advocates and leaders, she said. She has seen young people living with HIV move from simply trying to survive their diagnosis to becoming powerful voices in the response, and young women challenge systems, ask difficult questions and create solutions for their communities. "I am one of them," she said.

"That is the future I am working towards," Limo said, "one where young people are not spoken about only as vulnerable populations and beneficiaries, but recognized as people with agency, expertise and the ability to shape their own futures."

Through AYARHEP, she wants to keep building spaces where young people can access information, services, support and opportunities, and where they can also influence the systems around them. Ultimately, she said, she wants a future where a young person does not have to fight the system to access basic healthcare, accurate information, or dignity.

"And perhaps most importantly, I want young people to believe that their lives can be bigger than the challenges they were born into," said Limo.

World.title: Somalia: All 7 Surviving Pakistani Crew Members Rescued After Somalia Pirate Hijacking
World.content:
Islamabad — All seven Pakistani crew members who survived a pirate attack off Somalia's coast have been rescued, Pakistan's foreign minister said Monday.

The Palau-flagged oil tanker, MT Honour, was hijacked by Somali pirates in late April, around 30 nautical miles off Somalia's coast while sailing to Mogadishu. Ten of the 17 crew members aboard were Pakistani nationals.

The last three Pakistani survivors have been rescued and flown to Addis Ababa, accompanied by a team from the Pakistani Embassy in Djibouti, Ishaq Dar said on US social media company X.

They are expected to leave the Ethiopian capital for Karachi on the first available Ethiopian Airlines flight on Wednesday, he added.

Four other Pakistani crew members were rescued in late September, more than five months after the hijacking.

They arrived in Karachi on Sunday aboard an Ethiopian Airlines flight from Addis Ababa.

Three Pakistani crew members were killed during the incident, and their remains have also been repatriated to Pakistan.

World.title: Ghana: Cabinet Approves Establishment of Ghana Space Agency - Minister
World.content:
THE government is advancing plans to transform the Ghana Space Science and Technology Institute (GSSTI) into a fully-fledged Ghana Space Agency to strengthen the country's participation in the emerging global space economy.

The proposed agency is expected to provide a stronger institutional framework for coordinating Ghana's space activities, developing national space programmes, promoting research and innovation, facilitating public-private partnerships and strengthening international cooperation.

It will also support the development of space infrastructure and related technologies.

Speaking at a press conference in Accra yesterday, the Minister of Environment, Science and Technology, Dr Zanetor Agyemang-Rawlings, said the initiative formed part of her First 100 Days Public Engagement Agenda, aimed at moving Ghana's space science and technology agenda from aspiration to implementation.

Related Articles

She said processes were already underway to draft a Bill for the establishment of the agency following Cabinet's approval.

Dr Agyemang-Rawlings said the transformation would provide the country with the appropriate legal, institutional, technical and operational framework to coordinate its space activities. Read More

World.title: Ethiopia: Four African Countries Call for De-Escalation of Tension in Ethiopia
World.content:
This call comes amid the growing tension between Ethiopia's federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region.

Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan have called for a de-escalation of the conflicts across their region, including Sudan's civil war and the crisis in Ethiopia.

In a joint statement issued Sunday at the end of a meeting in New Alamein City, Egypt, the countries called for dialogue and a peaceful resolution of the conflicts.

The statement was signed by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Mohamud and Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, according to Al Jazeera.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The countries declared that cross-border challenges required "a dialogue, not confrontation."

They also demanded that the coastal states retain control of the Red Sea; a stance that appears to respond to Ethiopia's pursuit of sovereign access to the sea and a naval presence.

This call comes amid the growing tension between Ethiopia's federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region; a situation that has many in the country fearing that it could tip back into the kind of war that devastated it a few years ago.

PREMIUM TIMES reported renewed armed clashes in the northern Tigray region between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) two weeks ago.

The rebel forces also seized control of Mekelle and the Alula Aba Nega Airport.

Government and allied forces, however, retook the city of Mekelle on Sunday after the TPLF said it "temporarily moved out of" Tigray's regional capital to "operate from somewhere else."

According to local media, Tigray interim leader Abraham Belay accused the government of preparing a new temporary administration for the region and said it hopes to hold regional elections within months.

Meanwhile, Ethiopia has accused neighbouring Eritrea of directly backing the rebel alliance during Ethiopia's 2022 civil war. It also accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the armed alliance in the recent confrontation.

Sudan, which has been at war since April 2023, has accused Ethiopia of interfering in its crisis.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya Confirms First Ebola Case as Patient Returns From DRC
World.content:
Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola virus disease in Nairobi, ending months of heightened surveillance and preparedness following the spread of the deadly Bundibugyo strain in the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighbouring Uganda.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale confirmed the imported case on Tuesday, saying the patient had travelled from the DRC through Uganda before entering Kenya.

Duale said the patient, who had lived in the DRC for about seven years, developed illness approximately a month ago and sought treatment at several health facilities in the country before beginning his journey back to Kenya.

The patient travelled by road from the DRC into Uganda before boarding a flight to Nairobi, where he arrived at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) on Saturday, October 3, at about 1:10pm.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to Duale, the flight was carrying 23 passengers.

WHO declares Uganda Ebola-free

The patient underwent routine public health screening at JKIA before proceeding to the immigration desk, raising questions over how the infection was detected and the measures now being taken to identify and monitor people who may have been exposed during his journey.

“The Ministry of Health wishes to inform members of the public that it has confirmed the first imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease,” Duale said.

The confirmation marks a significant development for Kenya, which had remained free of confirmed Ebola infections despite mounting regional concerns.



The government had been preparing for the possibility of an imported case for several months as Ebola spread across the DRC and was reported in Uganda.

In June, Duale told Parliament that Kenya had activated its National Ebola Incident Management System and intensified screening at airports and land border crossings. More than 71,000 travellers had been screened at the time, while 22 suspected Ebola alerts reported in nine counties had all tested negative.

The Ministry of Health had also stepped up surveillance at the Malaba border because of the movement of people between Kenya and Uganda. By early June, authorities said 59 suspected Ebola cases tested in Kenya had returned negative results.

A national Ebola preparedness and response taskforce was subsequently established to coordinate surveillance, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, case management, risk communication and cross-border response.

The taskforce brings together national and county governments, health agencies, security authorities, development partners and technical experts.

Kenya’s first imported case comes as the Ebola outbreak in the DRC continues to grow.

The World Health Organisation said on September 25 that the outbreak had spread to 63 health zones across seven provinces, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, Bas-Uélé and Sud-Ubangi.

By September 23, the DRC had recorded 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 48.1 per cent. WHO warned that the geographical expansion of the outbreak was increasing the risk of cross-border transmission.

More recent figures reported by Congolese authorities showed the outbreak had surpassed 8,000 confirmed cases. On October 2 the DRC had recorded 8,300 confirmed cases and 4,018 deaths across seven provinces, making the current outbreak the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country’s history.

The outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, a strain for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment. WHO says insecurity, population movement and cross-border trade have complicated efforts to contain transmission.

The scale of the outbreak has also prompted experimental treatment efforts. More than 250 people exposed to the virus in Ituri are participating in a trial of obeldesivir, an experimental drug being studied as post-exposure protection against infection.

The patient’s movement through Uganda is particularly significant because the country had also experienced an outbreak of the same Bundibugyo strain after infections crossed its border from the DRC.

Close 

Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases during its 2026 outbreak, including imported and locally acquired infections. The country was declared Ebola-free on July 28 after completing the required 42-day period without a new confirmed case.

However, WHO has continued to warn that Uganda remains vulnerable to reintroduction because Ebola transmission has persisted in neighbouring DRC and people continue to cross the border.

Kenya’s confirmation therefore highlights the difficulty of containing the disease in a region characterised by extensive movement of people, goods and vehicles across borders.

The Ministry of Health had repeatedly cautioned that Kenya’s geographical position and extensive regional connectivity left it exposed to imported infections.

In May, the ministry announced heightened surveillance, laboratory testing, border screening and public awareness measures after WHO and Africa CDC classified the regional Ebola outbreak as a major public health threat.

World.title: Kenya: 3,6 Million Prepare For 2026 Exams
World.content:
Nairobi — The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) will deploy 342,005 contracted professionals to oversee national examinations and assessments involving 3,634,846 candidates between October 16 and November 20.

KNEC Chief Executive Officer David Njengere announced the figures on Monday during the launch of the 2026 National Examination and Assessment Season, saying extensive preparations had been put in place to ensure the exercise is conducted smoothly and with the required integrity.

"The Council will administer assessments and examination to a total of 3,634,846 candidates between 16th October and 20th November 2026. KNEC will engage a total of 342,005 contracted professionals to facilitate the conduct and management of the field administration process," Njengere said.

The 2026 exercise will cover the Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE), Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) and Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA).



The total candidature represents a 6.13 per cent increase from the 3,424,836 candidates registered for national examinations and assessments in 2025.

According to figures released during the launch, 1,380,463 learners have registered for KPSEA, while 1,206,028 will sit KJSEA. The KCSE candidature stands at 1,048,355, making 2026 the first year the number of KCSE candidates has crossed the one-million mark.

The KCSE examination season will begin with rehearsals on October 16, followed by papers with low candidature from October 19 to 30. Papers involving large numbers of candidates will then be administered from November 2 to 20.

The KPSEA and KJSEA assessments will run from October 26 to 30.

Tougher measures

KNEC has announced tighter security measures for this year's examination season, including the use of smart padlocks on all examination storage containers.

The technology was piloted in 250 containers last year and will now be rolled out across the country. The locks will be monitored from KNEC headquarters and will record access to the containers, helping the council detect unauthorised opening or tampering.

The containers will be opened only at designated times. KPSEA and KJSEA papers will be accessed from 6am, while KCSE centre managers will collect examination papers at 7am and 12.30pm for the morning and afternoon sessions respectively.

KNEC will also separate morning and afternoon KCSE papers in specially marked cartons to minimise the risk of mix-ups and unauthorised access.

The council has further personalised examination papers with candidates' details, although the identifying information will be removed before scripts are released to examiners for marking.

Njengere warned candidates and parents against paying individuals who claim they can provide examination papers before the scheduled dates.

He said candidates would see the actual papers for the first time when they sit the examinations, urging parents not to lose money to fraudsters promising advance access to examination materials.

Mobile phones have also been identified as a major threat to examination integrity. KNEC has warned that candidates and examination officials will not be allowed to have phones at examination centres during examination sessions, with violations treated as examination malpractice.

For KCSE alone, KNEC will deploy 10,765 centre managers, 12,274 supervisors, 57,432 invigilators and 21,388 security officers. At least two police officers will be assigned to each KCSE examination centre, with additional security provided at centres with larger candidate populations.

Heavy rains

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba also warned that heavy rains could disrupt the examination process and said the government had activated contingency measures to ensure candidates are not disadvantaged.

The Kenya Meteorological Department has forecast above-average rainfall associated with the El Niño phenomenon, prompting authorities to prepare for possible flooding, damaged roads and other challenges that could affect access to examination centres and movement of examination materials.

Ogamba said relevant government agencies would work together to respond to any disruptions during the examination period.

The government has also expanded storage capacity for examination materials, with 48 additional containers installed in sub-counties, bringing the total number of containers to 701.

Close 

Education officials have also raised concern over the growing use of artificial intelligence and digital technologies to facilitate examination malpractice.

Basic Education Principal Secretary John Ololtuaa urged examination officials to remain vigilant and ensure emerging technologies are not used to compromise the credibility of the assessments.

Education officials have warned that examination malpractice could undermine public confidence in the country's education system and said those found violating examination regulations would face disciplinary or legal action.

The 2026 examination season comes as Kenya continues its transition to the Competency-Based Education system, with KPSEA and KJSEA forming part of the new assessment framework.

Notably, 2026 will also be the second-last KCSE examination for the 8-4-4 cohort, with the final 8-4-4 class expected to sit the examination in 2027.

KNEC has said it will operate a 24-hour call centre throughout the examination period to allow candidates, officials and members of the public to report incidents and seek assistance.

World.title: Kenya: Govt Identifies 109 Criminal Gangs, Warns Against Political Violence Ahead of 2027 Polls
World.content:
Nairobi — The government has intensified its crackdown on criminal gangs and organised violence, identifying 109 organised criminal gangs and groups operating across the country as Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election.

Internal Security Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo said the government was particularly concerned about the use of organised youth groups for political intimidation, attacks and harassment.

He warned that the growing involvement of criminal groups in violence could undermine the rule of law, erode public confidence in state institutions and pose a serious security threat ahead of the elections.

The 109 groups identified by the government are an increase from the 89 criminal groups declared illegal in 2016 through Gazette Notice No. 10427.



According to the government, 38 of the groups are based in Western Kenya, 22 in the Rift Valley, 20 in Nairobi, 12 in Nyanza, 11 at the Coast, three in Eastern, two in North Eastern and one in Central Kenya.

Omollo said security agencies arrested and arraigned 1,827 suspects for offences linked to goonism and organised criminal activity between January 1 and August 31, 2026.

Trans Nzoia recorded the highest number of arrests at 491.

During the same period, courts secured 729 convictions, with the Rift Valley accounting for 36.5 per cent of all convictions.

A further 716 cases remain before the courts, according to the government.

Omollo said the figures demonstrate that the government's response extends beyond arrests to investigations, prosecution and convictions.

The government said security agencies have shifted their focus from individual offenders to the wider networks that facilitate and sustain organised criminal activity.

Through intelligence-led policing, investigators are targeting gang leaders, recruiters and financiers, while linking cases and investigating connections between seemingly unrelated incidents.

Financial investigations are also being pursued where evidence exists to trace proceeds linked to extortion, robbery, illegal businesses and other organised criminal activities.

However, the government acknowledged that the fight against organised gangs has become more difficult because of increasingly decentralised structures and the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, particularly along vulnerable border areas.

Authorities said they are strengthening multi-agency cooperation, community-based intelligence and collaboration with neighbouring countries to tackle criminal activities that cross borders.

The government said security agencies would remain alert to attempts to mobilise criminal gangs or organised youth groups for political intimidation, disruption or violence ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Omollo stressed that the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to participate in political life but warned that violence and intimidation have no place in the electoral process.

Security agencies will maintain visibility during political activities and take lawful action against criminal conduct, regardless of those involved, he said.

Those who recruit, finance or direct criminal groups will be held accountable alongside individuals who carry out acts of violence.

The Inspector-General of Police has directed regional police commanders to take firm, decisive and lawful action against criminal gangs and organised violence within their areas of command.

The government also warned that police officers found, through due process, to have facilitated criminal activities or failed to take appropriate action would face administrative or disciplinary measures.

The government acknowledged that enforcement alone cannot permanently eliminate organised criminality, particularly where former offenders return to the same environments and networks that initially drew them into crime.

Omollo said the government would therefore combine arrests and prosecutions with prevention, rehabilitation and reintegration programmes.

The initiatives will involve the Probation and Aftercare Service, Kenya Prisons Service, county governments, faith-based organisations and community leaders to help former members of criminal groups rebuild their lives and reintegrate into their communities.

The government also urged young people to take advantage of legitimate employment and enterprise opportunities available through programmes including the NYOTA Programme and Hustler Fund.

Close 

Omollo said some young people are recruited into criminal groups through promises of quick money, while others are coerced or exploited by individuals who finance and direct violence.

He said limited economic opportunities can leave young people vulnerable to such exploitation, although this does not excuse criminal conduct.

The government has called on parents, guardians, teachers, religious leaders and community leaders to work with security agencies to prevent young people from being recruited into criminal groups.

Members of the public have also been urged to report suspected criminal activity through credible channels.

The government cited the Fichua kwa DCI initiative, which can be reached through the toll-free number 0800 722 203, as one of the channels available for reporting suspected crime.

Omollo said the government would continue to strengthen intelligence-led policing, investigations and prosecutions while taking action to protect lives, property and communities.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 6, 2026
World.content:
press review

Nigeria Orders Probe into Tragic Ondo Military Plane Crash

Nigerian authorities are investigating the crash of a Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft near a naval base in Igbokoda, Ondo State, which had 25 passengers and seven crew members on board. The aircraft was travelling from Benin to Lagos on a routine mission when it crashed into a swampy area. President Bola Tinubu ordered a thorough investigation and declared three days of national mourning, with flags to fly at half-mast. The Nigerian Air Force said search and rescue operations were immediately activated. The Ministry of Aviation, Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau and Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority offered technical support. Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa also deployed emergency, health and security agencies to assist. Local officials and eyewitnesses reported finding wreckage, human remains and personal belongings at the difficult-to-access crash site, with early accounts indicating there may have been no survivors.

Abiy Ahmed Sworn In for Second Term as Ethiopia's Prime Minister

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has been sworn in for a second five-year term as the country formally begins a new parliamentary term amid renewed conflict in Tigray and worsening tensions with neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy took the oath during the inaugural session of the seventh House of Peoples' Representatives, with the new administration described as the "Medemer Government", reflecting his political philosophy of cooperation and national unity. The inauguration comes as federal forces and their allies consolidate control of Mekelle after the Tigray People's Liberation Front withdrew from the city. Fighting has continued elsewhere in the region, including reported airstrikes and artillery attacks. The renewed violence has raised fears of a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Ethiopia has also accused Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance, a claim Asmara denies, further straining regional relations and raising concerns about a wider Horn of Africa conflict.

Ugandan President Questions Progress on Appeal of Death-Row Daycare Killer

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni has questioned the handling of the appeal of Christopher Okello Onyum, who was sentenced to death after being convicted of murdering four toddlers at a daycare centre in Ggaba, Kampala. Speaking to the NRM Caucus, Museveni said the case appeared to have "disappeared" after the appeal was filed and questioned whether appellate proceedings could be held in the same community where the original trial took place. Onyum was convicted by the High Court in April following a mobile trial at Ggaba Community Church. The victims were Gideon Eteku, Keisha Agenorwoth Otim, Ignatius Sseruyange and Ryan Odeke, who were killed at the Ggaba Early Childhood Development Centre on April 2. Onyum has appealed both his conviction and sentence, arguing that the evidence was not properly evaluated and that his mental state was not adequately considered. The Court of Appeal remains responsible for determining the merits of the case.

Malawi Proposal Seeks Major Changes to Vice-Presidency

A Lilongwe resident, Boldwin Bickiel Dzuwalatsoka, has submitted a draft Constitutional Amendment Bill proposing major changes to Malawi's Vice-Presidency. The proposal would end the automatic succession of a Vice-President to the presidency, make the position appointive rather than elected on a joint presidential ticket, and allow the President to dismiss the Vice-President at any time without impeachment proceedings. The Vice-President would also have a largely ceremonial role, with executive powers delegated by the President. Under the proposal, if the presidency became vacant, the Speaker of Parliament would become interim President within 24 hours and organise a fresh presidential election within 90 days of the deceased President's burial. Dzuwalatsoka argued that the current system has contributed to political tensions and power struggles between presidents and their deputies. The proposal has not yet been tabled in Parliament and would require constitutional scrutiny and the necessary parliamentary support before it could take effect.

Close 

U.S. Supreme Court Ruling May Resume Deportation Flights to Liberia

The US Supreme Court's decision to allow the Trump administration to continue deporting migrants to third countries temporarily could lead to the resumption of deportation flights to Liberia. At least 20 people have already been deported to the West African nation, some of whom had never had any connection to Liberia. The policy has referenced the nation's long and complicated relationship with the United States, dating back to the early 19th century when the American Colonization Society advocated sending free Black Americans to Africa. Those settlers established Liberia, which became Africa's first independent republic in 1847. Thousands of Black Americans and others were transported there during the 19th century, although many died from disease and others faced severe hardship. The latest deportations are different in circumstances, but critics and historians have noted parallels with earlier US efforts to remove nonwhite people viewed as unwanted from American society. The Supreme Court is expected to consider the broader legality of the current third-country deportation policy.

Multiple reports that surfaced recently linked Tyreek Hill to a Kansas City Chiefs return and one report even quoted his agent as saying he expected the former All-Pro wide receiver to sign with a team in the coming days. That's before Hill's divorce trial began Tuesday.

And testimony from Lakeeta Vaccaro, the player's estranged wife, outlined incidents of domestic abuse. Her suit complaint outlined eight instances of abuse.

The divorce itself is of no interest to the NFL. But the allegations of abuse definitely are and could derail or at least significantly delay Hill's return to the field under the league's Personal Conduct Policy.

NFL FACES DOMESTIC ABUSE EPIDEMIC THIS OFFSEASON

Hill is a free agent but the NFL review of his domestic violence allegations by Vaccaro is ongoing with no timetable for a conclusion, a league source confirmed to OutKick.

Tuesday's accounting of those allegations in open court almost definitely will be taken into account as part of that review that will determine Hill's status to play when healthy.

RAVENS' RASHOD BATEMAN FACES DOMESTIC CHARGES FOR ALLEGED ATTACK ON CAR CARRYING EX-GIRLFRIEND AND THEIR BABY

Vaccaro, who is suing Hill for punitive and compensatory damages, testified during direct examination that in July 2024, she and Hill visited the ESPN campus in Orlando.

Later, at their hotel, Hill remained upset and became so heated he tried to punch her stomach, Vaccaro testified. She said she blocked the blow by putting her hands on her stomach, but the strike did hit her hands.

Vaccaro was pregnant at the time.

"But then the two weeks of, when it went back to this angry man, it was bad."

Vaccaro said Hill once picked her up physically to throw her out of their house. She said he once pushed her into a car door during an argument. She accused Hill of grabbing and hurting her breasts during multiple arguments.

She accused Hill of once leaving her on the side of a road after an argument in their car.

World.title: Trump says Putin call coming ‘very soon’ as US tracks suspected plague death in Russia
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump said Tuesday he will speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" as his administration closely tracks reports of a suspected pneumonic plague death in Siberia that have prompted a U.S. health alert and heightened health precautions across several countries bordering Russia.

Trump revealed the planned call while taking questions from reporters Tuesday.

Asked whether he had spoken with Putin about the situation, Trump said he already had a call scheduled.

"I have a call scheduled, yup," Trump said.

TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP'

Asked when the call would take place, the president responded, "Very soon."

Trump said the administration was in "very deep discussions" when asked what U.S. intelligence agencies were saying about the reports.

The president's comments came as the U.S. Embassy in Moscow issued a health alert Tuesday saying it was aware of press reports from Russia's Irkutsk region of "suspected pneumonic plague resulting in the death of an individual," along with associated quarantine measures and hospital closures.

"We continue to track the situation closely," the embassy said.

NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA

A State Department spokesman told Fox News Digital that the department, along with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other interagency partners, is "closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague" in Russia's Irkutsk Oblast.

"The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," the spokesman said.

The spokesman cautioned that "many details remain unconfirmed" and called on Moscow to provide greater clarity.

"We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," the spokesman said.

The alert advised Americans in the area to follow local health guidance, avoid affected medical facilities and seek prompt medical care if they develop fever or respiratory symptoms. Those who have traveled to an area experiencing an outbreak were advised to monitor their health for 14 days.

The State Department's existing Level 4 "Do Not Travel" advisory for Russia remains unchanged. The embassy reiterated that Americans currently in Russia should depart and warned that the U.S. government's ability to assist citizens there is limited, particularly outside Moscow.

UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE

Several countries bordering Russia are also implementing new health precautions in response to the reports.

Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan are moving to implement what their governments have described as "enhanced health and sanitary measures" in response to reports of pneumonic plague in Siberia.

A 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East died last week from what Russian authorities described as pneumonia of undetermined origin. Russia has not said the woman died of plague and said testing found no microorganisms in her body linked to her work.

Russian officials told the WHO that her contacts tested negative for dangerous infectious pathogens. The WHO has assessed the risk to the general population as low.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has also said it is closely monitoring the reports and working across the U.S. government as additional information becomes available. The agency said there is currently no indication of a broader threat to the United States.

Pneumonic plague is a serious bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis. It can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact and can progress rapidly if untreated. The disease can be successfully treated with antibiotics, particularly when identified and treated early.

For now, U.S. officials are continuing to seek additional information about what occurred in Irkutsk and whether the incident poses any wider threat.

The president suggested his administration could have more to say as soon as Wednesday.

"We'll be able to report about it probably tomorrow," Trump said.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

World.title: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning ‘On the Waterfront’ and ‘North by Northwest’ star, dead at 102
World.content:

Eva Marie Saint, the Oscar-and Emmy-winning actress who became one of the defining stars of Hollywood’s Golden Era, has died. She was 102.

Saint died Tuesday of natural causes at her Los Angeles home surrounded by family and loved ones, her representative confirmed to Fox News Digital.

The actress made an extraordinary film debut opposite Marlon Brando in the 1954 classic "On the Waterfront," winning the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress in her performance as Edie Doyle.

POST MALONE, EVA MARIE SAINT AND OTHER CELEBRITIES WHO SHARE A BIRTHDAY WITH THE FOURTH OF JULY

Five years later, Saint then firmly cemented her place in Hollywood's Golden Era history while starring opposite the legendary Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s "North by Northwest," playing mysterious "Hitchcock Blonde" Eve Kendall in the cult-classic 1959 thriller.

Over an incredible career spanning more than seven decades, Saint worked alongside some of Hollywood’s most celebrated leading men, including Montgomery Clift, Henry Fonda, Paul Newman, Gregory Peck, Richard Burton, Warren Beatty, James Garner, George C. Scott, Burt Lancaster and Tom Hanks.

OSCAR-WINNER BRENDA FRICKER, 'PIGEON LADY' FROM 'HOME ALONE 2,' DEAD AT 81

Other notable films featuring the actress included "A Hatful of Rain," "Raintree County," "Exodus," "The Russians Are Coming the Russians Are Coming," "Grand Prix," "Nothing in Common" and, later in her career, "Superman Returns."

Saint was also a regular fixture of television and the stage. She earned five Emmy nominations, winning in 1990 for the miniseries "People Like Us," and appeared on Broadway in "The Trip to Bountiful" before director Elia Kazan cast her in "On the Waterfront."

SHELLEY FABARES, STAR OF 'THE DONNA REED SHOW' AND 'COACH,' DEAD AT 82

Born in Newark, New Jersey, and raised in Albany and Delmar, New York, Saint attended Bowling Green State University in Ohio with plans to become a teacher before acting ultimately changed the course of her life.

Saint was married to director Jeffrey Hayden for 65 years until his death in 2016. She is survived by their two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

Saint's death closes a remarkable chapter in the Golden Era of Hollywood history, leaving behind performances alongside some of the biggest and brightest stars and filmmakers of the 20th century.

World.title: Anthony Rizzo, 2016 World Series champion, reveals most important piece to winning it all in MLB postseason
World.content:
With the MLB postseason in full swing, every team and its fan base vying for the World Series trophy is hoping that their superstars can rise to the occasion and get the job done.

However, every great team who has hoisted the hardware at the end of a grueling season knows it takes more than just those All-Stars to win it all. In fact, it takes every single person from the top down.

Just ask World Series champion and three-time All-Star first baseman Anthony Rizzo, who helped the Chicago Cubs break its 108-year streak without winning a World Series in 2016 after defeating the Cleveland Guardians in Game 7.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Of course, it was stars like himself, Kris Bryant and others celebrating on the field after he secured the final out at first base. But Rizzo can’t help stressing the importance of every player, coach, clubhouse attendant and more during October baseball.

"I just think that on every team you have the stars, the middle-of-the-tier players, and your role players. Everyone’s so important to a team," Rizzo told OutKick, while highlighting PAYDAY’s "Low Key Legends" initiative, which emphasizes the importance of the unsung heroes within an organization. "It takes all 26 guys, it takes your entire staff. So, in order for the superstars to win their championship – let’s say Aaron Judge. He’s the MVP of the Yankees, of the whole league. For him to win a championship, it’s going to take every single guy on that roster. It’s not just one guy who carries you.

"It’s the small things. It’s the baserunning, the pickoffs, the relays. It’s all the lowkey things that maybe don’t look as glitzy and glammy, but that’s what it takes to win a championship."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

We asked Rizzo who his "Low Key Legend" would be, and he didn’t even hesitate when thinking back to his career.

"In the baseball world, I would definitely say Danny Mueller," he responded. "He was the clubhouse attendant in Chicago. He was my guy. He always had me high-energy, ready, and always a bundle of joy when I walked in. Whatever I needed, he was there. Then, the hitting coaches. They are just behind the scenes doing their scouting reports, knowing everything I’m thinking, so when I walk in, I don’t have to think. They just have everything ready for me, knowing what I want so I can go out there and play effortlessly.

"Those are the guys behind the scenes that are just fueling this greatness you see on the field."

At this stage of the season, teams have completely bonded into a family rather than just colleagues, if they didn’t do so during spring training and the early-season grind. Rizzo enjoyed every "family" he was a part of in the bigs, where October baseball brought out that team chemistry.

"I think we’re together forever. We’re together for 200-plus days a year," he said. "In October, win or go home, you’re still saying to each other, ‘In a few weeks, I get to pick my own friends.’ So, we’re like family in the clubhouse. Guys know when to get on guys, when they need a little more love, when to back off – maybe they’re a little more sensitive. That’s the family and bond that’s created in a season. Every year is different. Every year is unique, but for me over my career, Danny’s been a low-key legend for me forever, and my hitting coaches I’ve always had a good relationship with them where they always had my dialed in."

Then, when it’s time to play ball, it’s not just the clean-up hitter or the ace that carries the load of winning a postseason game. It takes a village, and the Milwaukee Brewers gave a prime example of that in Game 2 of their NLDS series against the San Diego Padres.

YANKEES' JAZZ CHISHOLM JR MAKES WILD ADMISSION ABOUT COSTLY ERROR AS TEAM FACES POSTSEASON ELIMINATION

Of course, the highlights will capture the moment Jackson Chourio walked it off in the bottom of the ninth inning with bases loaded and two outs against the Padres’ dominant closer, Mason Miller. That grabs the headlines and fan appreciation.

However, Rizzo pointed to an unsung hero – a "Low Key Legend" – that helped make it all possible.

"It’s a team of destiny because they’re a smaller market, but this is how they’ve been all year. To stay on brand with Payday and low-key legends, Gary Sanchez in the at-bat before, pinch hitting, taking the walk to get the bases loaded. That’s the low-key legend moment of the game. The superstar moment is when Jackson Chourio coming up and getting that base hit."

DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS

CHINA ‘THROWING GASOLINE ON THE FIRE’ IN AI DATA CENTERS RACE, SAY LAWMAKERS

World.title: Drone strike sinks ship in NATO waters as Zelenskyy warns of looming ‘massive strike’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A commercial ship sank and its crew vanished Tuesday after an apparent coordinated air-and-sea drone attack off NATO member Bulgaria, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia before warning Moscow was preparing a broader "massive strike."

A second vessel was also heavily damaged and set ablaze inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, with a drone expert warning the dual precision strikes signaled a dangerous escalation and possible "larger invasion posture" by Russia.

"They were likely using the Geran-4 aerial drone to take the vessel out or the Maran surface vehicle to take it out," Cameron Chell, founder of drone manufacturer Draganfly, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday of the first strike.

RUSSIA MAY BE USING HIDDEN 'LUNCHBOX-SIZE' DRONE DEVICES TO COUNTER UKRAINE DEFENSES: EXPERT

"The reason it wasn't just an air vehicle or an air drone that took this ship out was that the Gerans generally come in at a pretty steep angle when they're on final attack," Chell said.

"There are not really any precision drones that fly closely above the surface, which is where they would have had to hit in order to create an impact that would sink this ship fast enough," he added.

"The nature of this strike suggests there was a combination of an air attack and surface attack," Chell said.

The dual attack occurred roughly 70 nautical miles off the eastern Bulgarian coastal town of Byala, according to Reuters, bringing the conflict into the economic zone of a NATO member.

Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence and security services were working to determine the full circumstances surrounding the attack.

US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS

"Our intelligence and special services are now working to establish all available information about yet another attack in the Black Sea targeting civilian vessels," he wrote on X.

"Our Navy contacted its counterparts in Bulgaria, and it has been established that this was a combined Russian attack using maritime and aerial drones."

Chell suggested the attack’s location and hybrid nature could serve Russia by sowing greater uncertainty across the region.

"We can see the amount of geopolitical chaos that's involved, and this is exactly the type of thing that would benefit Russia in the region," Chell said.

"The hybrid element here is really blurring the lines between traditional military actions," he added, describing the attack as "an expansion of strategy and tactics."

"This is indicative of this larger invasion posture that seems to be unfolding for Russia," Chell said. "And a real desire, what appears to be, for Russia to take things up a notch."

RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev also confirmed that aerial and maritime drones targeted two commercial vessels in shipping lanes inside Bulgaria’s EEZ, calling the attack a "gross, flagrant violation of international law," according to Reuters.

The sunken vessel, identified by British maritime risk group Vanguard as the cargo ship Alfa Watan, suffered catastrophic structural damage before submerging with an undisclosed cargo and an unknown number of crew members aboard.

A nearby Bulgarian ferry, the Dioscuria, diverted to the scene after witnessing an explosion and receiving distress signals, Reuters reported.

Rescuers found an overturned lifeboat, life rafts and life jackets floating in the debris field.

RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

Search-and-rescue operations involving the Bulgarian Navy, Air Force and Border Police remained underway to locate the missing crew and monitor for environmental threats, the outlet said.

Chell suggested the apparent coordination between the attacks was particularly significant.

"Not only are you using pretty sophisticated equipment, but you're also doing it in a coordinated manner," Chell said.

"These two ships were going opposite directions. One was actually just coming, and had left Ukraine the day before," he said.

"These things coordinated and were struck relatively at the same time. So another level of coordination has unfolded here," Chell added.

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

The second ship, identified by Vanguard as the general cargo vessel ABLE, caught fire after being struck while carrying grain.

A Bulgarian ferry crew evacuated all 18 seafarers aboard — 11 Turkish nationals and seven Indian nationals.

Two crew members suffered severe injuries and were airlifted to a medical facility in Varna, while the remaining 16 were transported safely to shore.

Radev convened an emergency government session following the strikes. While acknowledging it remained unclear whether the drones originated from Russia or Ukraine, he warned of the widening scope of the war.

"Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable," Radev told reporters.

REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

"If this war is not ended in time, it will continue to expand its spatial scope and increase the risk of even a global conflict."

Chell said striking the two ships inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone could also have the effect of disrupting a crucial shipping corridor and creating fear among commercial operators.

"It all adds up to a perfect little scenario for the Russians to create chaos there, not just to disrupt the lane of economics for the region and in particular for Ukraine — a lifeline," Chell said.

"The Russians are really taking a playbook out of the Iranians who have basically created enough chaos in the Strait of Hormuz where the operators can't take the chance to put their ships through there," he added.

The strikes came amid a surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident off Romania’s coast Monday in which two people died in a ship fire.

Ambrey, a British firm specializing in global maritime risk, recorded more than 210 strikes on commercial ships between July and the end of September.

UKRAINE LAUNCHES WHAT APPEARS TO BE ONE OF ITS LARGEST DRONE ATTACKS AGAINST RUSSIA: REPORT

Zelenskyy later warned that Ukrainian intelligence had obtained information indicating Russia was preparing a major new assault.

"We’ve got updated intel on Russia’s preparations for a massive strike," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "I ask you, please, to take care of yourselves and respond to missile threat alerts."

"Ukrainian services and our Air Force are ready to respond — as much as our defenses allow," Zelenskyy continued. "And a lot depends on our partners — every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us."

"It’s very important that there be the political will to do this — particularly in the United States and in Europe," he added.

World.title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson clash over Trump and seniority in Maine’s first Senate debate
World.content:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.

Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority, as they try to capitalize on the president’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that on Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking the president at least 20 times in one hour of debating on CBS13 News.

“It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.”

Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances where she opposed the Trump administration.

She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.”

“I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said.

Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time in the Senate. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited.

In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader, Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with the president if he visited Maine, with Trump recently teasing a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”

Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has come to Maine and backed her at events.

Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024.

Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars to hold a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority.

Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate.

Collins said she judges every nominee by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade.

“In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan, and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said.

Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referencing Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice and that’s me.”

Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the state Legislature.

Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier on Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years, should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats.

Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” which contains about $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that are unpopular.

That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the president’s signature second-term legislation when it came to final passage. The senator said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid.

“He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, while adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural health care fund.

Jackson doubled down.

“Senator Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.”

Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker in Maine, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She additionally questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate.

When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s fatal killing of a Mainer earlier this year, saying that it happened because “Senator Collins would not push back against ICE.”

Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras as well as training of officers and teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration.

In her closing statement, Collins said, “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority, and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.”

Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well.

“Tonight, Senator Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.”
