URUGUAY · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Uruguay is a small, stable South American democracy between Brazil and Argentina, where many savers still think in US dollars.

— What happened The Uruguay central bank, the Banco Central del Uruguay (BCU), published a 39-page policy paper on Monday 5 October on cutting dollar use.

— Why it matters Uruguayans who kept savings in dollar demand deposits lost on average about 6% a year of local buying power from 1972 to 2026.

— The numbers In July 2026, 72% of private non-financial deposits were in foreign currency, down from about 90% in the early 2000s, according to the BCU.

— The US link The BCU pays banks the top of the US Federal Reserve’s rate range minus 1.5 points on reserves for residents’ dollar demand deposits.

— Still open A third round of reserve changes is planned, tied to how market rates and bank lending respond, with no date given.

A new Uruguay central bank paper tells savers that the US dollar has been a poor home for their money. The Banco Central del Uruguay (BCU) says dollar deposits lost about 6% a year in local buying power since 1972.

The paper, published on Monday 5 October, sets out a four-part plan to reduce the economy’s heavy reliance on the dollar. For Americans, it shows how Uruguay’s banks are tied to US Federal Reserve rates, and why property there is often priced in dollars.

What the Central Bank Found

The dollar share of private deposits fell from about 90% in the early 2000s to 72% in July 2026, the Uruguay central bank paper says. Over the past year, it dropped about 3 percentage points, or 2.3 points once exchange-rate swings are stripped out.

Loans moved much faster: more than half of bank credit is now in pesos. Over 60% of public debt is in local currency too, up from under 10% in the early 2000s.

The bank says dollarisation is no longer mainly a threat to financial stability, since currency mismatches have shrunk and banks hold huge dollar buffers.

Instead, it calls dollarisation “a restriction on financial development” and, through that, on economic growth.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Uruguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Dollar Savers Lost Out

For a Uruguayan saving in foreign currency, the paper puts the chance of losing local buying power above 60% at every horizon studied. That chance rises from 63% over one month to 80% over 10 years and 93% over 12 years.

Those odds come from data running from March 1972 to June 2026, and they leave out interest. The paper notes that most dollar deposits already earn rates close to zero.

The value of dollar savings also swung far more. From 2005 to 2026, the yearly change in their local buying power had a standard deviation of 9.8%, against 1.5% for peso deposits.

The weekly paper Búsqueda noted that the BCU repeats arguments made by its president, Guillermo Tolosa, against saving in dollars while earning in pesos. The paper itself calls the habit “a puzzle from an economic point of view”.

The US Dollar Link

Uruguay’s banking system still runs heavily on foreign currency. Foreign-currency liabilities make up about 69% of the total, against a median of 20% among countries with a similar credit rating, the BCU says.

Banks must park part of their deposits at the central bank as reserves. Since September, the Uruguay central bank pays the top of the Fed’s rate range minus 1.5 points on reserves for residents’ dollar demand deposits.

The Fed raised that range to 3.75% to 4% on 16 September, so the payment now works out to about 2.5% a year. It was cut by half a point in March and again in September.

On the peso side, reserves on deposits of more than 30 days fell to zero in March. The requirement on peso demand deposits dropped step by step from 15% to 12% by September.

Rating agencies S&P Global Ratings, Fitch Ratings and Moody’s have all flagged dollarisation as a challenge, the paper says. Fitch said in September 2025 that reducing it could help lift Uruguay’s credit rating.

What It Means for You

People opening a dollar deposit in Uruguay now receive a specific notice on exchange-rate risk, in force since 1 October, the BCU said. The rule itself was issued in August, and existing dollar account holders are to be notified personally.

Citing the INE, Uruguay’s statistics institute, the paper says about 16% of consumer prices carry some dollar link. About 8% are set directly in dollars.

Taxes also favour the peso. Under the personal income tax, interest on fixed-rate peso deposits under one year is taxed at 5.5%, against 12% on foreign-currency deposits.

Banks also need more capital for dollar loans to households and to firms in sectors that do not earn foreign currency. Risk weights rose by 50%, up to a 150% ceiling, with exporters and other dollar earners exempt.

Property is the next target. The BCU wants homes built under the “promoted housing” (vivienda promovida) regime priced in pesos, especially in inflation-linked units (UI), the paper says.

What Is Not Known

A third stage of reserve changes is planned, with lower peso requirements and a further cut in pay on dollar reserves. The BCU says it depends on how lending and market rates respond, and gives no date.

The paper also says a decree requiring prices to be advertised in pesos is being evaluated, following Peru’s example. It gives no timetable for that decision.

In the cases the paper studied abroad, cutting excess dollarisation substantially took between 9 and 16 years. The BCU stresses that Uruguayans remain free to choose the currency they save and borrow in.

The next test comes on Thursday 8 October, when the BCU’s monetary policy committee reviews its 5.75% policy rate. Búsqueda reported that the bank will weigh a possible change that day.

More: Uruguay news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can people still keep their savings in US dollars in Uruguay?

Yes. The Uruguay central bank says its strategy preserves people’s freedom to choose the currency they save, borrow and pay in. Since 1 October, people opening a dollar deposit receive a specific notice on exchange-rate risk.

How much of Uruguay’s savings is in dollars?

According to the Uruguay central bank, 72% of private non-financial deposits were in foreign currency in July 2026. That share was about 90% in the early 2000s.

Why does the US Federal Reserve matter to Uruguayan banks?

The central bank pays banks on reserves held against residents’ dollar demand deposits at the top of the Fed’s rate range minus 1.5 percentage points. When the Fed moves, that payment moves with it.

Is Uruguay’s banking system at risk?

The Uruguay central bank calls the system solid against the dollarisation that remains, with capital about double the legal minimum. In a test assuming a 20% loss on dollar loans to firms that sell mainly at home, all banks stayed above the minimum.

Sources: Banco Central del Uruguay: policy paper “Uruguay: Profundización financiera en moneda nacional” (PDF), 5 October 2026; Banco Central del Uruguay: press release on the policy paper, 5 October 2026; Banco Central del Uruguay: agenda, monetary policy committee meeting, 8 October 2026; Banco Central del Uruguay: monetary policy committee communiqués, 18 August 2026; Banco Central del Uruguay: Tolosa in Salto, 25 September 2026; US Federal Reserve: FOMC statement, 16 September 2026; Búsqueda: Desdolarización, Banco Central defiende su campaña a favor del peso, 5 October 2026; Búsqueda: La inflación se aceleró en setiembre, 5 October 2026; El Observador: Ahorrar en dólares, el análisis del BCU, 6 October 2026.

World.content:

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS 2026

Runoff · Sunday, 25 October Flávio Bolsonaro vs Lula: what happens next First-round results, how the runoff works, the key dates and who backs whom, in one guide. Read the runoff guide →

Key Facts — The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, holds runoffs on Sunday 25 October for president and for governors who missed 50% of valid votes.

— What happened Former Rio governor Anthony Garotinho dropped his appeal on Monday 5 October; on Tuesday, electoral prosecutors asked the court to accept that step.

— The numbers Without Garotinho’s 274,411 annulled votes, Douglas Ruas of Jair Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party has 50.88% of valid votes, enough to win outright.

— Who decides Justice Floriano de Azevedo Marques of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) can accept the withdrawal alone or refer it to the full court.

— Prediction markets Polymarket gives Douglas Ruas a 95.2% chance of becoming Rio de Janeiro governor (6 October, 4:54 p.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 85% and Kalshi at 85% (Lula: 15% and 16% ), as of 6 October, 7:20 pm ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

— Still open No date is set for the decision, and the left-wing PSOL party has asked the court to keep Garotinho’s votes in the count.

The Rio governor runoff set for Sunday 25 October may not take place. On Tuesday, Brazil’s electoral prosecutors backed former Rio de Janeiro governor Anthony Garotinho’s request to drop his court appeal, Agência Brasil and g1 reported.

If the court accepts, Douglas Ruas of Jair Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) wins Rio, Brazil’s third-most-populous state, in the first round. That would hand a key state to the party of Trump ally Bolsonaro, after Donald Trump praised Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round result.

Why Garotinho’s Votes Decide the Race

A first-round win needs more than half of valid votes. Blank and spoiled ballots do not count, Agência Brasil noted.

The electoral court’s official results give Ruas 4,271,199 votes and Eduardo Paes 3,706,984. Garotinho’s 274,411 votes are listed as annulled, pending a final ruling.

With those votes left in the total, Ruas has 49.27% and would face a governor runoff. With them removed, his share rises to 50.88% of the 8,394,627 valid votes.

Rio’s regional electoral court rejected Garotinho’s candidacy in September under the Clean Slate Law, which bars politicians with certain convictions for eight years. It cited a 2018 conviction for administrative misconduct.

On Friday 2 October, TSE Justice Floriano de Azevedo Marques ordered Garotinho’s votes recorded as annulled pending a final ruling. His name stayed on the voting machines because the regional ruling came after the system closed.

On Monday afternoon, Garotinho said he was giving up the appeal freely and irrevocably, citing the result at the ballot box, Agência Brasil reported. His vote share of 3.17% left him third.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Brazil Elections 2026 Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Prosecutors Asked the Court

On Monday, Justice Floriano gave the electoral prosecutor’s office two days to give its view, Agência Brasil reported. The office answered on Tuesday 6 October.

Vice Prosecutor-General for Elections Alexandre Espinosa asked the court to accept the withdrawal, g1 reported. As a fallback, he asked it to reject Garotinho’s appeal, which would also keep the votes annulled.

Espinosa noted that the TSE normally bars dropping such appeals after an election, because the voters’ will is at stake. He argued this case is an exception, since a ruling on the merits would lead to the same result.

Justice Floriano can now accept the withdrawal alone or take it to the full court. If it is accepted, the votes are retotalled and Rio’s regional court can proclaim Ruas elected, Agência Brasil reported.

The left-wing Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), whose candidate came fourth, has asked the TSE to keep Garotinho’s votes in the count. Its Rio branch filed the request on the night of 5 October, Metrópoles reported.

Who the Candidates Are

Douglas Ruas, 37, is a state lawmaker and speaker of Rio’s state assembly, Gazeta do Povo reported. He runs for the Liberal Party, the conservative party of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Eduardo Paes, a former mayor of the city of Rio de Janeiro, runs for the centrist Social Democratic Party (PSD), led by Gilberto Kassab. His coalition includes President Lula’s left-wing Workers’ Party (PT).

On Sunday night, Paes said a governor runoff would show what the fight is about, Gazeta do Povo reported. “It will not be Flávio Bolsonaro and it will not be Lula who governs Rio de Janeiro,” he said.

Ruas asked the TSE for a quick and final decision. “We trust in the courts,” he said, according to the same report.

Garotinho, of the Republicanos party, was Rio’s governor from 1999 to 2002. His wife, Rosinha Garotinho, succeeded him from 2003 to 2007, Agência Brasil noted.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bets give Ruas a 95.2% chance of becoming Rio’s governor (6 October, 4:54 p.m. ET), down 1.1 points in 24 hours. About US$711,000 has been bet on that market.

In the national race, the same platform gives Flávio Bolsonaro an 84.2% chance of beating Lula on 25 October (6 October, 4:54 p.m. ET).

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro 84.5% · Lula 14.5% (US$175 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 85% · Lula 16% As of 6 October, 7:20 pm ET (00:20 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

Rio’s governor runs the state police and state finances in the home of Petrobras, the state-controlled oil company. A first-round win would end Rio’s own race three weeks early.

Travellers face no change for now. The US State Department rates Brazil at Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, in its travel advisory.

Rio voters should still plan for 25 October, because the presidential runoff takes place in every state. A 5 October overview of the seven governor runoffs explains the wider map.

What Is Not Known

No date is set for Justice Floriano’s decision. He has not said whether he will rule alone or refer the case to the full court.

It is also unclear how the court will treat the PSOL request. Until it rules, the official tally still lists a governor runoff between Ruas and Paes.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Background: Flávio and Lula Head to Brazil Runoff, 99.9% Counted.

Background: Brazil Tax Reform 2026 Replaces Five Taxes With Two VATs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will Rio de Janeiro hold a governor runoff on 25 October?

It depends on the Superior Electoral Court. If Garotinho’s votes are annulled for good, Douglas Ruas has 50.88% of valid votes and wins outright, and the Rio governor runoff is cancelled.

Why do Garotinho’s votes matter if he came third?

Brazil counts only valid votes. His 274,411 votes are annulled because his candidacy was barred, which shrinks the total and lifts Ruas above 50%.

What did the prosecutors say?

On Tuesday 6 October, Vice Prosecutor-General for Elections Alexandre Espinosa asked the court to accept Garotinho’s withdrawal. Failing that, he asked it to reject the appeal, which also keeps the votes annulled.

Who is Douglas Ruas?

He is a 37-year-old state lawmaker and speaker of Rio’s state assembly, from Jair Bolsonaro’s conservative Liberal Party. He won 4,271,199 votes in the first round on Sunday 4 October.

Does this change the presidential runoff?

No. Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula still meet on 25 October, and Rio’s 12.8 million voters take part either way.

World.content:

PARAGUAY · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Paraguay, a landlocked soy and beef exporter between Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia, holds the lowest US travel-warning level.

— What happened Police arrested Junior Ramón Delvalle Almeida, 30, the main suspect, at about 7:30 a.m. on Tuesday 6 October in Paraguarí department.

— The crime Two young women were abducted after a rodeo festival and shot in the cemetery of Eusebio Ayala before dawn on Monday 28 September.

— The victims Rebeca Martínez Aricaye, 28, was killed, and Carolina Raquel Aguilar, 32, was still in intensive care on Tuesday.

— The other suspects Police said on Tuesday they hold five people, including Édgar Clodomiro Rodríguez Merlo, 28, and Alcides Osorio, 39.

— For US visitors Washington rates Paraguay Level 1, and the central departments in this case are not among the five it flags for crime.

— Still open Ballistic tests must still show who fired, and all suspects are presumed innocent until a court rules.

Police in Paraguay arrested the main suspect in a cemetery killing on Tuesday 6 October, eight days after the attack on two young women. Officers found Junior Ramón Delvalle Almeida, the last fugitive in the case, at a rural bus stop south-east of the capital, Última Hora reported.

The attack took place in central Paraguay, outside the five departments that the US State Department flags for crime. Washington still rates the country at Level 1, calling it “generally a safe destination for travelers”.

How the Cemetery Killing Unfolded

The two women were riding a motorcycle after a jineteada, a rural rodeo festival, early on Monday 28 September. At about 5 a.m. a white Toyota Fortuner SUV rammed them, and the attackers forced both into the vehicle, Última Hora reported.

About 20 minutes later both were shot inside the cemetery of Eusebio Ayala, a town east of the capital. Rebeca Martínez Aricaye died, and Carolina Raquel Aguilar survived with serious wounds.

Eusebio Ayala lies in the Cordillera department, and the cemetery killing drew wide coverage in Paraguay’s national press. Prosecutors first treated it as a femicide, then reclassified it as aggravated homicide, Última Hora reported on Thursday 1 October.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Paraguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Police Say About the Motive

Abel Cantero, head of the National Police homicide investigation department, set out the police theory of the motive in a radio interview. “Their aim was to kill the two girls,” he told the station 650 AM, as quoted by Hoy.

Cantero said the trouble began at the festival, when someone pushed one of the suspects, Alcides Osorio, alias Ka’i, in the chest. On the drive to the attack, Delvalle allegedly said he would not accept disrespect towards friends he had invited to his town.

According to Cantero, the group set out to find Martínez’s former boyfriend, the man in the festival dispute, and found the two women instead. Martínez recognised Delvalle and called him by name, and the attackers then shot the women to leave no witnesses, he said.

At a police news conference on Tuesday, officers called the cemetery killing revenge for a shove on the dance floor. Police now suspect that Delvalle fired the shots, but the head of the organised crime department said they still lacked “concrete proof”, NPY reported.

That differs from the prosecutors’ charge sheet, which named Rodríguez Merlo and a still-unidentified man as the gunmen. It cast Delvalle as the man who gave the orders, and both he and Rodríguez Merlo were charged as co-perpetrators, according to Última Hora.

The Manhunt and the Arrests

Rodríguez Merlo, alias Chule, whom the charge sheet names as one of the gunmen, was caught on the morning of Monday 5 October. Police found him at a guesthouse in Valle Pe, in the Borja district of Guairá department.

Before the capture, gunmen fired M4 rifles at officers from a white Kia Sportage, ABC Color reported. The suspects fled into woodland, and police then closed a cordon around Rodríguez Merlo.

After the attack, Rodríguez Merlo cut off the electronic ankle tag that monitored him, which led to an international arrest warrant. Its GPS records placed him at the festival, on the road where the women were seized and inside the cemetery, according to ABC Color.

Police detained José Quintín Velázquez Martínez, 44, after a clash in Borja on Sunday night, Última Hora reported. Ka’i, 39, was caught in woodland in Guairá on Monday.

Police said on Tuesday that Velázquez and a fifth detainee, Braian Matías Funes Galeano, 26, allegedly helped the main suspects hide and flee.

Delvalle, the last man sought, was arrested on Tuesday morning after an anonymous tip, Última Hora said.

“He did not resist,” said Emilio Alvarenga, an officer at the police station in Tebicuarymí, in Paraguarí department. He added that Delvalle was unarmed and cooperated throughout.

Speaking to reporters after his arrest, Delvalle denied any part in the attack. “At no time did I go near that girl, or even greet her,” he said, ABC Color reported.

He said he left the festival in a Kia Sportage, not in the white Fortuner that investigators link to the abduction.

Police also suspect Delvalle of leading a gang of robbers. He was wanted over an attempted robbery of a cash truck on 1 July, Última Hora reported.

Prosecutor Norma Salinas of the Public Ministry, Paraguay’s state prosecution service, is handling the cemetery killing case.

What It Means for You

The US State Department last updated its Paraguay advice on 19 August 2026, rating the country Level 1, “exercise normal precautions”. It asks for increased caution only in Alto Paraná, Amambay, Canindeyú, Concepción and San Pedro.

The department says criminal groups in those areas smuggle weapons, drugs and other goods along the northeastern border with Brazil. Cordillera, Paraguarí and Guairá, where the cemetery killing and the manhunt played out, are not on that list.

The same advisory bars US government employees from using municipal buses in Paraguay because of the risk of robbery and assault. Visitors who attend rural events at night should arrange known transport and avoid isolated roads after the event ends.

The manhunt ran in the same days as Paraguay’s municipal elections on Sunday 4 October, which elected mayors and councils nationwide.

What Is Not Known

Who fired the shots in the cemetery killing is not settled, since the charge sheet and the police account point to different gunmen. Ballistic tests on a seized weapon are still under way, according to police.

No ruling on pretrial detention for Delvalle had been reported by Tuesday evening, although prosecutors requested it when they charged him. Rodríguez Merlo stayed silent when reporters questioned him at police headquarters in Asunción, ABC Color reported.

Última Hora and NPY placed Delvalle’s arrest near Tebicuarymí, while Hoy, La Nación and ABC Color named La Colmena. Both towns lie in Paraguarí department, south-east of Asunción.

Carolina Raquel Aguilar, the survivor of the cemetery killing, was still in intensive care at the Trauma Hospital in Asunción on Tuesday. Doctors have not disclosed her prognosis.

More: Paraguay news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Eusebio Ayala?

Two young women were abducted after a rural festival and shot in the town cemetery before dawn on Monday 28 September. In the cemetery killing, Rebeca Martínez Aricaye died and Carolina Raquel Aguilar was seriously wounded.

Who has been arrested in the cemetery killing?

Police said on Tuesday they hold five people. They name Delvalle, Rodríguez Merlo and Alcides Osorio as the main suspects, and two men as helpers in their escape. All are presumed innocent until a court rules.

Who fired the shots in the cemetery killing?

That is not settled. The prosecutors’ charge sheet names Rodríguez Merlo and an unidentified man, while police said on Tuesday that Delvalle may have fired, pending ballistic tests.

Is Paraguay safe for American travellers?

The US State Department rates Paraguay Level 1, its lowest warning, and calls it generally safe. It urges more caution in five northern and eastern departments because of organised crime and smuggling.

Where is Eusebio Ayala?

Eusebio Ayala is a town in the Cordillera department, east of Asunción. It lies outside the areas the US government flags for crime.

World.content:

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic shares the Caribbean island of Hispaniola with Haiti and its beach resorts draw large numbers of US visitors.

— What happened Police spokesman Colonel Diego Pesqueira said neither the police nor the government has a guideline to kill wanted suspects (Diario Libre, Tuesday 6 October).

— The numbers Of 125 homicides the National Police reported for September, 55, or 44%, were deaths in alleged exchanges of gunfire with officers.

— Why it matters to Americans The deaths occurred across the country, including Verón-Punta Cana, the eastern resort area popular with US visitors.

— The trend Homicides rose 34.4% from September 2025 while robberies fell 38.6%. The January to September homicide rate was 7.35 per 100,000 people.

— Still open Whether prosecutors will investigate any of the September deaths, and whether the pace continues in October.

Dominican police deny that officers have orders to kill wanted suspects, after 55 people died in alleged shootouts with officers in September. That was 44% of the 125 homicides recorded in the Caribbean country last month.

The denial matters to American visitors and to the large Dominican community in the United States. Deaths were recorded from Verón-Punta Cana, the eastern resort area, to the Haitian border.

What the Police Spokesman Said

Colonel Diego Pesqueira is the spokesman of the National Police, the country’s main police force. “Neither the National Police nor the government has a guideline to that effect,” he said in remarks reported by Diario Libre.

He was asked about criticism of putting people “en 29”, slang for the deaths of young people in alleged shootouts with officers. Several organisations have questioned the practice, Diario Libre noted.

Pesqueira said more than 120 people wanted on arrest warrants had turned themselves in since September, many through the police press office. All were placed before the justice system, he said.

Officers use “a proportional use of force” against suspects who resist arrest with weapons, Pesqueira added. Any case that raises doubts goes to the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which investigates crimes in the Dominican Republic.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the September Figures Show

The National Police counted 125 homicides in September, 34.4% more than in September 2025, in figures released on Monday 5 October. Of these, 55 were deaths in alleged shootouts with officers, which police classify as “legal action”.

Another 42 killings grew out of personal disputes, which police classify as social conflicts. Dominican police said those killed by officers were allegedly linked to crime and wanted on arrest warrants.

The deaths spread over at least 12 provinces and the capital district, from La Altagracia in the far east to Dajabón on the Haitian border. The same report lists 1,476 arrest warrants executed and 448 firearms seized in September.

On Tuesday 6 October, Dominican police said Estarlin Emilio Rodríguez Ramos died after allegedly firing at detectives in Sabana Iglesia, Santiago province. He was the second man killed in an alleged shootout with police in Santiago in under 24 hours, Diario Libre reported.

Why the Deaths Are Disputed

The police version of these deaths is contested. Legal groups have already demanded independent investigations of Dominican police killings.

At the president’s weekly press conference in late September, police director Major General Ernesto Rodríguez García spoke of a list of suspected repeat offenders. He said the force aims to find them before they offend again.

President Luis Abinader, of the social-democratic Modern Revolutionary Party (PRM), used the same press conference to warn wanted criminals to surrender. Pesqueira cited more than 120 surrenders since September to back his denial.

What It Means for You

The US State Department rates the Dominican Republic at Level 2, “exercise increased caution”, on a scale of 1 to 4. Its travel advisory warns that violent crime is a concern “despite more police presence in areas often visited by tourists.”

Dominican police describe those killed in September as suspects wanted on arrest warrants. For travellers, the more relevant figure is street crime: robberies fell 38.6% from September 2025 to 4,214 cases.

Homicides from January to September were 5.8% below the same period of 2025, even though September alone was up 34.4%. The police put the homicide rate for the first nine months at 7.35 per 100,000 people, down 15.9% from a year earlier.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether prosecutors have opened inquiries into any of the 55 September deaths. It is also not known who is on the police list of suspected repeat offenders.

Dominican police shared the September breakdown in a press note and later withdrew it, Diario Libre reported. Why it did so is not known.

It is also unclear whether the pace will continue in October. The body of the man killed in Sabana Iglesia was sent to the National Institute of Forensic Sciences for an autopsy.

More: Dominican Republic news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does “en 29” mean in the Dominican Republic?

It is slang for the death of a suspect, usually a young person, in what police call an exchange of gunfire. Several organisations have questioned the practice, and the police deny any order behind it.

How many people did Dominican police kill in September 2026?

Dominican police figures reported by Diario Libre show 55 deaths in alleged shootouts with officers in September. That was 44% of the 125 homicides recorded that month.

Is the Dominican Republic safe for American tourists?

The US State Department keeps the country at Level 2, exercise increased caution, citing violent crime. In September, robberies fell 38.6% from a year earlier while homicides rose 34.4%, and police describe those killed by officers as wanted suspects.

World.title: World Bank Lifts Mexico Growth Forecast to 1.4%
World.content:

MEXICO · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Mexico is one of Latin America’s two largest economies; the US bought US$419.3 billion of its goods in January–August 2026.

— What happened On Tuesday 6 October, the World Bank raised its Mexico growth forecast for 2026 to 1.4%, from 1.3% in April.

— The numbers The bank now expects 1.8% growth in 2027 and 2.2% in 2028, after an estimated 0.5% in 2025.

— Why it matters to the US The bank says domestic and external policy uncertainty is holding back private investment, as talks on the North American trade pact run into 2027.

— Prediction markets Polymarket’s most-backed range for Mexico’s third-quarter growth, 2.0% to 2.5% year on year, stands at 29.5% (6 October, 4:46 p.m. ET).

— Still open How the 2027 review of the USMCA trade pact ends, and whether US tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminium are cut.

The World Bank raised its Mexico growth forecast on Tuesday 6 October and now expects the economy to expand 1.4% in 2026, up from 1.3%. Even so, Mexico is the second-slowest of the six large Latin American economies the bank groups together.

The Mexico growth forecast matters to Americans: the US bought US$419.3 billion of Mexican goods from January to August 2026, Census Bureau data show. The bank says trade policy friction and uncertainty are still holding back private investment in Mexico.

What the World Bank Said About Mexico

The World Bank is a Washington-based development lender owned by its member governments. Its Latin America and the Caribbean Economic Update, published in April and October, sets out growth forecasts for most countries in the region.

In the October edition, the Mexico growth forecast is 1.4% for 2026, 1.8% for 2027 and 2.2% for 2028. In April it had expected 1.3% for 2026 and 1.7% for 2027.

The bank also trimmed its estimate for 2025 to 0.5%, from 0.6% in April. Its figures use data available up to Wednesday 23 September 2026.

“In Mexico, growth remains modest, with private investment constrained by both domestic and external policy uncertainty,” the report says. It adds that large public infrastructure projects are giving the economy less of a lift than before.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Mexico Compares in Latin America

The bank expects Latin America and the Caribbean to grow 2.2% in 2026, broadly in line with 2.4% in 2025. Among the six biggest economies, it sees Peru growing 3.2%, Colombia 2.3%, and Argentina and Brazil 2.1% each.

Only Chile, at 0.8%, has a weaker 2026 outlook in that group, so the Mexico growth forecast ranks second-lowest. The bank says Brazil and Mexico are growing at or below the regional average.

It blames “tight monetary conditions needed to continue disinflation, policy uncertainty, and fading public investment impulses.” In plain terms, high interest rates, uncertainty over policy and smaller government building programmes are all slowing growth.

The region “has the potential to achieve stronger and more ambitious growth,” said Susana Cordeiro Guerra, the World Bank’s vice president for the region. She urged “consistent policies and investment” to raise productivity and incomes.

Why Trade With the US Weighs on Mexico

The bank says trade policy friction is damping confidence in Mexico, where domestic demand remains constrained. Mexico’s trade with the US runs under the USMCA, the pact linking the US, Mexico and Canada.

On Monday 5 October, the US Trade Representative’s office, the White House trade agency, opened public comments ahead of the pact’s 2027 joint review. At the first review in July 2026, the US did not agree to extend the deal for another 16 years, Proceso reported.

Economy minister Marcelo Ebrard said in a radio interview Mexico’s main goal is cutting US tariffs on cars, steel and aluminium, La Jornada reported. He said Mexico cannot accept higher tariffs or stricter origin rules than rivals such as Japan, Korea and the European Union.

Trade has held up despite the friction: Mexico’s exports to the US hit a record in August. The bank also notes that Mexico’s proximity to the US makes it a natural hub for data centres serving US customers.

What Prediction Markets Say

Bettors on Polymarket are pricing Mexico’s third-quarter growth, a separate measure from the World Bank’s yearly Mexico growth forecast. The most-backed range for Mexico’s third-quarter growth, 2.0% to 2.5% from a year earlier, stood at 29.5% at 4:46 p.m. ET on 6 October.

The 2.5% to 3.0% and 3.0% to 3.5% ranges were close behind at 27.5% each. The 3.0% to 3.5% range jumped 15.5 points in 24 hours.

About US$43,600 has been bet on the market. It settles on the quick estimate from INEGI, Mexico’s statistics institute, which the market’s rules date to Friday 30 October.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For US investors and companies with plants in Mexico, the higher Mexico growth forecast signals steady but slow growth, not a slump. The upgrade is small, though, and the bank still places Mexico near the bottom of the region’s big economies.

The catch is private investment, which pays for new factories and jobs. The bank links weak private investment to policy uncertainty at home and abroad, so the trade talks with Washington remain the main thing to watch.

What Is Not Known

The bank does not say how its Mexico growth forecast would change if the USMCA review fails or if US tariffs rise again. Its numbers include only data up to 23 September, so later news is not reflected.

No deal to cut the US tariffs on Mexican cars, steel and aluminium has been announced. The next official growth figure is INEGI’s quick estimate for the third quarter, which the betting market expects on 30 October.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the World Bank’s Mexico growth forecast for 2026?

The World Bank’s Mexico growth forecast for 2026 is 1.4%, up from the 1.3% it expected in April. It sees 1.8% growth in 2027 and 2.2% in 2028.

Why is Mexico’s economy growing slowly?

The World Bank cites policy uncertainty at home and abroad, trade friction and high interest rates. It also says large public infrastructure projects are giving less of a lift than before.

How does Mexico’s outlook affect the United States?

The US bought US$419.3 billion of Mexican goods from January to August 2026, so Mexican demand and supply chains matter to US firms. The 2027 review of the USMCA trade pact will shape that trade.

World.content:

CUBA · SOCIETY

Key Facts — The country Cuba is a one-party communist state under a US trade embargo, in a deep economic crisis marked by blackouts.

— What happened A US government aid shipment of 700 food kits and 700 hygiene kits landed in Santa Clara on Tuesday morning, 6 October.

— Who gets it Vulnerable families in the Catholic Diocese of Ciego de Ávila, starting in the parish of Gaspar, according to Cáritas Cuba.

— The US angle The kits come from a US$100 million US aid fund; Cuba’s Catholic Church channels US$60 million of it, Cáritas says.

— Who hands it out Trained Cáritas volunteers deliver the kits directly to families chosen by vulnerability, such as people over 60 and children under 5.

— Still open How many families in the diocese will be reached, and how much of the US$100 million has been spent so far.

A new shipment of US aid landed in Cuba on Tuesday morning, 6 October, for poor families in central Ciego de Ávila province. The 700 food kits and 700 hygiene kits arrived at Abel Santamaría International Airport in Santa Clara, the Catholic charity Cáritas Cuba said.

For Americans, the cargo shows how part of the US taxpayer money set aside for Cubans reaches them: through the Catholic Church’s charity network. It is part of a US$100 million US aid fund, of which Cuba’s Catholic Church channels US$60 million, according to Cáritas.

What Landed in Santa Clara

Cáritas Cuba is the Catholic Church’s social and charity arm on the island. Its statement on Tuesday said the cargo came from the US government and was meant for the families in greatest need.

Father Dariusz Chalupczynski, who heads the Ciego de Ávila diocese, and Roberto Armas Carbonell, the diocese’s Cáritas director, received it. They oversaw the unloading together with airport staff and volunteers, Cáritas said.

Santa Clara is the capital of Villa Clara province in central Cuba, west of Ciego de Ávila. Handouts will begin in the parish of Gaspar, which the Church had identified in advance.

Priority goes to people over 60, people with disabilities or who are bedridden, pregnant or breastfeeding women and children under five. Cáritas volunteers, trained beforehand, will deliver the kits directly to the selected families.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Cuba Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the US$100 Million Fund Works

Cáritas describes the fund as US$100 million in humanitarian assistance approved by the US administration to support the Cuban people. The Catholic Church in Cuba channels US$60 million of it, the charity says.

CiberCuba, an independent Cuban news site, reported that the US$60 million runs through Cáritas Cuba and Catholic Relief Services, a US-based Catholic aid agency.

According to CiberCuba, the remaining US$40 million of US aid is handled by independent organisations.

The Church has stressed that Cáritas does not receive the money in cash, CiberCuba added. The funds buy the food and hygiene goods and pay for getting them to the families.

In the town of Nuevitas, each kit came with a printed list of its contents and contacts for complaints, Cáritas said on Friday 2 October.

Part of a Wider Rollout

The same airport handled earlier US shipments of the same size, 700 food kits and 700 hygiene kits, Cáritas said. They went to the Diocese of Santa Clara on Thursday 10 September and the Diocese of Cienfuegos on Thursday 17 September.

Camagüey, the next province to the east, received its first 700 kits at its own airport on Thursday 1 October, Cáritas Camagüey said. Volunteers then began handing out 400 kits in Nuevitas and 300 in the rural community of Lugareño, where 300 families received them.

The Diocese of Holguín-Las Tunas got a US air shipment of 700 food and 700 hygiene kits on Tuesday 29 September, Cáritas reported. It went to families in eastern Cuba hit by Hurricane Melissa, which struck in October 2025.

Near the capital, Cáritas began handing out US kits in the towns of Bejucal and Alquízar on Wednesday 22 July, the charity said. They lie in Mayabeque and Artemisa provinces, next to Havana.

In mid-September, the United States announced new shipments for Camagüey, Ciego de Ávila, Cienfuegos, Matanzas and Pinar del Río, according to CiberCuba. In Matanzas, Cáritas said on 20 September that its volunteers were preparing to reach 18,200 families.

Aid Alongside Pressure

The deliveries run in parallel with heavy US pressure on Cuba’s communist leadership. The United States has kept a trade embargo on the island since the early 1960s.

Ordinary Cubans are struggling. On Tuesday, CiberCuba reported, citing the state newspaper Granma, that blackouts, poor transport and teacher shortages marked the first month of the school year.

On Monday, the Cuban news site Periódico Cubano reported remarks by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a Cuban American from Florida. In a US television interview, he said he hoped some of those who control Cuba’s weapons would open their eyes to reality.

What It Means for You

For Cuban Americans with relatives in Ciego de Ávila, the US aid kits go only to families the Church has already selected by need. The elderly, disabled people, pregnant women and small children come first.

For US taxpayers and policy watchers, each shipment shows a two-track policy at work. Washington is sending part of its help to ordinary Cubans through the Church while keeping up pressure on the government in Havana.

What Is Not Known

The number of families in Ciego de Ávila who will get kits, and what this batch contains, have not been made public. Nor has a start date for handouts in Gaspar.

Cáritas has not said how much of the US$100 million has been spent so far. Nor has it said how many families the programme has reached across Cuba.

More: Cuba news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who pays for the aid that arrived in Cuba on 6 October?

The US government. Cáritas Cuba says the kits are part of a US$100 million humanitarian fund approved by the US administration.

Who distributes the US aid inside Cuba?

Cáritas Cuba, the Catholic Church’s charity, hands out the kits through trained volunteers. According to CiberCuba, the Church’s share runs through Cáritas Cuba and Catholic Relief Services.

Who receives the kits?

Families the Church selects by vulnerability. Priority goes to people over 60, people with disabilities or who are bedridden, pregnant or breastfeeding women and children under five.

Where else in Cuba has the aid arrived?

Before this shipment, Cáritas reported US aid deliveries in the dioceses of Havana, Santa Clara, Cienfuegos, Holguín-Las Tunas and Camagüey. The US also announced shipments for Matanzas and Pinar del Río in mid-September, CiberCuba reported.

World.content:

GUATEMALA · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Guatemala borders Mexico and ranks 128th of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index of Reporters Without Borders (RSF).

— What happened Local reporter Evelio López Sánchez, 34, was shot dead on the night of Friday 2 October in San Pedro Necta, in Huehuetenango department.

— The response On Tuesday 6 October the government promised to finish its press protection mechanism for journalists this year and then publish it.

— The US angle The US Embassy condemned the killing on Monday 5 October, and the State Department tells Americans not to travel to Huehuetenango.

— The pattern RSF counts him as the second journalist killed in Guatemala in 2026, after Carlos Humberto Cal Ical in April.

— Still open Prosecutors had announced no arrest warrants by Tuesday 6 October, and the Interior Ministry says the motive has yet to be established.

Guatemala’s government promised on Tuesday 6 October to finish a long-delayed press protection plan for journalists this year and then publish it. The pledge came four days after a local reporter was shot dead in Huehuetenango, a department on the Mexican border.

The US Embassy in Guatemala City condemned the killing on Monday 5 October, noting the reporter had received death threats over his work. The State Department already tells Americans not to travel to Huehuetenango, the department where he died.

What Happened in San Pedro Necta

Evelio López Sánchez ran Huehue Es Noticias HNT2, a local news page on Facebook. He was also a sports commentator and an active member of the Huehuetenango Press Association (APEHUE), a professional group of local reporters.

He was shot on the night of Friday 2 October while heading home in San Pedro Necta, a municipality in Huehuetenango, according to RSF. The press freedom group said he had spoken publicly about threats linked to his journalism and was the father of a young daughter.

The killing set off unrest in the town. Residents demanding an arrest set fire to the local police substation, a house and a pickup truck, Prensa Libre reported.

The National Civil Police (PNC), Guatemala’s national police force, sent officers from elsewhere in Huehuetenango and from Quetzaltenango, plus a riot squad. It called for calm and said its investigation was under way, Prensa Libre reported.

APEHUE filed a complaint with the special prosecutor for crimes against journalists at the Public Ministry (MP), Guatemala’s prosecution service, in Quetzaltenango. That office has since given protection measures to several reporters in San Pedro Necta, APEHUE’s president told RSF.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Guatemala Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Washington and Press Groups Demand Answers

“We deeply regret the murder of journalist Evelio López Sánchez in Huehuetenango,” the US Embassy wrote on social media on Monday 5 October. It noted that he “had received death threats related to his journalistic work” and sent condolences to his family, colleagues and APEHUE.

“A free society needs a press that reports without threats, without fear and without self-censorship,” the embassy added, as quoted by Prensa Libre. It said it hoped the case would be solved and those responsible held to account.

The Inter American Press Association (IAPA), which groups news outlets across the Americas, urged an exhaustive, timely and transparent investigation. Reporters Without Borders, the Paris-based group known as RSF, asked prosecutors to treat a professional motive as a priority line of inquiry.

Artur Romeu, RSF’s director for Latin America, said the investigation “must take into account the threats he had received” because of his reporting. He also urged protection for local reporters before the 2027 general and municipal elections.

RSF said Carlos Humberto Cal Ical, an independent reporter, was killed on 26 April 2026 in San Cristóbal Verapaz, in northern Guatemala. Ismael Alonzo González, who ran a local news page in Quetzaltenango, was killed on 21 March 2025.

The Government’s Promise

The government of President Bernardo Arévalo, a centre-left anti-corruption reformer who took office in January 2024, responded on Tuesday. It condemned the killing and told executive agencies to help solve the crime and capture those responsible, the state news agency AGN reported.

The presidential communications office told La Hora that the protection plan is in a final round of review with groups that work on reporters’ safety. “The commitment is to conclude this process during this year and move forward with its publication,” it said.

The government also urged journalists who face threats to file a complaint with the Interior Ministry, so that protection measures can be activated, AGN said.

The plan, formally the Protection Mechanism for Journalists, is being drafted by COPADEH, the presidential commission for peace and human rights. The promise is not new: Arévalo’s then communications secretary, Santiago Palomo, said on 21 April 2025 that a press protection policy was nearly finished.

Palomo said again on 5 May 2025 that the policy would be presented “soon”. Seventeen months later, the government says the press protection plan is still in final review.

What It Means for You

The State Department rates Guatemala at Level 3, “reconsider travel,” in an advisory issued on Thursday 12 March 2026. On Huehuetenango it is blunter: “Do not travel to Huehuetenango Department for any reason.”

The same do-not-travel warning, citing the risk of crime and terrorism, covers San Marcos department, Zone 18 of Guatemala City and Villa Nueva. Huehuetenango is a border region where, two Guatemalan journalists told RSF, drug trafficking, people smuggling and local political interests converge.

US government employees and their families cannot go to Huehuetenango for personal travel, the advisory adds.

Popular destinations such as Antigua, Lake Atitlán and Tikal are not on the do-not-travel list, and US government staff may visit them, the advisory says. The Rio Times guide to safety in Guatemala explains where the violence is concentrated.

What Is Not Known

Neither prosecutors nor police had confirmed any arrest by Monday evening, La Hora reported. By Tuesday, prosecutors had still announced no arrest warrants and had not said whether they link the killing to the threats.

Guatemala’s Interior Ministry, which runs the police, says the investigation must establish the motive. It added that any accusation against possible suspects must rest on evidence.

It is also unclear whether López had formally reported the threats he described. APEHUE’s president, Estefany Martínez, has asked for that to be checked, and the group criticised prosecutors for reaching the scene only the next morning.

The government has given no publication date for the press protection mechanism, only the aim of finishing it “this year”. COPADEH had not answered La Hora’s questions about when and how it will be published.

More: Guatemala news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was the journalist killed in Guatemala on 2 October?

Evelio López Sánchez, 34, ran the local news page Huehue Es Noticias HNT2 in Huehuetenango. He was shot dead while heading home in San Pedro Necta, and after his death the government renewed its press protection pledge.

What did the US Embassy say about the killing?

The embassy said it deeply regretted the murder and noted that López had received death threats over his work. It said a free society needs a press that reports without threats, fear or self-censorship.

What is Guatemala’s press protection mechanism?

It is a planned government press protection system for reporters at risk, drafted by COPADEH, the presidential human rights commission. The government said on 6 October that it aims to finish the review this year and then publish it.

Is it safe to travel to Huehuetenango?

The US State Department tells Americans not to travel to Huehuetenango department because of crime and terrorism. It rates Guatemala as a whole at Level 3, reconsider travel.
