World.title: Kharkiv mayor: No safe place left in the city as winter approaches
World.content:
The northern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv is now targeted by Russian drones as well as missiles, but the city lives on mayor Ihor Terehhov told ERR.

Being just 30 kilometers from the Russian border, Kharkiv has suffered a lot over the past four and a half years but is unbowed and is trying to rebuild what has been destroyed,

The mayor noted the coming winter will be very hard without any "energy truce", but the city survived the last winter and the previous ones too.

Mayor Terehhov was talkng to ERR at a time when Russia has been hitting Kharkiv in lethal strikes involving bombs, missiles and drones.

It is mid-autumn already and winter is approaching. How is Kharkiv preparing, and how did it survive the last winter?

If there is no so-called energy truce — Ukraine ending strikes on Russian oil refineries in exchange for Russia ending attacks on energy and other critical infrastructure in Ukraine, which is currently widely under discussion — then the coming winter will be very hard. We understand that perfectly.

I warned everyone last autumn that the winter would be tough, and so it has turned out to be. The enemy has been destroying energy infrastructure, targeting thermal power plants and water supply, leaving residents without basic utilities.

We all understand this all too well, yet we survived last winter, even though it, too, was hard. Due to the strikes on the power plants, we had not a single megawatt of electricity generation of our own. The heating system was damaged. There had been 50 attacks on electricity and heating networks. So it was a hard winter, but we held out. As for next winter, we are preparing for that too. We have been preparing since 2022.

Two years ago, in our previous interview, you spoke about the need to create energy "islands". What are these islands, and have they been created?

We wouldn't have survived last winter without those energy islands. I can't tell you everything, but if I were Estonia, I would be setting up energy islands too. It is effective. In essence an energy island is an autonomous energy source fed by small boiler houses. People get electricity, heat and water from it.

How many people currently live in Kharkiv? Initially people left, and then, as you said, they began to return. Two years ago you estimated the population at 900,000. Kharkiv has also become a destination for internally displaced people from the front line and occupied areas. What is the trend today?

During the war there have been times when the city's population fell to 350,000 and even to 320,000. But the trend has been positive, and currently around 1.4 million people live in Kharkiv, of whom 225,000 are internally displaced persons. This is a serious challenge for the city — these people have to be resettled and cared for.

Our hospitals cater to these people; their children attend our schools. They have lost everything, and it is our duty to care for them, but they also need help from the state. They have been left homeless, so the state should issue them housing certificates, but so far no state program has been implemented. So there are many challenges we face every day. But the fact that there are 1.4 million people living in Kharkiv today is actually good news.

How is responsibility for internally displaced people divided between the city, the oblast and the central government? Is the city obliged to provide them with housing?

In my view, providing housing for those who have lost everything — that is, internally displaced people — is the state's obligation. I mean a construction program for internally displaced people, so they have the opportunity to get living space where they want. The situation is not like this in Kharkiv alone. Yes, most of our people are displaced from Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. So such a program is needed.

As for Kharkiv residents, we currently have 160,000 people who have been left without shelter. No other major Ukrainian city has suffered destruction like Kharkiv has. As of today, we have 10,000 damaged, severely damaged or completely destroyed residential buildings, but during the war we have managed to repair and restore nearly 4,000 buildings. Of course, the city's budget deficit is very large, and according to government forecasts it will be even larger next year.

Where is the money coming from?

Financial assistance from international partners is required. It is no secret that we depend on funds allocated by our international partners. This is public information; both the president and the government have said so. We have to use state and city budget funds very carefully.

Ihor Terehhov- Source: Tarmo Aarma

On September 28, Russian attack drones destroyed practically the entire stairwell of a multi-story block. Do you have reserve apartments to relocate residents somewhere?

We offered people accommodation in a dorm. Two families initially agreed, but then said they would go to live with relatives. Most of the residents of that building are internally displaced people who were renting apartments there. And now they are looking for other apartments.

For our part, we closed the building shell (a temporary measure where holes in walls and broken windows are covered with plywood — ed.), restored the electricity supply and restarted the heating and water systems. All of this is financed out of the city budget. The victims have been documented and are receiving payments. But the stairwell is still destroyed, from the third floor to the fifth, and with this I think the state should already allocate money for restoration. At first we were restoring everything ourselves at our own expense, but the city budget is already exhausted.

So what is the city's current budget deficit? How much money do you need?

That is a complicated question. You could say there is a deficit, but also say there isn't, depending on how you calculate it. Without reconstruction costs, we are on the edge, but still not in deficit. If we want to carry out the programs we consider necessary, then a deficit comes up. For us, the most important thing is to ensure reconstruction support and that payments are not delayed, as sometimes happens.

I saw three buildings in [residential district of Kharkiv] Saltivka that had been heavily damaged at the start of the war, then repaired, and now they are in order and people are starting to return (apartment repairs are not the city's responsibility but the residents' — ed.). But the Saltivka area is not the safest place in Kharkiv, to put it mildly. Is it worth spending money on rebuilding something that could be destroyed again the very next day?

I am convinced that rebuilding is essential. If we don't do it, people will stay in other countries and not return. People do not come back to places where there is nowhere to live, work or educate their children. We consider it important that Ukrainians, Kharkiv residents, come back from abroad, which means we have to rebuild in any case. Moreover, the current situation is such that a strike can hit practically any Ukrainian city. There is no city in the country so safe that you could say it definitely won't be attacked.

Have you been taking part in international conferences on Ukraine's reconstruction? In June a conference like that took place in Gdansk, Poland; next January one is going to be held in Tallinn.

I was at the Gdansk one. We held a special event and we managed to attract money from international partners, specifically for preparing for the heating season. That meeting was a productive one for Kharkiv.

I was in the Pyatykhatky neighborhood, and anti-drone nets are being installed over the road there. At the same time, some nearby streets are not covered with nets; I saw at least one car destroyed by a drone strike. On what criteria do you decide what to cover with nets and what not to?

The nets are not installed by the city but by the regional military administration, and they are installed where the military says so. Only the military decides where the anti-drone nets get placed. For our part, we are also installing protection against fibre-optic FPV drones. We do this in conjunction with the military, but at the city's expense. This protection is our know-how, developed in cooperation with the military and engineers.

Which places in Kharkiv are currently the most dangerous, and which are the safest?

In Kharkiv, as in the rest of the country, there is no safe place. I can't tell you that Pyatykhatky is dangerous but the city center — say Shevchenkivskyi or Kyivskyi districts — is more or less safe, because at any moment it could be hit by anything, from a missile to an FPV drone. As long as the war continues, nowhere in Ukraine can be a hundred percent safe.

Do you have any advice for your Estonian colleagues — mayors, municipal leaders — on preparing for crises?

Estonia is a sovereign state and we respect that. If you need our advice, there is no problem there. We will talk and show everything as openly as possible, though that information is not intended for the wider public consumption.

World.title: Pay raises drive surge in applications for senior teacher status in Estonia
World.content:
Interest among teachers in obtaining senior‑ and master‑teacher qualifications has grown, as these come with higher salaries. But a larger number of higher‑paid teachers is putting additional pressure on school budgets.

This academic year, a national teacher career model took effect in Estonia, linking qualification levels to salary. Since higher levels bring a pay increase, interest has tripled in just a couple of years.

On Monday — Teachers' Day — the autumn application round ended. As of that day, 170 portfolios had been submitted for senior‑ or master‑teacher qualification.

"Already now we have as many senior‑teacher applications as we had in the entire previous year. We have several rounds, so the number will definitely rise," said Margit Timakov, board member of the Estonian Teachers' Union.

However, not all applications meet the criteria for a higher qualification level.

"It's clear from the portfolio whether a person takes the application seriously or not. When the number of applications grows, the number of rejections grows as well — we still have those who come just to try their luck," Timakov noted.

At Mahtra Basic School, five of the school's 60 teachers are considering applying for senior‑teacher status, and two senior teachers already work there. Mahtra school also pays both senior and master teachers more than one‑third above the national minimum salary. This makes managing the budget more difficult.

"I often wonder how to make ends meet, but in the end it works out. The most important thing is that the person standing in front of the class knows what they're doing and wants to be there. And they want to be there when they receive fair pay," said Mahtra Basic School director Edgar Roditšenko.

At Nõmme Basic School, three teachers are considering a higher career level. For now, there is enough salary funding.

"If you want good teachers, you must also find the finances. As far as I know, we currently have the resources, but what happens when interest grows significantly — that's hard to predict. School leaders are beginning to question how sustainable this system is," said Nõmme Basic School director Õnnela Leedo‑Küngas.

It is also unclear how many higher‑level teachers the education system actually needs.

"We haven't yet analyzed nationally how many master‑teacher‑profile teachers the system requires. Right now, it's trial and error," Timakov said.

World.title: Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center director Hendrik Agur suspected of fraud
World.content:
Hendrik Agur, director of the Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center (IVKHK), has been formally named a suspect in fraud committed as a public official. According to the suspicion, Agur submitted false information to receive compensation for using his personal car.

The Prosecutor's Office confirmed that Agur is suspected of fraud as a public official.

"According to the suspicion, Agur submitted expense‑compensation requests to the Ministry of Education and Research for nearly a year starting in August 2025, claiming reimbursement for personal car use on trips that did not actually take place. The initial suspicion is that he requested compensation amounting to €4,500. He has since repaid the damage caused to the ministry," said lead prosecutor Daniel Toom.

As the criminal investigation is ongoing and evidence collection continues, both the time period covered by the suspicion and the estimated damage amount may still be clarified.

Agur told ERR that he misunderstood the nature of the compensation and has now repaid it.

"The suspicion is justified, and in summary, I submitted false information," Agur said.

"From the beginning, I misunderstood the nature of the car‑use compensation and treated it as part of my salary. But that understanding was incorrect, and I have now repaid the compensation in full," he said, adding that he is cooperating fully with the police.

On Tuesday, Agur sent a letter to colleagues, noting that media coverage about him will likely appear soon, concerning the personal car‑use compensation he received as a school director.

"During job interviews with the school's governing body before I started, I misunderstood the concept of personal car‑use compensation and treated it as a component of monthly salary. From August 2025 to June 2026, I submitted monthly compensation requests in the state employee portal totaling €5,500 (€500 per month)," he wrote.

Agur said he was summoned for questioning by police in early August regarding suspected false information in his compensation requests.

"I realized I had fundamentally misunderstood the nature of the personal car‑use compensation and on 12 August repaid the full amount to the Ministry of Education and Research," he added.

Agur assured colleagues that despite the situation, he remains fully committed to developing the school.

The Ministry of Education and Research is aware of the criminal investigation involving Agur and is cooperating with law‑enforcement authorities.

"Hendrik Agur has acknowledged errors in the travel logs submitted to the ministry, expressed regret over the incident, and repaid the compensation he received," said ministry spokesperson Kersti Ringmets.

She added that the ministry's priority is ensuring stability at the Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center and continuity in the transition to Estonian‑language education. If new circumstances emerge during the investigation, the ministry will take them into account in future decisions.

The ministry will also review its internal control and oversight systems in connection with the case.

Agur took office as director of the IVKHK on 1 August 2025. Before that, he served as director of Kohtla‑Järve High School.

World.title: Risky maneuvers preceded deadly 2025 helicopter crash in Finland
World.content:
The investigation into the helicopter crash in Finland that killed five people found that the aircraft had been flying in a formation‑like manner while disregarding standard group‑flying practices, and had performed several dangerous maneuvers before the collision.

On 17 May 2025, two helicopters were en route from Tallinn to Piikajärvi airfield in Finland. Both took off from the Linnahall heliport in Tallinn at 11:17.

The two Robinson R44 helicopters carried five people: businessman Priit Jaagant, his wife, and Mihkel Kapp in one aircraft; Oleg Sõnajalg and Tiit Kuusk in the other.

The helicopters flew together and collided near Eura airfield at 12:34 at an altitude of about 200 meters. All five people on board were killed.

Finland's Safety Investigation Authority (OTKES) and Estonia's Safety Investigation Bureau (OJK) presented their findings on Tuesday.

Investigators determined that the helicopters flew in a manner resembling formation flight but did not follow the principles required for such operations. In group flying, pilots must agree in advance on key procedures, positioning, and designate a lead aircraft. In this case, the helicopters' positions changed repeatedly — one leading at times, then the other.

OTKES lead investigator Janne Kotiranta said the dangerous maneuvers were such that the accident could have occurred already over the Gulf of Finland.

Investigators noted that without agreed positioning and procedures, predicting the other aircraft's movements becomes extremely difficult, increasing the risk of collision.

After one hour and 16 minutes of flight, the helicopters approached Eura airfield.

Over the airfield, the Jaagant helicopter on the left suddenly turned sharply right toward the north. The second helicopter continued on its original course.

The aircraft collided at 12:34 over the northeastern corner of Eura airfield at roughly 200 meters above ground.

Emergency services received several calls, including an automatic emergency call from a mobile phone onboard one of the helicopters.

The first call came at 12:35 from an airfield employee, triggering rescue operations. The caller reported seeing two small helicopters collide about one kilometer north of the airfield. He said the helicopters broke apart in the air and had people onboard.

The crash sites were located in dense spruce forest, about 150 meters from the nearest forest road and roughly 100 meters apart.

Paramedics and a medical helicopter doctor confirmed all occupants dead at the scene.

Limited visibility and distraction

Trajectory analysis showed that neither pilot recognized the other's intentions or noticed the other aircraft before the collision.

A reconstruction by OTKES indicated that the pilot of the helicopter that veered dangerously right may have had his view obstructed by the passenger seated beside him.

Investigators also found that the pilots' attention may have been focused on aircraft controls, conversations with passengers, or external distractions such as events, people, or other traffic at Eura airfield — rather than on monitoring each other. Attention may also have been directed toward approach procedures for the destination.

Investigators could not determine from onboard systems whether autopilot was used. They said it is possible it was engaged at some point. Autopilot use can reduce situational awareness, including monitoring surroundings during turns, because the pilot is no longer actively executing the maneuver.

No technical faults were found that could have contributed to the collision.

A collision‑avoidance system would not have helped in this case, investigators said. Because the helicopters flew close together for most of the journey, such a system would have issued continuous alerts.

The ELT emergency locator transmitter did not activate during the crash. The device is designed to send a radio signal to help rescuers locate the aircraft. Failure to activate can slow rescue efforts and delay aid.

In this case, the ELT's non‑activation did not affect locating the wreckage, as eyewitnesses immediately began searching, investigators noted.

World.title: Estonian justice ministry after tougher penalties for migrant smuggling
World.content:
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta has submitted a proposal to the Riigikogu and the government seeking significantly tougher penalties for illegally transporting foreign nationals across the state border.

Pakosta (Eesti 200) sent the Government Office and the Riigikogu Legal Affairs Committee a proposal to amend a bill changing the Penal Code that is currently awaiting its second reading. The ministry wants to significantly toughen penalties for illegally transporting foreign nationals across the state border, or migrant smuggling.

Under the bill, the maximum prison sentence for organizing a standard illegal border crossing would be increased to five years, while offenses committed under aggravating circumstances would be punishable by one to seven years in prison.

Aggravating circumstances would include committing the offense in a life-threatening manner, repeatedly or involving two or more people. The maximum penalty under the relevant section would also be increased from one year to three years in prison.

The Ministry of Justice cited hybrid attacks originating in neighboring countries and a sharp rise in the number of migrants and smugglers in Estonia as reasons for the changes.

"Countries near Estonia have recently come under hybrid attack, with hostile neighboring countries facilitating attempts by large numbers of migrants from third countries to cross state borders. In connection with this, there has also been a noticeable increase in the number of illegal border crossers arriving in Estonia. Illegal border crossers are often assisted by criminals whom migrants pay to smuggle them into the European Union and arrange their illegal border crossings," Pakosta said in the proposal.

While 11 such crimes were registered in Estonia last year, 26 were registered in the first eight months of this year. According to the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), 27 people who were in Estonia illegally were caught while traveling onward within the Schengen Area in 2025, compared with 181 in the first eight months of this year.

Pakosta said that both organizing illegal border crossings and facilitating illegal stays in Estonia are serious crimes that currently carry relatively lenient penalties. Existing law does not even allow authorities to take into account whether an offense is a repeat violation or involves bringing several migrants into the country at once for greater financial gain.

She added that the recent rise in the number of such criminal incidents, as well as the apparent lack of difficulty criminal networks face in recruiting accomplices, shows that the risk of punishment is not sufficiently deterrent.

Estonian police detained suspects in organizing illegal migration. Source: PPA

"In other words, the penalties introduced into the existing law in 2015 no longer reflect the current situation, are not sufficiently deterrent and must therefore be increased. In addition, to deter repeat offenders, the maximum possible penalty for such offenses must also be increased so that repeatedly transporting foreign nationals illegally across the border or transporting several foreign nationals illegally across the border becomes a first-degree criminal offense," Pakosta wrote in the proposal.

Both the Ministry of the Interior and the Prosecutor's Office have said tougher penalties are necessary, she noted.

Pakosta also wants to add a provision to the bill under which damaging an object of importance to national defense would be punishable by one to eight years in prison.

Under the proposal, objects of importance to national defense would include buildings, structures, vehicles, equipment or other property used for activities essential to carrying out crisis-related duties by the Estonian Defense Forces, the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit), a security agency, a rescue agency, the Police and Border Guard Board or a defense industry company.

As an example, Pakosta cited the fire in Tallinn in August this year at a building used by defense industry company Milrem Robotics.

Milrem Robotics. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

World.title: UK prog band Marillion to perform in Tallinn
World.content:
In April, the neo‑prog band Marillion will give two full‑length concerts in Tallinn on two consecutive evenings, each with a different setlist.

Marillion will take the stage in Tallinn on Friday, 16 April, and Saturday, 17 April — together forming a single, cohesive Marillion Weekend.

Marillion Weekend is a format created by the band itself, built around specially curated setlists for each night and offering fans a chance to experience Marillion's work more broadly than during a typical concert.

Since 2002, Marillion Weekend repertoires have ranged from well‑known concert favorites to rarely performed tracks and long epics, and in some years have included full albums played in their entirety.

Marillion will perform a different concert programme on each of the two nights. Only two-day tickets will be available for the event, providing admission to both concert evenings.

Each evening will also feature a local guest act: Indrek Patte band on 16 April and Pantokraator on 17 April.

Formed in Aylesbury in 1979, Marillion became one of the best‑known representatives of emotionally charged, dramatic progressive rock in the 1980s. The band, whose name was inspired by JRR Tolkien's "Silmarillion", released its debut studio album in 1983. In total, they have released 20 albums, the most recent in 2022.

World.title: Gallery: Young Estonian artists' fall exhibition opens in Tallinn
World.content:
The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition has opened at Tallinn's Art & Tonic gallery where visitors can see works by 88 young Estonian artists free of charge. The exhibition will conclude with an art auction on October 23.

Nearly 400 works by 203 artists were submitted for this year's fall exhibition, with the jury selecting works by 88 artists. According to Reigo Kuivjõgi, organizer of "Buy Young Art" and gallerist at Art & Tonic, this year's selection is characterized by the high quality and diversity of the works.

"I am pleased that this time the selection includes more completely new artists than usual who will make their debut at the fall auction. This also makes the exhibition particularly interesting, as young artists with very different styles and approaches have come together under one roof," Kuivjõgi said.

Now in its 11th year, the "Buy Young Art" exhibition and auction gives young artists an opportunity to introduce their work to a wider audience while also bringing young Estonian art closer to enthusiasts and buyers.

"This year's selection is truly diverse and offers an opportunity to explore different artistic media, as in addition to painting, it also features graphic art, drawing, collage, photography and sculpture. The prices of the works also vary widely and start at just €1. When it comes to young art, there is always something for everyone, whether an experienced collector or someone buying art for the first time," Kuivjõgi explained.

Entrepreneur and art enthusiast Kristjan-Thor Vähi, head of Invego and a member of the selection jury, said the high quality of the works made choosing among the candidates quite a difficult task.

"There are many different approaches and truly fresh ideas in the work of young Estonian artists and I really like the fact that they dare to experiment. The exhibition offers a good opportunity to become better acquainted with their work and see what our young artists are doing right now," he said.

According to Vähi, initiatives such as "Buy Young Art" are important for young artists because they help their work reach a broader audience beyond the art world.

"When an artist is at the beginning of their career and is still relatively unknown, an opportunity like this to show their work is very important. It is important for young Estonian art to be visible and accessible and the more young art reaches the public, the more confident people will become about buying it and thereby supporting local artists," he said.

The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition is open at the Art & Tonic gallery through October 22. All works displayed at the exhibition will be offered at a public auction on October 23.

World.title: Evelin Kasenõmm: Asia puts drones to work — Estonia should follow suit
World.content:
Europe may lead on drone rules, but Asia leads on putting them into practice — and Estonia's first move should be establishing two or three permanent drone corridors, writes Evelin Kasenõmm.

A new economic layer is emerging in Asia, often called the low‑altitude economy, meaning business activities and public services operating in low airspace, along with the infrastructure needed for them.

There is no point for Estonia to compete with Asian countries in drone manufacturing volume. Our opportunity may instead lie in developing digital services needed for safe and automated drone use. Estonia's long‑term experience in spatial data and 3D city models provides a strong technological foundation for this.

China is building an industry out of low‑altitude airspace

China has made the low‑altitude economy a national economic policy area, covering drones, air taxis, logistics, agriculture, urban monitoring, rescue operations, and the necessary infrastructure. According to China's civil aviation authority, by the end of 2025 the country had nearly 3.3 million registered drones — 51 percent more than the year before. Low‑altitude traffic service stations were already operating in 23 provinces1. In major Chinese cities, drones are used for delivering food and medical supplies, firefighting, urban monitoring, and maintaining public order.

Rapid growth has also brought stricter control: in 2026, mandatory drone registration and electronic identification requirements took effect, and conditions for airworthiness and operating permits for larger drones were clarified.

Japan uses drones to solve labor shortages

In Japan, drone adoption is accelerated by an aging population, labor shortages, mountainous terrain, and the difficulty of serving sparsely populated areas.

A framework created in 2022 allows compliant drones to fly beyond the pilot's line of sight even over populated areas. This enables inspection of power lines, railways, or coastlines without the pilot needing to follow the entire route.

Japan's next step is a national drone corridor system. A drone corridor is a digitally managed flight path with predefined routes, permitted altitudes, obstacles, network quality, possible landing sites, and safety requirements.

Technical specifications, guidelines, and a nationwide development map for the corridors were completed in 2025. Corridor management software was published as open source, and an official registration system is planned for 20262.

Drone logistics focus mainly on mountainous regions, small islands, and depopulating areas, where mail, medicines, and small parcels are delivered. Drones are also used in disaster zones. In agriculture, they are integrated with autonomous machinery, satellite data, and shared data platforms to reduce labor needs and improve precision.

Japan's experience shows that drone services are most likely to become permanent where they solve a clear and growing societal problem.

South Korea turns trials into standardized services

South Korea is expanding its drone industry through municipalities and standardized service models. Since 2019, drone delivery, rescue, monitoring, and other public services have been tested. In 2025, 26 municipalities participated.

In the national drone delivery program, services were launched in 2024 on 32 islands, 17 parks, and one port, with flight bases, delivery points, routes, ordering apps, and real‑time flight monitoring. In 2025, the service expanded to 166 areas. Korea is also testing medical logistics, safety monitoring, and transporting island‑produced goods to the mainland3.

Standardization is at the core of Korea's model. The state creates a unified safety and service model that different regions and companies can use. Drone delivery is becoming a practical service that people can order.

The country is also investing in the K‑UAM program. UAM (urban air mobility) refers to air taxis and other new aircraft used in and between cities. Although air taxi timelines have proven overly optimistic, the infrastructure created by the program enables smaller cargo and service drones.

Europe leads regulation, Asia leads implementation

Are Asian industrial countries far ahead of Europe in civilian drone use? Such a generalization would be misleading. The European Union has created one of the world's most comprehensive drone regulatory frameworks. The rules are based on flight risk rather than whether the drone is used for hobby or business.

Europe's strength also includes U‑space, whose legal framework has been in force since 2023. Essentially, it is a digital drone traffic management environment that allows filing flight plans, checking restrictions, issuing flight permissions, tracking drones, and avoiding conflicts with other aircraft.

SESAR — Single European Sky ATM Research — is Europe's joint air traffic modernization program. It has tested cooperation between drone service providers, integration of drones with conventional air traffic, medical logistics, and simultaneous beyond‑visual‑line‑of‑sight flights. Trials show that the technology can work in urban and cross‑border environments4.

Europe's bottleneck is slow and fragmented implementation, as decisions are made by member states. As a result, Europe has many successful pilot projects but fewer everyday services. Europe leads drone regulation; Asia leads drone deployment.

Estonia's opportunities

Estonia's strengths in the drone field include high‑quality spatial data, digital public services, a small and relatively manageable airspace, strong communications and cybersecurity competence, and the ability to integrate state and private‑sector information systems5.

We also have practical use cases. Islands are suitable for transporting medicines and small parcels. Power lines, railways, coastlines, and wind farms require regular inspection. Security agencies need rapidly collected spatial information. Estonia's variable and cold weather allows testing systems in conditions valuable for many foreign markets.

Currently, Estonia often treats drone flights as individual operations where the operator checks restrictions, requests permission, plans the route, and conducts the flight. In a service‑based world, much of this information exchange must happen automatically.

A flight‑planning system should be able to request up‑to‑date data on airspace restrictions, buildings and obstacles, terrain height, weather, and mobile network coverage. The system could evaluate the route, submit a permit request, and transmit drone identification data during the flight. Creating such a digital layer may be Estonia's opportunity.

I see Estonia's first step as creating two or three permanent drone corridors. One would serve logistics between islands and the mainland, another would support energy infrastructure inspection, and a third would handle coastal, forest, or rescue monitoring. A corridor must include reliable connectivity, spatial and weather data, agreed safety requirements, digital permitting, and shared infrastructure for multiple companies. Pilot projects for drone corridors are already underway in Estonia.

In parallel, public‑sector demand must be created. Multi‑year service contracts for detecting power line faults, assessing forest damage, or transporting lab samples and medicines would give the private sector reason to invest in automated solutions and create validated services in Estonia that could later be exported.

In the drone economy of the next decade, a significant part of the value will come from systems that allow drones to fly safely, with minimal human intervention, and legally. Estonia has succeeded before by turning a complex state process into a simple digital service. Opening our low‑altitude airspace to new services could be the next such field — but we must act much faster than we are now.

World.title: Iraqi policeman killed in terrorist attack near Kirkuk
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Two security sources told Reuters that ISIS terrorists assaulted a federal police post near the northern Iraqi city of Kirkuk on Monday, killing at least one Iraqi federal policeman and injuring four others.

The assailants used semi-automatic machine guns and sniper fire on the federal police unit stationed in Hawija, around 70 kilometers (43 miles) southwest of Kirkuk.

No one immediately claimed responsibility. However, security and army officials indicated ISIS militants, who are still active in the area, were responsible for the attack.

The raid is the first documented assault by ISIS terrorists on Iraqi security forces since US troops withdrew from the country on September 30, terminating the military operation in Iraq.

The United States led the international coalition that aided Iraqi forces in their war against terrorism, including measures to keep the extremist organization from reorganizing.

Washington said that it will continue to offer targeted training and intelligence assistance following the departure, but Iraqi forces would be fully responsible for the country’s security and the suppression of remnants of terrorist groups.

Despite the defeat of the terrorist group over a decade ago, Iraqi security officials told Reuters that the organization still has sleeper cells in the country.

The pullout of the US-led international coalition raised concerns that a security vacuum would allow the terrorist group to recover momentum, with some officials warning that Iraqi security forces would now have to hold the group without the coalition’s military presence.

World.title: Iraq estimates oil price at $58 per barrel in 2027 federal budget
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi government aims to spend 217 trillion Iraqi dinars (around $166 billion) in 2027, assuming an oil price of $58 per barrel, according to parliamentarians familiar with the draft budget.

The measures would result in a fiscal deficit of around 40 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $30.6 billion).

Members of the parliamentary finance committee told Reuters that the draft budget anticipates crude oil exports of around four million barrels per day, including shipments from Iraqi Kurdistan.

The Iraqi cabinet is also studying raising the local currency’s exchange rate to between 1,400 and 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar, up from roughly 1,300 now, according to legislators.

Oil exports generate the majority of the Iraqi government’s revenue, accounting for roughly 80 percent of the general budget’s resources.

The US-Israeli military conflict with Iran has disrupted shipping via the Strait of Hormuz, prompting Iraq to seek other routes for its crude oil exports.

The Iraqi parliament is about to start official deliberations on the 2027 federal budget.

The 2027 budget represents a structural transformation by allocating 150 trillion ($114.5 billion) for traditional line items and 50 trillion Iraqi dinar ($38.2 billion) for a new World Bank-coordinated program-and-performance model to measure expenditure efficiency.

World.title: Chinese refiners increase oil imports from Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Chinese independent refiners are swiftly increasing their imports of Iraqi and Qatari crude to compensate for a sharp decline in Iranian oil supplies.

As their stockpiles near depletion, private refineries in China are paying considerable premiums to acquire alternatives, according to Reuters.

Experts see that the step represents a desperate search for alternatives due to logistical obstacles, rather than a true rebound in Chinese domestic crude demand.

Private refineries in China have historically relied on deeply discounted, sanctioned Iranian oil to optimize their refining margins, previously importing over one million barrels per day. However, the US naval blockade and the higher cost of Russian oil alternatives are two major geopolitical factors that have forced a shift.

A rigorous US blockade linked to the larger crisis involving Iran has trapped at least 50 tankers transporting mostly Iranian petroleum off the Chinese coast, cutting off the refiners’ key supply source.

State-owned Chinese refiners have successfully secured the majority of the available Russian crude oil. As a result of the fierce competition, Russian barrels now command significant premiums of roughly $30 per barrel above Brent, driving smaller independent refiners out.

Refiners have purchased at least 12 million barrels of Iraqi and Qatari oil for October and November delivery, with total estimates ranging from 15 million to 20 million barrels.

Buyers are mostly interested in the sulfur-rich Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy grades. Independent refiners normally reject these higher grades in favor of lighter Iranian or Russian choices, but they are embracing them since they are readily available.

Major global commodities trading firms such as Vitol Group, Trafigura Group, Mercuria Energy Group, and TotalEnergies SE are facilitating the deals.

This move is being aided by a steady recovery in total exports leaving the Arabian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz, making Middle Eastern options physically available even as regional tensions remain.

World.title: Turkey to turn Iraq’s Development Road into multi-fuel energy corridor
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkey intends to develop the planned Development Road from Iraq’s southern ports to Europe into a multi-fuel energy corridor worth $80 billion annually.

According to Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, this strategic route will go beyond typical freight transit by incorporating crucial infrastructure for oil, natural gas, and power transmission.

In a statement to Anadolu Agency (AA), Bayraktar expressed Turkey’s enthusiasm for building the Development Road not merely as a transport corridor but also as a strategic energy route. This route would be bolstered by the inclusion of oil, natural gas, and electricity transmission lines along its path.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi instructed in July the establishment of a defined structure to finance and implement the strategic project of the Development Road, assuring the start of practical steps within a planned timeline.

In early June, the head of the state-owned General Company for Ports of Iraq (GCPI), Farhan al-Fartousi, said that the planning process for the project and the al-Faw Grand Port has made tremendous progress, with essential operating plans already submitted to the government.

The project will enter the implementation phase following government approval in the coming months, according to al-Fartousi.

The $17 billion project, which will connect the al-Faw Grand Port in southern Iraq to the Turkish border by constructing a railway and road network, is anticipated to transform Iraq into a transit center by cutting the time it takes to travel from Asia to Europe.

In addition to pipelines for energy transportation, the project’s railway will significantly assist in the transportation of commodities, with a first-phase capacity of 3.5 million tons and a second-phase capacity of 7.5 million tons.

By connecting the port city of Basra to Turkey via an overland route, the logistics project will compete with Egypt’s Suez Canal and establish Basra as a gateway to Europe.

In 2024, Turkey formed a council involving Bulgaria, Hungary, and Serbia to arrange the connection of Europe with Iraq’s Development Road.

As a worldwide corridor for commodities and energy transportation, the project is expected to attract international commerce and create considerable employment opportunities and investment possibilities in Iraq and other countries in the region.

World.title: Iraq’s seaborne oil exports jump to 2.57 million bpd in September
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s crude oil exports rose for the fourth consecutive month in September, growing by over nine percent—equivalent to 218,000 barrels per day—to reach their highest level since the start of the Iran war.

Iraq’s seaborne crude oil exports jumped to 2.57 million barrels per day in September, up from 2.35 million barrels per day in August.

Despite the monthly improvement, Iraqi oil exports in September remained 25 percent lower than the 3.41 million barrels per day recorded during the same month in 2025.

Iraq’s oil exports gradually recovered in September, after hitting a low of 98,000 barrels per day in May.

Iraq’s average crude oil exports plummeted by 52 percent between January and September 2026, to an average of 1.6 million barrels per day, down from 3.34 million barrels per day in the same period in 2025.

The volume of oil exports surpassed three million barrels per day at the beginning of the year before experiencing a major shock due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which caused shipments to collapse to 540,000 barrels per day in March.

Exports continued to fall sharply, reaching historic lows of more than 90 percent in April and May before gradually recovering to 2.57 million barrels per day in September.

World.title: Iraq targets 1M electric vehicles via Green Taxi initiative
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Environment reaffirmed on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, that private sector investment forms the bedrock of its national “Green Taxi” initiative and the phased transition toward deploying one million electric vehicles (EVs).

Speaking to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Haidar Qasim Al-Darraji, Director General of the General Company for Carbon Economics at the Ministry of Environment, outlined a comprehensive framework to transform Iraq’s transportation grid into an investable, eco-friendly ecosystem.

Al-Darraji emphasized that the green transit transition cannot operate as a conventional state-run enterprise, but rather as an integrated public-private partnership (PPP) bringing together government regulators, commercial banks, private equity investors, energy providers, and automotive innovators.

Under this model, the state will establish statutory and technical codes, streamline the regulatory climate, lay foundational infrastructure, and verify carbon credit baselines. In turn, private industry will handle capital expenditure, vehicle manufacturing, importation, fleet operations, maintenance logistics, and the rollout of solar-powered charging networks.

Inter-agency groundwork is already underway through coordinated channels involving the Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Transport, and the General Company for Private Transport Management. The bodies are evaluating existing municipal transit garages and public transport depots for conversion into EV charging hubs powered by distributed solar photovoltaic systems.

Clarifying the scale of the transition, Al-Darraji noted that the target of one million electric vehicles is a phased, metrics-driven national roadmap rather than an overnight influx. Rollouts will begin via scalable pilot projects across Baghdad before expanding into the provinces.

The strategic objective is to cultivate an integrated domestic industrial value chain around e-mobility—spanning local assembly, maintenance, bank lending, commercial insurance, ride-hailing software, and monetization under sovereign carbon credit mechanisms—thereby curbing state fiscal burdens and generating skilled technical employment.

In tandem with public sustainability policies, regional automotive distributors are expanding their electrified footprints across the domestic market. Ahmed Al-Ani, Branch Director of Toyota Iraq, revealed to INA that Iraq has emerged as a major regional adopter of hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), ranking as the second-largest consumer of hybrid cars in the Middle East.

Highlighting consumer demand for green mobility, Al-Ani announced the official domestic market launch of two electrified Toyota flagships: the all-electric bZ4X Touring SUV and the RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicle (PHEV), offering extended electric range and modern efficiency tailored to Iraq’s expanding charging landscape.

World.title: US dollar holds above 160,000 IQD in Baghdad, Erbil, and Basra
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The U.S. dollar held firm above the 160,000-dinar threshold across Iraq’s parallel currency markets on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, consolidating Monday’s steep gains across trading hubs in Baghdad, Erbil, and Basra.

The persistent gap between free-market rates and the Central Bank of Iraq’s official peg of 131,000 dinars per $100 continues to hover near 22.5 percent as exchange bureaus navigate heavy cash demand.

Market data showed that exchange bureaus and trading counters in the capital city of Baghdad maintained cash selling rates at 160,500 dinars per $100, while buying bids ticked slightly higher to 160,150 dinars, narrowing the intraday bid-ask spread.

In Erbil, the regional hub of the Kurdistan Region, parallel counters offered greenbacks at 160,000 dinars per $100 against purchase bids of 159,750 dinars. In the southern trade center of Basra, rates rose to match the 160,000 mark, with cash sales quoted at 160,000 dinars per $100 and buying bids settling at 159,500 dinars.

The elevated rates across major cities reflect ongoing liquidity pressures as retail merchants and unbanked importers seek physical foreign currency outside the formal electronic transfer platform. Despite regular market interventions and central bank oversight, speculative buying and regional fiscal uncertainties continue to anchor cash prices above key psychological thresholds.

World.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim attack on Riyadh airport, deny losing territory
World.content:
Sanaa – Yemen’s Houthis claimed an attack on the main airport in the Saudi capital while also denying on Tuesday losing territory to government forces, as fighting intensified.

After declaring a counter-offensive, government forces claimed Monday to have pushed the Houthis out of the Bab al-Mandab area, a key shipping route in the Red Sea, as well as the port city of Mocha, which was captured last month.

Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify with the situation on the ground moving fast and access for journalists difficult.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed on Telegram that the group still held all territory recently seized, including strategic areas along the Red Sea coast.

Their fighters “have full control over all their advances on the ground”, he said.

He said the Houthis had carried out dozens of strikes in the past few hours targeting government forces in Yemen’s Al-Jawf and Marib regions, while also attacking Taiz governorate.

On Monday night, the Houthis said they had struck Riyadh airport and a refinery belonging to Saudi state oil giant Aramco.

Loud explosions rattled the Saudi capital on Monday evening.

On Tuesday Saudi Arabia’s civilian aviation authority said at least three people were also wounded in attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemen border a day earlier.

Saudi Arabia, the main backer of the Yemeni government, has been providing air support for a counter-offensive launched by government forces.

– ‘Victories on several fronts’ –

Yemen’s government forces claimed late Monday that they had achieved “victories on several fronts”, but military sources with the government nevertheless refrained from officially confirming taking Mocha, only saying they had cut the one supply route to the area.

They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the southwest, where fighting has surged in recent days.

Yemen’s government has announced a goal of retaking all Houthi territory — home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

Yemen’s civil war flared up again in July after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the wider Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

The Houthis last month seized control of the entire western coastline of Yemen along the Red Sea in the country’s deadliest fighting in years.

Since then, they have regularly targeted oil and military installations in Saudi Arabia and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.

Pakistan and Turkey have pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks.

The Yemen conflict has caused a humanitarian crisis. Since the renewed fighting broke out, more than 184,000 people have been displaced from their homes, according to the United Nations.

A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”. He condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia.

World.title: 80% vote in West Bengal bypolls amid rigging, intimidation charges
World.content:
KOLKATA/CHENNAI/GUWAHATI: Bypolls across three states and one Union territory saw high but uneven turnouts Tuesday, with Bengal's Nandigram and Rejinagar recording 80% turnout amid allegations of rigging, voter intimidation and police interference, while polling in one Puducherry and two Tamil Nadu assembly seats and Assam's Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency remained largely peaceful.

Nandigram recorded above 80% turnout by 7pm, but voters reported being turned away from booths. CM Suvendu Adhikari, who had vacated the seat after winning both Nandigram and Bhowanipore in May, said: "In 2016, I won by 82,000 votes, my highest margin ever. I believe that record will be broken this time."

Congress candidate Milan Pradhan, out on bail following his arrest in a 2007 case after he filed his nomination, said the election had been "looted" and complained of blocked agents, voters being denied entry, assault and vandalism.

CPI and ISF candidate Sabe Mirza Khan also alleged rigging.

Rejinagar recorded 80% turnout, with allegations of police interference dominating polling. AJUP chief Humayun Kabir, who gave up Rejinagar and kept Nowda after winning both in May, was detained after police accused him of provoking tension. Videos showed police grabbing Kabir by his shirt and taking him away. He was released after 12 hours. His son Golam Nabi Azad is the AJUP candidate.





Congress and TMC alleged widespread rigging and removal of polling agents. BJP's Shankharavh Sarkar clashed with central forces after being asked to move away from voters.

Tamil Nadu saw a turnout dip from April's elections. Madurantakam recorded 86%, down from 93%, while Dharapuram saw 80%, against 89% in April. Both saw three-way contests involving TVK, DMK and AIADMK.

World.title: From Gujarat CM to India's PM: Modi's 25 years in office
World.content:
Narendra Modi was thrust into the thick of governance in 2001 as the party suffered a setback in local polls in Gujarat and the response of the state government headed by CM Keshubhai Patel to the massive Kutch earthquake was found wanting.

Within months of his swearing-in as CM, riots swept the state in the wake of the Godhra train-burning incident. BJP's win in the 2002 assembly polls cemented his position and dissidents in the party were marginalised as he set about implementing his governance agenda.

Oct 2001-May 2014: Gujarat CM

Kutch rebuilt. In 2003, Gujarat passed India's first state disaster management law.

Vibrant Gujarat Summit launched in 2003 to showcase its strength & attract investors.

Jyotigram Yojana, launched in 2006, prioritised reliable power supply over subsidised but erratic electricity to villages. Soon, all 18,000 villages had access to reliable three-phase power as non-farm economic activity expanded and subsidies were nearly halved.

Sagarkhedu Sarvangi Vikas Yojana launched in 2007 adopted an outcome-oriented mission for coastal communities, combining infrastructure, livelihoods, irrigation, salinity control, coastal security and fisheries development.

Launched in 2009, Garib Kalyan Mela took welfare delivery to citizens.

Check dams, farm ponds, recharge wells, canals and inter-basin transfers were planned as surplus floodwater was carried through 332km of canals and Narmada water reached reservoirs across Saurashtra, opening over 10 lakh acres of irrigation potential. A CAG report in 2017 recorded groundwater recharge roughly 50% above 2002 levels.

His government linked ports with power, roads, rail and industrial estates. Mundra, Hazira and Pipavav grew into major private ports.

Nudged by RSS, the BJP brass named Modi in June 2013 as its campaign committee head for the 2014 polls and soon elevated him as its PM candidate. When results were announced on May 16, BJP more than doubled its tally to 282, its first majority in the then 545-member Lok Sabha.

It was the first majority government since 1984.

2014-2019: First term as PM

His government launched Jan Dhan Yojana, and 59 crore accounts were opened with over Rs 3.1 lakh crore in deposits. Women owned 33 crore of these accounts. This helped in ushering in direct benefit transfer, changing welfare delivery. By Aug 2026, DBT had transferred Rs 53.2 lakh crore across 320 schemes and 56 ministries.

In his Aug 15 speech at Red Fort, Modi spoke of the indignities women suffer due to lack of toilets and announced a sanitation campaign. Swachh Bharat Mission was launched. PM Ujjwala Yojana, launched in 2016, gave 10.5 crore free LPG connections to women from poor households by May 2026.

His government expanded the social security net, including free treatment for the poor under Ayushman Bharat. By 2025, official estimates say 94.3 crore Indians were covered by some form of social protection, up from 19% in 2015 to 64%.

GST was rolled out in July 2017 in what the PM lauded as economic unification of India as tax borders came down and the market became one.



2019-24: Second term as PM

Few people outside the top echelons of government were aware when it took probably its most significant political calls: revoking the special constitutional status enjoyed by J&K under Article 370, downgrading the state to the status of UT and hiving off Ladakh as a UT.

A verdict from SC paved the way for construction of Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. The idol was consecrated in Jan 2024.

CAA was passed in 2019, providing a path to citizenship for persecuted non-Muslim communities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.

The Covid pandemic and lockdowns tested government as India suffered a large human toll. Scaling up of indigenous vaccines and the world's largest vaccination campaign helped. Government launched the Atmanirbhar Bharat programme. It was also a period when UPI use began zooming and has become a definitive success.

2024: Wins a third term

BJP went into the 2024 elections with supreme confidence and was humbled as a section of voters balked at its "abki baar 400 paar" slogan. However, it won a majority with its allies even as it lost its own majority after a decade.

Operation Sindoor targeted terrorist hideouts in Pakistan in May 2025 after the Pahalgam attack.

World.title: ED summons Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann kin in 5 crore graft case
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The alleged Rs 5 crore bribery allegation against Punjab CM

's wife

has taken a new turn with ED summoning his brother-in-law Amardeep Singh Grewal for questioning in the case.

Grewal, a prominent Punjabi film personality, was asked by ED to appear before it Wednesday, sources said, adding he sought an adjournment. ED issued a second summons for Friday for him to appear for recording his statements.

Kaur had earlier denied the allegation against her and sent a legal notice to ex-Punjab and Haryana HC judge Ranjit Singh for claiming she had demanded Rs 5 crore to suppress a rape case.

Grewal's summoning comes a day after the high court ordered a CBI investigation against Mann's OSD in another bribery allegation.

ED is probing Grewal's links to the alleged bribery deal and the role of his East Sunshine Production Pvt Ltd.

The overseas transactions of the company are also being trailed to verify any bribery or alleged money laundering accusations.

World.title: Flydubai flight incident: Cockpit attack left Captain Smit Machchhar with 'depressed skull fracture'
World.content:
File photo: Captain Smit Machchhar

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Captain Smit Machchhar's heroic act of saving flydubai FZ1073 has acquired another dimension with the extent of the injuries he was fighting to save the plane from its suicidal Omani co-pilot now coming out.Sources say co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami hitting him with the axe kept in the cockpit had led to a "depressed fracture fragment of skull". An emergency surgery is learnt to have been performed in Saudi Arabia before Captain Machchhar could be flown back to the UAE for further treatment.Dr (Air Cmde) Krishan Kumar Yadav, senior clinical director and professor of neurosurgery and neuro-spine surgery at Marengo Asia Hospitals, told TOI: "A depressed skull fracture is serious. Put simply, a piece of the skull has been pressed inward toward the brain. During surgery, doctors make a careful incision, lift or remove the pressed-in fragment, and check the protective membrane around the brain for tears. They clean the area, repair any damage, and then either replace the bone or reconstruct it. It is delicate work, but it is work we are trained for, and many patients do very well afterwards."The Indian embassy in the UAE said on X Tuesday: "Capt Smit continues to make steady progress and is regaining his health.The embassy remains in close touch with his family, doctors and local authorities, extending all possible assistance. We thank everyone for their prayers & wish him a speedy recovery.""Recovery is not a straight line. The first days are quiet ones: rest, careful monitoring, and keeping him comfortable. Then, bit by bit, strength returns. There will be good days and slower ones. Headaches, tiredness, or trouble concentrating are common while the body heals, and they don't mean something is wrong," Dr Yadav said.Captain Machchhar had told Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu: "It was a normal flight, and the co-pilot wanted to pray, which a lot of locals do. While he was praying, out of respect, I just looked at the front and not at the back." He said that about four or five minutes later, he suddenly felt a heavy blow to the back of his head, which he initially thought was an impact involving the aircraft."After about four or five minutes, my first thought was damage to the aircraft and something is not right. But then the blow kept coming, one after the other. And that's when I realised that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me."He tried to stop the co-pilot but was badly affected by the initial blows. "I did try to stop him, but because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing. And I was completely blurred out," the captain said. He then realised the aircraft was descending sharply.

World.title: ED unearths bribe racket involving top executives of 40 PSUs, banks & companies
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate has unearthed a bribery racket involving top executives of at least 40 public sector undertakings and government banks, besides some corporate houses engaged in siphoning off and laundering hundreds of crores of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds channelled through multiple charities promoted by a class XII dropout, who has been caught impersonating as a medical doctor for close to three decades.

According to ED, the fake doctor, Dharmendra Kumar Chandradev, received CSR donations in his multiple trusts registered for the purpose of laundering money meant for charity and exempted from taxation. These funds were further returned back to the "donor" in cash, after retaining his commission. The racket involved some corporate houses, hospitals, public sector companies and govt banks. Top executives of these PSUs were heavily bribed for releasing CSR funds.

On Oct 1, the central agency carried out searches at eight locations across Maharashtra, Bengal, Gujarat and Delhi-NCR related to these bogus donations cases. The agency seized several pieces of evidence and details of transactions related to PSU executives and corporate hospitals, in addition to Rs 21 lakh in unaccounted cash.

"The CSR mechanism was utilised as a conduit for conversion of accounted funds into unaccounted cash.





Funds amounting to Rs 200 crore have been routed through the above mechanism," ED has estimated through its preliminary investigation.

The agency further said its probe revealed that CSR contributions from corporate houses were "returned substantially in cash" to the contributors after deduction of a small commission.

World.title: Election Commission: Was ready to meet 240 opposition MPs but not at their chosen venue
World.content:
Till 4 pm, no political party had sought an appointment, EC said

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Tuesday, while willing to meet the 240 opposition party MPs at their request conveyed through Delhi Police, declined to do so at their suggested venue of Parliament House annexe, saying the poll panel's protocol required such meetings to be held only on EC premises and based on a request from the parties' authorised representative."EC considered this request as unusual and therefore, it could not be accepted," the panel said in a statement.As an alternative, EC proposed that its most senior officer on duty could be sent to the meeting venue to receive a memorandum, "which in itself would have been an unprecedented step", said an EC spokesperson. However, this offer was declined by the MPs.While emphasising that any political party may request for a meeting with EC, which would then schedule a date and time, the commission said it must balance its respect for parliamentary and democratic processes with that for its own protocols and conventions, "which are of utmost importance".EC said during the march by certain political parties towards Nirvachan Sadan, "it was learnt through the media that some MPs wished to meet the commission along with their delegation"."It is clarified that, till 4pm, no political party, through its representatives, had sought an appointment for a meeting with EC," the commission said. EC said around 4pm, information was received from police that a delegation of MPs led by Rahul Gandhi wished to meet and submit a memorandum.Referring to the procedure laid down in 2025 for meetings with political parties, EC said if a delegation wishes to meet, it seeks an appointment through its authorised representative. The meeting is thereafter held at a time mutually agreed upon by both sides. "This is a regular practice," EC said.When the panel was considering the proposal, it was informed by the Delhi Police DCP that the meeting was sought to be held with 240 MPs and the proposed venue was the Parliament House annexe, it said. "EC, considering its protocol to meet political parties only on its own premises and its procedure to only schedule such meetings in consultation with the parties' authorised representative, declined the offer," it said.

World.title: SIR in Delhi: disposals of Form 7 nearly six times those of Form 6
World.content:
For every Form 6 application for inclusion in Delhi’s electoral roll disposed of during the ongoing claims and objections phase of the special intensive revision (SIR), nearly six Form 7 applications seeking objections to the inclusion of names or their deletion from the draft roll have been cleared, data accessed by The Hindu showed.

According to the weekly constituency-wise forms disposal report, only 569 Form 6 applications were disposed of between August 31 and October 4. In comparison, 3,209 Form 7 applications were cleared during the same five-week period covered by the data. More than two-thirds of these Form 7 applications, or 2,352, were disposed of in the last two weeks alone, while no Form 6 application was disposed of last week.

Since the claims and objections phase began on August 31, 1.94 lakh applications seeking enrolment and 5,431 forms seeking deletion of names have been received so far, according to data from Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Ashok Kumar’s office.

The data also showed that 2.12 lakh Form 6 and 51,747 Form 7 applications had already been received before the claims and objections period began, between June 16 and August 30.

The claims and objections period ends on October 30, while disposal of the applications and notices has to be completed by November 30. The final roll is set to be published on December 4.

During the claims and objections period, an Indian citizen aged 18 or above can submit Form 6 to seek inclusion of their name in the final SIR roll, either as a first-time voter or if their name was left out of the draft roll published on August 31. An elector can simultaneously file Form 7 to object to or seek deletion of another elector’s name from the roll.

Once an objection is received, a poll official serves a notice on the concerned elector, giving them 15 days to respond before any action is taken. A Booth Level Officer (BLO) is also required under the rules to verify the address and make three attempts to deliver the notice. For Form 6 applications, a BLO is assigned to conduct physical verification and submit a report, based on which a decision is taken. “There is a seven-day window for assigning a BLO; however, there is no set deadline for disposing of Form 6 applications,” an official said.

Queries were sent to Mr. Kumar’s office over the lower rate of Form 6 disposal compared with Form 7, but no replies were received till the time of going to press.

Special camps

Meanwhile, Mr. Kumar’s office is organising a special camp at all polling station locations on October 11 to maximise enrolment of electors left out of the draft roll. Another round of special camps for enrolment of young electors will be held at all colleges, universities and other educational institutions in Delhi on October 7 and 8, his office stated in an official release.

World.title: Morning Digest: Rahul calls SIR ‘treason’ as INDIA unites against ECI; SC to hear Punjab’s plea against CBI probe linked to CM Mann’s office
World.content:
Rahul, Priyanka among 260 detained during INDIA bloc march to ECI in Delhi

“What has been done to my country is treason,” Leader of the Opposition (LoP) in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said even as the Opposition parties closed ranks, marching from Parliament to the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) headquarters to demand the scrapping of special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, restoring the names of deleted voters and sacking of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Later in the evening, Mr. Gandhi, his sister, the Wayanad MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and other MPs were forcibly removed, detained and huddled into a bus even as Mr. Gandhi resisted, attempting to wriggle out of the vehicle’s window.

Bypolls held in five Assembly seats, one Lok Sabha constituency

Bypolls were held in five Assembly seats in Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Puducherry, and one Lok Sabha seat in Assam. The Madurantakam Assembly constituency in Tamil Nadu recorded the highest polling percentage of 86%. The other Assembly seat which went to the polls in Tamil Nadu was Dharapuram, which saw a turnout of just over 80%. Both seats in the State were reserved for Scheduled Caste candidates.

The protest that wouldn’t end: Inside Rahul Gandhi’s daylong siege of Akashvani Bhawan

After police appeared to have broken up the Opposition’s march against the Election Commission of India, Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi improvised by turning the All India Radio campus in the national capital into the unlikely centre of an all-day sit-in that lasted well past sunset.

‘Targeting of commercial shipping must end’: India condemns latest attack on vessels

The Ministry of External Affairs condemned the targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers, and civilian infrastructure following two separate attacks in the Black Sea and off Oman that left two foreign seafarers dead and several Indian crew members injured. Eleven Indian crew members were injured on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) after a Panama-flagged commercial vessel MT On Peace was hit by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

Not part of INDIA bloc, BJD issues long clarification

The Biju Janata Dal (BJD) clarified that it was not part of the INDIA bloc, despite its Rajya Sabha MPs joining the Opposition alliance’s protest march against the alleged arbitrary actions of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in connection with the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The clarification came after BJD MPs were seen alongside Congress leaders, actively participating in the protest over alleged irregularities in the electoral roll revision exercise, in New Delhi.

Two arrested; 13 Navy personnel among 18 under scanner for alleged leaks to Pakistan intelligence operatives

The Counter Intelligence Cell (CIC) of the Andhra Pradesh Intelligence Department has uncovered an espionage module in which 18 people including 13 Navy personnel are suspected of passing sensitive information to Pakistani intelligence operatives. Two of them have been arrested. The suspects were allegedly sharing information related to defence establishments and strategic locations at the Visakhapatnam Naval Base and other parts of the country with Pakistani Intelligence Operatives (PIOs), the intelligence officials said in a release.

Deleted in SIR, four Bengal men now locked at Chhattisgarh detention centre for over a month

After their names were deleted from the voters list during the recent special intensive revision (SIR) exercise, four migrant workers from West Bengal’s Murshidabad now find themselves in an uncanny situation. It’s been a month; they have been detained by Chhattisgarh Police and lodged at a detention centre in Raipur on suspicion of being Bangladeshi nationals despite being a long-time resident of India over generations.

Cabinet clears apex body to handle roads, rail, ports as one network

The Union Cabinet approved a Special Purpose Vehicle — the Integrated Transport & Logistics Authority (ITLA) — which will be the apex body to plan, appraise and monitor transport and logistics projects that are now handled separately by different ministries and agencies. Its central task will be a National Transport Master Plan with a horizon of 10 years or more, covering every major mode.

Centre to propose five-pronged reform plan at GST Council meeting on October 8

The Centre will propose a five-pronged plan for the next set of reforms to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) system at the upcoming GST Council meeting on October 8, according to sources in the Ministry of Finance. These reforms are aimed at automating and easing a lot of the current administrative bottlenecks in the GST system, and reducing the compliance burden, especially for small businesses. Rates, including the GST on the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions, will not be on the agenda.

Rajnath Singh launches Navy’s first indigenous fleet support ship ‘Surya’ at Visakhapatnam

Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh launched the Indian Navy’s first indigenously built Fleet Support Ship FSS-1 named Surya and laid the keel for the fifth vessel of the series FSS-5 at Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL) in Visakhapatnam. The five Fleet Support Ships are being built under a single contract with 82% indigenous content. HSL has used integrated modular construction to cut build times while meeting naval specifications.

One more FIR over alleged fake Form-7 applications to delete 136 voters at Malleswaram in Bengaluru

The Yeshwantpur police have registered an FIR against a BJP-linked Booth Level Agent (BLA-2) for allegedly submitting false Form-7 applications seeking deletion of 136 voters from the electoral rolls in Malleswaram Assembly constituency in Bengaluru. The FIR was registered on October 5 based on a complaint by a Congress leader.

World Bank ups India’s GDP growth projection to 7.1% for FY27

The World Bank raised India’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth forecast for the current fiscal to 7.1%, up 0.5 percentage points from its April projections, driven by better-than-expected print for the first quarter.

Obituary | Jeffrey Archer: politician, novelist, conman, jailbird and survival specialist

With a combination of charisma and chutzpah, Jeffrey Archer survived everything life threw at him and was loved by hordes of readers, especially in India

Israel puts military on alert for October 7 anniversary, warns Gazans

Israel’s Defence Minister said he had put the military on high alert before the anniversary of Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, warning Gazans would pay a “heavy price” if forces were harmed. The office of Defence Minister Israel Katz said the instruction came “in light of intelligence regarding Hamas’s intentions to attempt to carry out attacks and terror operations against our forces in Gaza on that day”.

Paramount and Warner Bros merge to become one Hollywood giant, Skydance

It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its USD 81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. The companies completed the deal, ushering in a new Hollywood giant with the now shorter “Skydance” name tag. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together. And HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners,” and even networks like CNN find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather”.

Students, teachers march in France on biggest day of school protests

Students, teachers and parents marched in cites across France and protesters blockaded hundreds of schools, in the ‌biggest day of action in a wave of demonstrations demanding the government tackle understaffed and ​dilapidated classrooms.

Smriti Mandhana appointed Indian women’s cricket team captain

Senior opener Smriti Mandhana was appointed captain of the Indian women’s cricket team after Harmanpreet Kaur stepped down from the role. Harmanpreet announced her decision to step down as India captain in a social media post, following a review meeting with the BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia, women’s team head coach Amol Muzumdar, and Mandhana in Guwahati.

India, six other countries express interest to host 2036 Olympics; to present Games projects in Nov.: IOC

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) said that India, Germany, Qatar and Turkiye are among seven countries with a stated interest in hosting the 2036 Olympic Games and have been invited to present their projects to the Future Host Commission in November.

World.title: CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s Chhattisgarh visit postponed
World.content:
A two day visit of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and a couple of senior officials of the Election Commission of India (ECI) to Chhattisgarh has been postponed due to “unavoidable reasons”, according to a government order issued on Tuesday (October 6, 2026).

Mr Kumar — who is facing criticism over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls — and the fellow ECI officials were scheduled to travel from Delhi to Chhattisgarh for the visit spanning October 7 and 8.

“It is informed that the Commission [ECI] has postponed the Chhattisgarh visit programme of Shri Gyanesh Kumar, Hon’ble Chief Election Commissioner, and other senior officials of the Commission, due to unavoidable reasons.The revised date of the visit will be communicated separately once it is received from the Commission,” the letter issued by the office of the Chief Electoral Officer in Chhattisgarh.
