World.title: LIST: Duterte-Carpio bank accounts, balances detailed in impeachment trial
World.content:
FINANCIAL RECORDS. The Senate impeachment court receives tax and bank records of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 30, 2026.

Here is a summary of the banks testifying on the Duterte-Carpio money trail as prosecutors try to determine whether year-end account balances line up with what was declared in the Vice President's SALNs

MANILA, Philippines – After examining billions of pesos in reported transactions through the Anti-Money Laundering Council, prosecutors in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial are now going to what could be the most consequential part: the banks that actually held the accounts.

More representatives from several banks are expected to authenticate the underlying accounts and records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, as prosecutors seek to establish whether the couple’s bank balances were properly reflected in the Vice President’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs).

Private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said the records cover at least 30 active accounts across eight banks for the years 2022 to 2025.

According to the prosecution’s offer of testimony, the accounts had combined year-end balances of more than P59 million in 2022, P71 million in 2023, P22 million in 2024, and P35 million in 2025.

UNDECLARED? Screenshot from prosecution’s offer of testimony on Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

Yet recall that in each of those years, Duterte’s SALNs did not separately list any cash on hand or cash in bank.

The prosecution alleges that the balances do not match Duterte’s SALNs. Her lawyers have previously argued that cash and bank deposits were included under the broader “other personal properties” category. The testimonies of bank officials are expected to provide the more precise year-end balances needed to make that comparison.

Here are the banks and officers identified so far:

1. Land Bank of the Philippines (LandBank)

Eunice Sumatra, manager of LandBank’s San Pedro-Davao City branch, became the first bank witness on Tuesday, October 6. Prosecutors called her to authenticate records involving one payroll bank account with account number ending 8998 in the name of Sara Zimmerman Duterte.

Raquel Dela Cerna, manager of LandBank’s Davao R. Magsaysay branch, followed Sumatra and authenticated an active account belonging to Carpio ending in 2730. She disclosed year-end balances of P505,517.35 in 2022, P953,681.42 in 2023, P115,824.20 in 2024, and P1,358,373.07 in 2025.

LANDBANK. Screenshot during the direct examination of Cerna on October 6.

Cerna also mentioned that the branch had two accounts linked to the Vice President, which were now closed.

During cross-examination, Cerna agreed that marriage alone does not make one spouse a joint account holder or authorized signatory of an account held by the other.

2. Asia United Bank

AUB is among the banks the prosecution is expected to present. As of October 6, no representative from the bank had yet taken the stand.

3. Philippine Savings Bank (PSBank)

PSBank is among the banks the prosecution is expected to present. As of October 6, no representative from the bank had yet taken the stand.

AMLC earlier presented an August 1, 2024 suspicious transaction report involving Carpio’s PSBank accounts that cited “drug trafficking and related offenses.” The STR narrative referred to a criminal complaint over the alleged 2017 importation of P6.4 billion worth of shabu and noted that Carpio had active peso and dollar accounts with the bank.

4. Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co.

Metrobank is among the banks the prosecution is expected to present. As of October 6, no representative from the bank had yet taken the stand.

5. Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI)

BPI is among the banks the prosecution is expected to present. As of October 6, no representative from the bank had yet taken the stand.

BPI is already a significant part of the impeachment record because it asked AMLC to correct 13 covered transaction reports involving Carpio after discovering erroneous amounts caused by what the bank described as a system bug.

AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura confirmed Tuesday that AMLC validated BPI’s corrections.

6. Philippine National Bank (PNB)

PNB is among the banks the prosecution is expected to present. As of October 6, no representative from the bank had yet taken the stand.

PNB records could be notable because AMLC testimony on October 5 identified P18 million in withdrawals from a Carpio account at PNB on August 6, 2024, part of P41 million he withdrew from PNB and BDO that day.

7. BDO Unibank

BDO is among the banks the prosecution is expected to present. As of October 6, no representative from the bank had yet taken the stand.

BDO records could likewise draw scrutiny after AMLC testimony identified P23 million in withdrawals from Carpio’s account at BDO on August 6, 2024, forming part of the same P41-million single-day withdrawal total.

The prosecution is expected to complete the bank-by-bank presentation over the succeeding trial days. – Rappler.com

World.title: Want to buy GCash shares? How retail investors can join the IPO
World.content:
Here’s what you need to know about the offer period and what to consider before deciding whether to buy

MANILA, Philippines – Filipinos can now buy into GCash before it officially makes its Philippine Stock Exchange debut, with the public offer period starting Tuesday, October 6.

One of the easiest routes is through GStocks PH inside the GCash app itself. Investors can open Invest, select GStocks PH, then tap the IPO banner. GStocks PH requires an eligible account with enough money in its trading wallet. Opening an account generally requires users to be at least 18 years old, have a Philippine SIM, a fully verified GCash account, and a valid government ID.

The minimum GCash IPO order through GStocks PH is 100 shares, worth P660 at the P6.60 offer price.

Retail investors can also participate as local small investors through PSE EASy. The PSE said all LSI subscriptions for the Mynt IPO must be submitted through the platform, which requires investors to nominate a PSE trading participant or broker. The usual LSI ceiling is P100,000. Investors with existing brokerage accounts may also check whether their broker is accepting IPO orders.

The offer period runs until noon on Monday, October 12, giving retail investors until then to submit their subscriptions and complete any required payment and documentation.

Regular trading under the ticker GCASH is scheduled to begin on October 20, when allocated IPO shares can start trading on the PSE.

As always, do your own research

In an investor briefing on Tuesday, GCash’s top executives made their case for why the homegrown e-wallet is a good buy.

Mynt had 41.5 million monthly active users by June, about four times the active users of its nearest competitor. Its adjusted revenue grew at a 54% compound annual growth rate from 2023 to 2025, while net income rose at a 64.4% CAGR over the same period, reaching P17.25 billion in 2025.

In other words, both revenue and profit were growing quite strongly over that two-year stretch. Net income reached another P10.82 billion in the first half of 2026. Management is eyeing lending, merchant services, overseas users, and deeper use of the app as the next avenue of growth.

But investors also have reasons to look closely at the deal. Around 80% of the IPO consists of secondary shares being sold by existing shareholders, meaning most of the money raised from those shares goes to the sellers rather than Mynt as fresh capital. Management has stressed that this does not represent a full exit by its strategic shareholders, but it does show that several early private equity investors see this as a good time to cash out. (READ: Meet the new cornerstone investors lining up for GCash’s record IPO)

Remember too the oft-repeated investing maxim that a good company can still be a bad investment at the wrong price. GCash is also coming to market at a hefty valuation. At P6.60, its roughly P442-billion valuation works out to about 24.6x its latest trailing 12-month earnings through June, against the PSEi’s 9.87x multiple as of October 2. – Rappler.com

World.title: Health groups to lawmakers: Increase PhilHealth budget, not MAIFIP funding
World.content:
PHILHEALTH BUDGET. Advocates led by the Healthcare Professionals Alliance After COVID-19 push for a higher 2027 budget for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation in a press conference on October 6, 2026.

Funding for MAIFIP — described as 'soft pork' — could double in 2027, while PhilHealth may face a significant budget gap

MANILA, Philippines – Healthcare workers and advocates criticized the House of Representatives’ budget amendments review subcommittee (BARSc) for not recommending an increase in the proposed 2027 budget of the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) and instead seeking to hike funding for controversial medical aid.

On Tuesday, October 6, some 70 medical societies and healthcare workers’ groups under the Healthcare Professionals Alliance After COVID-19 (HPAAC) urged Congress to “decisively close” the P170-billion funding shortfall for PhilHealth.

Even after the BARSc hearing last Thursday, October 1, PhilHealth’s proposed spending plan for 2027 is set to remain at P74.4 billion — at least in the House’s version.

In a press conference on Tuesday, Dr. Antonio Dans, HPAAC convenor, said that amount may be exhausted by PhilHealth as early as March next year.

“Naghihingalo ang PhilHealth (PhilHealth is at risk),” Social Watch Philippines co-convenor Maria Victoria Raquiza also said.

“One of the best ways to sabotage PhilHealth is to not provide it the funding that it needs. And because it is not being given the funding that it needs, it’s not able to do its job in the right way,” she added.

HPAAC also called for the transfer of the budget for the Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) program directly to the state health insurer.

Civil society groups have branded MAIFIP as “soft pork,” describing it as a “politicized discretionary program” that forces Filipinos to “beg for life-saving services.”

The BARSc recommended an additional P24.97 billion for MAIFIP, pushing it to P49.19 billion from the P24.23 billion under the 2027 National Expenditure Program.

It’s the second biggest proposed increase from the BARSc. The subcommittee also suggested boosting funding for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, nationally procured commodities for prevention and control of communicable disease, and operations of regional hospitals, all under the Department of Health.

HPAAC also sought the immediate release of P311 billion to PhilHealth — accumulated from previous years — to strengthen benefit packages and reduce Filipinos’ out-of-pocket healthcare spending. The total figure includes around P133 billion in sin tax collections, some P62 billion from revenues of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation and the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, and over P112 billion appropriated by law.

While having an original proposal of P379 billion for the state insurer, health officials have asked lawmakers to restore at least P244 billion to fully implement benefit expansion, as well as cover projected insurance claims of indirect contributors next year.

Dr. Jeremy Cordero, also from HPAAC, said not granting a budget of at least P244 billion to PhilHealth may result in late payments, which could push hospitals to opt out of the state insurer. He said geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas “could be left behind” in this scenario.

Advocates now plan to raise the issue to senators. They expect senators to decrease funding for MAIFIP, with Dans saying that lawmakers from the upper chamber have a “very jaded view” of the program.

Worries remain, however, that when the bicameral conference committee convenes, higher MAIFIP funding would emerge — just like the experience in the 2026 budget.

“We’re just hoping they feel the burden,” Dans said, referring to lawmakers. “Nakikita lang nila ‘yong naabutan nila ng pera. ‘Yong mga ‘di nila naabutan ng pera, ‘yon ‘yong mga lumalapit sa amin.” (The lawmakers only see those they give aid to. But those who were not able to receive money are the ones who come to us doctors.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan, Oman Push for Stronger Trade, Investment Ties at Business Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Oman outlined new opportunities to expand investment, financial cooperation, energy, logistics and agricultural ties at a Kazakh-Omani business forum held during Omani Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said’s state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 6.

Investment cooperation

Addressing the forum, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the high-level talks during the visit had laid a strong foundation for closer economic cooperation.

Tokayev called for a stronger legal and institutional framework for trade and investment, saying greater protections for investors would help create more predictable, transparent and reliable business conditions.

He also urged business to establish stronger direct ties.

“I am confident that the establishment of the Kazakh-Omani Business Council will become a practical platform for active interaction between business representatives,” he said.

Financial partnership

President Tokayev welcomed an agreement to establish a joint investment structure between Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and the Oman Investment Authority, describing it as an important mechanism to mobilize financing and attract additional investment.

“We also see significant potential for cooperation with the recently established Oman International Financial Center. Establishing direct relations between the financial institutions of our two countries opens up new opportunities and avenues for mutual investment,” Tokayev said.

Energy and mining

Tokayev identified energy and mining as another area for expansion, saying existing cooperation could pave a way for new joint ventures.

“Combining our capabilities in these vital areas will enable us to create new joint ventures that ensure the long-term prosperity of both countries,” Tokayev said.

Transport and agriculture

Tokayev described Oman as an important transit and logistics partner, citing its strategic geographic position, port infrastructure and access to Middle Eastern and African markets.

Kazakhstan, he said, brings extensive natural resources, an established industrial base and a strategic position along emerging transport routes connecting Asia and Europe, alongside plans to further strengthen connectivity.

Tokayev also called for greater cooperation in agriculture and food security, highlighting Kazakhstan’s large agricultural land base.

“Kazakhstan, with its extensive agricultural lands, is ready to become a reliable partner in ensuring the long-term food security of the entire Gulf region,” Tokayev said.

From agreements to projects

He identified implementing agreements reached at the political level as the key priority for the next stage of bilateral relations.

“By actively engaging our business communities, we can take economic relations to a new level,” Tokayev said.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Cross-Border Hubs Take Shape as New Trade and Logistics Gateways
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is moving its cross-border trade hubs from planning to implementation, with new production facilities, logistics infrastructure and cargo flows emerging along the country’s borders and Caspian coast.

The five priority hubs are designed to strengthen trade with the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan, Russia, China and the Caspian region, attract investment and support the government’s goal of raising non-resource exports to 30%, the Ministry of Trade and Integration reported on Sept. 6.

Khorgos emerges as major eastern gateway

The strongest growth is at the Khorgos-Eastern Gate Special Economic Zone (SEZ), where the number of projects rose from 14 in 2022 to 69, while investment grew from 340 billion tenge (US$755.1 million) to 652.8 billion tenge (US$1.5 billion).

Currently, 40 projects worth 75 billion tenge (US$166.6 million) are under implementation, creating 864 jobs. In January-June, nine new participants registered projects totaling 9.3 billion tenge (US$20.7 million), creating 230 jobs. Production reached 12.7 billion tenge (US$28.2 million), up 74% year on year.

The SEZ already hosts a dry port with an annual capacity of 540,000 containers and a 25,000-square-meter Class A warehouse. Two additional major logistics projects are being designed.

By 2028, 28 projects worth 577.7 billion tenge (US$1.3 billion) are planned, with nearly 2,800 jobs. Key projects include the Kazakhstan-China International Industrial City, valued at 330 billion tenge (US$733 million), and an international cargo and passenger airport worth 250 billion tenge (US$555.2 million).

Central Asia hub advances

On the southern border, the Central Asia International Industrial Cooperation Center is moving into the construction and commissioning phase.

External construction and installation work is complete, and commissioning is underway. Internal engineering infrastructure is 55% complete and is expected to be finished by December.

Eight production buildings have already been constructed, while the center’s investment project portfolio totals 89.4 billion tenge (US$199 million). Construction has started on a 75.3-billion-tenge (US$167.2 million) industrial park, one of the center’s largest projects.

In the Zhambyl Region, the Industrial Trade and Logistics Complex received SEZ status in April. The 165-hectare site is being prepared for development, with infrastructure connections planned. Construction of the first-stage substation began this year, with around 4 billion tenge (US$8.8 million) allocated this year from a total planned 12 billion tenge (US$26.7 million).

Western hub targets production and trade

The Eurasia Cross-Border Trade Center in the West Kazakhstan Region covers 281 hectares. Part of its external infrastructure, including gas, electricity, water supply and wastewater systems, has already been completed.

The industrial zone is attracting projects ranging from asphalt production and tire recycling to aerated concrete manufacturing and a gas-turbine power plant.

Authorities are also considering creating the Eurasia SEZ, which would provide additional incentives for investment and local production.

Caspian corridor gains container capacity

The Caspian leg is already generating tangible cargo flows. The Aktau International Container Hub received its first container train on July 14. Since then, it has handled 233 containers, or 444 TEUs.

The project is being developed in stages and is expected to raise the port’s container-handling capacity from 70,000 TEUs to 240,000 TEUs annually.

Another major project is the Ersai container terminal at the Industrial Port. Construction is nearly 85% complete. Ten kilometers of internal railway tracks have been built, while the container yard and crane tracks are nearing completion.

The terminal is scheduled to open on Oct. 1. At full capacity, it will handle up to 120,000 TEUs annually and accommodate up to 300 vessels a year. Private investment in the project exceeds 15 billion tenge (US$33.3 million).

From border infrastructure to trade network

The five hubs are gradually becoming part of a broader trade and logistics network connecting Kazakhstan with neighboring markets and international transport routes.

The emerging model goes beyond border checkpoints and warehouses. Industrial production, logistics services, investment projects and container infrastructure are developing alongside one another, creating new points of economic activity across the country.

The next priority is to bring the facilities to full capacity, attract more investors and increase trade and transit volumes through Kazakhstan’s border corridors.

World.title: Turkmenistan Launches E-Visas and Online Registration for Foreigners
World.content:
ALMATY – Turkmenistan has launched an electronic visa system and an online registration portal for foreign nationals, moving parts of the country’s migration procedures to digital platforms.

The State Migration Service of Turkmenistan presented the new services with representatives of foreign diplomatic missions accredited in the country attending the event. Turkmen ambassadors abroad also joined via videoconference.

The electronic visa system operates through the migration service’s portal, allowing foreigners to submit documents online to obtain authorization to enter Turkmenistan. A separate platform has been launched for the online registration of foreign visitors.

The service is intended for tourists, entrepreneurs and diplomats, who can submit documents for migration registration through the platform. Authorities expect the digitalization of migration procedures to reduce processing times and the amount of paperwork required from foreign nationals.

Previously, foreigners traveling to Turkmenistan for tourism generally had to obtain an invitation through a host organization or tour operator before applying for a visa.

World.title: Eleven Years in WTO: What Has Kazakhstan Gained
World.content:
ASTANA – Eleven years after Kazakhstan joined the World Trade Organization, the country trades across a far wider global market under internationally agreed rules. However, one of the central challenges that preceded accession remains: reducing its dependence on commodity exports.

Kazakhstan became the WTO’s 162nd member in 2015 after nearly two decades of negotiations. Its experience since then offers a measure of how deeply the economy has integrated into global trade and whether greater market access has translated into a more diversified export base.

“It is important to understand that today, 98% of Kazakhstan’s trade is conducted with WTO member countries. The organization remains a key element of the global trade architecture,” said Minister of Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev during a briefing in September.

Sagyndyk Kosherbayev, director of the Center for Trade and Investment Policy at the Astana-based Economic Research Institute, describes Kazakhstan’s accession to the WTO as one of the key stages in the country’s integration into the global economy.

According to him, by the end of 2025, Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover had reached $144.7 billion, up 89% from 2015. Over the same period, exports increased by 72%, while imports more than doubled. During Kazakhstan’s first WTO Trade Policy Review in 2024, WTO members also noted that the country’s trade volumes had roughly doubled since accession.

Kosherbayev cautioned against attributing all of that growth directly to WTO membership. A more useful measure, he said, is how membership has changed the conditions under which Kazakhstan trades with the rest of the world.

“Kazakhstan remains a major exporter of commodities, meaning the value of its foreign trade is heavily influenced by global prices for oil, metals and uranium. Trade dynamics have also been shaped by the development of the Eurasian Economic Union, geopolitical shifts, exchange-rate fluctuations, transport and logistics constraints, and changes in the geography of trade flows,” Kosherbayev told The Astana Times.

What WTO membership changed

According to Kosherbayev, some of the clearest gains from WTO membership have come through more predictable market access, lower tariffs and simpler customs procedures.

“As part of its commitments, Kazakhstan bound tariffs across all product lines, while its average applied most-favored-nation tariff fell from 7.8% in 2015 to 5.6% in 2025. A more open tariff regime lowered barriers to imports of equipment and production inputs, while binding maximum tariff levels made foreign trade conditions more predictable for businesses and investors,” Kosherbayev said.

The expert also pointed to the progress in simplifying trade procedures, including introducing electronic customs declarations, a single-window system for export and import operations, and a customs risk-management system.

“This is where one of the more underestimated benefits of membership lies. The WTO is not so much a mechanism for increasing exports in itself as it is a system of rules that makes international trade more predictable,” he said.

This predictability also matters for investors, particularly companies considering export-oriented production, because it allows them to better assess the cost of importing equipment and components and the conditions for exporting finished goods.

WTO membership also provides a rules-based forum to challenge trade measures that might otherwise be difficult to contest through bilateral pressure alone.

Kosherbayev said that in April, Kazakhstan used the WTO dispute settlement system as a complainant for the first time, requesting consultations with Indonesia over additional import duties on hot-rolled steel coils from Kazakhstan.

“Kazakhstan argued that the measures may be inconsistent with provisions of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 1994, the Anti-Dumping Agreement and the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the WTO. The case illustrates one of the practical advantages of membership, particularly for economies with less negotiating weight,” he explained.

Diversification challenge

However, more predictable trade rules did not fundamentally transform the structure of Kazakhstan’s exports.

“In 2025, crude oil accounted for around 50.5% of Kazakhstan’s merchandise exports. Other major export categories included radioactive elements and isotopes, refined copper, copper ores and concentrates and ferroalloys. This is a crucial point when assessing the results of WTO membership,” said the expert.

A highly concentrated export structure doesn’t necessarily mean the WTO membership has been ineffective. Rather, as Kosherbayev said, it shows the limits of what trade policy alone can achieve.

“Export diversification is shaped primarily within the domestic economy. It requires competitive businesses, technological development, higher labor productivity, access to financing, transport connectivity, compliance with international standards and the ability of companies to integrate into global value chains,” he explained.

“International trade rules can provide access to markets, but it is the domestic economy that must produce goods and services capable of competing in those markets,” he added.

WTO under pressure

The predictability may matter even more today, as protectionism, wars and geopolitical rivalry increasingly reshape global trade. WTO itself describes the current period as the “most serious and sustained disruptions since the multilateral trading system was created 80 years ago.”

The shift has been especially visible in U.S. trade policy, with the Trump administration expanding the use of reciprocal, country-specific and sectoral tariffs in pursuit of what it describes as fairer trade.

“Trade conflicts among the world’s largest economies, industrial policies, subsidies for strategic sectors, sanctions-related restrictions and efforts by governments to reduce dependence on individual suppliers are accelerating the fragmentation of global trade,” said Kosherbayev.

At the same time, WTO’s World Trade Report indicated that around 72% of global merchandise trade still takes place under the WTO’s most-favored-nation terms. The organization says decades of trade cooperation have supported economic growth, helped narrow income gaps between developing and advanced economies, and contributed to greater stability among its members.

The WTO said it now faces a paradox partly of its own making. The more open and integrated trading system it helped build has also become more complex, multipolar and difficult to govern. Its challenge is no longer simply to preserve that system, but to adapt to the world it helped create.

So the next phase will depend on whether Kazakh companies can use that access to expand beyond commodities and compete in higher-value segments of global trade at a time when the multilateral trading system itself is becoming more fragmented.

As Kosherbayev said, Kazakhstan’s trade policy should increasingly be judged not by the number of markets formally open to the country, but by how effectively its businesses can compete in them.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Oman Deepen Ties During Sultan’s First Central Asia Visit
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Oman agreed to deepen strategic partnership across energy, transport, logistics, agriculture and digitalization on Oct. 6, as Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said made his first visit to Central Asia.

During the talks in Astana, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described Oman as a “time-tested and reliable partner” of Kazakhstan in the Arab world. He noted that the two countries will mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations next year.

“We have laid a solid foundation for moving to a new dynamic stage of partnership,” Tokayev said.

The two leaders also adopted a joint statement that sets out the main areas of the bilateral partnership, Akorda reported. The document reaffirms the two countries’ commitment to strengthening cooperation based on mutual respect, trust and shared interests, while outlining priorities ranging from trade and investment to transport, energy, agriculture, digital technologies, education and tourism.

Tokayev highlighted several ongoing joint projects, including the development of the Dunga oil field, Solidcore Resources’ operations in the Pavlodar and North Kazakhstan Regions, the joint investment fund with Oman Investment Authority, and projects in the hotel and resort sector.

New agreements strengthen investment and business ties

During the visit, Kazakhstan and Oman signed an intergovernmental agreement to promote and mutually protect investments, an air services agreement, an agreement establishing the Oman-Kazakhstan Business Council, and an agreement establishing a joint investment fund.

The leaders also signed an agreement setting the terms of the Eurasian Development Bank’s presence in Oman, along with several interagency memoranda covering cooperation in various fields.

The leaders agreed to diversify bilateral trade, address trade barriers and improve market access for products from both countries. They also endorsed stronger investment cooperation in energy, natural resources, manufacturing, food, healthcare, logistics, tourism, renewable energy and mining.

Transport connectivity identified as strategic priority

The joint statement highlights the strategic importance of stronger transport and logistics links between Central Asia and the Gulf region.

Kazakhstan and Oman intend to develop efficient transport corridors connecting Central Asian markets with the Gulf, the Middle East and Africa, among other key regions.

The countries also agreed to work toward launching direct, regular flights as soon as possible, saying improved air links would support business, tourism and people-to-people ties.

“We see significant opportunities for growth, investment and cooperation with Kazakhstan,” Sultan Haitham said.

Energy, digital technologies and AI

The two countries also expressed interest in joint projects in energy, petrochemicals, manufacturing and processing, while identifying agriculture and food security as promising areas for deeper cooperation.

Digital technologies, artificial intelligence, innovation and human capital development emerged as another priority. The officials will encourage partnerships between technology companies, innovation hubs and academic institutions, including through knowledge exchange and joint initiatives.

The leaders also expressed interest in expanding educational cooperation through student and academic exchanges, joint programs and collaborative research.

Sultan Haitham thanked President Tokayev for his hospitality and reaffirmed Oman’s commitment to strengthening relations with Kazakhstan. He also invited President Tokayev to visit the Sultanate of Oman.

World.title: Digital Bridge 2026: New AI Order Beyond US-China Race — Who Gets to Act for You?
World.content:
ASTANA – The emerging AI order may look bipolar from a distance, with the United States (U.S.) and China dominating the most advanced models, chips and computing infrastructure. But the discussion at Digital Bridge 2026 in Astana on Oct. 2 suggested a more complex picture: the technology may be concentrated, while its applications, standards and economic benefits are likely to spread far more widely.

Olaf J. Groth, founder and CEO of Cambrian Futures, described the emerging system as a “G2 plus X” order.

“The G2 with regard to AI and cognitive technology is dominated by the U.S. and China,” Groth said during the New AI World Order panel moderated by Financial Times China Technology Correspondent Eleanor Olcott.

But the question, in his view, is who the “X” will be.

“There’s lots of room for smaller economies, including, of course, middle powers, as well as some larger economies like India, Europe, to be the X,” he said, pointing to countries such as Kazakhstan, Singapore, Vietnam and Malaysia as economies that could play differentiated roles.

That distinction is important. The countries outside the two AI superpowers may not need to reproduce the entire technological stack to have a meaningful place in the new economy.

Ya-Qin Zhang, founder of the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua University, noted that most countries should not try to build frontier models entirely on their own.

“I wouldn’t say it’s a good idea to develop a trillion-parameter super frontier model for every country, probably not for Kazakhstan,” Zhang said.

Instead, he suggested countries focus on areas where they can build their own strengths while selectively using frontier models developed elsewhere.

His “TAP” model, including token, agent or application, and people, offered one way of looking at that division. Applications and people can be developed locally, while countries make choices around the infrastructure behind the models, including electricity, chips and access to frontier systems.

The emphasis on choice is important. Zhang said that countries should avoid becoming locked into a small number of technology providers and retain the ability to combine different models, infrastructure and applications. That also shifts the discussion away from the race to build the biggest model and toward the less visible infrastructure that lets AI function across economies.

Data, security and the limits of doing it alone

For financial networks in particular, AI’s value is closely linked to the breadth of data available to it. Ian Slater, Executive Vice President at Mastercard, made that point when the discussion turned to fraud and cybersecurity. According to him, global payment systems can benefit from drawing on patterns across markets rather than operating on data from a single country.

“A single country data set from a fraud and risk management perspective doesn’t work very well,” Slater said.

His argument was not simply that more data is always better. Fraud itself is increasingly cross-border, meaning that systems designed to detect it can be disadvantaged if they see only a fraction of the picture. That same logic applies to the wider question of access to technology.

Slater said that AI could create new opportunities for financial inclusion, but those opportunities depend on whether markets can connect to the technology and standards already developing globally.

“It is not efficient nor is it possible for every market in the world to develop its own capability,” he said.

The point fits into a broader tension running through the discussion: how to develop domestic capability without turning technological sovereignty into technological isolation.

Groth said that open-weight models could help widen access, while Zhang pointed to the cost-effectiveness of open models and the possibility for countries to combine them with their own data centers, electricity and applications.

“Open models can be an equalizer to democratize AI,” Zhang added.

But greater accessibility introduces another problem. The more models spread, the harder they may become to monitor. Groth warned that a world full of customized open models could also become “very unwieldy” from a governance perspective, raising questions about how governments would monitor systems operating outside traditional institutional structures. That makes the emerging AI architecture not only a technological and economic question, but a regulatory one.

The panel also returned repeatedly to the issue of trust, particularly as AI moves into financial services, digital identity and autonomous systems. Zhang said that increasingly capable AI systems will require clear boundaries, testing and mechanisms that allow potentially dangerous systems to be monitored or shut down. Slater approached the same issue from the consumer side, noting that people are still trying to understand what AI actually means for them. The challenge, then, is no longer simply whether AI works. It is whether the systems built around it are understandable, secure and governed well enough to become part of everyday economic life.

What comes after the technology?

In a separate conversation with The Astana Times after the panel, Slater returned to a question that came up several times during the discussion: what actually makes AI useful to an economy? His answer was not about building ever-larger models.

“I think the government needs a plan. They need to know what they’re doing it for,” he said.

He said there is a risk that AI becomes a target in itself, much as happened with other technology cycles.

“The danger with anything like AI … is that the term itself becomes the end. People talk about AI for the sake of AI,” he said.

For Slater, governments should start with a use case and work backward, building the institutions and partnerships around it. He pointed to Singapore and the United Arab Emirates as examples of countries that approached digital transformation with a relatively clear sense of what they wanted to achieve.

The same practical approach, he said, will be needed as AI agents begin to enter commerce. Slater sees agents as an extension of how people already interact with the internet rather than a replacement for existing commerce. Someone could eventually ask an agent to search for a flight, compare options and make a purchase according to permissions given in advance. But the technology is moving faster than consumer familiarity with it.

“We talk about these things, but we’re not at the end of the point where a consumer actually knows how to do it,” he said.

That gap matters because giving an agent the ability to act on someone’s behalf raises questions as much about behavior and responsibility as about software.

Slater also sees a similar challenge around biometrics and digital identity. He said he prefers biometrics to passwords, but as AI agents become more sophisticated, systems will still need to distinguish the real individual from the digital representation acting on that person’s behalf.

“We have some work to do to figure that piece out,” he said.

For a panel framed around a contest between the world’s biggest AI powers, that may have been one of the more telling conclusions. The next chapter will certainly be shaped by who controls frontier models, computers and chips. But it will also depend on what countries do with technologies they did not necessarily invent themselves and whether people are willing to let those technologies make increasingly consequential decisions for them.

World.title: Astana School Named Finalist for 2027 Zayed Sustainability Prize
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana’s General Education School No. 101 has been named one of three finalists representing Europe and Central Asia in the Global High Schools category of the 2027 Zayed Sustainability Prize, organizers announced.

The school was selected for an artificial intelligence-based system that monitors air quality in classrooms, allowing schools to detect changes in indoor conditions and respond before they affect the learning environment. The project is designed to help create safer and healthier conditions for students and teachers.

“General Education School No.101, Astana, a public school in Kazakhstan with 3,800 students, aims to develop an AI-supported indoor air quality system using LEGO Spike Prime and Raspberry Pi sensors to monitor classroom conditions and predict periods of poor air quality,” reads the official website of the prize.

The school is competing against Agrupamento de Escolas Gândara Mar of Portugal and Keban Multi-Program Anatolian High School of Türkiye. Overall, 18 schools from six regions were selected as finalists in the Global High Schools category.

The UAE-based award received a record 10,233 submissions from 177 countries in the 2027 cycle, up 32% from the previous year. Finalists were selected across six categories: health, food, energy, water, climate action and global high schools.

Other finalists include U.S.-based Elythea, which uses artificial intelligence to identify pregnancy complications using first-trimester data, and Japan’s TOWING, which uses biochar technology to improve soil health.

Each organizational finalist will receive $100,000, while school finalists will receive $25,000. Winners in the organizational categories will receive $1 million, while winning schools will receive $150,000.

The winners will be announced on Jan. 12, 2027 at the Awards Ceremony during Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week.

“The most powerful solutions are those rooted in real-world needs,” said Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Director General of the Prize.

The Zayed Sustainability Prize says projects supported through the award have reached more than 411 million people worldwide.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Partners Target Falling Caspian Sea Levels With New Monitoring Project
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and international partners are stepping up efforts to address falling Caspian Sea levels, biodiversity loss and pollution, as Aktau hosted a high-level dialogue on Oct. 5 that also launched a Japan-funded monitoring and water management project.

The Caspian Sea has been shrinking for decades, raising concerns over biodiversity, coastal communities, infrastructure and economic activity across the five littoral states. Kazakhstan, which has the sea’s longest coastline, has increasingly sought regional and international cooperation as scientists warn that climate change and declining river inflows could accelerate the retreat.

Organized by the United Nations Development Programme in Kazakhstan with the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources and the Mangystau Region akimat (administration), the dialogue brought together government institutions, diplomats, international organizations, scientists, civil society and the private sector.

The participants discussed changes in the Caspian Sea’s water balance, geological risks, pollution, marine litter, biodiversity conservation and the circular economy, the UNDP reported.

Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Alibek Kuantyrov emphasized the need for coordinated action to address the Caspian Sea’s environmental challenges.

“For Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea is a vital part of the country’s environmental, social and economic development, a source of livelihoods for coastal communities, and a space connecting five states. That is why Kazakhstan has consistently advocated moving from discussions of individual environmental challenges towards systemic and coordinated action,” said Kuantyrov.

Japan-funded project to strengthen Caspian Sea monitoring

The Japan-funded project will support joint research involving experts from Caspian countries and establish a regional scientific coordination platform for exchanging data and expertise. It will also strengthen Kazakhstan’s capacity to monitor the Northern Caspian Sea, including through upgraded monitoring and laboratory equipment and professional training.

The project will help improve monitoring of sea level, river discharge, water temperature and salinity, and evaporation. The data, combined with meteorological, bathymetric and satellite observations, will support improved models and projections of Caspian Sea level changes and related risks.

Japanese Ambassador to Kazakhstan Yasumasa Iijima highlighted Japan’s expertise in water resources management, disaster risk reduction and environmental protection.

“The project will focus on two main areas: establishing a platform to strengthen cooperation among the Caspian littoral states, and advancing scientific monitoring, transboundary data exchange, dialogue and joint action. Japan has extensive experience and expertise in water resources management, disaster risk reduction and environmental protection,” he said.

The event was the first held under the Friends of the Caspian initiative, which aims to bring together Caspian states, international organizations, financial institutions, donors, scientists and civil society around the shared goal of preserving the Caspian Sea.

The initiative is expected to be presented to international partners on the sidelines of the UN Climate Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, in November.

World.title: Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev’s statement about ‘Ukrainisation’ of Armenia
World.content:
Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia

“Armenia turning into a new Ukraine represents another sign of Russia’s geopolitical anxiety and the deepening crisis in Armenian-Russian relations,” political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan said in response to Dmitry Medvedev’s sensational statement.

“Armenia’s current leadership decided that changing the country’s course would serve its interests. I am sure that this will not lead to anything good either. The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” said Russia’s deputy Security Council chairman.

By a change in course, he meant Armenia’s drive towards European integration. Yerevan has not officially responded to his remarks.

Only parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan told journalists: “Armenia cannot be anything else. Armenia is Armenia, and it will always be Armenia.”

Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan believes that Russia “is irritated and unbalanced because the situation in the war is not just bad, but very bad”. At the same time, the analyst says Armenia should take the statement from Moscow seriously and try to assess how real the threat is:

“We should not treat this threat as either an absolutely inevitable scenario or empty bravado. It involves real risks stemming from Armenia’s energy and economic vulnerabilities. It also contains elements of psychological pressure.”

Comment

Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan says Russia fears losing its influence in the South Caucasus:

“Against the backdrop of setbacks on the Ukrainian front, Moscow’s resources remain limited, while its influence across the post-Soviet space has weakened. But the most unwelcome development for Russia is that all of this now shows a clear trend towards further deterioration.”

In his view, Russia can still wage a war of attrition in Ukraine, but casualties, economic sanctions and international isolation are creating significant tensions inside the country.

The analyst says that under these conditions, Russia sees the departure of any ally as a “stab in the back”. This leads to an unbalanced response, as Medvedev’s statement demonstrates:

“The aim of the threat is to instil fear in Armenian society and stop the process of rapprochement with the West, which stems from our security and development interests.”

Mehrabyan believes the threats from Moscow carry some real risks:

“The possibility of a direct military invasion is currently close to zero for one simple reason. No matter how many threats Medvedev spews, Russia has no way to invade a country with which it has no border. But Russia has powerful hybrid tools, and it can and does use them.”

Among the existing risks, the political analyst highlights Armenia’s economic and energy dependence on Russia.

He points to the Upper Lars checkpoint, the only land route linking Armenia with Russia. Whenever the route closes, it creates problems for Armenian exporters and importers. Mehrabyan also notes that Armenia receives gas from Russia, as well as fuel for its nuclear power plant:

“Cutting off gas supplies or suspending deliveries under the pretext of repairs, or closing the border on sanitary grounds, could trigger internal upheaval in Armenia and force the country to operate under a state of emergency.”

According to Mehrabyan, Yerevan has so far managed the potential risks without shocks or conflicts, but he is not confident that it will continue to do so.

He stresses that the current situation also creates potential security risks. In particular, he suggests that “Baku could sell its pressure on Armenia to Moscow”, and that Russia would have no objection to such a deal.

The political analyst says Russia is behaving like a wounded beast. He urges the Armenian authorities to summon the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry and hand him a formal protest note instead of making public demarches.

At the same time, he says Armenia needs to emphasise once again that its closer ties with the European Union and the United States serve Armenia’s interests and do not target Russia.

Mehrabyan identifies energy and economic diversification among Yerevan’s priorities. He says Armenia urgently needs to secure gas supplies from Iran, which could cover 85% of the country’s needs. He also expects the authorities to:

continue army reforms and work to strengthen the country’s borders;

deepen military and technical cooperation with various countries, including France, India and Greece;

ensure domestic stability and resilience;

strengthen strategic communications and combat disinformation.

Ruben Mehrabyan believes Armenia needs to prepare for modern warfare, including hybrid attacks:

“Armenia must not give Azerbaijan or Russia any reason to be tempted to commit aggression against us.”

Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia

World.title: Giorgi Davitadze case: how it drew attention to what is happening in Georgia’s prisons
World.content:
36-year-old prisoner Giorgi Davitadze says that about 10 prison staff at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi, Georgia, sexually assaulted him.

Authorities have not yet investigated Davitadze’s case. The Penitentiary Service, however, calls his allegations “a complete lie” and has released silent video footage as evidence. Davitadze’s family says the footage is incomplete and that authorities have not released the actual footage showing the alleged abuse.

Georgia’s Public Defender says the video provided to the office does not show the abuse Davitadze described.

Davitadze’s case has unfolded in a particularly sensitive context for Georgia. The allegations concern sexual abuse inside the very system that Georgian Dream made one of the main targets of its promised reforms when it came to power.

What Giorgi Davitadze says

The public learned about the alleged sexual abuse of Giorgi Davitadze on 2 October, during a hearing at the Court of Appeals.

Davitadze told the court that on 21 December 2025, about 10 prison staff sexually assaulted him and subjected him to degrading treatment in a de-escalation room, a special facility for temporarily isolating prisoners experiencing severe emotional or psychological distress.

“They took me down to the de-escalation room and raped me — with a finger, with a hand. […] Ten people, the guards, raped me. You can see everything on the camera,” Davitadze told the court.

He said he later attempted suicide.

Davitadze demanded that the authorities punish the prison staff he named, threatening to go on hunger strike if they failed to do so.

Davitadze’s allegations sparked widespread attention in the media and society.

The severity of the allegations drew particular attention, as did Davitadze’s claim that surveillance cameras should have captured the incident he described.

Davitadze’s family demanded the full release of the footage, while civil society organisations said the prisoner’s allegations required an effective and comprehensive investigation. The Penitentiary Service, in turn, categorically denied the allegations of sexual abuse.

It later emerged that government agencies had known about the alleged abuse since December 2025.

The Public Defender’s Office was also aware of the case. On 26 December, Davitadze’s lawyer told the office that his client had suffered ill-treatment.

That same day, a representative of the Public Defender’s Office went to the Rustavi prison and spoke with Davitadze. He repeated his account, saying prison staff had subjected him to abuse, including sexual abuse.

The Public Defender’s Office passed the information to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which opened an investigation. The office also demanded that video footage from the period identified by Davitadze be preserved in the archive.

More than nine months have passed since then. The investigation remains incomplete, and Davitadze is still being held in the same prison whose staff he accuses of abuse.

What the video released by the Penitentiary Service shows

On 2 October, the Penitentiary Service released footage that, according to the agency, shows Davitadze being taken to the de-escalation room on 21 December 2025 and the events that followed.

The video has no sound.

The footage shows Davitadze and about 10 prison staff members. One of them wears disposable medical gloves.

The staff search Davitadze, including with a metal detector. Several people hold the prisoner’s arms behind his back. The staff then forcibly search Davitadze after pinning him down on a bed.

The Penitentiary Service says prison staff must search prisoners when moving them to a de-escalation room. According to its account, Davitadze refused to undergo the search and insulted the staff, so they carried out the search by force.

The service calls the allegations of sexual abuse “a complete lie” and says “there was not only no sexual violence against Davitadze, there was no violence of any kind.”

The Penitentiary Service says it had not previously released the footage because the case remains under investigation. The agency also says it has continuously archived video footage related to Davitadze since 3 March 2026.

Family says the released video is incomplete

Davitadze’s family says the video released by the Penitentiary Service is incomplete.

His mother, Irma Davitadze, says she saw five video files covering about 20 minutes in total and believes the footage had been edited.

On 3 October, family members and Davitadze’s supporters held a protest outside the prison. They demanded the release of the full footage, an impartial investigation and the resignation of prison director Shota Trapaidze.

Another demand from the family is to transfer Davitadze to another prison, away from the staff members he accuses of abuse.

The prisoner’s father, Avtandil Davitadze, says:

“[These staff members] come to his cell, shout something, say something that insults his dignity, provoke him, and then what should never happen begins.”

However, Justice Minister Paata Salia says transferring a prisoner to another facility requires the authorities to follow certain procedures and meet specific conditions. The minister says officials are considering the request and will transfer Davitadze if he meets those conditions.

What the ombudsman says

The Public Defender’s position has become one of the most contentious aspects of the case.

According to an official statement from the Public Defender’s Office, its representatives requested and reviewed the relevant video footage but found no details showing the severe abuse Davitadze described.

However, the office stresses that authorities must investigate the allegations regardless and verify the prisoner’s complaint by collecting and comparing all available evidence.

The Public Defender also calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make the findings of the investigation public as soon as possible.

On 5 October, Public Defender Levan Ioseliani repeated on TV Pirveli that the footage released so far does not show sexual abuse itself. When asked whether inserting a finger into a prisoner’s body could form part of a search procedure, Ioseliani initially said he needed to check the relevant regulation:

Journalist: [Davitadze says] he felt a finger penetrate his body. Is that part of the search procedure?

Public Defender: We need to see what the regulation says — whether it allows such a thorough search. However, the regulation does require searches, including with a detector and scanner.

When the presenter asked whether he therefore ruled out the possibility of something that does not appear in the footage, Ioseliani replied: “The Prosecutor’s Office must investigate what we cannot see.”

Questions that remain unanswered

Public organisations say the footage and explanations released by the Penitentiary Service cannot provide an adequate response to such a serious allegation. More than ten organisations have called for an effective and comprehensive investigation. They include the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), the Social Justice Center, Transparency International — Georgia, the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED), the Institute for Development of Freedom of Information (IDFI), the Civil Society Foundation, Safari and others.

In their statement, they raise eight main questions:

Why did authorities need to move Davitadze to the de-escalation room?

What exactly did he do before the authorities took this step?

Was the measure necessary and proportionate?

Why were about ten staff members in the room?

Who were they and what did each of them do?

Does the published video show the full sequence of events without interruption?

Does the original video still exist, and can an independent expert examine it?

Do recordings from other cameras exist?

“The video released by the Penitentiary Service cannot replace an independent and effective investigation,” the organisations say.

Why the video has no sound

Another question concerns the fact that the released footage has no sound.

On 5 October, journalists asked Justice Minister Paata Salia whether the original recording had sound. The minister did not answer. When they asked whether cameras installed in de-escalation rooms can record sound at all, Salia said he could not comment. Later, speaking on Imedi TV, the minister said Georgian law does not provide for audio recording.

Salia also could not explain why authorities moved Davitadze to the de-escalation room on 21 December 2025 and referred journalists to the Penitentiary Service for an answer.

The minister says authorities are investigating Giorgi Davitadze’s original allegation and that they need to complete the investigation before giving a final answer.

“If anyone attempts to destabilise or disrupt the operation of penitentiary institutions, whether from inside or outside, the authorities will respond strictly, as provided by law,” Salia said.

He also mentioned that some public statements may contain signs of a criminal offence, but he did not name any specific individuals or give examples.

Prisons — one of the most painful issues in modern Georgia

The issue of violence in Georgian prisons goes beyond human rights.

It holds a special place in the country’s recent political history. In 2012, conditions in the penitentiary system became one of the key factors behind the change of government.

On 18 September 2012, less than two weeks before the parliamentary elections, Georgian television channels broadcast footage recorded at Prison No. 8 in Tbilisi.

The footage showed guards beating, humiliating and sexually abusing prisoners. The broadcasts triggered mass protests in Tbilisi and other cities.

The footage exposed a problem that human rights groups had already raised. A 2013 Human Rights Watch report said the images highlighted a longstanding problem of torture and ill-treatment of prisoners.

The government at the time acknowledged the systemic nature of violence in prisons. The ministers responsible for prisons and internal affairs resigned, and authorities arrested several penitentiary staff members. Within days, the prison system became one of the central issues of the election campaign.

In the parliamentary elections on 1 October 2012, Mikheil Saakashvili’s United National Movement lost power, and Bidzina Ivanishvili’s Georgian Dream coalition took control of the government.

One of the new government’s main political promises was to reform the penitentiary system that had developed under the previous government and protect prisoners’ rights.

But data from recent years and reports by human rights organisations show that violence and ill-treatment by security, law enforcement and penitentiary authorities remain serious concerns. The problem extends beyond prisons to police stations, the detention process and protests.

In June 2026, Georgian human rights organisations said in a joint statement that, in their assessment, torture and ill-treatment in Georgia had become a “systemic and widespread practice”. Amnesty International describes a similar situation.

At the same time, the penitentiary system continues to grow in scale. According to official statistics, Georgia’s penitentiary system received a total of 22,767 convicted people in 2025 — 25.5% more than the previous year. This marks the highest figure since the authorities began keeping the relevant statistics.

In 2024, Georgia ranked second among 46 Council of Europe countries in terms of the number of prisoners per 100,000 people.

What is happening in Georgia’s prisons

After the allegations by Giorgi Davitadze became public, several incidents occurred at Rustavi Prison No. 6. According to the Public Defender, its representatives met three prisoners on 3 and 4 October who had protested against the treatment of Davitadze. They told the representatives why they were protesting and described their conditions in prison.

The Penitentiary Service denies that the authorities moved these prisoners to de-escalation rooms because they had expressed solidarity with Davitadze. According to the agency, the authorities moved them to protect the safety of the prisoners and prison staff.

For example, the service says that on 2 October one prisoner kicked the prison’s deputy director in the stomach. On 4 October, two other prisoners allegedly “physically insulted” staff members — that is, attacked them — while returning from a walk. The agency also released video footage showing these incidents.

Later that same evening, on 4 October, an incident also involved Davitadze himself. According to the Penitentiary Service, he called over a prison employee and, in front of him, swallowed “several small objects of unknown origin”. Staff offered to transfer Davitadze to Vivamedi Clinic, but he refused.

The following day, the Public Defender’s Office said its representative had met with Davitadze. According to the prisoner, he felt well and had refused the transfer to the clinic as part of his protest. Davitadze said he would not go to the clinic until the authorities returned the three prisoners who had protested in his support from the de-escalation rooms to their cells.

Amid these events, reports also emerged of possible violence against another prisoner. According to lawyer Anna Akopova, her client Lasha Chachanidze suffered a beating at the same Prison No. 6 after he shouted from his cell to express solidarity with Davitadze. The lawyer says authorities transferred Chachanidze and two other prisoners to Prison No. 3 in Batumi.

Akopova says the prisoner has multiple injuries on different parts of his body. According to her, about ten people took part in the alleged assault. The lawyer is demanding a medical examination and the preservation of the relevant video footage, which could establish Chachanidze’s condition when staff took him out of his cell and when they returned him.

The Penitentiary Service categorically denies the allegation and says nothing of the sort happened. The Public Defender’s Office said it had received information about the case and would visit the prisoner.

Saba Skhvitaridze, who authorities detained during pro-European protests, also wrote about the tense situation at Prison No. 6. According to a statement published on his Facebook page, authorities transferred some prisoners to other facilities, placed others in de-escalation rooms and several prisoners went on hunger strike. Skhvitaridze also reported that authorities beat a prisoner and that some prisoners injured themselves.

Giorgi Davitadze remains in the same prison, whose staff he accuses of sexual abuse.

The Prosecutor’s Office investigation, which it launched in December 2025 after the Public Defender’s Office filed a complaint, remains incomplete. The Public Defender’s Office says it continues to monitor the investigation and calls on the Prosecutor’s Office to make its findings public as soon as possible.

The Penitentiary Service denies all the allegations, including reports of a hunger strike among prisoners, and insists that “complete calm” prevails at Rustavi Prison No. 6.

The Giorgi Davitadze case

World.title: SJC: Extradition of prisoners from Georgia to Russia must be stopped immediately
World.content:
Following the killing of Dmitry Pushkaryov, who Georgia extradited to Russia, the Georgian Social Justice Center (SJC) said that Georgia should immediately halt the extradition of prisoners to Russia.

The organisation said resuming the practice of extraditing prisoners to Russia was incompatible with human rights.

After Georgia extradited Dmitry Pushkaryov, he was killed in an attack on Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) officers. According to Russian authorities, Pushkaryov killed one officer and wounded three others while attempting to escape.

“The mere fact that Dmitry Pushkaryov was killed does not directly establish that Georgia violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by extraditing him. However, his death raises even more serious questions about how thoroughly the Georgian authorities assessed the risks he faced in Russia, what guarantees they obtained from Russia, whether an independent mechanism existed to monitor compliance with those guarantees, and whether the Georgian side subsequently monitored the person’s situation,” the SJC said.

According to the organisation, the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) indicates that information that emerges after a person’s transfer can also matter when assessing how well-founded the state’s initial risk assessment was.

The SJC believes that continuing extraditions to Russia — particularly without proper public justification, a rigorous individual risk assessment and effective independent monitoring mechanisms — could put Georgia in breach of its international human rights obligations.

The organisation calls on the Georgian government, the Ministry of Justice and the Prosecutor General’s Office to immediately suspend extraditions to Russia. The SJC believes the practice should remain suspended until the situation in Russia changes significantly and the international community reaches a consensus on the issue.

The Centre also calls on the Prosecutor General’s Office to publish statistical data on extradition requests received from Russia since 16 March 2022, the decisions made on those requests and the extraditions carried out.

The organisation is also demanding that the Ministry of Justice explain the legal grounds for changing the moratorium recorded before the European Court of Human Rights in the case of Sumbaev v. Georgia.

The ECtHR found Georgia’s 2021 extradition of Aslan Sumbaev, who faced serious criminal charges in Russia, lawful only after Russia provided official diplomatic assurances that it would prevent torture and ensure proper detention conditions.

“Please also specify what individual guarantees and subsequent monitoring mechanisms were applied in relation to the extraditions that have already taken place,” the Social Justice Center wrote.

World.title: Georgia without an opposition? How ruling party moved to ban its opponents through constitutional lawsuit
World.content:
The ruling party Georgian Dream has asked Georgia’s Constitutional Court to ban five opposition parties. Four of them crossed the five per cent threshold in the 2024 parliamentary elections. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, election stability risks, a total of 784,820 voters — 37.79% of those who took part in the election — voted for the four parties.

What legal grounds does the government cite for seeking to ban the five parties? What does the term “collective United National Movement” mean? How has the list of parties facing a ban changed, and under what conditions does European law allow such a ban? JAMnews examined the Georgian Dream lawsuit, relevant legislation and European practice to answer these questions.

Georgian Dream registered its latest lawsuit with the Constitutional Court on 24 September 2026, under case No. 1979.

The list of parties facing a ban includes Unity — National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia — Lelo, Gakharia for Georgia and Federalists.

As of 5 October 2026, the court has not yet published a decision on whether it will accept the lawsuit for consideration on the merits, and it has not yet set a hearing date.

The First Chamber is hearing the case, with Vasil Roinishvili serving as the reporting judge. Under the law, the court must issue its final decision within nine months of the filing — no later than 24 June 2027.

If the court upholds the lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the electoral threshold in the last parliamentary elections could disappear from the country’s political system.

Under current legislation, the authorities can also ask the court to ban another political organisation that acts as a “successor” to an already banned party.

An election campaign promise

Bidzina Ivanishvili at a Georgian Dream rally, April 2024.

The idea of banning opposition parties did not emerge spontaneously within Georgian Dream. Its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili, publicly stated even before the 2024 parliamentary elections that, after the vote, the government would deliver a “strict political and legal verdict” to the “collective National Movement”.

In other words, the idea of banning the opposition did not emerge after the election. It formed part of the election campaign itself.

“After the election, we will have the opportunity to deliver a strict political and legal verdict to the collective National Movement.”

Ivanishvili also explained why, in his view, this did not happen in 2012. He said the government did not yet have sufficient resources at the time:

“Over these years, we have accumulated enough resources to begin fully strengthening our sovereignty…”

A statement made almost six months before the election gradually turned into a concrete political plan. In August 2024, Georgian Dream openly announced that it needed a constitutional majority in the election to declare the “collective National Movement” illegal. The European Commission included the plan in its report that year.

Then EU High Representative Josep Borrell, speaking in the European Parliament, described the promise to ban opposition parties as one of the worrying developments during Georgia’s election campaign.

Two years later, that campaign promise has turned into a concrete lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

Three lawsuits, three lists — how the number of parties facing a ban grew

The lawsuit changed three times over the course of one year.

The Constitutional Court registered the first lawsuit on 31 October 2025, under case No. 1912. Eighty-eight members of parliament signed it. They sought to ban three political forces:

Unity — National Movement

Coalition for Change

Strong Georgia — Lelo

Later, on 21 April 2026, 89 MPs filed a second lawsuit, No. 1958. They added a fourth party, Federalists, to the list.

The list of parties facing a ban grew again in September 2026.

On 24 September, the Constitutional Court registered lawsuit No. 1979, signed by 88 MPs. This time, the authorities are seeking to ban five parties, including former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s party, For Georgia.

The law gives the Constitutional Court a maximum of nine months to rule on such a case. Each new lawsuit has therefore sparked debate over whether that period starts again from the beginning.

The authors of the lawsuit hope the Constitutional Court will complete the process by January 2027, by which time all five parties would have been banned.

Opposition representatives, meanwhile, argue that Georgian Dream is actually prolonging the process by adding new parties.

On what grounds can a party be banned?

Georgia’s Constitution sets out specific grounds for banning a political party.

It prohibits parties whose goals include overthrowing or forcibly changing the constitutional order, undermining the country’s independence or violating its territorial integrity. The authorities can also ban parties that promote war or violence or incite national, ethnic, regional, religious or social hatred.

Only the Constitutional Court can ban a political party.

The Georgian Dream lawsuit relies on these constitutional grounds and argues that the listed parties’ activities target the state.

A significant part of the argument draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission, known as the Tsulukiani Commission.

One of the lawsuit’s key arguments concerns the opposition parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the 2024 election, parliament and the government.

The plaintiffs also link the opposition parties’ actions to “sabotage”, calls for Western sanctions against the Georgian authorities and attempts to “punish” the country.

The lawsuit, for example, treats the opposition’s refusal to recognise the election results and its view that Georgian Dream is an illegitimate government as “sabotage”.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also cited the legitimacy of the government when explaining why the authorities added Gakharia’s party to the list.

He said that although the party, unlike its “fellow opposition parties”, agreed to take part in parliamentary work, it still does not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government:

“It is true that they entered parliament, but to this day they do not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government. Under these circumstances, the spirit of this political party’s activities is no different from that of the other relevant political parties,” he said.

Why these parties?

The lawsuit explicitly cites the parties’ political influence as a reason for seeking their ban. It also mentions other opposition parties, such as the Republican Party, which does not appear on the list, and says:

“At present, they do not have significant influence on politics or a realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold. Accordingly, at this stage, there is no apparent need to ban them.”

A brief overview of the five parties facing a ban: Политические силы, объединенные “Грузинской мечтой” в единый “черный список”, имеют разное происхождение, историю и идеологию. Некоторые из них действительно произошли из политической семьи «Единого национального движения». Некоторые пытались занять независимое пространство именно между ЕНД и «Грузинской мечтой». Политическое же ядро партии Гиорги Гахария и вовсе вышло из самой «Грузинской мечты». «Единство — Национальное движение» «Единое национальное движение» экс-президента Михеила Саакашвили — самая старая партия в этой пятерке и единственная, имеющая опыт пребывания у власти: в течение 9 лет она являлась правящей партией Грузии. На выборах 2024 года ЕНД официально получила 211 216 голосов — 10,17%. Уже долгие годы партия переживает кризис лидерства и на данный момент находится в режиме переходного управления. В августе 2026 года был создан временный управляющий совет, руководителем которого стал Иракли Павленишвили. Избрание постоянного председателя партии должно состояться позже. Главным лицом, принимающим решения в партии, по-прежнему остается Михеил Саакашвили, который уже пять лет находится в тюрьме. ЕНД позиционирует себя как резко проевропейская и евроатлантическая политическая сила. Её историческое ядро — это политическое наследие правительства Саакашвили. Именно правление ЕНД в 2004-2012 годах является главной мишенью большей части иска «Грузинской мечты» и обвинений комиссии Цулукиани. Coalition for Change Coalition for Change was created ahead of the 2024 elections and brought together several different political forces. The coalition included Nika Melia and Nika Gvaramia’s Akhali party, Zurab Japaridze’s Girchi — More Freedom and Elene Khoshtaria’s Droa. Akhali is a pro-European centre-right liberal party. Girchi — More Freedom has a more distinctly right-libertarian economic platform, while Droa has a liberal and activist profile. In the 2024 election, the coalition received the largest number of official votes among the opposition forces — 229,161, or 11.03%. Most of its leaders had previously been associated with the UNM. The coalition brings together parties that broke away from the UNM or emerged independently at different times. Strong Georgia — Lelo The core of Strong Georgia is the Lelo party, which Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze founded in 2019. Both entered politics after careers in business. A broader coalition formed around Lelo in 2024. It included Ana Dolidze’s For People, Aleko Elisashvili’s Citizens and Levan Tsutskiridze’s Freedom Square. The coalition sought to present itself as an independent alternative to both Georgian Dream and the former ruling UNM. The party has a pro-European, centrist-liberal profile. Economic development, institutional reform and Western integration have remained central themes in Lelo’s programmes. In 2024, Strong Georgia officially received 182,922 votes, or 8.81%. Gakharia for Georgia Giorgi Gakharia’s party stands out from the other four parties in the group because of its origins. Gakharia was not a member of the government under Mikheil Saakashvili. Instead, he served as economy minister, interior minister and eventually prime minister under Georgian Dream. He resigned as prime minister in February 2021 and founded his own For Georgia party in May. The party initially sought to present itself as an alternative to both Georgian Dream and the UNM. It received 7.79% in the 2021 municipal elections and 161,521 votes, or 7.78%, in the 2024 parliamentary election. Gakharia’s case shows how broadly Georgian Dream applies the concept of the “collective National Movement”: today, the category also includes a political force led by one of Georgian Dream’s former leaders.
