World.title: Bear’s Wine Bar
World.content:
You might expect a wine list of this calibre to be the draw at Bear’s. Instead, it bolsters a wider offering of clever snacking and wine-friendly feasting. The brainchild of Supernormal alumni Austin Kangket and Nathan Schofield (the one responsible for the wine), this beacon of warm light and red brick feels like a haven just off North Melbourne’s main strip.

Stracciatella and tomatoes reads like a Melbourne wine bar standby, but is handily reimagined with the earthy addition of zaatar. Tender barbecued cabbage sits under a bed of craggly, crisp tobacco onions, begging for a glass of mineral-driven txakolina.

The lamb ribs, proudly pink, would look right at home in a much finer diner. End on deep-fried Tim-Tams. They’re exactly how they sound and encapsulate what Bear’s does best: playful excellence.

Best for: A casual first date with an emphasis on good food.

World.title: The Lincoln
World.content:
The pub has been around for over 100 years.

16 / 16 The pub has been around for over 100 years.

Is The Lincoln a great local pub? A casual dinner spot? A solid cocktail bar? The magic is that it manages to be all three. A line of 12 taps pours craft beers at the charmingly old-school front bar, while the back is jam-packed with diners enjoying table service.

Whichever side you settle into, there’s a solid range of Australian and European wines and the full dinner menu to choose from. You’ll see thick-cut chicken schnitzels arriving with a large dollop of herb butter and iceberg lettuce. You’ll see baked scallops under a blanket of buttery chorizo bechamel and herb-flecked bread crumbs.

You’ll see deeply golden-brown prawn toast brightened by coriander, lightly pickled cucumber there to cut right through the richness. None of it would look out of place in a neighbourhood bistro, but the Lincoln’s warm staff and easygoing demeanour means this place exudes the charm of a proper local.

Good to know: The Sunday roast is one of Melbourne’s best.

World.title: ‘I made a pretty strong stand’: How Travis Head stamped out a ball-tampering plot
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I made a pretty strong stand’: How Travis Head stamped out a ball-tampering plot Daniel Brettig October 7, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Durban: Travis Head has spoken for the first time about how he shut down a dressing room ball-tampering plot as captain of his state, and why the memories of “sandpapergate” remain key to how the Australian team now plays the game. Eight years ago, Head was 24 years old and about to start playing a lot more often for Australia, having seen Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft cop heavy punishment for their parts in the Newlands scandal. He was also captain of a South Australian side that was in the midst of a run of five consecutive seasons at the bottom of the Sheffield Shield table. Travis Head leading South Australia in 2018. AAP It’s in that context that Head swiftly slammed the door shut on a discussion about whether the SACAs needed to be more aggressive in the way they managed the ball to make it reverse swing. Some players held suspicions that other teams were still sailing close to the wind in how they prepared the ball to reverse. Head went as far as to tell those making the suggestion that they would lose their place in the side if they attempted to tamper in line with what they believed some opponents were doing. SA had long been saddled with the perception that their state team was not as “hard” as others, and it was a moment in which Head – backed up by his South Australian deputy Alex Carey – put the game first.



“I made a pretty strong stand at that point, and I was captain at the time, that they weren’t going to be in the dressing room if that’s the case, if that’s what [they want to do],” Head told this masthead in Durban ahead of Australia’s first Test in South Africa since the infamous 2018 tour. “I didn’t care what other teams did. I didn’t care if we were facing it. “I just knew what a couple of close friends had gone through, and knew what the [Australian] team had gone through, and the flow-on effect of that. I don’t care if we’re bottom of the table, as long as we play the game the right way. That was my opinion, and still is my opinion.” ‘You never play better when you’re tense and feel pressured’ Head declined to go into further details about the discussion, including exactly when it took place, but said that the current team, led by Pat Cummins, would never forget the importance of keeping cricket in perspective: the 2018 team had lost their moorings and paid a heavy penalty as a result.



“It’s driven from Pat. Pat’s always said it’s a game, and it’s not do or die,” Head said. “If South Africa play really, really well, and we lose 3-0, that’s OK; it’s not the end of the world. We’ll wake up tomorrow. I think that then brings in, I guess, that freer side of yourself to go out and express yourself. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Just be careful, they’re on you’: Inside cricket’s greatest scandal “We’ve seen other teams around the world hold on to certain things or think it’s the most important thing they’re ever going to do, and sometimes you can play on that. You can see that they get tense and feel pressure, and you never play better when you’re tense and feel pressured.” Head is critical of some of the extremes he sees in the way Test cricketers are judged and critiqued, and said it was duly vital for the players themselves to stay level amid the madness. “Yes, we’re playing in front of billions of people. Yes, it’s important,” Head said. “Yes, everyone’s got you scrutinised to the absolute tip of it, every single day. The game’s changed a lot over even the little period that I’ve played it.



“It’s not just ‘they batted well and they bowled well’. It’s their career is over. That team’s shit. That team’s not. Do you know what I mean? So the storylines of media now is through the roof. So if you can’t enjoy it within the four walls, then you’re never going to. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot “That’s the one little piece that we’ve got to keep it sane, I guess, because everything around us is pretty much chaos.” Head had some fun with his teammates when he claimed an unexpected catch on the boundary in the final over of their warm-up game in Potchefstroom this week, wheeling away in celebration as though the moment was as important as his blinder to catch Rohit Sharma in the 2023 World Cup final. Head acknowledged his place as a back-up leader for both Cummins and Steve Smith in the three-Test series, which begins on Friday in Durban. It will be the first time the Australians have played Tests in South Africa since the acrimonious 2018 series.



“There’s a world where I can see it not bothering me too much,” he said laconically of the day he might be captain. “I think I bring something to this team. Well, I hope I do, and it doesn’t have to be in that [captaincy] space either. “So I’m really, really enjoying where I’m at. It’s an exciting 12-18 months, but also a few years in Australian cricket. I want to be as involved as much as I can and support and help everyone and just be me.” Mitchell Starc dismissed Faf du Plessis during the first Test in South Africa in 2018. AP Aside from being vice-captain, Head is now the main ball shiner for the team, and said the reduction of reverse swing in the international game since 2018 was a combination of ball management methods and conditions. “I’ve been shining it, so yeah, it’s going to be important if we can get it,” he said. “Wickets have been green over the last two or three years, so we haven’t really needed to worry too much about that. But with a fair few used wickets around South Africa, it may come in naturally too.”



Do the bowlers miss reverse swing? Ask captain Cummins or Mitchell Starc about how rarely reverse swing has been seen since 2018 – apart from some striking instances on the 2022 tour of Pakistan – and they weigh up its disappearance. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Sandpaper series was radioactive from the start. Then a USB stick was delivered to my room “I wouldn’t put it on the overrated list, but it’s normally when there’s not much else happening, there’s no traditional swing or seam and you kind of shift into that role as a pace bowler,” Cummins said. “Normally, the ball is a bit softer and you’re not necessarily getting catches behind square. “It is fun when it’s going, but I think our jobs have been easier in the last couple of years where it’s swinging and seaming up front with the new ball, rather than trying to take wickets with the reversing ball.



Mitchell Starc believes he’s a more rounded bowler these days. Getty Images “It is part of red-ball cricket and Tests and it is interesting, but I’m not saying I miss it too much. A lot of the time I think reverse swing only excites people because the ball’s been doing nothing for the previous 40 overs.” Starc believes that he has become a more rounded and versatile bowler than the one who used to revert to trying to reverse the ball from around the wicket at the first sign of a partnership. “I have a few extra strings to the bow now,” he said. “The wobble seam and a bit more control and more comfortable in my own skin. Whereas before I had swing with the new ball, bowled fast, and when reverse started I had more to offer as well. “So I think that and conditions around the world have changed a bit. Whether that’s the introduction of the World Test Championship and teams looking for results, or just the nature of the wickets, you don’t see a lot of reverse swing outside the subcontinent any more.



“Even the practice game the other day, it was more like a day-five wicket and both teams had a small hint of reverse, but you just don’t see it much. You get a little more now in a one-day game back to one ball for the innings, but not a whole lot of it the last seven years.” Jonny Bairstow is stumped by Alex Carey at Lord’s in 2023. Getty Images 'Australia were no longer the favourite villains in world cricket' As he nears the end of his tenure as Cricket Australia chair, Mike Baird believes there was a signal moment when he knew that the shadow of sandpapergate had receded. It arrived at Lord's in 2023, when England were outraged by the stumping of Jonny Bairstow, but the balance of world cricket opinion was firmly with Australia.



“I think everyone was with Australia at that time. He walked out of his ground, pretty simple,” Baird said. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot “But it’s true. Australia were no longer the favourite villains in world cricket. They were identified as fair and tough cricketers and that was shown at Lord’s. “[2018] was a dark period, dark days indeed as a fan of the game. But there isn’t a person in Australia who hasn’t made mistakes and sometimes really big mistakes, and it’s about what you do from there. “I’ve been in public life, so I’ve got a bit of understanding of what some of those pressures are like. But to see them respond and come back and have success is inspiring. Culturally, Australian cricket has really changed off the back of those days.”

World.title: Shrugging off war, the bond rout and oil crunch: Why Wall Street keeps rallying
World.content:
BusinessMarketsSharemarket Opinion Shrugging off war, the bond rout and oil crunch: Why Wall Street keeps rallying Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 7, 2026 — 12:18pm

October 7, 2026 — 12:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US sharemarket hit another record overnight, even as US bond yields reached levels last seen in 2002. There’s something unusual happening in financial markets. Share prices and bond yields generally have an inverse correlation. As yields go up, increasing the cost of credit and tightening financial conditions while producing near risk-free income streams, the appeal of riskier stocks and their dividends reduces. That isn’t happening in the US, or at least it is not being reflected in the overall sharemarket indices. Defying the concerns over the Iran war, bond yields and fuel prices, Wall Street’s S&P benchmark goes up and up. But it’s not a broad-based bull run. Bloomberg The explanation is obvious. Investors are still piling into the stocks powering the boom in artificial intelligence investment.



The S&P 500 is up just over 14 per cent so far this year, but the more tech-laden Nasdaq index is up more than 18 per cent, and the NYFANG+ index, which reflects the performance of the biggest of the tech stocks, is up by about 25 per cent. The significance of the AI-related stocks to the wider sharemarket’s performance is underscored by the underperformance of the S&P 500 equal weight index, which assigns every stock the same weighting, against that of the primary S&P 500 index, which uses their market capitalisation. The equal weight index has risen 10.8 per cent this year and has actually fallen almost 3 per cent in the past month – the market might be at record levels, but its performance is very narrowly based. Indeed, only four stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Micron and AMD – account for roughly half the S&P 500’s rise this year. If you look at the market’s performance since mid-August, had it not been for the performance of two of those stocks – chipmakers Nvidia and Micron – the market would have actually fallen from that point.



Last month, roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 fell. Mid-August is an important reference point because it was from about that point that US bond yields started their recent climb, a shift that accelerated after the Federal Reserve Board chairman Kevin Warsh dispelled doubts about his inflation-fighting credentials by giving a clearly “hawkish” speech at the annual Jackson Hole conference of economists and academics. The narrow base for growth in the economy and the sharemarket makes both extremely vulnerable to any adverse development or shift in confidence in AI. The Fed followed that up last month with its first interest rate increase in more than three years. Thus, while the index might suggest otherwise, most stocks in the S&P 500 are now going backwards, which is more in keeping with the normal relationship between bonds and shares.



Bond yields are being driven by a number of influences. A US inflation rate of 3.4 per cent is the most obvious, but a budget deficit of $US2 trillion ($2.9 trillion), or 6 per cent of GDP, and gross government debt of more than $US40 trillion not only raise concerns about the sustainability of America’s finances and how the Trump administration might seek to stabilise them, but are swelling the supply of bonds the market is being asked to absorb. The supply issue is being exacerbated by the increasing amounts of AI-related debt hitting debt markets and providing alternative investments to Treasury securities. The AI boom has significance beyond the sharemarket. The vast amounts of investment being made are supporting the wider US economy, its solid 2.2 per cent growth rate and the stable jobs market. The headline GDP numbers, however, contrast with what most Americans feel about the state of their economy, with consumer sentiment at record lows. The US savings rate is also at historic lows and consumer debt at record highs.



Consumer spending has, however held up, strongly. That suggests that those wealthier households that are exposed to the AI boom, either directly or via the sharemarket, are feeling positive and are spending. There are wealth effects on the broader economy that flow from sharemarket gains. Related Article Opinion

World markets Trump’s bluff is too late to save him Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Like the sharemarket, it would appear that America’s economic growth is also narrowly based. Below the broad indices, only two of the 11 sectors in the sharemarket – IT and communications services – rose last month. Higher interest rates, inflation, the surge in gasoline and diesel prices flowing from the conflict in the Middle East and the rise in input costs as a result of Donald Trump’s trade wars are having an effect on those companies not benefiting from AI.



An increasing volume of securitised corporate debt is now trading at material discounts to its face value – JPMorgan says there are about $US140 billion of loans trading at less than 80 per cent of their face value. Spreads and defaults in the leveraged loan and distressed debt markets have been surging. Bets on AI stars like Nvidia and Alphabet parent Google are powering the US sharemarket. Bloomberg While there might be a tale of two economies and two markets underlying the aggregated numbers, analysts remain bullish. Expectations for the third-quarter profit reporting season starting next week is that it will produce an average 25 per cent increase in earnings over the same quarter last year. That, too, is deceptive. This year, a handful of the big tech stocks, notably Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, have accounted for most of the increase in the earnings expectations for the entire S&P 500, and their reported earnings – like those of most of the key players in AI -- lean heavily on their investments in, and contracts with, other AI companies. The narrow base for growth in the economy and the sharemarket makes both extremely vulnerable to any adverse development or shift in confidence in AI.



For the moment, investors are clearly capitalising an extraordinarily lucrative future for the hyperscalers and frontier labs and AI infrastructure providers into their valuations. Related Article Opinion

AI Billion-dollar losses but worth $2.9 trillion? The mind-boggling maths of AI Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist They don’t seem concerned about the impact of higher interest rates on companies increasingly reliant on debt to fund unprecedented levels of investment whose pay-off, if there is a payoff, is uncertain and may not be known for some years. There also appears to be some level of expectation (despite the evidence to date) that the war in the Middle East will end and oil, gasoline and diesel prices will subside. The bond market is volatile and signalling risk and concern.



The sharemarket, thanks to AI, isn’t. While it is conceivable that the sharemarket could keep rising off its narrow base in the face of a continuing surge in interest rates, there would be a point where the resilience of the AI sector and its investor base was tested. It probably won’t come this month – the odds on another Fed rate hike in October have been receding – but the market is pricing in another one for December and more next year. Without a conclusive end to the war in the Middle East and a fall in oil, gasoline and diesel prices and with Trump continuing to slap new tariffs on America’s trading partners, the environment for AI, its backers and the broader sharemarket can only become more challenging and risky. World.title: ‘Direct line between October 7 and Bondi’: Vigil remembers Jewish massacre
World.content:
NationalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Direct line between October 7 and Bondi’: Vigil remembers Jewish massacre Ben Cubby October 7, 2026 — 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The coarse wail of the shofar - a ceremonial ram’s horn trumpet - echoed across the Bondi Pavilion courtyard at 6.29am on Tuesday as around 700 people gathered to mark the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel. NSW opposition leader Kellie Sloane, federal Liberal senator Dave Sharma and Israel’s ambassador to Australia Hillel Newman spoke at the event, metres away from the site of December’s Bondi terrorist attack. A man sounds the shofar, a ceremonial trumpet, at the Bondi Pavilion during a vigil on the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel. Audrey Richardson They all drew a link between the events of October 7, 2023, when thousands of militants crossed from Gaza to assault Israel, and the Bondi attack, in which 15 people were killed by gunmen at a Jewish festival. “There is a direct line between the shooting at Nova and the shooting at Bondi,” said Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman.



“We have witnessed verbal violence and bullying which led to vandalism, arson and culminated in the murder of 15 people right here … It is not the actions of Israel, it is the hatred of Jews.” Among the speakers was 11-year-old Ben Carasso, the grandson of a Holocaust survivor who became a child influencer on social media after the father of his friend went missing from the Nova festival in Israel and was later found to have been killed. Ben Carasso, 11, poses for a portrait as people gather at Bondi Pavilion to commemorate the three-year anniversary of the October 7th attack on Israel. Audrey Richardson “I’m very glad we began the connection in Bondi with the Israel children and the Jewish children, they’ve both suffered since October 7,” said Carasso, who lives in Tel Aviv but has travelled widely among the global Jewish diaspora. “We don’t have a normal childhood for three years now. I want to get to speak for the children. We didn’t get a chance to grow up.



“Since October 7, I saw what the children of Israel were going through. My friend lost his father. They didn’t know where he was for months, he was at the Nova festival. Related Article Analysis

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘The world will never be the same again’: How October 7 changed Israel, Gaza and Australia “Israeli children are forced to learn what to do in a rocket attack. It’s a side that is not talked about. For three years we have had this, and I want the world to know.” Sloane told those at the vigil that vision of the October 7 attacks had moved her deeply. “Little boys running from a shelter after their father was attacked, a woman on the back of a ute, kids slaughtered. It was brutality at its worst,” she said.



“What was done to them deserved to be seen, and it can never been denied.” Sloane said people who chose today to protest Israel’s action in Gaza should be ashamed of themselves. Leader of the NSW Opposition Kellie Sloane, whose electorate lies in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, attended the event. Audrey Richardson “On this day, can I just say ‘shame on you’ to the people that have held protests.” Pro-Palestine vigils have been organised in the Sydney CBD and Wollongong today.



Sharma called the Hamas attacks on October 7 “an organised and systematic massacre of Jews … a pogrom,” and said it had created the conditions for the Bondi attack. “It was the terrible tragic result of a culture that took root in Australia after the Hamas terror attack and the war that followed,” Sharma said. Senator Dave Sharma at the Bondi Pavilion to commemorate the third anniversary of the October 7 attack. Audrey Richardson “This was a culture where vilification was permitted to go unchecked, where antisemitism was excused, or tolerated, or met with moral equivocation and where Australian leaders went missing in action and lost their moral compass.” While the Jewish community in Australia is united in grief by the October 7 atrocities, there are diverse views on the way forward.



Alex Ryvchin of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry said the event had exposed antisemitism in sections of the community. “We saw it in Lakemba and the Opera House,” he said. “We saw it among religious fanatics, the far-left and the resurgent neo-Nazis. It made everything clear at once. It exposed the rank hypocrisy of human-rights advocates who lined up to explain why rape and murder were resistance in certain cases.” About 1200 people were killed, and 250 taken as hostages in the October 7 attack. Audrey Richardson The progressive Jewish Council of Australia used the date to call for sanctions against Israel. “Every life lost is a whole universe, both Palestinian and Israeli,” said the group’s executive director Sarah Schwartz. “But as Jews, we refuse to allow our identities to be weaponised to enable further killing and the silencing of advocacy for Palestinian rights.”



Another commemoration event is to be held in an undisclosed location in Sydney’s eastern suburbs on Tuesday night. Over 1200 people were killed and over 250 taken captive on October 7, 2023, when militants crossed the Israeli border from Gaza to attack on a Jewish holiday. Israel responded with attacks on Gaza that are estimated to have killed over 70,000 people. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ASX turns lower as banks decline, gold miners shine; Wall Street hits record
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX turns lower as banks decline, gold miners shine; Wall Street hits record Staff writers Updated October 7, 2026 — 12:01pm ,first published October 7, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket wobbled in early trade on Wednesday, even after Wall Street traders drove US stocks to all-time highs overnight on growing bets that companies will be able to weather the threats from elevated energy costs and interest rates. The S&P/ASX 200 opened higher but then swung into the red, trading down 30.5 points, or 0.3 per cent, at 8705.20 at 11.20am AEDT, even though eight of the 11 industry sectors were in the green. Gold miners and consumer stocks were higher, while the bank and iron ore heavyweights declined. Wall Street’s benchmark index posted a record closing high, but failed to take the ASX along for the ride. AP The Australian dollar was flat at US69.81¢. The local bourse added 0.6 per cent on Tuesday, led higher by property stocks and miners. Gold miners led gains in early trade after bullion prices edged higher overnight as easing oil prices helped to ease investor worries about inflation and the trajectory for interest rates in the world’s largest economy. Spot bullion rose as much as 0.5 per cent, climbing alongside US stocks and bonds while oil dropped on signs of increasing exports from the Middle East.



Gold fell more than 6 per cent last month on concerns over energy-driven inflation as well as the prospect for higher US rates. Higher rates are typically negative for bullion, relative to yield-bearing assets like Treasuries. “Gold has stabilised for the time being,” Barbara Lambrecht, an analyst at Commerzbank, said in a note. “After all, concerns about a rapid interest rate rise in the US have eased somewhat recently.” Local goldminers advanced, with Northern Star Resources up 3.2 per cent, Evolution Mining up 1.8 per cent and Newmont Mining up 1 per cent, leaving the iron ore and copper giants in the dust. BHP and Rio Tinto both slipped 0.7 per cent and Fortescue Metals fell 1.6 per cent. Consumer-related stocks fared well. Wesfarmers, the owner of the Bunnings, Officeworks and Kmart chains, was up 1 per cent, while Rebel-owner Super Retail Group rose 2 per cent and fashion jewellery brand Lovisa gained 1.5 per cent. Woolworths and Coles were up 0.2 per cent and 0.4 per cent, respectively. But the banking heavyweights struggled, with all big four banks down between 0.5 per cent (ANZ Bank) and 1.3 per cent (Commonwealth Bank). Energy stocks were mixed, with oil and gas giant Woodside flat and Santos up 0.2 per cent, while Ampol shed 0.8 per cent.



On Wall Street overnight, the US stock market hit a record even as the list of challenges chipping away at it keeps growing. The S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent to a fresh all-time high after topping its prior record set in August. Despite worries about everything from war to high inflation to pressure from the bond market, the index at the heart of the US sharemarket has soared 23 per cent since hitting a bottom in late March. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 253 points, or 0.5 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite tacked 0.4 per cent onto its own all-time high set the day before. The record-high stock prices are helping investors feel better about their finances, or at least less bad, when Americans are generally feeling discouraged about keeping up with the fast-rising cost of living. Related Article Opinion

Government debt FROGS, not PIIGS, could spark the next global financial crisis Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Many of the fears that sent the US stock market to its bottom in March have indeed come true. Oil prices are high because of the war with Iran, which has made inflation worse. Yields have cranked higher in the bond market, which threatens to slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. And Americans broadly say they’re feeling more pessimistic about the economy and where it’s heading. But one vital source of support has remained resolute for the US stock market throughout: the relentless ability for companies to make more money.



Lamb Weston, which sells frozen fries and other potato products, said on Tuesday that its profit and revenue during its latest quarter topped its projections, for example. The results also beat analysts’ expectations, and its stock rallied 7.5 per cent. CEO Mike Smith said the company continues to deal with unexpected increases in freight and other expenses. But the company nevertheless raised its forecast for an underlying measure of profit for its full fiscal year. It’s not just potato products proving to be profitable. All kinds of companies are lining up to report soon how much profit they made from July through September, and expectations are high. Delta Air Lines will report its third-quarter results on Friday, with several of the country’s biggest banks headlining the following week. Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30 per cent in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25 per cent. That’s crucial because corporate profits are one of the main levers that set prices for stocks, along with interest rates. At the moment, high bond yields are making investors less willing to pay high prices for investments that aren’t bonds. But the simultaneous strength for corporate profits is allowing the market to stay high and “to win the tug-of-war against yields,” according to strategists at Barclays.



To be sure, much hinges on companies actually meeting those expectations for fatter profits. If they fail to do so, stock prices could easily fall off their records. Some critics also point to a possible bubble in stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry after how much they soared in the frenzy around the technology. Overnight, Paramount Skydance closed its $US110 billion ($157.5 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, completing one of the biggest media mergers of all time. The merger brings two of America’s oldest movie-making studios together under a new name: Skydance. The deal, which followed a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight, further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. AI stocks have been a huge force driving the US market to records, including Nvidia’s 28.3 per cent surge so far this year. That’s roughly double the broad market’s gain. Constellation Energy jumped 12.2 per cent for one of Tuesday’s biggest gains in the S&P 500 because it’s also riding that rising tide. It announced a long-term deal to supply Google with about as much electricity as a new nuclear reactor makes. The boom in AI data centers has made not just electricity more in demand but also construction crews and materials throughout the economy.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, Option Care Health soared 32.6 per cent after CD&R and McKesson said they’re buying the provider of infusion services. The two are paying $32.05 for each Option Care Health share, valuing it at roughly $5.8 billion. Bond yields offered some slack on Tuesday after falling back from their highest levels in years or even decades. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the focal point of the US bond market, eased to 5.28 per cent from 5.31 per cent late Monday. Related Article Exclusive

AI Sneak peek: Government gave AI giant early look at data centre rules It fell after oil prices steadied themselves somewhat. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, dropped to roughly $US97 in the morning before pulling back to settle at $US100.58. While that was up 0.3 per cent from Monday’s settlement price, it’s still below the nearly $US110 it was at a few weeks ago. In other international markets, indexes ticked higher in Europe as yields continue to swing in their bond markets amid concerns about high government debts and tight budgets. In France, tens of thousands of demonstrators marched in support of protests by students demanding more funding for schools.



In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 1.1 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng climbed 1 per cent, but South Korea’s Kospi dropped 0.9 per cent. with AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Mr Security’ led Germany’s top spy agency for years. He’s now suspected of selling state secrets
World.content:
WorldEuropeCrime ‘Mr Security’ led Germany’s top spy agency for years. He’s now suspected of selling state secrets James Rothwell , Joe Barnes and Alexandra Snow October 7, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Berlin: The former head of Germany’s top intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason, in what could amount to Europe’s gravest postwar spy scandal. August Hanning, 80, is suspected of spending 16 years illegally collecting classified documents and selling some of the information to an undisclosed foreign power. August Hanning, the former president of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND). Michael Kappeler/DPA via AP Hanning – who was president of the Federal Intelligence Service, known as the BND, until 2005 – was arrested at his home on Tuesday morning (German time) in Steinfurt county, near the Dutch border. He was taken into custody under orders from Germany’s federal prosecutor. During a separate raid, a senior BND official – named only as Manfred D under German privacy laws – was arrested at his home in Bavaria on suspicion of aiding in treason.



“Both suspects are believed to have agreed in the spring of 2010 to have Manfred D continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service to Hanning in exchange for remuneration,” German prosecutors said. They also alleged that Hanning drafted an analysis for an officer of a “foreign intelligence service”, without identifying them, and said it was unclear if the material reached its recipient. Police officers outside Henning’s home in Nordwalde, Germany, on Tuesday. Christoph Reichwein/DPA via AP German magazine Der Spiegel alleged in a report on Tuesday that the analysis was prepared for the intelligence services of Azerbaijan, one of Turkey’s closest allies. Hanning is reportedly a member of the board of the “German-Azerbaijani Forum”. The explosive allegations against Hanning are the latest embarrassment for the BND, which is still reeling from the 2023 arrest of Carsten Linke, a BND desk chief, for allegedly passing material to Moscow. Linke was charged with treason and his trial is ongoing.



According to Süddeutsche Zeitung, a German newspaper, the data obtained by Hanning allegedly includes “highly sensitive situation assessments, classified material from foreign partner agencies, and reportedly also papers on the Iranian nuclear program and the Russian military”. Nicknamed “Mr Security”, Hanning led the BND from 1998 to 2005, steering German intelligence agents through 9/11, the second Gulf War and the invasion of Afghanistan. The BND headquarters in Berlin. Christophe Gateau/dpa via AP During his term, he led about 6000 agents on foreign intelligence work, worked closely with the CIA and MI6, and took part in a key weekly security meeting in the German chancellery. Across all three roles, he would have been privy to highly sensitive intelligence gathered by allied agencies, as well as state secrets involving German security weaknesses.



German security sources said some of the high-level information the pair handled came from partner intelligence agencies abroad, raising fears that other nations’ human sources – either agents or informants operating in the field – could be identified through information that has been shared. British intelligence agencies are now investigating whether their classified information or spies were compromised. Several US agencies are also believed to be undergoing a systematic internal review of all sensitive information shared with European allies during the relevant period. Police allegedly found thousands of sensitive security documents at the house. Christoph Reichwein/DPA via AP The investigation into Hanning began virtually by accident in 2025, when police raided the ex-BND chief’s home in connection with an unrelated abduction case. Police had been investigating Hanning’s links to Christina Block, the heiress of a German steakhouse restaurant chain who was suspected of abducting her children amid a custody battle.



During the raid on Hanning’s home, police allegedly found 2000 highly sensitive security documents which at that time he had no right to possess, having left the agency two decades prior. Among the cache, reports on the BND’s senior leadership and briefing materials for the weekly intelligence meeting at the German chancellery were allegedly found. The headquarters of the UK’s Secret Intelligence Service, known as MI6, left, on the River Thames in London. Henning worked closely with the agency during his time at the BND. Bloomberg Germany’s ARD broadcaster claimed that some of the information that Manfred D passed on to Hanning included material on the Russian army and from partner intelligence agencies abroad. A key focus of the investigation is likely to be Hanning’s alleged links to Russia and whether any of the material he handled had fallen into the hands of Moscow.



Hanning made at least seven trips to Russia after leaving the BND, The Insider claimed in a report. He made the trips, often spending just a single day in Moscow, between 2015 and 2019, the news website alleged. Manfred D was Hanning’s chief of staff at the BND and later also went on to work at the German interior ministry. After Hanning’s departure, Manfred D served as chief of staff for several BND presidents between March 2012 and March 2026. Hanning used the information he received from Manfred D in his private consulting work, German prosecutors said. “On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service,” their statement said. “It has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient.”



Marc Henrichmann, the chairman of the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said on Tuesday that Germany would “not tolerate the betrayal of secrets”. “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” he told AFP. He said Hanning’s alleged behaviour would represent “trampling his official duties underfoot”. Martin Jäger, the president of the BND, said the agency had “initiated comprehensive internal investigations at an early stage and without delay. These have confirmed the suspicion. The federal public prosecutor general has taken over the investigation. “For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security. None of my goals or priorities are being called into question by this incident.” Hanning has been a hawkish voice on Moscow in Germany’s national security debate. In a 2024 interview with The Telegraph, he warned that his country was “naive” and needed to “wake up” to the reality of a potential war. “Many haven’t realised that we are in a conflict with Russia – that’s been underestimated,” he said.



Hanning is known to have kept close relations with various Russian businessmen and organisations since his time as a diplomat in East Berlin in the late 1980s. He appeared as a witness in a London court in support of Oleg Deripaska, a Russian oligarch, who was known to be closely associated with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the time. He also worked as a consultant on Russia issues for G3, a London-based consultancy firm. According to Der Spiegel, one of Hanning’s favourite perks as BND president was being ferried around on a private jet. But when police closed in on him on Tuesday, a much less glamorous form of transport was waiting outside his home to transport him to custody: a blue and grey Polizei wagon.

World.title: Kmart’s $89 camera glasses removed from sale online amid privacy backlash
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyPrivacy Kmart’s $89 camera glasses removed from sale online amid privacy backlash David Swan October 7, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kmart has removed its $89 camera glasses from sale online, two months after the cut-price devices sparked a national privacy backlash and calls for the federal government to step in. The Anko smart glasses, which shoot video and take photos through a camera built into the frame, no longer appear on Kmart’s website. The retailer still sells a $39 pair of speaker glasses, which play music and take calls but have no camera. The Anko smart glasses from Kmart. Kmart was contacted for comment. The development follows a campaign by activist Gina Martin, who petitioned Kmart group managing director Aleksandra Spaseska to remove the glasses from stores and online. GetUp, which hosted the petition, said more than 57,000 of its members had joined the push.



The glasses went on sale on July 28 and sold out in less than a week, undercutting Meta’s Ray-Ban models by hundreds of dollars. When this masthead reported on the backlash in August, Kmart described them as part of an “established and increasingly mainstream category” of wearable technology. Kmart has removed its $89 camera glasses from sale online, two months after the cut-price devices sparked a national privacy backlash and calls for the federal government to step in. Privacy commissioner Carly Kind on Wednesday announced an investigation into Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology, the Chinese company whose HeyCyan app runs the Anko glasses, as well as cheap glasses sold on Big W Marketplace and Amazon. Kind’s office began questioning Meta, Kmart, Google and Shenzhen Qingcheng on August 12, after attorney-general Michelle Rowland asked it to examine smart glasses because of the risk of women and children being filmed covertly. Shenzhen Qingcheng did not respond. “In the absence of any response from Shenzhen Qingcheng to the OAIC’s preliminary inquiries, I have no assurance that it is protecting personal data of Australians as required by the Privacy Act,” Kind said.



Kind has written to retailers selling devices that use HeyCyan, urging them to “consider whether it is appropriate to continue making these devices available”. The investigation gives Kind compulsory information-gathering powers, and she can seek civil penalties in the Federal Court if she finds serious or repeated interferences with privacy. Opening an investigation does not mean the commissioner has found the company broke the law. Shenzhen Qingcheng was contacted for comment. Milica Stilinovic, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Sydney’s Governing Immersive Tech project, said cheaper glasses often came with questionable data-retention practices and recording lights that were hard to see or missing altogether. Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg wears a pair of Meta Ray-Ban Display AI glasses. Bloomberg “State and federal governments must urgently answer the call to step up and protect Australians against non-consensual recording, data breaches, and basic notions of privacy,” Stilinovic said.



Her team’s research, released in August, found that in Instagram videos where women appeared not to know they were being filmed, about 60 per cent of the interactions could be classed as potential harassment. The more expensive glasses remain on sale. Meta has sold more than 7 million pairs of its glasses, and Google and Apple are both preparing rivals. Loading Ferris said Meta was still selling millions of pairs, and that Australia’s privacy laws “weren’t written for a world with hidden cameras on people’s faces”. Meta has said every pair carries a white light that flashes during recording and cannot be switched off without disabling the camera. Local councils have already acted. Brisbane City Council has banned non-consensual filming with camera devices, including smart glasses, at its 21 public pools, and Yarra, the City of Sydney and Canterbury-Bankstown have brought in similar rules at pools and leisure centres. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has asked the Australian Public Service Commission whether the glasses should be banned in public service workplaces.



Related Article City life ‘No-brainer’: Sydney council targets smart glasses in city-first ban on AI tech The federal government is not planning an outright ban. Consultation on its draft Privacy Act reforms closed in mid-September, and legislation is expected before the end of the year. The Greens want a 12-month import ban on camera-enabled wearables, with an exemption for disability aids.
