World.title: Bear’s Wine Bar
World.content:
You might expect a wine list of this calibre to be the draw at Bear’s. Instead, it bolsters a wider offering of clever snacking and wine-friendly feasting. The brainchild of Supernormal alumni Austin Kangket and Nathan Schofield (the one responsible for the wine), this beacon of warm light and red brick feels like a haven just off North Melbourne’s main strip.

Stracciatella and tomatoes reads like a Melbourne wine bar standby, but is handily reimagined with the earthy addition of zaatar. Tender barbecued cabbage sits under a bed of craggly, crisp tobacco onions, begging for a glass of mineral-driven txakolina.

The lamb ribs, proudly pink, would look right at home in a much finer diner. End on deep-fried Tim-Tams. They’re exactly how they sound and encapsulate what Bear’s does best: playful excellence.

Best for: A casual first date with an emphasis on good food.

World.title: The Lincoln
World.content:
The pub has been around for over 100 years.

16 / 16 The pub has been around for over 100 years.

Is The Lincoln a great local pub? A casual dinner spot? A solid cocktail bar? The magic is that it manages to be all three. A line of 12 taps pours craft beers at the charmingly old-school front bar, while the back is jam-packed with diners enjoying table service.

Whichever side you settle into, there’s a solid range of Australian and European wines and the full dinner menu to choose from. You’ll see thick-cut chicken schnitzels arriving with a large dollop of herb butter and iceberg lettuce. You’ll see baked scallops under a blanket of buttery chorizo bechamel and herb-flecked bread crumbs.

You’ll see deeply golden-brown prawn toast brightened by coriander, lightly pickled cucumber there to cut right through the richness. None of it would look out of place in a neighbourhood bistro, but the Lincoln’s warm staff and easygoing demeanour means this place exudes the charm of a proper local.

Good to know: The Sunday roast is one of Melbourne’s best.

World.title: ‘I made a pretty strong stand’: How Travis Head stamped out a ball-tampering plot
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I made a pretty strong stand’: How Travis Head stamped out a ball-tampering plot Daniel Brettig October 7, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Durban: Travis Head has spoken for the first time about how he shut down a dressing room ball-tampering plot as captain of his state, and why the memories of “sandpapergate” remain key to how the Australian team now plays the game. Eight years ago, Head was 24 years old and about to start playing a lot more often for Australia, having seen Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft cop heavy punishment for their parts in the Newlands scandal. He was also captain of a South Australian side that was in the midst of a run of five consecutive seasons at the bottom of the Sheffield Shield table. Travis Head leading South Australia in 2018. AAP It’s in that context that Head swiftly slammed the door shut on a discussion about whether the SACAs needed to be more aggressive in the way they managed the ball to make it reverse swing. Some players held suspicions that other teams were still sailing close to the wind in how they prepared the ball to reverse. Head went as far as to tell those making the suggestion that they would lose their place in the side if they attempted to tamper in line with what they believed some opponents were doing. SA had long been saddled with the perception that their state team was not as “hard” as others, and it was a moment in which Head – backed up by his South Australian deputy Alex Carey – put the game first.



“I made a pretty strong stand at that point, and I was captain at the time, that they weren’t going to be in the dressing room if that’s the case, if that’s what [they want to do],” Head told this masthead in Durban ahead of Australia’s first Test in South Africa since the infamous 2018 tour. “I didn’t care what other teams did. I didn’t care if we were facing it. “I just knew what a couple of close friends had gone through, and knew what the [Australian] team had gone through, and the flow-on effect of that. I don’t care if we’re bottom of the table, as long as we play the game the right way. That was my opinion, and still is my opinion.” ‘You never play better when you’re tense and feel pressured’ Head declined to go into further details about the discussion, including exactly when it took place, but said that the current team, led by Pat Cummins, would never forget the importance of keeping cricket in perspective: the 2018 team had lost their moorings and paid a heavy penalty as a result.



“It’s driven from Pat. Pat’s always said it’s a game, and it’s not do or die,” Head said. “If South Africa play really, really well, and we lose 3-0, that’s OK; it’s not the end of the world. We’ll wake up tomorrow. I think that then brings in, I guess, that freer side of yourself to go out and express yourself. Related Article Australian cricket ‘Just be careful, they’re on you’: Inside cricket’s greatest scandal “We’ve seen other teams around the world hold on to certain things or think it’s the most important thing they’re ever going to do, and sometimes you can play on that. You can see that they get tense and feel pressure, and you never play better when you’re tense and feel pressured.” Head is critical of some of the extremes he sees in the way Test cricketers are judged and critiqued, and said it was duly vital for the players themselves to stay level amid the madness. “Yes, we’re playing in front of billions of people. Yes, it’s important,” Head said. “Yes, everyone’s got you scrutinised to the absolute tip of it, every single day. The game’s changed a lot over even the little period that I’ve played it.



“It’s not just ‘they batted well and they bowled well’. It’s their career is over. That team’s shit. That team’s not. Do you know what I mean? So the storylines of media now is through the roof. So if you can’t enjoy it within the four walls, then you’re never going to. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot “That’s the one little piece that we’ve got to keep it sane, I guess, because everything around us is pretty much chaos.” Head had some fun with his teammates when he claimed an unexpected catch on the boundary in the final over of their warm-up game in Potchefstroom this week, wheeling away in celebration as though the moment was as important as his blinder to catch Rohit Sharma in the 2023 World Cup final. Head acknowledged his place as a back-up leader for both Cummins and Steve Smith in the three-Test series, which begins on Friday in Durban. It will be the first time the Australians have played Tests in South Africa since the acrimonious 2018 series.



“There’s a world where I can see it not bothering me too much,” he said laconically of the day he might be captain. “I think I bring something to this team. Well, I hope I do, and it doesn’t have to be in that [captaincy] space either. “So I’m really, really enjoying where I’m at. It’s an exciting 12-18 months, but also a few years in Australian cricket. I want to be as involved as much as I can and support and help everyone and just be me.” Mitchell Starc dismissed Faf du Plessis during the first Test in South Africa in 2018. AP Aside from being vice-captain, Head is now the main ball shiner for the team, and said the reduction of reverse swing in the international game since 2018 was a combination of ball management methods and conditions. “I’ve been shining it, so yeah, it’s going to be important if we can get it,” he said. “Wickets have been green over the last two or three years, so we haven’t really needed to worry too much about that. But with a fair few used wickets around South Africa, it may come in naturally too.”



Do the bowlers miss reverse swing? Ask captain Cummins or Mitchell Starc about how rarely reverse swing has been seen since 2018 – apart from some striking instances on the 2022 tour of Pakistan – and they weigh up its disappearance. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Sandpaper series was radioactive from the start. Then a USB stick was delivered to my room “I wouldn’t put it on the overrated list, but it’s normally when there’s not much else happening, there’s no traditional swing or seam and you kind of shift into that role as a pace bowler,” Cummins said. “Normally, the ball is a bit softer and you’re not necessarily getting catches behind square. “It is fun when it’s going, but I think our jobs have been easier in the last couple of years where it’s swinging and seaming up front with the new ball, rather than trying to take wickets with the reversing ball.



Mitchell Starc believes he’s a more rounded bowler these days. Getty Images “It is part of red-ball cricket and Tests and it is interesting, but I’m not saying I miss it too much. A lot of the time I think reverse swing only excites people because the ball’s been doing nothing for the previous 40 overs.” Starc believes that he has become a more rounded and versatile bowler than the one who used to revert to trying to reverse the ball from around the wicket at the first sign of a partnership. “I have a few extra strings to the bow now,” he said. “The wobble seam and a bit more control and more comfortable in my own skin. Whereas before I had swing with the new ball, bowled fast, and when reverse started I had more to offer as well. “So I think that and conditions around the world have changed a bit. Whether that’s the introduction of the World Test Championship and teams looking for results, or just the nature of the wickets, you don’t see a lot of reverse swing outside the subcontinent any more.



“Even the practice game the other day, it was more like a day-five wicket and both teams had a small hint of reverse, but you just don’t see it much. You get a little more now in a one-day game back to one ball for the innings, but not a whole lot of it the last seven years.” Jonny Bairstow is stumped by Alex Carey at Lord’s in 2023. Getty Images 'Australia were no longer the favourite villains in world cricket' As he nears the end of his tenure as Cricket Australia chair, Mike Baird believes there was a signal moment when he knew that the shadow of sandpapergate had receded. It arrived at Lord's in 2023, when England were outraged by the stumping of Jonny Bairstow, but the balance of world cricket opinion was firmly with Australia.



“I think everyone was with Australia at that time. He walked out of his ground, pretty simple,” Baird said. Editor's pick Updated

Australian cricket Cameron Green out of Durban Test, Connolly and Maddinson in duel for spot “But it’s true. Australia were no longer the favourite villains in world cricket. They were identified as fair and tough cricketers and that was shown at Lord’s. “[2018] was a dark period, dark days indeed as a fan of the game. But there isn’t a person in Australia who hasn’t made mistakes and sometimes really big mistakes, and it’s about what you do from there. “I’ve been in public life, so I’ve got a bit of understanding of what some of those pressures are like. But to see them respond and come back and have success is inspiring. Culturally, Australian cricket has really changed off the back of those days.”

World.title: 'Suspicious circumstances': Woman found dead in Waiheke Island home an hour after welfare check
World.content:
The death of a woman on Auckland's Waiheke Island is being treated as suspicious after police were called to her home twice on the day she died.

Detective Senior Sergeant Martin Friend, said police believe a select few people have information on the circumstances of the death of Chantelle McLaughlin-Middlemiss on June 2.

He urged those people to come forward and said the 32-year-old's death was suspicious.

Friend said emergency services were called the home of McLaughlin-Middlemiss on Waiheke Rd, Onetangi twice on the day she died - within an hour of each other.

The first time was at 2.42pm, after information was reported that she might be dead, Friend said.

"These concerns were allayed and no immediate concerns required any intervention."

But an hour later, emergency services were called back.

Friend said people had gone to the home after calls were made to the family.

"At around 3.30pm, people known to the family located Chantelle unresponsive in bed. First aid was provided and emergency services were called," he said.

"Fire and ambulance staff attended but sadly could not revive her, and Chantelle was pronounced deceased."

A police investigation, Operation Gannon, had been underway since June.

"Our investigation is focusing on what took place the hours before emergency services first attended the address finding Chantelle alive and well, to being found unresponsive around an hour later, and those persons Chantelle may have had contact with that day.

"From our investigation we believe that there are some people that have information that is important to the case."

Police were urging those people to come forward.

"I recognise there may be mixed loyalties at play, and some people might feel challenged to come forward," Friend said.

"We are determined on finding out what has led to Chantelle's death. We owe it to her whānau and children to find these answers, so we ask you to speak with us."

World.title: Finance debate: Where National and Labour agree, and where they don't
World.content:
4_jpg" crop="16x10" layout="full"]

Audio player for " Finance Debate: Barbara Edmonds, Nicola Willis go head-to-head " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1779926%2Ffinance-debate-where-national-and-labour-agree-and-where-they-don-t

Finance Debate: Barbara Edmonds, Nicola Willis go head-to-head Morning Report Download MP3 24m

National and Labour's finance spokespeople agree on some things - New Zealand should make the most of its renewable energy, and education is important.

But they disagree on many others, including the best way to help households start to feel better about their financial lives, and the sentiment of the public on the campaign trail.

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis faced off against Labour's Barbara Edmonds on Morning Report on Wednesday.

While Willis said she was told by people she met while campaigning that it seemed that, finally, progress was being made, and if National wasn't in power after the election they would go to Australia, Edmonds said people were still telling her they were finding it hard to put food on the table or petrol in their cars.

Willis said some households were better off than three years ago, and the country needed to stay on track to grow the economy, create jobs and lift incomes.

She said there was better ahead, and the country had a lot going for it. "We just need to back it and know that what has been a tough time is going to pay off. We have got to stick with the plan."

Where money was coming from to pay for election promises was up for debate.

Willis argued that Edmonds was having to take money from the National Land Transport Fund to pay for Labour's public transport cap. That money was used to rebuild roads, she said.

Edmonds said Willis was spending too much time attacking Labour's numbers and not enough talking about what National planned to do. "In that last piece of monologue you just heard from Nicola Willis, not one did she answer your question, which is 'what are you going to do?' It was all about Labour, attacking Labour on numbers, attacking Labour on our economic choices. I'm confident in the numbers but, Nicola Willis, show us your numbers."

Both agreed addressing supermarket prices was a priority.

Edmonds said Willis's meeting with Fonterra chief executive Miles Hurrell about butter prices was "drama for the sake of drama".

"Butter is up by 71 percent. Bread is up by 68 percent. The key thing for Labour is ensuring that there is more competition, which is why our supermarket policy is around splitting the wholesale and the retail."

Willis said the important thing was that there was competition to drive down prices for customers, including between Pak'nSave and New World.

When asked about ways to help children growing up in poverty, Edmonds said she had come through "struggle street" herself.

"I was brought up in a benefit household. When I think about the policies we need to focus on to help lift our children out of poverty, having been through it myself, having been brought up in a benefit household there are three things that stick out for me. One is getting people into work. When my father retrained to become a social worker, he had to get off the benefit after mum died. That's what helped lift our household income.

"The second thing is housing, ensuring people who are vulnerable or do not have the money to keep up with market rents, ensuring they're supported through their housing, building more social housing, and not lifting up social housing rents, which the current government has done, which we will reverse. And the third key thing that helps children out of material poverty is education.

"My father made the call to send us to a school because we could stay in one place. We were brought up in one place and we built a community. But ensuring that the education system is able to teach children of all diversities, to help them teach for the future, the skills that they're going to need in the future."

Willis said she agreed education was vital and said the Government had made good progress in getting more kids to school regularly, and improving outcomes with the focus on things like structured literacy.

Both parties committed to renewable energy, including encouraging households to put solar power systems on their roofs.

Barbara Edmonds and Nicola Willis RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Willis said it was important to build more solar and wind farms and keep looking for gas in New Zealand, as an alternative to importing fossil fuels from offshore.

Edmonds said renewable energy was the future.

"Building more of it is our future, and ensuring that more households have access to solar is exactly the same policy. We have different ways of doing it, but we believe that that's one way to support our customers."

Neither was keen to see house prices increase quickly. Edmonds said they had to be stable and Willis said she wanted to see moderate price rises over time with incomes rising more quickly.

Edmonds said unemployment should be included in the Reserve Bank's mandate because it was just as important as inflation. Willis said the focus should only be on inflation because the country had experienced what could happen when it got out of control.

World.title: ACT vows to scrap donations tax-break limit
World.content:
The ACT Party is promising to scrap a cap on charitable donations being able to receive tax benefits.

Announcing the policy on Wednesday as a preview to the party's fiscal plan coming on Sunday, leader David Seymour says the tax system should encourage charitable generosity rather than imposing an arbitrary ceiling on it.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406384761112

He says the opening of a new children's hospital in Wellington would not have been possible without the backing of Sir Mark Dunajtschik and Dame Dorothy Spotswood.

"Starship is another example of what New Zealand can achieve, and it wouldn't be possible without the kindness of people who are willing to give some of what they've earned to help someone else live a better life.

"ACT's plan for New Zealand's first Comprehensive Cancer Centre will also be achieved by partnering with New Zealand's leading philanthropists, families, businesses, charitable trusts, community organisations and successful Kiwis, we can build something extraordinary.

"If New Zealanders want to give $1 million, $10 million or more to cancer care, medical research or other causes, the tax system should encourage that generosity."

Seymour said the policy would reduce government revenue by $15 million in the first year, and $19 million in subsequent years - but $57 million would be injected into the charity sector annually.

World.title: Woman charged with attempted murder over knife attack unable to appear in court again
World.content:
An Auckland woman charged with attempted murder over a knife attack in which a baby was critically injured has again been unable to appear in court.

The 33-year-old was being treated in hospital after she, the baby, and another person were found injured at a home on Kirby St in Glendene on Sunday night.

The baby remained in critical condition, and the third person was recovering at home.

On Tuesday, police confirmed the baby had undergone surgery.

The accused woman was due to appear before the Waitakere District Court from hospital this morning, after her appearance was delayed yesterday, but was still in a serious condition.

Police said the woman had been charged and thanked neighbours for their bravery on Sunday night.

"Neighbours came to these people's aid prior to emergency services arriving on the scene.

"We are very grateful for their assistance and bravery with what can only be described as a very confronting and upsetting scene."

A neighbour at the scene on Kirby St told RNZ on Monday she heard a woman crying shortly before midnight on Sunday and asked her partner and her brother to go with her to see what had happened.

She said they opened the door and found blood on the floor inside and called 111.

Her brother tended to an injured baby, she said, and applied pressure to a wound it had.

Police were not looking for anyone else in connection to what had happened.

World.title: Explainer: What is the 'purple vote' and why is it shrinking?
World.content:
Explainer - You'll see a lot of red and blue, pink and green signs leading up to Election Day - but purple might be the colour to keep a close eye on.

One month out from the election, one thing is becoming clear - voters are turning away from Labour and National as minor parties reap the rewards.

The "purple vote" has been dropping in recent elections and polling shows it might reach a new low this year.

What is the 'purple vote' anyway?

It's just a way of describing the combined vote for National (who favour blue) and Labour (who favour red).

Election results over the past 10 years and polling for this year's election are showing a steady decline in their overall share of the pie as smaller parties like the Greens and New Zealand First take bigger slices.

"People are switching off from the so-called major parties," RNZ's political editor Jo Moir said after the latest poll numbers came in Tuesday.

"There's a broader trend away from major political parties around the world," said analyst Lara Greaves, an associate professor in politics at Victoria University of Wellington and a senior research fellow in statistics.

What do the last few elections tell us?

The purple vote has been steadily declining since the 2005 election, with a bit of a shift upwards in the 2017 election.

In 2005, Labour and National combined took 80.2 percent of the party vote, but by 2014 that had fallen to 72.17 percent.

In the 2017 general election, the purple vote rose back up to 81.3 percent, in an election which saw NZ First and the Greens fall under 8 percent and ACT getting only 0.5 percent of the party votes.

But after 2017, it started to fall again, and by the 2023 election the purple vote only managed 64.97 percent.

That was the lowest purple vote since the 1996 election, the first under MMP, when only 62 percent of the party vote went to National and Labour, and NZ First, the Alliance Party and ACT all finished strongly.

Greaves said that first MMP election saw a shift away from Labour and National, "and then people kind of went back to them, which was kind of interesting".

MMP "kind of rewards us as voters for moving away from the major parties," Greaves said.

Audio player for " Political editor Jo Moir analyses latest RNZ poll " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1776776%2Fexplainer-what-is-the-purple-vote-and-why-is-it-shrinking

Political editor Jo Moir analyses latest RNZ poll Morning Report Download MP3 11m

"We don't have to worry as much about a wasted vote, although some people still do."

After 30 years, many voters have never known the old first-past-the-post system of voting, she noted, and tend to vote more strategically.

What do the polls tell us about this year?

The polls if anything show an even sharper drop could be possible on November 7.

Reid Research polling dating back to 2021 shows a steady downward trajectory for the combined purple vote.

The latest RNZ-Reid poll released this week had Labour and National getting just 56.7 percent of the party vote, which if repeated on Election Day would be by far the lowest result for the two in MMP's history.

Other polls this season have generally showed similar trends. The latest 1News-Verian Poll released Tuesday night showed National at 29 percent and Labour at 28 percent.

Moir called the 56.7 percent for the purple vote in the latest RNZ-Reid poll "jawdropping".

"That is down from 61.3 in August in our poll then and it is down from 64.9 at the 2023 election."

It might ultimately lead to a change in how "major" and "minor" parties are defined, Greaves said.

"You know, when you start to get minor parties solidly in the teens, and the major parties heading into the 20s, it's like at what point are they no longer a major party? And at what point do they have less of the cards?"

If a major party did dip below 20 percent in the party vote, "that would be shocking to me, but stranger things have happened," she said.

It's all a sign that the purple vote is "just continuing to slide away, people are switching off from the so-called major parties and it's creating all sorts of weird things," such as the talk about strategic voting to engineer potential overhangs, Moir said.

Politicians worldwide have ridden a wave against business as usual. BILL PUGLIANO / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP

Are voters just perpetually dissatisfied now with the status quo?

It's hardly a New Zealand phenomenon to see minor parties romping ahead of the established players in polls and a growing anti-incumbent movement.

In Britain, Nigel Farage's Reform UK has been leading many polls for months, while in Australia Pauline Hanson's One Nation has also seen a resurgence.

And it's hard not to note that the steeper decline in the purple vote began in 2017, around the time Donald Trump first assumed the US presidency and a general wider shift in global politics began happening.

So many normal political processes have become unsettled in the past 10 years, Greaves said.

"There is this argument that people are turning to the minor parties because the major parties haven't fixed anything.

"It is this genuine swing towards more radical change or more action or someone a bit different because the major parties have held power for so long and they haven't actually helped our lives improve so much more than where they were, say, 20, 30 years ago."

In the end, voters may decide to try something new like the novelty of the Opportunity party or give established smaller parties a go.

The latest RNZ-Reid poll also found 53 percent of people responding said they think the country is on the wrong track.

World.title: NZ Cricket reveals decision-making behind controversial NZ20 call
World.content:
New Zealand Cricket has admitted its decision to pursue the NZ20 league went against the initial lean of a key piece of independent advice.

A Deloitte analysis commissioned by the national body favoured further exploration of a New Zealand team entering Australia's Big Bash League, despite the NZC board ultimately voting unanimously to pursue a privately-owned domestic franchise competition.

In a statement released on Wednesday, NZC board chair Diana Puketapu-Lyndon said the Deloitte report identified financial upside and governance advantages in the Big Bash option, but the board decided those benefits were outweighed by the strategic value of establishing NZ20.

For the first time, NZC has detailed how that process unfolded, revealing that the Deloitte report was one of four separate pieces of expert analysis commissioned as weighed up changes to the domestic game.

The revelation comes after mounting criticism from high profile members of the New Zealand Cricket community, including Sir Richard Hadlee and former NZC President Lesley Murdoch, who have questioned the organisation's governance, transparency and future direction and called for the release of the Deloitte report.

Puketapu-Lyndon said the board is confident it made the right decision in choosing NZ20, but accepted it did not explain the process well enough when the decision was made in March.

She said the Deloitte report was only one part of the information considered by the Board and was never intended to be made public because of the confidential information provided by individuals, entities and stakeholders.

"We acknowledge we should have provided more information about the process to get there and the rationale for where we finally landed," she said.

"People who love this game deserve to know how we made the decision - we've heard that, and want to make it right."

Former NZ Cricket chief executive Scott Weenink stepped down in December last year after a relationship breakdown with the players' association, the MAs, and eventually his own board. Photosport / RNZ composite

Puketapu-Lyndon said the decision came down to which option offered the best long-term future for New Zealand cricket, particularly the grassroots game, domestic player pathways and NZC's ability to retain control over the direction of the sport."

Our constitution says the amateur game is the reason NZC exists, and NZ20 was the superior option in that respect with the development of a Capital Fund from the sale of teams which would help underpin the community game for years to come."

NZ20 would also provide a domestic competition of around six teams spread around the country, which Puketapu-Lyndon said would offer greater opportunities for players and fans while creating a platform to grow the game in New Zealand.

NZC said it also took into account the views of its cricket network, with the six Major Associations and NZ Cricket Players Association backing the NZ20 option.

"We listened and took into account the views of our cricket network who are our most important stakeholders. These are the people our game relies on to function and prosper, and the message was clear, from our Major Associations (MAs) and our professional players - they wanted us to pursue NZ20."

The Board also considered how the global game was changing and which option would allow NZC to retain control over the future direction of cricket in New Zealand.

"When all of that was considered, alongside the Board's own due diligence, the Board voted unanimously, 7-0, to support NZ20 as the preferred option."

Puketapu-Lyndon said the Deloitte report was only one part of the information considered by the Board and was never intended to be made public because of the confidential information provided by individuals, entities and stakeholders.

"Confidentiality is standard practice for Deloitte when they produce reports of this nature," she said.

While Deloitte has not identified any record of a commitment to provide participants with a copy of the report, Puketapu-Lyndon said it had acknowledged that Sir Richard Hadlee and Lesley Murdoch came away from the process expecting to receive one.

Deloitte had apologised for any lack of clarity, or anything said during the consultation process, that created that expectation, she said. NZC has not released the full report, but Puketapu-Lyndon has now disclosed its key finding on the Big Bash.

"At the time of Deloitte's report earlier this year, its analysis favoured exploring the Big Bash opportunity further, for reasons including financial upside and governance, but it also said weighing the options was for the Board and encouraged us to continue exploring both options."

Sir Richard Hadlee played 86 test matches for New Zealand and 115 one day internationals. RNZ / Conan Young

The failure of NZC to disclose of the Deloitte report is at the heart of Sir Richard Hadlee's criticism of the national body.

Hadlee, who played 86 test matches for New Zealand and 115 one day internationals, had contributed to the consultation process and said he was told the report would be shared with participants.

In a statement released last Friday, Hadlee raised concerns about the "governance, transparency, accountability and the future direction of cricket in New Zealand".

"My view is simple. The longer the report remains unavailable to key stakeholders, the greater the speculation regarding its findings, recommendations and the decision-making process that followed.

"Transparency builds trust. A lack of transparency creates uncertainty, misinformation, speculation and mistrust. That was my view when I served on the Board and it remains my view today."

His criticism came amid a turbulent period for NZC, including the departure of chief executive Scott Weenink and the resignation of former Black Cap Dion Nash from the NZC Board following the debate over the future of domestic T20 cricket.

Hadlee said the developments over the past 12 months, including changes in Board composition, the departure of senior executives and staff, concerns about staff morale and concerns expressed by commercial partners and sponsors, "warrant serious reflection by the Board and leadership of the organisation".

Puketapu-Lyndon acknowledged the national body had been through a difficult period.

"It's been a time of change and uncertainty, and we put our hand up in saying we could have handled things better," she said.

World.title: Where you can vote in advance and on election day
World.content:
There will be more than 2300 voting locations open on election day - 7 November.

The Electoral Commission says of these, 67 will be bilingual - voters can go through the voting process in te reo Māori or English - and six will have sign language interpreters.

There will be 1679 fully accessible polling locations, and three locations with quiet times.

"Our voting places are in locations people go in their daily lives including community halls, schools, shopping malls, places of worship, tertiary education providers and marae," chief electoral officer Karl Le Quesne said.

Though votes would be taken at a total of 2638 locations during the voting period, only 2315 will be open on election day on 7 November.

Advance voting will begin on Monday 26 October, the day after enrolments close.

Where to vote

A list of voting places is available online and at local supermarkets.

Le Quesne said the days and times voting places will be open during advance voting varies, so people are asked to check before they go to vote.

"During advance voting, look out for a list of your nearest voting places at your local supermarket as this is a really easy way to find out where to vote in your community. People can also call us for free on 0800 36 76 56 and our team will be ready to help you find your nearest voting place.'

"Anyone who cannot make it to a voting place should also give us a call. We have alternative voting options available."

World.title: 'Let's rally behind them': PNG commits to help Tuvalu at Pre-COP climate meet
World.content:
Papua New Guinea has committed around US$5.5 million (K$25m) to Tuvalu over five years in aid of its coastal reclamation efforts.

PNG's Prime Minister James Marape made the announcement at the Pre-COP31 climate meeting in Tuvalu.

Speaking at a joint press conference with Tuvaluan Prime Minister Feleti Teo in Funafuti, Marape confirmed that funding would be allocated from each annual budget over the five-year term.

He said climate change is playing out in real time in the atoll nation, and that even a relatively small amount of investment will make a significant difference.

"It would buy them two or three more generations of life, if they buy ten soccer fields in land reclamations where ever you can," Marape said.

Tuvalu consists of low-lying atolls encompassing a total land mass of 26 square kilometres, making the country highly exposed to sea level rise and environmental degradation.

"Let's rally behind them (Tuvalu), let's help them preserve their sovereignty, and let's move on in this instead of going to COPs with no serious commitments," Marape said.

'Talk fests'

Teo acknowledged PNG's contribution, stating that the financial resources will be utilised to secure the island nation's highly vulnerable coast line.

But he noted that while international bodies recently adopted a political declaration on sea level rise at the UN General Assembly, declarations alone cannot physically fix eroding coastlines without substantial capital.

Marape also criticised the lack of actionable progress at global climate forums, referring to them as "talk fests" with few serious commitments.

He said he would not attend the global COP-31 summit in Türkiye next month, choosing instead to focus resources on regional solidarity and localised adaptation projects.

The PNG leader also issued a formal appeal to industrialised nations, including the United States. China, Japan, India, and the United Kingdom, to provide direct financial assistance to small island states facing immediate existential threats.

Target call

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the Pacific cannot afford to lose sight of the 1.5 degrees Celcius target as rising seas, extreme weather and El Niño conditions intensify across the region.

Albanese has been in Tuvalu and Fiji attending the Pre-COP climate meetings with other leaders from the Pacific region.

The Post-Courier reports him saying Pacific nations must convert their shared concern about climate change into collective action.

He argues the 1.5 degrees target on global warming remains vital as sea levels rise and extreme weather worsens.

World.title: Athletes drive to make table tennis a smash at national Special Olympics debut
World.content:
The repetitive click-clack of a small white ball paddling back and forth over a net may seem like a simple game of ping pong, but for these three teammates, it could be their ticket to the world stage.

The Bundaberg athletes are gearing up to compete in the Special Olympics Australia in Melbourne later this month, where table tennis is making its competitive debut.

Oscar Quarrell, 16, is diligently working to perfect his pendulum — a serve with a bit of side and back spin.

Oscar Quarrell (right) talks with coach Ha Bui as he prepares to play in his first Special Olympics. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Oscar is one of three from his regional club, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, to be selected as part of the 14-strong Queensland table tennis team.

"I love table tennis because it's something that takes my mind off thinking and gives me a break," he said.

"It's also very fun to do with people that actually enjoy hanging around you."

Celebrating 50 years

The Special Olympics is for people with intellectual disabilities, cognitive delays or autism. It is also an organisation that supports community-based clubs and participation.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Special Olympics movement in Australia.

Oscar Quarrell, Taylah Sim and Nicholas Jefferson train with coach Ha Bui. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Special Olympics Australia CEO Jamie O'Connor said 850 athletes across 13 sports would compete at the 2026 games.

"Special Olympics provides programs at a grassroots level week in, week out, at a community level," he said.

"But it also has the path that goes through local competitions to state events, to national events, to international events.

"Our Special Olympics is more about participation opportunities than it is about winning gold medals."

Mr O'Connor said that, in addition to the inclusion of table tennis, dance sport would be a demonstration sport for the first time this year.

Oscar Quarrell practises with Taylah Sim. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

"As sport evolves, and the demand for different sports evolves, then we try and provide options for people with intellectual disability and the sports that they want to compete in," he said.

About 60 athletes who are successful in the national games will go on to compete at the Special Olympics World Games in Santiago, Chile, next October.

Trio take on games

As the excitement builds towards the national games alongside his backhand, Oscar was also preparing for a big leap in independence.

"I'm excited to do something different, and it's also the first time I haven't had my parents with me, so they are going to come and watch, but I'm not allowed to speak to them," he said.

Clubmates Taylah and Nicholas will be joining Oscar in Melbourne.

Taylah Sim has been putting in the hours to prepare for her Special Olympics debut. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Taylah has her eyes firmly on the prize, saying she looks forward to winning then going on to compete at the world games.

Nicholas is also hoping to win a medal, having played the game for 13 years.

His mum, Margaret, said table tennis had opened doors for her son and she enjoyed watching the competition.

"They all want to do their best but, at the end of the day, whoever gets first, second or last, they're all rewarded, and they are happy for them," Ms Jefferson said.

"There's cheering, there's no jealousy, they're here to support each other."

Table tennis has opened doors for Nicholas Jefferson. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Queensland table tennis head coach Kim Hammermeister had high hopes for her Queensland team when they competed at the national level for the first time.

"Bundaberg has always been very strong with their school program for people with an intellectual impairment," she said.

Ms Hammermeister said any Special Olympics sport provided opportunities for friendship.

"People with an intellectual impairment can become very isolated, especially after school," she said.

"Of course, the physical benefits of being active are amazing; you can't put a price on that."

World.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after China Open incident
World.content:
Coco Gauff says she received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after beating local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open.

The ‌American won 7-5, 6-1 on Monday to reach the fourth round but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set.

She raised her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner.

After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed.

Gauff won the replayed point and held serve ⁠for 5-5 before cruising to victory against her 16-year-old opponent.

De Minaur retires from China Open with injury Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

The two-time major singles champion said she received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match.

"You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote on X in reply to a post containing a racial slur.

"The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane.

"Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."

The WTA has made efforts to ‌tackle ⁠online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system that monitors thousands of players and officials on social media.

A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier.

Gauff explained she was ⁠following the rules when she challenged the point.

Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgement calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play.

Gauff said she spoke to Sun about the ⁠point at the end of the match.

"I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff wrote.

"I didn't like to see ⁠her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it's like but this is the beginning of an incredible career.

"It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd."

Reuters

World.title: Aussies dealt major injury blow ahead of first South Africa Test
World.content:
Cameron Green has been ruled out of the first Test against South Africa in Durban after succumbing to an abdominal strain.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald said Green failed to overcome the injury, which he suffered in the final one-day international (ODI) played in Potchefstroom last week.

McDonald said it was "highly unlikely" Green would bowl later in the series, should he prove his fitness for the remaining two Tests.

The injury blow is likely to leave Australia with a choice to make between Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson at number five in the batting order for the first Test, which begins on Friday night, AEST.

Travis Head is expected to remain as opener, with Alex Carey to bat at six.

Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Green appeared to be finding some rhythm with the bat, having scored a century against Bangladesh in Darwin in August.

"He is progressing pretty well, all things considered … he is still here for a reason, so there is some light at the end of the tunnel," McDonald said

"It will just be a matter of going through the rehab. He has a pretty demanding week as he reintroduced some activities.

"It's a bit of an unknown, but there is still optimism that he will take part in the series at some stage."

Green had been managing a shoulder injury that stopped him bowling in the white-ball matches against the Proteas.

His planned bowling return in the final ODI was aborted due to the abdominal injury.

"We would be solely focused on getting him to return as a batter. We wouldn't be putting that demand on him to return as a bowler," McDonald said.

"That would be too high-risk, is the information I have."

Maddinson has not played a Test for Australia since 2016 but was a surprise addition to the squad last week when Josh Inglis suffered a fractured finger.

Australia is also weighing up whether a dry Durban surface pushes them towards picking Connolly, with an expectation the Kingsmead wicket will turn later in the match.

Matt Kuhnemann is also on the tour as a second spinner, but it would appear unlikely Australia will opt to play him ahead of one of the three frontline quicks.

Green's injury also increases the chances of Beau Webster holding his spot as a fourth seamer, after he played in the last three Tests batting at number seven.

AAP

World.title: Geelong scores major coup with Matildas-Colombia clash
World.content:
The Matildas will return to Victoria this year, with Geelong's Kardinia Park named as the venue for the second leg of a two-match series against Colombia.

The Victorian government today announced the December 2 fixture, two years after 30,000 fans packed out the regional stadium to see the "Tillies" beat Chinese Taipei 6-0.

The announcement is a major coup for Geelong, which will be the only Victorian city to host the Matildas this year.

The national team last played in Victoria in May 2025.

"This blockbuster clash will drive visitation across the Geelong region, support local businesses and showcase Victoria's unmatched ability to host world-class sporting events," Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements said.

Football Australia deputy chief executive Heather Garriock said Victorians' support of the Matildas was "always outstanding".

"We're delighted to bring the CommBank Matildas back to Victoria for what promises to be a special occasion for football fans, as our FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 preparations intensify," Ms Garriock said.

The first leg of the Colombia series will be played at Canberra Stadium on November 28, with the games expected to serve as a valuable test ahead of the World Cup in Brazil in June.

Both Australia and Colombia have already qualified for the World Cup.

Matildas fans were out in force in 2023, and will be raring to go in Brazil (AAP Image)

The Matildas finished fourth in the 2023 World Cup, and earlier this year were runners up in the AFC Women's Asian Cup.

Ms Garriock, who is also Football Australia's executive director of football, in August said the Colombia series would be an opportunity to give younger talent a chance to impress.

"We sat down with (coach) Joe (Montemurro) some 12 months ago when he started in the Matildas position, and we asked him what his ideal preparation was in the lead-up to the Women's World Cup," Ms Garriock said.

"It was very evident that different styles of play were important to him, but also trying to blood some of the next generation as well.

"We've seen that (younger players getting an opportunity) at the recent World Cup in the US with (Socceroos coach) Tony Popovic as well."

World.title: Kostecki loses engineer to bike accident as he goes for Bathurst record
World.content:
Supercars star Brodie Kostecki can surpass Australian motor racing legends Peter Brock and Allan Moffat with a Bathurst record this weekend, but will do it without the support of his engineer.

Kostecki has claimed pole position at the previous three Bathurst 1000s, trying the record for most consecutive poles for the great race with Moffat (1970-72) and Brock (1977-79).

Should the West Australian be the fastest in Saturday's top-10 shootout, he will become the first driver to secure four consecutive poles for the great race.

Kostecki is the only driver to secure pole position at Bathurst in the Gen3 era which began in 2024, and he put the number 17 Dick Johnson Racing entry on pole position for the last Supercars round at The Bend.

However, there will be a change on the pit wall for Kostecki, with his engineer George Commins not attending Mount Panorama this weekend.

Dick Johnson Racing announced that Commins, who was Kostecki's engineer for this Bathurst triumph in 2024 with Erebus Motorsport, had been injured in a mountain biking accident.

"Car 17 race engineer George Commins will miss the Repco Bathurst 1000 after sustaining injuries in a mountain biking accident prior to the race weekend," the team said in a statement.

"Team manager Tom Moore will take over race engineer duties for Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood at Mount Panorama while George recuperates at home."

Moore is no stranger to the engineering role, or Kostecki. The pair have been working in the same team since 2021. Moore was the race engineer for Kostecki's then-teammate Will Brown at Erebus.

Kostecki has been very good in qualifying this season, with six pole positions from 28 races.

His shootout laps at Mount Panorama for the past three years have been excellent, with Kostecki claiming pole position by margins of 0.483, 0.131 and 0.176 seconds.

Qualifying for the Bathurst 1000 will be held on Friday afternoon. That will set the grid for positions 11 to 27.

The top 10 from Friday will participate in Saturday's top-10 shootout to determine the grid from pole to 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

World.title: Jannik Sinner to miss rest of tennis season with knee injury
World.content:
World number one Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery ‌from a knee injury that has kept him out of action ‌since his ⁠triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.

"Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee, which means that the 2026 season is officially over," Sinner said in a video message on Instagram.

" I also need to think about my long-term career so I will do everything possible to get back 100 per cent. "

Sinner has not played since beating Alexander Zverev in the All England Club final on July 12, with the 25-year-old missing the North American hardcourt swing, the US Open as well as the ongoing slate of tournaments in Asia.

He will now miss the European indoor hardcourt swing as well as the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin, where he won the title in the last two years.

Sinner's team said in a statement that he would follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee.

"The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027."

Sinner's absence could open the door for Zverev to finish the year at the top of the world rankings.

The German world number two has cut the gap to Sinner after winning the French Open and US Open titles.

World.title: Zach Merrett staying 'open-minded' after high-profile AFL move to Hawks
World.content:
Boom AFL recruit Zach Merrett is open-minded over what role he will play at Hawthorn under coach Sam Mitchell.

More than a year after the bombshell revelation that the Hawks were trying to lure Merrett from Essendon, a deal was finally struck for the former Bombers captain when the trade period opened on Monday.

Essendon will receive the number 15 and 25 picks in this year's national draft, as well as Hawthorn's 2028 second-round selection.

The bitter rivals were unable to reach a deal for Merrett in trade talks a year ago.

Merrett would obviously boost Hawthorn's midfield, but he noted on Tuesday in a club interview that he could also play in defence or across half-forward.

"It is funny that Gia and I are back together," he said of former Essendon assistant coach Daniel Giansiracusa, who is now at the Hawks.

"We worked for three years on trying to be the most flexible player in the competition, being able to play a number of different roles.

"I have no preconceived ideas with Sam. We're going to be pretty open-minded, to what that could look like.

Loading Instagram content

"There are already so many incredible players out there for the Hawks, so wherever I fit in, I will make sure I make that work — whether that's back, forward, mid, or wing, or whatever it looks like."

Merrett has toured Hawthorn's Dingley headquarters and met with captain Jai Newcombe.

"It's been a bit overwhelming, the last 24 hours," Merrett said.

"To see the whole facility and to get so many incredible messages, I feel extremely welcomed, and so is my family."

Last Thursday Merrett became the third player to win Essendon's best and fairest award seven times, alongside Dick Reynolds and Bill Hutchison.

"It was a really hard decision, it was probably something I weighed up for six to nine months," Merrett said of the move.

"It felt like Hawthorn was going to be the best place for me and my family, moving forward, to keep achieving, to achieve out of footy.

"I also have so much respect and love for Essendon as well, so it is a unique feeling, a little bit.

"But I'm keen to move forward, get stuck into work."

Hawthorn, whose season ended with an epic preliminary final loss to premiers Brisbane, are also expected to recruit key forward Ben King from Gold Coast.

Tech.title: OpenAI drops another batch of mathematical breakthroughs
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

OpenAI has revealed solutions to a number of long-standing mathematics problems produced by an unreleased frontier model in a batch of 722 manuscripts, covering 372 result families that group related papers. It extends a run of breakthroughs that have both impressed and unsettled parts of the mathematical community while raising questions about research ethics and academic conduct. According to AGMAI, the newly formed independent advisory group of elite mathematicians put together to work on communicating the results responsibly, the release includes solutions to “hundreds” of open questions.

The results have been expected for weeks, although until now OpenAI had not provided details about which problems the model had solved or exactly when they would be published. In September, the company said its model had “resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.” The released papers and other details also include some summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimates of the compute used, and stats about the number of problems attempted. OpenAI claims the “average result” used the equivalent of three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

AGMAI, or the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, published its first recommendations in late September, urging AI labs to release mathematical results promptly and through established academic channels where possible, while disclosing details such as the name of the model used, prompts, and compute costs. The group also implored AI companies to “refrain from treating the release of mathematical results as marketing vehicles to promote their models,” a practice they said inflicts significant harm on the mathematical community.

Here’s how OpenAI described its process for this release:

For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding

The full impact of the results will likely take some time to be felt as mathematicians assess and digest them. They add to a rapidly growing body of mathematical results from OpenAI and rival labs like Anthropic that the field is still processing, including results concerning a Millennium Prize problem, among the most famous open questions in the field. The speed at which AI labs have barreled into the discipline this year — particularly their handling of announcements — has provoked fierce debate over research practices, ethics, and how companies credit the human mathematicians whose work their systems build upon and potentially use to produce results.

Tech.title: Xbox has secured exclusive GTA 6 streaming rights
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that Microsoft is getting ready to do something around Grand Theft Auto VI that “no other platform holder is doing” during an employee all-hands this morning. According to sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans, Xbox has managed to land a deal for the exclusive game streaming rights for Grand Theft Auto VI.

The deal will mean only Xbox Cloud Gaming can stream Grand Theft Auto VI to players at launch, but it’s not clear how long the agreement will be in place. Rockstar Games still hasn’t announced a PC version of Grand Theft Auto VI, so this deal will allow Xbox to market its Xbox Cloud Gaming service to PC players who would otherwise need an Xbox Series X / S or PS5 console.

News of the streaming rights comes around a month after Microsoft announced some major changes to Xbox Cloud Gaming. From November, the same month Grand Theft Auto VI releases, Microsoft is limiting streaming hours to just 15 hours for Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers, 10 hours for Premium subscribers, and just five hours for Game Pass Essential.

Microsoft is also opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with a pay-as-you-go option next month, rather than being limited to Game Pass subscriptions. The pay-as-you-go option is perfectly timed for Grand Theft Auto VI, allowing those who don’t own an Xbox, or who primarily play from a phone, to stream the game by paying for a bundle of hours.

During the Xbox all-hands, Sharma also told employees that Project Helix, the next generation of Xbox hardware, will be a “family of devices” and that Microsoft will partner with others on some of those devices. Sharma first called Helix a family of devices last month in an interview, after Microsoft and AMD announced a “strategic multi-year partnership” last year to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console.
